Alemanha planeja dobrar sua capacidade de data centers
11 de outubro de 2026
O futuro digital na Alemanhaestá tomando forma na cidade de Dietzenbach. Google, EdgeConnex e Maincubes – duas empresas de tecnologia americanas e uma alemã – reservaram terrenos para a construção de centros de dados (data centers) nessa pequena cidade próxima a Frankfurt.
Dietzenbach é um polo logístico nas proximidades do aeroporto da metrópole financeira e tem cerca de 35 mil habitantes. A região de Frankfurt é um dos locais mais atraentes do mundo para operadores de computação em nuvem.
À medida que a demanda por capacidade computacional continua crescendo, mais centros de dados estão sendo planejados no local.
Consumo de eletricidade e água
No entanto, a notícia sobre os planos para um quarto megacentro de dados encontrou resistência entre os moradores.
As dezenas de milhares de computadores instalados num data center precisam de um enorme fornecimento de energia para funcionar ininterruptamente.
Esses equipamentos geram grandes quantidades de calor e necessitam de sistemas de refrigeração, que, por sua vez, consomem enormes volumes de água.
As pessoas entrevistadas pela DW em Dietzenbach demonstraram preocupação com o aumento das contas de água e energia, além de possíveis elevações da temperatura local.
"Queremos saber duas coisas: quais são os benefícios para a comunidade local aqui em Dietzenbach? E quais são os impactos ambientais?", afirmou o morador Wilhelm Sauer, apontando para as quatro imponentes chaminés que se erguem do centro de dados da EdgeConnex.
Ele e outros ativistas locais acreditam que o impacto dos centros de dados sobre os recursos da região talvez não seja compensado pelo número relativamente baixo de novos empregos anunciados.
Já o prefeito de Dietzenbach, Dieter Lang, do Partido Social-Democrata (SPD), de centro-esquerda, mostra-se otimista. Segundo ele, cerca de cem empregos de alta qualificação deverão chegar à cidade por meio do centro de dados da Google. Ele também disse esperar benefícios para as finanças municipais por meio de impostos.
Mas a pesquisadora Tara Merk, do projeto Community Data Centers no Instituto Weizenbaum, é cética. Ela acredita que a Alemanha provavelmente arrecadará pouco com centros de dados operados por empresas americanas "porque os lucros podem ser tributados em outros lugares".
Em especial as grandes empresas de tecnologia, diz ela, não vão pagar seus impostos em Dietzenbach.
Falta de informação sobre data centers
Em agosto de 2026, o governo alemão lançou um cadastro nacional de centros de dados que lista consumo de energia e de água e medidas de eficiência energética dos centros já em operação.
No entanto, a lista inclui apenas cerca de 300 instalações, muito menos que os aproximadamente 2 mil centros de dados que, segundo o próprio governo, operam no país.
"Algumas empresas informam seus projetos menores, mas não os grandes", disse Werner Neumann, membro da diretoria da organização ambientalista Bund.

artigo.texto: How Chiplets Could Transform Server Design – And Data Centers Chiplets are reshaping CPU design, enabling data centers to do more without increasing space or power consumption. Since the advent of microprocessors more than 50 years ago, CPUs have typically been built as single pieces of silicon. As a result, servers and the data centers that house them have largely been designed around that model. However, that is beginning to change. The growing adoption of chiplets – small modular dies that can be combined in a single processor package – is giving chipmakers a new way to build CPUs. By improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling more specialized processor designs, chiplets could reshape not just server architecture but also how data centers approach compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. What Are Chiplets? A chiplet is a small integrated circuit designed to perform a specific function within a larger processing package. Depending on the design, chiplets may handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as AI acceleration. When combined, chiplets can provide the same overall capabilities as a traditional CPU. The key difference is that, instead of manufacturing a processor as one large monolithic die, chipmakers can build it from multiple smaller dies assembled in a single package. The chiplet concept has existed for decades, and related multi-die approaches are not entirely new. But adoption accelerated in the late 2010s as chipmakers sought more efficient ways to improve processor performance, manage manufacturing complexity, and scale designs across different workloads. The Benefits of Chiplets A chiplet-based approach to CPU design offers several potential advantages. Reduced manufacturing costs. Smaller dies are often easier to manufacture with higher yields than a single large, complex die. If a single die has a defect, the loss is usually less significant than losing an entire monolithic processor. It can also be easier to engineer and optimize a smaller die for a specific function than to design one large chip that must handle multiple functions at once. Design freedom. By separating functions such as compute and I/O into different dies, chipmakers can tailor processor designs more efficiently for different types of workloads and product segments. Potentially higher compute density. In some cases, chiplets allow chipmakers to pack more processing capability into a single processor package, helping to enable more powerful servers without necessarily increasing physical server size. Supply chain flexibility. Because smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than very large monolithic chips, chiplet-based designs may reduce some production constraints. That said, they do not eliminate supply chain risk altogether, because advanced packaging and integration can create bottlenecks on their own. In short, chiplets can make it easier for chipmakers to scale processor designs, improve yields, and optimize hardware for growing demand. What Do Chiplets Mean for Data Centers? Although chiplets directly affect processor design, their impact could extend well beyond the chip itself. One important implication is the potential for increased compute density inside data centers. If chiplets allow server vendors to deliver more processing power within a single server platform, operators may be able to support heavier workloads without expanding physical footprints at the same pace. Historically, higher compute density has often meant higher power draw and greater cooling requirements. Chiplets do not automatically solve that problem. However, if they enable more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt, they could help offset some of the infrastructure strain that typically comes with denser compute environments. A key result of greater chiplet adoption, then, could be data centers that support higher IT loads without requiring proportionally more space or power. In that scenario, existing facilities could become more valuable because operators would be able to do more with the infrastructure they already have. Chiplets may also help reduce the risk of server procurement delays by giving manufacturers more flexibility in how processors are designed and produced. This does not remove supply chain challenges altogether, but it could make sourcing CPUs and servers somewhat easier over time. In the longer term, chiplets could also encourage more specialized server designs. As chipmakers gain flexibility to mix and match dies optimized for different functions, server platforms may become increasingly tailored for workloads such as AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing. That would give data center operators more options, but it could also make infrastructure planning more workload-specific than it is today. A Shift Worth Watching Chiplets are no longer a futuristic concept. They are already becoming an important part of modern processor design, especially as chipmakers look for new ways to improve performance and efficiency. For data centers, the biggest impact may not come from chiplets themselves, but from the servers they enable. If chiplet-based designs continue to improve compute density, efficiency, and workload specialization, they could play a major role in shaping the next generation of data center infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Virginia Tops AI Data Center Readiness Ranking as Smaller Markets Advance TRG DataCenters’ August 2026 ranking places Virginia in the lead, while states with abundant power, low-carbon electricity, and favorable water conditions gain ground. Power supply and water availability could help states outside established data center hubs compete for AI infrastructure investment, according to a new survey of US states from TRG DataCenters. The report, published in August 2026, compares 24 states using measures of infrastructure scale and environmental exposure and points to a more geographically diverse market as AI demand expands. Virginia topped the August ranking of states positioned for AI data center growth, but the findings also suggest smaller markets can compete by offering a favorable combination of electricity supply, lower-carbon generation, and water availability. “When planning infrastructure for the long term, that balance between scale and resource efficiency matters as much as raw megawatts,” Chris Hinkle, CEO of TRG DataCenters, told Data Center Knowledge. TRG’s analysis considered mapped large-scale AI data center sites, power capacity, electricity use, estimated annual carbon emissions, and the proportion of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Capacity figures reflect the AI infrastructure included in TRG’s dataset and do not represent each state’s total data center market. Virginia’s Lead Comes with Water Constraints Virginia received a readiness score of 100, followed by Ohio at 88.2, Tennessee at 83.7, Georgia at 81.8, and Texas at 80.8. TRG’s dataset mapped seven large AI sites in Virginia totaling 1,085 MW of capacity, while Ohio and Tennessee showed higher mapped capacities – 1,410 MW in Ohio and 1,373 MW in Tennessee. Virginia’s advantage reflects performance across several measures, including lower estimated grid carbon intensity serving the mapped facilities. Hinkle said Ohio’s mapped AI capacity was around 30% greater, but the grid serving Virginia’s facilities had roughly one-third lower carbon intensity than Ohio’s. “As a result, the AI facilities in our dataset are associated with around 2.3 million tons of CO2 emissions annually, compared with roughly 4.5 million tons in Ohio and 4.3 million in Tennessee,” he said. Water – or lack thereof – is a complicating factor. About one-third of Virginia’s mapped data centers are located in areas of high water stress, compared with none in Ohio and just 7% in Tennessee. “One factor Virginia will need to continue managing as the market expands is site selection around water availability,” Hinkle said. Those differences make the ranking a starting point for evaluating markets rather than evidence that development conditions are uniform within a state. Smaller Markets Offer Competing Advantages South Carolina placed sixth with a score of 80.5, just behind Texas, despite having only one large AI site and 142 MW of capacity in the study. “What surprised us most was South Carolina,” Hinkle said. “It has just one large AI data center site and around 142 MW of capacity, yet it finished almost level with Texas in our overall readiness ranking, despite Texas having 13 large sites.” He attributed that performance partly to the state’s nuclear-heavy electricity supply and the absence of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Hinkle also pointed to New York, Iowa, and Mississippi. New York combined relatively limited large-scale AI capacity with one of the lowest-carbon grids in the dataset, while Mississippi already supported more than 500 MW of AI capacity. “States that can combine reliable power with a relatively low-carbon electricity mix and favorable water conditions could become increasingly attractive as demand expands,” he said. Texas Faces a Siting Challenge Texas had the largest number of AI sites in the study – 13, with a combined capacity of 1,301 MW. However, 58.8% of those facilities were located in areas of high water stress. Hinkle said he expects those conditions to influence cooling choices and project locations. “That is likely to encourage more sophisticated siting and infrastructure strategies rather than simply slowing development,” he said. “We could see greater use of approaches such as closed-loop or air-based cooling, recycled water, and locations where local water conditions are more favorable.” TRG notes that the water-stress measure describes facility locations and does not establish actual water consumption or the impact of individual cooling systems. Developers still need to assess those conditions at the project level. From Readiness to Deliverable Infrastructure Statewide advantages must also translate into infrastructure that developers can use. A relatively small share of statewide electricity use does not, by itself, establish that a particular site has power available for expansion. “Grid connections, transmission capacity, fiber connectivity, build-ready sites, and long-term power availability can all influence where major projects ultimately land,” Hinkle said. For emerging markets, those requirements determine whether attractive resource conditions can support projects at scale. For established hubs, the requirements shape where additional development can proceed. “The result could be a more geographically diverse AI infrastructure market as developers match projects with the locations best equipped to support them.”

artigo.texto: How to Secure Data Centers During the Construction Phase Before operations begin, layered defenses at the site and in the supply chain help prevent theft, vandalism, counterfeit gear, and covert endpoints. As data center build-outs accelerate, most conversations about physical security focus on operational facilities, with threats ranging from mundane events, such as break-ins, to novel threats like drone attacks. Yet the period of greatest exposure is often earlier: during construction. Sites are porous, contractor populations are large and fluid, and high-value materials and preinstalled equipment can be targeted or tampered with. Protecting the build phase should be a core pillar of any data center’s broader physical security strategy. Construction-Phase Risks to Data Centers Physical intrusions during construction come in many forms: Material theft. Theft of construction materials is common on open or lightly controlled construction sites. Copper, cabling, generators, and networking gear are all attractive targets, leading to financial losses and construction delays. Vandalism and sabotage. In some markets, community opposition to data center expansion can increase the likelihood of on-site disruption or damage. Deployment of spy devices. More covertly, malicious actors may attempt to plant devices – such as rogue wireless access points, small network switches, or hidden sensors – during construction to enable remote backdoor access once the facility is operational. Supply chain tampering. Risks also extend into supply chains: tampering with shipments, swapping components, or introducing counterfeit or compromised gear can create backdoors or degrade reliability before the facility ever goes live. Aerial reconnaissance or nuisance activity. Hobbyist drones can expose site layouts and procedures or create safety hazards. Practical Strategies to Secure Data Center Construction Sites While the overarching goal is simple – prevent unauthorized access to construction sites and their supply chains – executing this amid complex projects and large contractor populations is challenging. The following layered controls help reduce risk while maintaining construction speed. Establish a strong perimeter and active monitoring. Build robust physical barriers, ensure all ingress/egress routes are controlled, and funnel all foot and vehicle traffic through staffed gates. Pair this with temporary but professional-grade surveillance cameras covering the perimeter, material laydown yards, and sensitive areas; lighting designed with Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design principles; and motion or thermal sensors where feasible. Verify and control who enters the construction site. Vet contractors and delivery personnel before granting access, consistent with local laws and company policy. Require visible badges and use zoned access so workers can enter only the areas relevant to their tasks. This is no guarantee that bad actors won’t find their way in, but it’s one way to reduce risk. Grant access in phases. Bringing contractors on-site in smaller groups (e.g., having electricians complete their work before allowing HVAC workers to begin) reduces crowding and makes anomalous activity more visible. The trade-off is that this may slow construction by reducing the amount of work contractors can perform in parallel. Rope off construction areas. In addition to establishing a strong perimeter around the data center site, roping off or caging high-value storage (e.g., copper, cabling, generators, and networking equipment) provides another layer of defense against theft and sabotage. Harden the supply chain and track custody. Vet vendors for chain-of-custody controls, tamper-evident packaging, and secure transit practices. Upon receipt, record serial numbers and MAC addresses of networked devices, use barcodes or RFID to track movement, and keep sensitive equipment in controlled cages until deployment. Prepare for drone threats. Use drone detection where appropriate for visibility into potential aerial activity. Many forms of active drone interdiction are illegal, so coordinate with local authorities and legal teams, emphasizing deterrence, detection, and evidence capture rather than unlawful countermeasures. Validate what’s installed before commissioning. Another way to detect supply chain abuse is to compare installed assets against purchase orders and approved bills of materials. Conduct technical sweeps for unauthorized wireless signals or unexpected network endpoints to identify situations where someone installed a device that isn’t supposed to be included. Balancing Speed and Security Complete eradication of construction-phase physical security risks isn’t realistic, just as fully preventing cyberattacks isn’t. However, a multilayered defense strategy based on practices like those described above goes a long way toward reducing the likelihood and impact of intrusions, while improving your chances of detecting and remediating those that do occur.

artigo.texto: [Photo: MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND CLIMATE CHANGE/ FACEBOOK] Fiji has launched a five-year $5.2 million plan aimed at preparing the country to enter international carbon markets by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan was launched yesterday during the opening of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan sets out the regulatory, technical and institutional systems Fiji needs before its first international carbon trade under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. It focuses on sectors including energy, transport, agriculture, waste and forestry, with strong emphasis on forests, mangroves, wetlands and other nature-based solutions. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu says carbon markets must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners.” The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre, with provisions for fair benefit-sharing, social and environmental safeguards and Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Fiji will also establish a Fijian Transactional Registry and a National Carbon Market Inter-Agency Technical Working Group to manage and track carbon market activities. The Government will use the plan to engage development partners, donors and potential carbon buyers to secure the finance and technical support needed for implementation. Conservation International says the plan could help Fiji attract high-integrity carbon finance while protecting ecosystems and supporting resilient livelihoods.

A empresa russa de tecnologia e inteligência artificial Yandex informou na madrugada deste domingo (11) que um ataque com drones danificou suas instalações e provocou o fechamento completo de seu centro de dados na região de Vladimir, na Rússia.
Segundo a companhia, ninguém ficou ferido, mas alguns de seus serviços estão indisponíveis para os usuários.
Este é o terceiro grande centro de dados da empresa a ficar fora de operação nos últimos dias.
Na sexta-feira (9), a Yandex informou que outro de seus centros de dados, localizado na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou, havia sido atingido por drones ucranianos. O ataque danificou parcialmente as instalações e comprometeu seu funcionamento.
Um dia antes, um ataque ucraniano havia paralisado o centro de dados da empresa em Sasovo, a sudeste de Moscou. O local abriga dois dos três supercomputadores usados no desenvolvimento do modelo de inteligência artificial da companhia.
Yandex: a "Google da Rússia"
A Yandex é uma das principais empresas russas de tecnologia e tem participação importante no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial no país. Por sua atuação em serviços digitais, como buscas na internet, é frequentemente chamada de “Google da Rússia”.
Centros de dados são instalações que abrigam servidores e outros equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar e processar informações e manter serviços digitais em funcionamento.
Data center da Yandex, o 'Google russo' fica em chamas após ser atingido por drones em 8 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/redes sociais via REUTERS

A partir de 2027, os leilões de energia realizados pelo governo federal poderão contratar termelétricas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis, além de hidrelétricas com a capacidade instalada de até 50 megawhats (MW) e soluções de armazenamento de energia, incluindo as baterias. As hidrelétricas de até 50 MW serão contratadas por meio de Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade no primeiro semestre de 2027. Neste tipo de leilão, o empreendimento fica disponível, mas só produz energia, quando é necessário ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A expectativa é de aumentar o mercado dos biocombustíveis com a realização destas novas concorrências.
Os novos leilões também devem aumentar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico brasileiro. Serão contratadas térmicas flexíveis, que podem começar a gerar energia de uma forma mais rápida, quando for necessário. Atualmente, no Brasil, há térmicas que começam a produzir pela manhã, embora a sua energia seja necessária no final da tarde, quando as renováveis diminuem a sua produção.

Já o leilão de potência, vai incluir as termelétricas e sistemas de armazenamento – em baterias químicas e no sistema hidráulico – e deve ocorrer no segundo semestre de 2027.
Portaria estabelece cronograma de leilões até 2029

A portaria foi elogiada por agentes do setor por trazer previsibilidade na compra de energia e da potência instalada. A contratação desta última é importante para ter capacidade disponível para atender, rapidamente, aos horários de maior consumo, quando, por exemplo, a geração solar diminui.

Geralmente, as térmicas movidas a biogás e biometano usam resíduos como matéria-prima, aproveitando o que seria descartado no meio ambiente.

artigo.texto: Environment ministers, meeting in Luxembourg on Monday 12 October, held their first formal debate on the revision of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS, or ‘ETS’) presented by the European Commission on 17 July (see EUROPE 13912/1). On the first question raised by the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union – the climate ambition of the proposed revision – little new emerged. Both camps are growing. The most ambitious countries – Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Luxembourg – want to change the current system as little as possible or propose a more demanding linear reduction factor, which determines how many allowances are removed from the European carbon market each year. Some of these countries, including the Nordic countries, opposed including international credits in the ETS, advocating domestic CO2 emissions reductions instead. Nevertheless, some of these same Member States favour the inclusion of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies, not least because they benefit from them (see EUROPE 13941/4). The countries calling for a further easing of the linear reduction factor are Poland, Austria, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Romania, Cyprus, Malta, Italy, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Belgium. Many of these countries also want to postpone or make optional ETS2, the system covering emissions from buildings and road transport, which is not due to enter into force until 2028. France and Germany clarify their positions. Germany and France clarified their positions on the various elements of the revision and they are both concerned about carbon leakage if the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is not operational before the next phase of the ETS begins. Nine other Member States share that concern. “Work on the CBAM is not finished ”, French Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut summed up. German Federal Minister for Climate Action Carsten Schneider told the press that “the free allocation of allowances must be conditional on investment commitments to ensure that companies and their expertise remain in Europe”. He also reiterated that any weakening of the ETS’s ambition would have to be offset by greater climate ambition in other sectors, echoing an argument put forward by Denmark. France, for its part, opposed the European Commission’s proposal to make free allowances conditional on investment in Europe. According to Monique Barbut, this would create an additional administrative burden for businesses. Use of European funds for modernisation and decarbonisation. Several Member States expressed alarm at the planned reduction in the Modernisation Fund’s allocation from 4.5% to 2%. These include Poland, Hungary, Romania, Slovenia, Croatia and Lithuania. In the forthcoming negotiations, the fact that several countries complaining about the reduction in this allocation also favour easing the ETS and reopening ETS2 could work against them. On the use of ETS revenues as an EU own resource – an issue being discussed in negotiations on the EU’s next Multiannual Financial Framework (see EUROPE 13957/1) – many Member States, including Belgium, Estonia, Hungary, Romania and Latvia, clearly opposed the proposal. As for extending the scope of the ETS to maritime transport, aviation and waste incinerators, Agence Europe will come back on this subject. (Original version in French by Nadège Delépine)

artigo.texto: JANESVILLE – This week, The Gazette is taking a closer look at three questions we originally wrote for a public forum we hosted Sept. 30 on the GM/JATCO ballot referendum that's set for the Nov. 3 election ballot. The referendum asks Janesville residents to respond “Yes” or “No” to a question that asks if they'd want voters to have the authority to decide whether to approve any development project worth more than $450 million at the GM/JATCO site. The Gazette didn’t get to all the questions we’d hoped to ask at our forum, so we posed three unasked questions to the public — and to panelists who attended the forum. We received several responses, and we plan to examine them this week in a three-part series, with each story focusing on one question and the range of views it drew from some of those who responded. The first question: Q: The Janesville City Council has approved a 12-month, citywide moratorium on all data center developments, which it says would allow the city more time to research and craft policy and guardrails tied to data centers. Should voters take that moratorium into consideration when deciding on the GM/JATCO site referendum in the Nov. 3 election? Why or Why not? Mandy Witt is a local commercial property realtor and one of the six panelists at our forum. She opposes the referendum because she says if it passes, it could bring unpredictability to decisions usually made based on local planning and economic development policies — structures developers are accustomed to working with. In her response to this question, Witt said she thinks a residents’ vote on projects bigger than $450 million at the GM site could deter developers. She thinks voters should pay attention to the moratorium’s intent, which she believes is to give the City of Janesville extra time to research data centers and develop standards and local protections for the projects. Witt points out a contrast between the two measures: The referendum would apply to a variety of large-scale projects at the GM/JATCO site, not just data centers, while the city moratorium only applies to data centers only. “I am voting “No” (on the referendum) because I want clear requirements, early communication, and a predictable approval process,” Witt said. “The moratorium provides an opportunity to develop data center rules. The referendum adds a separate voter approval requirement without establishing those rules or a timetable for that vote.” Cathy Erdman fronts SNOW Janesville, a grassroots group that advocates for south-side Janesville residents and businesses, and one of the six panelists at our forum. She was another forum panelist. Erdman supports a “Yes” vote on the referendum, which would give voters authority over whether to approve large-scale projects at the GM/JATCO site. She says she’s more interested in what a citywide data center moratorium eventually accomplishes than the city's stated intentions going into the moratorium. In her response, Erdman said she believes it’s impossible to separate data centers from the conversation on the GM/JATCO referendum – despite the city’s recent passage of a data center moratorium. Erdman points out the city’s nearly more than year-long rewrite of the city’s zoning code has rolled out during the period in which the city was considering a proposal by Viridian Partners. During that time, Erdman notes, planners have not written standards for data centers that would require impact studies, setback requirements or neighbor notification rules. She points out a zoning reboot with fewer data center rules than she thinks is appropriate could get approved before the city drafts and OKs companion ordinances tied to the moratorium. Meanwhile, Erdman said, a new data center proposal should come after the moratorium ends. Now, there’s no clarity on what new rules the moratorium will produce. She thinks that’s why voters should weigh both the moratorium and the possibility of data centers when they vote on the referendum. “Despite the presence of a moratorium, future data center projects at GM/Jatco remain a possibility, and that should be a part of a voter’s decision-making process,” Erdman said. “Voters should be asking 'What happens when the moratorium expires, and who should have the final say on any exceptionally large development project at the publicly-owned GM/Jatco site, including data centers?'" Elaine Strassburg is a Janesville resident who responded to The Gazette’s request for local reader feedback on our questions on the referendum. Strassburg opposes the referendum. In her response, she says she thinks residents should separate the city’s data center moratorium from their consideration of the GM/JATCO site referendum, in part because Strassburg takes a more measured stance on data centers. “I’m hopeful the strong feelings against data centers will motivate the industry to innovate because unless we put a lid on AI, and I doubt that will happen, we will need data centers,” Strassburg said. The city of Janesville cut short a due-dillegence process at the GM/JATCO site with data center developer Viridian Partners earlier this year after the company failed in six months to show any concerted plans on how it might pursue a data center project. Strassburg believes public pressure against against Viridian Partners’ proposal is what led the city to in turn enact a data center moratorium. She believes public pressure against data centers provides reason enough for the city to use the moratorium period to craft data center protections that respond to residents’ concerns. “Interested citizens had sufficient influence on city government to ensure there will be no data center anywhere in Janesville until environmental issues such as water and electrical usage, and noise levels of current data centers, are cared for to the satisfaction of Janesville citizens,” she said. In her response, Erdman said she believes it’s impossible to separate data centers from the conversation on the GM/JATCO referendum – despite the city’s recent passage of a data center moratorium. Erdman points out the city’s nearly more than year-long rewrite of the city’s zoning code has rolled out during the period in which the city was considering a proposal by Viridian Partners. During that time, Erdman notes, planners have not written standards for data centers that would require impact studies, setback requirements or neighbor notification rules. She points out a zoning reboot with fewer data center rules than she thinks is appropriate could get approved before the city drafts and OKs companion ordinances tied to the moratorium. Meanwhile, Erdman said, a new data center proposal should come after the moratorium ends. Now, there’s no clarity on what new rules the moratorium will produce. She thinks that’s why voters should weigh both the moratorium and the possibility of data centers when they vote on the referendum. “Despite the presence of a moratorium, future data center projects at GM/Jatco remain a possibility, and that should be a part of a voter’s decision-making process,” Erdman said. “Voters should be asking 'What happens when the moratorium expires, and who should have the final say on any exceptionally large development project at the publicly-owned GM/Jatco site, including data centers?'" Elaine Strassburg is a Janesville resident who responded to The Gazette’s request for local reader feedback on our questions on the referendum. Strassburg opposes the referendum. In her response, she says she thinks residents should separate the city’s data center moratorium from their consideration of the GM/JATCO site referendum, in part because Strassburg takes a more measured stance on data centers. “I’m hopeful the strong feelings against data centers will motivate the industry to innovate because unless we put a lid on AI, and I doubt that will happen, we will need data centers,” Strassburg said. The city of Janesville cut short a due-dillegence process at the GM/JATCO site with data center developer Viridian Partners earlier this year after the company failed in six months to show any concerted plans on how it might pursue a data center project. Strassburg believes public pressure against against Viridian Partners’ proposal is what led the city to in turn enact a data center moratorium. She believes public pressure against data centers provides reason enough for the city to use the moratorium period to craft data center protections that respond to residents’ concerns. “Interested citizens had sufficient influence on city government to ensure there will be no data center anywhere in Janesville until environmental issues such as water and electrical usage, and noise levels of current data centers, are cared for to the satisfaction of Janesville citizens,” she said. artigo.texto: - United States - / - Construction - / - NasdaqGS:MTRX 3 U.S. Infrastructure Stocks Tied To SPR Refill And Energy Storage Demand The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, sitting near multi decade lows, has turned what used to feel like a sleepy government stockpile into a live market risk. Supply shocks now carry more bite, and pricing power can shift quickly when barrels are scarce and storage is constrained. This piece walks through how that backdrop hits the SPR value chain and profiles 3 U.S. stocks whose businesses are directly exposed to those pressures. The three stocks covered next are a sample set. The full screen surfaced 10 more U.S. energy infrastructure and engineering contractors tied by business description to SPR style storage and fuel terminal work that are not detailed here. To identify and analyze your own highest conviction angles in this theme, head straight into the U.S. Strategic Energy Infrastructure & Engineering Contractors screener. Beam Global (BEEM) Beam Global fits this screener as a clean-tech player focused on distributed, off grid energy and storage that can complement government efforts to build more resilient back up capacity when traditional fuel reserves look less secure. Beam Global designs and manufactures renewably energized infrastructure and battery solutions, with all reported revenue of about US$26.5 million coming from solar products and proprietary technology solutions, and the stock carries a market value of roughly US$24 million. "Beam's privileged government-backed partnerships in the Middle East and strategic manufacturing footprint give it fast-track access to over $1 trillion in near-term sustainable infrastructure spending, which may affect its gross and net margins as high-value projects ramp." What that ultimately means for Beam Global’s profitability depends on how one underappreciated pressure on its future contract mix and pricing unfolds. If that contract tilt is what you care about, read the full narrative for Beam Global to see how that pressure could reshape the next phase for Beam Global. Matrix Service (MTRX) Matrix Service sits much closer to the traditional heart of the SPR theme than Beam Global, because its core business is designing, building and maintaining the large storage tanks and terminals that keep crude, LNG and other fuels available when physical reserves run thin. Matrix Service Company focuses on large scale storage and terminal solutions, which generated about US$461 million of the US$874 million segment revenues, with utility and power infrastructure adding roughly US$283 million and process and industrial facilities about US$132 million, and the stock carries a market value near US$298 million. "Exposure to large LNG and NGL projects, including peak shaving and specialty storage, is feeding into a US$1.1b backlog and guided full year revenue of US$875 million to US$925 million." What really matters now is how one less visible constraint on future storage project timing shapes Matrix Service’s pricing power and eventual margins. That hidden timing pressure is exactly what full narrative for Matrix Service unpacks, including how Matrix Service’s backlog could accelerate or stall as SPR linked projects shuffle in the queue. Quanta Services (PWR) Quanta Services plugs directly into the SPR theme because it actually builds and maintains the electric and underground infrastructure that keeps strategic energy systems running, from transmission lines to storage-related pipelines, and its scale gives it a front row seat to long duration grid and energy security projects. Quanta Services generates about US$26.9b of revenue from Electric Infrastructure Solutions and roughly US$6.0b from Underground Utility and Infrastructure Solutions, with the stock valued around US$106.1b by market cap. "The long case is simple: Quanta sits at the intersection of several unusually durable spending waves: aging grid replacement, transmission expansion, utility hardening, manufacturing reshoring, renewable interconnection, and AI-driven power demand." The real swing factor is how one less visible constraint on future large project execution shapes Quanta’s ability to turn backlog into sustained margin strength. That execution swing factor is exactly what the full narrative for Quanta Services unpacks, including how project bottlenecks, risk sharing and capital cycles might be reshaping Quanta Services’ long run earnings power. artigo.texto: Mercado global de equipamentos de teste Ethernet: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do Mercado de Equipamentos de Teste Ethernet até 2035: Crescimento Impulsionado por 800GbE e Data Centers de IA Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de equipamentos de teste Ethernet, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de equipamentos de teste Ethernet entra em uma fase decisiva à medida que a infraestrutura de rede avança para 800GbE e as primeiras implantações de 1.6TbE, impulsionadas por cargas de trabalho de IA, expansão da nuvem e backhaul 5G-Advanced. Os equipamentos de teste Ethernet abrangem instrumentos e sistemas especializados que verificam, analisam e validam o desempenho, a conformidade e a funcionalidade de redes e dispositivos baseados em Ethernet ao longo de todo o ciclo de vida, da pesquisa e desenvolvimento à fabricação, chegando à implantação em campo e à manutenção. O mercado é definido por um conjunto diversificado de produtos, incluindo analisadores de rede, analisadores de protocolo, testadores de cabos, testadores de taxa de erro de bit, emuladores de rede, equipamentos de teste óptico, testadores de campo portáteis e equipamentos de laboratório de bancada. A demanda concentra-se na implantação de redes de telecomunicações, testes de infraestrutura de data centers, manutenção de redes corporativas, validação de Ethernet industrial, testes de Ethernet automotiva, sistemas aeroespaciais e de defesa, garantia de qualidade na fabricação e pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Com o crescimento do tráfego de dados e a evolução dos padrões Ethernet, a necessidade de ferramentas de validação precisas e de alta velocidade torna-se ainda mais crítica. O período de previsão de 2026 a 2035 será moldado pela comercialização da Ethernet de maior velocidade, pelo amadurecimento das operações de rede orientadas por IA e pela exigência de arquiteturas de data center energeticamente eficientes. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados sobre tamanho de mercado, estrutura, principais tendências, vetores de demanda, restrições de oferta e dinâmica competitiva para fabricantes, distribuidores, investidores e consultores. O cenário-base para o mercado de equipamentos de teste Ethernet de 2026 a 2035 prevê expansão sustentada, com taxa de crescimento anual composta de 6,2% e índice de mercado atingindo 182 em 2035 (2025=100). Essa perspectiva é sustentada pela aceleração da implantação de 800GbE e pela adoção inicial de 1.6TbE em data centers de hiperescala, que exigem soluções de teste avançadas para integridade de sinal, conformidade de protocolo e interoperabilidade. As operadoras de telecomunicações continuarão investindo em 5G-Advanced e backhaul pré-6G, impulsionando a demanda por testadores de campo portáteis e equipamentos de teste óptico. A manutenção de redes corporativas continuará sendo uma fonte estável de receita à medida que as organizações migram para Ethernet de maior velocidade para suportar aplicações intensivas em largura de banda. A validação de Ethernet industrial e os testes de Ethernet automotiva representam áreas de crescimento emergentes, impulsionadas pela manufatura inteligente e pelo desenvolvimento de veículos autônomos. O mercado também se beneficiará da crescente complexidade das arquiteturas de rede, incluindo redes desagregadas e abertas, que exigem testes e monitoramento abrangentes. No entanto, restrições como o alto custo dos equipamentos, a escassez de técnicos qualificados e os longos ciclos de substituição de equipamentos de teste legados podem moderar o crescimento. O cenário competitivo deverá registrar consolidação contínua e uma transição para soluções de teste definidas por software, que oferecem escalabilidade e automação. Geograficamente, a Ásia-Pacífico liderará o consumo, seguida pela América do Norte e Europa, enquanto a América Latina e o Oriente Médio e África apresentam oportunidades ainda não exploradas. No geral, o mercado está preparado para um crescimento robusto, com inovação tecnológica e transformação digital como principais viabilizadores. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Aceleração da implantação de 800GbE e 1.6TbE em data centers de hiperescala, impulsionada por cargas de trabalho de IA e nuvem - Implantações globais de 5G-Advanced e backhaul pré-6G que exigem validação de Ethernet de alta velocidade - Adoção crescente de Ethernet industrial na manufatura inteligente e em iniciativas da Indústria 4.0 - Crescimento dos testes de Ethernet automotiva para veículos autônomos e conectados - Aumento da complexidade das redes e necessidade de soluções de teste automatizadas e definidas por software - Expansão das redes corporativas para suportar aplicações intensivas em largura de banda e o trabalho remoto Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Altos custos de capital de equipamentos de teste avançados, limitando a adoção entre empresas de menor porte - Escassez de técnicos qualificados para operar e interpretar instrumentos de teste complexos - Ciclos de substituição prolongados de equipamentos de teste legados, desacelerando o ritmo de atualização - Interrupções na cadeia de suprimentos de semicondutores especializados e componentes ópticos - Incerteza econômica e restrições orçamentárias em alguns segmentos de usuários finais Estrutura da Demanda por Indústria de Uso Final Implantação de Redes de Telecomunicações (participação estimada: 28%) A implantação de redes de telecomunicações continua sendo o maior setor de uso final para equipamentos de

artigo.texto: Highlights - Repeat orders from a Hungarian partner. - Flow batteries support solar projects. - Long-duration storage demand rises. Invinity Energy Systems, a maker of vanadium flow batteries, secured new sales to a Hungarian partner for solar-plus-storage projects. The repeat order shows growing demand for long-duration energy storage as renewable energy expands. This update falls within our Energy Stocks coverage. Energy Storage for a Renewable Future Energy stocks include companies producing oil and gas, generating electricity and developing technologies for the energy transition. Invinity Energy Systems falls into the last category, manufacturing vanadium flow batteries that store energy for long periods. The company secured repeat sales to a Hungarian partner, adding to its growing presence in the Hungarian market. The systems will support solar-plus-storage projects, helping store solar power for use when the sun is not shining. What Invinity Does Vanadium Flow Batteries Invinity's batteries store energy in liquid electrolytes containing vanadium. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, flow batteries can discharge for many hours and degrade very little over time. Long-Duration Storage Flow batteries are suited to long-duration storage, providing power for several hours. This complements shorter-duration lithium-ion systems. Applications Invinity's systems support solar farms, wind projects, industrial sites and grid services. Why the Hungary Orders Matter Repeat Customer Repeat orders show that the customer is satisfied with performance, which builds credibility. Market Expansion Hungary is becoming an important market for Invinity, with multiple sales to the same partner. Solar Integration Pairing batteries with solar allows energy to be used in the evening, improving project economics. The Long-Duration Storage Opportunity Renewable Growth As wind and solar grow, storage is needed to balance supply and demand. Grid Stability Long-duration storage helps maintain grid stability during periods of low renewable output. Policy Support Governments are introducing support mechanisms for long-duration storage, including in the UK. Advantages of Flow Batteries Durability Flow batteries can operate for many years with minimal degradation. Safety They use non-flammable electrolytes, reducing fire risk. Recyclability Vanadium electrolyte can be reused, supporting circular economy goals. Risks to Consider Cost Competitiveness Flow batteries must compete with falling lithium-ion costs. Scaling Production Manufacturing at scale requires investment. Funding Growth companies may need additional capital. Order Timing Revenue depends on project timelines. How Investors Can Follow Invinity Readers will watch new orders, deliveries, manufacturing capacity, cost reductions and policy developments in key markets. The Role of Vanadium Vanadium is a metal that can exist in multiple charge states, making it ideal for flow batteries. Supply comes mainly from China, Russia and South Africa. Securing reliable vanadium supply is important for flow battery manufacturers. Why Europe Needs Storage European countries have ambitious renewable energy targets. Storage helps integrate renewables by smoothing output and reducing curtailment. Markets such as Hungary, with growing solar capacity, need storage to make the most of renewable generation. Hungary's Solar Growth Hungary has seen rapid growth in solar power capacity in recent years. As solar output rises, the grid faces challenges during peak production, when supply can exceed demand. Storage helps absorb excess solar power and release it later, improving grid balance and project returns. Repeat orders from a Hungarian partner suggest that solar developers in the country see value in long-duration storage. Building a track record in one market can help Invinity win business in neighbouring countries with similar needs. The UK Long-Duration Storage Scheme The UK government has developed a support mechanism for long-duration electricity storage, designed to encourage investment in technologies that can store energy for many hours. This scheme could create opportunities for flow battery manufacturers, including Invinity, by providing revenue certainty for projects. Competition in Energy Storage Lithium-ion batteries dominate the energy storage market because of falling costs and widespread manufacturing. Flow batteries compete by offering longer duration, greater cycle life and enhanced safety. The right choice depends on the application, with flow batteries suited to projects needing daily cycling over many hours. Manufacturing and Partnerships Invinity has worked with manufacturing partners to scale production. Expanding capacity while reducing costs is central to competing with alternative technologies. Partnerships can help share investment and accelerate deployment. Financial Considerations As a growth company, Invinity has invested heavily in product development and manufacturing. Revenue growth from orders like those in Hungary is important for reaching profitability. Investors watch cash balances, order backlogs and delivery schedules closely. The Energy Transition Context Global investment in renewable energy continues to grow, and storage is an essential part of integrating renewables into power systems. Long-duration storage is expected to become increasingly important as renewable penetration rises. Companies with proven technologies and growing order books may benefit from this trend. Why Durability Matters Energy storage assets are expected to operate for many years. Flow batteries can cycle many times with minimal degradation, which can lower lifetime costs. For project developers, durability and predictable performance improve the economics of storage investments. Final Thoughts Invinity Energy Systems' repeat Hungarian orders highlight demand for long-duration energy storage as renewable energy expands. Its vanadium flow batteries offer durability, safety

artigo.texto: Recently, the strategic cooperation signing ceremony between Rockcheck New Energy Group and Suzhou Qingde Hydrogen Energy Technology Co., Ltd. was held in Tianjin. Relying on the Sunan Institute of Molecular Engineering at Peking University, the two parties will focus on the field of hydrogen agriculture to jointly develop and promote hydrogen molecular fertilizers, while deepening cooperation in hydrogen beauty and health and hydrogen industry sectors, working together to open up new tracks for diversified hydrogen energy applications. Peking University professor and doctoral supervisor Li Xingguo, Qingde Hydrogen Energy General Manager Xie Lei, and Rockcheck Group Director, Vice President, and Rockcheck New Energy Group Chairman Zhang Lihua attended the ceremony. Hydrogen energy industry enters a new era of multi-scenario large-scale application Currently, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the Ministry of Finance, and the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) have approved five major urban clusters including Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei to carry out comprehensive hydrogen energy application pilot projects. China's hydrogen energy industry has officially moved from single-point breakthroughs in fuel cell vehicles into a period of multi-scenario large-scale application. The strategic cooperation between Rockcheck New Energy and Qingde Hydrogen Energy is an important initiative by the two enterprises to actively implement the national hydrogen energy pilot deployment, which will continue to broaden the boundaries of hydrogen energy applications and build a diversified hydrogen energy industry ecosystem. Strong alliance between technology R&D and scenario operations This cooperation achieves a strong alliance and complementary advantages between technology R&D and scenario operations. Rockcheck New Energy is a benchmark enterprise in the commercial and large-scale implementation of hydrogen energy, positioned as an integrated solution provider for the hydrogen energy industry. It has built an entire industry chain layout covering "production, storage, transportation, refueling, application, research, and equipment manufacturing," and created a "one core, two poles" development model centered on a digital and intelligent big data platform, with the "hydrogen +" economy and "vehicle +" economy as the two poles. To date, it hascumulatively put into operation 1,255 hydrogen fuel cell heavy trucks and 17 hydrogen refueling stations, with mature project implementation capabilities, rich multi-scenario operation experience, and a complete industrial supporting system. Qingde Hydrogen Energy is a hydrogen energy technology innovation enterprise relying on the Sunan Institute of Molecular Engineering at Peking University. The company has developed efficient and safe nano-hydrolysis hydrogen production materials, which are widely used in hydrogen molecular biomedicine and hydrogen agriculture. It holds multiple independent intellectual property rights and has carried out project cooperation with multiple industry leaders, demonstrating outstanding strength in technological innovation and commercialization of research outcomes. Industrial layout implemented across three major tracks According to the agreement, the two parties will implement industrial layout across three major tracks: first, jointly promote the civilian application, productization, and scenario-based implementation of hydrogen health technologies, creating a new sector in the hydrogen beauty and health industry; second, use hydrogen-enriched technology to empower the transformation of modern agriculture,jointly develop and promote hydrogen molecular fertilizers, and explore a new model of green, efficient, and low-carbon smart hydrogen agriculture; third, tap into the value of hydrogen energy storage, promote the large-scale application of hydrogen energy in scenarios such as renewable energy consumption and power grid peak shaving, and cultivate new growth poles for the hydrogen energy industry. The two parties will establish a special working group, build an industry-academia-research collaboration mechanism, and jointly carry out technical research, demonstration project construction, and market expansion, promoting the extension of hydrogen energy applications from transportation and logistics to diversified scenarios such as public health, modern agriculture, and new-type industry.

artigo.texto: SWI arrecada US$ 894 milhões para reestruturar a antiga mineradora de bitcoin da FTX, Genesis Digital, para IA O Grupo SWI afirmou que utilizará os recursos provenientes de uma captação de fundos de 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) para transformar a Genesis Digital Assets, adquirida da falência da FTX, de um minerador de bitcoin para um data center focado em IA. - O Grupo SWI levantou 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) de investidores institucionais, avaliando a empresa em 6,1 bilhões de euros, para expandir projetos de inteligência artificial e data centers na Europa e nos Estados Unidos. - A empresa planeja reutilizar as instalações nos EUA e na Suécia da Genesis Digital Assets, a mineradora de bitcoin anteriormente apoiada pela FTX que agora controla como SWI Digital, para cargas de trabalho de IA, enquanto vende os locais da unidade no Cazaquistão. - A estratégia da SWI reflete uma mudança mais ampla na indústria, à medida que os mineradores de bitcoin transformam conexões de energia e capacidade de data center em receita de IA e computação de alto desempenho. SWI Group (SWICH), que controla a mineradora de bitcoin Genesis Digital Assets, anteriormente pertencente à FTX, afirmou ter levantado 800 milhões de euros (894 milhões de dólares) junto a investidores institucionais para expandir seus projetos de data center e de computação em inteligência artificial (IA) na Europa e nos Estados Unidos. A empresa listada na Euronext Amsterdã, uma firma de investimentos focada em infraestrutura digital, anunciou o aumento de capital avalia-o em 6,1 bilhões de euros. Anunciou a aquisição de cerca de 40% da Genesis Digital em junho por 500 milhões de dólares, concluindo o aquisição em agosto com 70% dos direitos de voto e renomeando a unidade para SWI Digital. A estratégia da empresa ilustra o que se tornou uma operação conhecida para as empresas de mineração de bitcoin. Seu ativo mais valioso não são mais suas máquinas de mineração, mas as conexões de energia e os locais dos data centers que podem ser reaproveitados para clientes de IA. Mineradores de bitcoin assinaram mais de US$ 70 bilhões em contratos de IA e computação de alto desempenho, à medida que buscam uma receita mais estável do que a mineração de bitcoin atualmente oferece. A mudança do foco da mineração de criptomoedas para o processamento de computações de IA coloca a empresa na mesma corrida que os mineradores listados como a TeraWulf e Core Scientific , que estão convertendo o acesso à energia e a capacidade de data centers em negócios de hospedagem de IA. O CEO da SWI, Max-Hervé George, disse ao Wall Street Journal que ele “"juros zero” na mineração de bitcoin. A empresa está vendendo os sites da Genesis Digital Assets no Cazaquistão e pretende utilizar suas instalações nos EUA e na Suécia para cargas de trabalho de IA em vez disso. Alameda Research, a empresa de negociação de criptomoedas pertencente ao ex-CEO da FTX, Sam Bankman-Fried, investiu mais de US$ 1 bilhão na Genesis Digital Assets desde 2021 e detinha cerca de 20% da mineradora, informou o WSJ. FTX declarou falência em novembro de 2022, deixando esse investimento entre os muitos ativos analisados pelo espólio. artigo.texto: Maryland regulators denied financial credits for a controversial battery storage project proposed for Harford County, but the decision does not necessarily stop the project from moving forward. The 500-megawatt Oystercatcher Energy Storage System is proposed near BGE's Conastone substation in White Hall. Harford County has opposed the project and has been involved in the Public Service Commission proceedings surrounding the proposal. According to the PSC decision provided to WMAR-2 News, regulators denied the project's application for Energy Storage Capacity Credits, citing concerns about whether the project would be cost-effective and provide enough benefit to ratepayers. The decision does not prevent developers from continuing the project's separate approval process. Oystercatcher could also seek the financial credits again during the state's next round of applications after Jan. 1. Regulators also called for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project moves forward. WMAR-2 News previously reported on opposition to the proposed facility, particularly over its location near Deer Creek. Residents have raised concerns about lithium-ion battery fires and potential impacts to the air and nearby water. Supporters of battery storage have argued that the technology could help support Maryland's electric grid as demand grows and other sources of electricity generation are retired. Harford County created a workgroup involving county agencies, fire companies, health officials, community organizations and residents to examine battery energy storage projects proposed in the county. The county says it has also explored legal action over environmental and public-safety concerns. The Oystercatcher project would connect to BGE's Conastone substation near Norrisville Road and Deer Creek. County materials describe the proposed facility as capable of storing 500 megawatts of energy. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. Email the WMAR-2 Newsroom if you have info, photos or videos to share. This story was initially reported by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

artigo.texto: Behind-the-Meter Power Offers Control, Flexibility and Speed for the AI Age Key Highlights - AI is driving data centers to rethink their relationship with power. - BESS helps data centers manage volatile AI compute loads and grid constraints. - UPS, BESS and on-site generation create a coordinated energy stack. - Virtual power plants can turn backup assets into strategic grid resources. - Energy-as-a-Service can reduce upfront costs for behind-the-meter infrastructure. For the last decade, the data center industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy, but today, the explosive rise of AI is exacerbating power sourcing issues that must be solved to keep building at the speed of innovation. Electric Power Research Institute projects that data centers could consume as much as 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, more than triple their current 4-5% share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid. At the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of new generation and storage capacity was represented by projects actively seeking interconnection to the U.S. grid. In turn, data center operators are fundamentally rethinking their relationship with power, shifting from passive grid consumers to active, localized energy producers. Grid capacity is no longer the ceiling. Instead, the next chapter of digital infrastructure will be written behind the meter. Behind-the-meter (BTM) refers to energy assets located on the customer side of the utility connection, including battery systems, microgrids, generators, fuel cells, and distributed energy resources that can operate independently of grid constraints. The Role of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) While every data center developer face grid constraints, the industry’s two dominant business models are adopting distinctly different strategies to bypass the power bottleneck. Hyperscale Operators Hyperscale operators (tech giants like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) utilize their massive balance sheets to secure gigawatt-scale capacity directly. Rather than acting as passive grid customers, hyperscalers are taking direct, active control of their energy supply chains. They negotiate custom, state-level tariffs directly with utilities, co-locate facilities next to large nuclear or baseload assets, and sign massive off-site Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Increasingly, hyperscalers are also deploying large-scale, on-site Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to bypass grid delays and accelerate their projects, or turning to behind-the-meter natural gas generation to provide additional power on-site. Colocation Providers In contrast, colocation providers lease space, power, and cooling to third-party tenants. Colos operate on a highly competitive, faster-to-market model where speed-to-revenue is the primary metric. Colocation facilities are geographically constrained, as their facilities must be located close to business hubs to minimize latency rather than simply next to remote power plants. Consequently, data center and colocation developers are increasingly integrating on-site, behind-the-meter energy solutions. In highly congested markets, BTM generation and battery storage can provide a path to power while developers wait for grid interconnection. In Virginia, for example, LS Power is pursuing a 300 MW data center project designed to receive power directly from its adjacent natural gas-fired Doswell power plant, creating a behind-the-meter supply arrangement that can help accelerate access to power. The New Coordinated Energy Stack: UPS + BESS + Generators Historically, a data center’s power architecture was passive, consisting of an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to bridge 5-to-15 minutes of downtime and backup diesel generators to handle prolonged outages. AI has shattered this legacy design. Although many enterprise deployments still operate below 20 kW per rack, next-generation AI clusters are increasingly exceeding 100 kW per rack, with some designs targeting significantly higher densities. Furthermore, AI training runs create highly volatile, synchronized compute loads, causing electricity draw to spike and drop in massive, sub-second waves. To protect both sensitive computing equipment and the local grid from these fluctuations, operators are deploying a layered, grid-interactive energy stack: - UPS (Instant Protection): Positioned in series with the servers, the traditional UPS remains essential for providing millisecond-fast power conditioning and preventing data loss during transient voltage sags. - BESS (On-site Shock Absorber & Optimizer): Connected in parallel at the facility level, BESS acts as a real-time shock absorber. It smooths out volatile AI compute spikes, stores cost-effective off-peak power for use during peak hours, and participates in grid-balancing services. - On-site Generation (Long-Term Firm Power): Customer-sited generation, including natural gas microturbines, provides the ultimate firm baseload capacity, insulating the facility from grid failures for days or weeks. By layering these technologies, operators can stop treating their power systems like a pricey “insurance policy” that sits idle, and start using them as a smart, money-saving asset. By discharging on-site batteries during peak demand periods — a strategy known as peak shaving — operators can reduce the peak loads used to calculate demand charges, potentially lowering electricity costs significantly. Turning Backup Assets into Strategic Grid Partners Historically, backup diesel generators sat untouched, accumulating maintenance costs unless a blackout occurred. Today, utilities and data center operators are establishing mutually beneficial partnerships. Through Virtual Power Plants (VPPs), utilities can aggregate a data center’s distributed backup generators and BESS capacity into a single, software-controlled resource. artigo.texto: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has recently inaugurated two projects in Tamil Nadu. These projects are expected to support renewable energy integration ports and address growing demand for Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects in Tamil Nadu. One of the projects involves the development of port infrastructure across the country to help the shipping sector reach new heights. Tamil Nadu is expected to play an important role in this initiative. The central government has recently taken a significant decision In this direction with approximately Rs. 17,000 crore investment. The VOC Port in Thoothukudi is being developed into a mega container port and green energy hub. Once completed, the port will be able to accommodate even the ultra-large container vessels. This development is expected to help transform Tamil Nadu into a global hub for industry and transportation. BESS Project in Tamil Nadu Prime Minister Narendra Modi also laid the foundation stone for the 250 MW/500 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, on October 11, 2026. According to the tender, awarded to NLC India Renewables Limited (NIRL), a subsidiary of NLC India Limited (NLCIL), last year, it would develop this project across Ottapidaram, Anuppankulam, and Kayathar. The systems are designed to support two full charging and discharging cycles daily, enabling them to manage peak power demand and improve energy availability during critical load periods. It will follow a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model under which the company will receive financial assistance under the State component of the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme. Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) will procure the energy storage services from NIRL for a period of 12 years through a Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). About NLC India's 250 MW/500 MWh BESS Project The 500 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project was originally awarded to NLC India Renewables Limited (NIRL), a subsidiary of NLC India Limited (NLCIL), following a tender issued by Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Limited (TNGECL) in June 2025. It is the first large-scale energy storage initiative for NLCIL. The project involves the development of three standalone BESS units with a combined capacity of 250 MW/500 MWh. These units will be installed at three substations in Tamil Nadu—Ottapidaram, Anuppankulam, and Kayathar—each operating at 400/230/110 kV. The systems are designed to support two full charging and discharging cycles daily, enabling them to manage peak power demand and improve energy availability during critical load periods. The project will follow the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model and was awarded through a tariff-based competitive bidding process. It will receive financial assistance under the state component of the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme. As part of the agreement, Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) will procure energy storage services from NIRL for 12 years under a Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). This long-term arrangement is expected to provide reliable support for Tamil Nadu's grid infrastructure and energy requirements.

artigo.texto: A well-known local engineer said he's completely reimagined the concept of data centers — and he said it addresses just about every concern communities have expressed. Opposition to data centers has exploded almost as quickly as the industry itself. Channing Blackwell believes he's got the solution. Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. “We're not putting off any pollution, we're not putting off any noise,” he said. Blackwell is a professional engineer, and whether or not you know his name, you know his work. His firm designed several monuments in D.C., including the National Museum of African American History and Culture. His father's company helped design the underground Metro system. When it came to looking at data centers, Blackwell said the solution was as easy as turning the problem upside down. “Once I put it underground, then I started really pushing on optimizing the building,” he said. He calls it “The Renaissance System.” Northern Virginia Northern Virginia news, events and updates “For 12 months, they've worked quietly fixated on three core principles: community security, environmental security, national security. That work gave birth to The Renaissance System,” a corporate video described the project. Buried below the ground, crowned by a berm adorned with solar panels, the subterranean data center concept would be powered by geothermal energy, relying on zero fossil fuel. At hyperscale, it would span 30 acres, cost less than half of the current hyperscale data center and be nearly as powerful as the largest data center currently operating in the U.S. — not to mention that Blackwell said it wouldn't need to plug into the electric grid. “People that are 20 miles down the road that are protesting the power lines — Are they really needed if you get rid of the above-ground data centers that are obsolete technology and go to something that we've designed?” he said. Just last week the U.S. Department of Energy released a report suggesting geothermal technology could solve one of the largest issues current data center design creates: heating and cooling. Blackwell explained that above ground, data centers struggle to keep the thermostat at a comfortable level for their servers, and it costs a lot of money to do it. Underground cooling comes naturally and requires zero community water. Blackwell said mother nature will work for us — all she requires is that we listen to her. “If you're sloppy with your design, she can't close it for you. But, if you're mindful, it's there,” he said. As Blackwell launches his Renaissance System, he's not the only game in town. Other companies around the country are working on similar projects. In fact, a company based in Texas just inked a deal with Google to provide geothermal energy to a data center out west. While the future of this technology has yet to be proven, one thing is certain: There are people hearing the concerns about the data center industry, and they are working on solutions. This Saturday, the Piedmont Environmental Council is hosting a march in Leesburg, calling for a statewide data center moratorium. News4 asked a council spokesperson about using geothermal energy to power data centers. The spokesperson was unfamiliar with the Renaissance System but said they hope it works.

artigo.texto: Diagnóstico de 90 dias vai mapear a infraestrutura do estado para disputar a instalação de empresas de tecnologia e data centers junto ao resto do Nordeste por Cynara Maíra Publicado em 12/10/2026, às 12h26 - Atualizado às 12h51 Estudo encomendado: Governo de Pernambuco e LIDE contrataram a Deloitte para fazer um raio-x da infraestrutura digital do estado em 90 dias. Financiamento privado: Os custos do levantamento são pagos pelas empresas Cavalcanti Petribu, Estratégica Engenharia e Dislub Equador. Secretarias envolvidas: Participam do projeto as pastas de Administração, Ciência e Tecnologia e Desenvolvimento Econômico. Objetivo: O documento vai apontar gargalos e orientar ações do governo para atrair empresas de tecnologia e investimentos privados. Lançamento: O encontro de apresentação ocorre nesta quarta-feira (14), às 10h30, na sede da Secti, no Bairro do Recife. O Governo de Pernambuco e o LIDE Pernambuco iniciam nesta semana a elaboração do Estudo Estratégico do Ecossistema de Infraestrutura Digital do estado. O levantamento, conduzido pela consultoria Deloitte com prazo de conclusão de 90 dias, vai traçar um diagnóstico técnico para orientar políticas públicas e atrair investimentos privados voltados à conectividade, inteligência artificial e centros de processamento de dados (Data Centers) no estado. A ideia é que o anúncio do início dos trabalhos ocorra nesta semana, na quarta-feira (14), como a primeira entrega formal da parceria entre o Governo do Estado e o Lide, após o início do acordo de cooperação técnica firmado em julho de 2026. A ideia é que o grupo de cooperação continue pelos próximos quatro anos. Na parte do Executivo, participarão as secretarias de Administração; Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação e a pasta de Desenvolvimento Econômico. No lado privado, bancarão os custos o Grupo Cavalcanti Petribu, a Estratégia Engenharia e o Grupo Dislub Equador. A partir das conclusões da Deloitte, a gestão estadual pretende definir prioridades para modernizar a rede, ampliar a conectividade e aumentar a competitividade econômica local. Quando o relatório for entregue, os dados ficarão disponíveis para consulta pública. A apresentação oficial do estudo acontece nesta quarta-feira (14), às 10h30, no auditório da Secti, no Bairro do Recife. O encontro reúne as titulares das secretarias envolvidas, lideranças do LIDE e dirigentes das empresas que patrocinam o projeto. O Lide Pernambuco é uma organização empresarial que reúne diversas empresas do estado que defendem o fortalecimento do ambiente de negócios e o desenvolvimento econômico do estado. Parte do acordo de cooperação técnica com o estado já previa o incentivo a projetos nas áreas de conectividade, data centers sustentáveis, atração de investimentos e desenvolvimento da economia digital no estado.
