artigo.texto: Concept mockup to be showcased at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, with functional battery segment development planned as the next phase of cell and system integration work PARIS, Oct. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ProLogium today announced progress in its collaboration with Rimac Technology on next-generation electric vehicle battery pack development. The companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in September 2025 to develop a next-generation battery platform and have completed a battery pack concept mockup, which will be displayed at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The next phase will focus on developing a functional battery segment to establish a basis for testing the thermal management and cell-integration concepts and support battery pack applications in the battery electric vehicle (BEV) market. The collaboration combines ProLogium's next-generation cell technology with Rimac Technology's battery system development expertise, focusing on a pouch cell-to-pack architecture. Through a staged development path from concept mockup to functional battery segment, full-scale functional battery pack and in-vehicle testing, the companies will progressively evaluate cell and system integration approaches, connecting next-generation cell technology with automotive product development. From Concept Mockup to Functional Hardware Bringing cell technology into automotive applications requires more than cell-level performance. It also involves addressing thermal management, cell integration and battery pack architecture at the system level. With battery pack integration at its core, the collaboration brings together cell technology and systems engineering to examine the design requirements for next-generation batteries in automotive applications. The completed concept mockup is an initial milestone in this development process. The ongoing development will move the project from a conceptual representation toward functional hardware, using a battery segment as the platform for subsequent testing. This work will assess the feasibility of thermal management and cell-integration concepts and inform full-scale battery pack development. By developing a battery segment before expanding to a full-scale system, the companies will gather test results and design feedback at each stage to assess whether the integration approach can meet automotive battery-systems requirements. Vincent Yang, Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said: "Since jointly announcing our collaboration with Rimac Technology at IAA in 2025, both teams have continued to advance the project, translating our shared technical vision into concrete engineering development work. What we are presenting at the Paris Motor Show is the baseline of that collaboration. Building on the completed concept mockup and the functional segments currently in development, we are preparing to move into the development and production of a functional battery progressing toward a full-scale battery pack and subsequent vehicle integration validation. Bringing next-generation batteries to the automotive market requires more than cell technology. It also takes the engineering expertise to integrate those cells into a battery pack with optimized architecture and thermal management. We look forward to combining our technical strengths through hardware development and testing to address the engineering challenges of automotive integration and translate the value of next-generation cell technology into solutions that can be adopted in vehicles.” Daniel Kišić, Principal Product Architect of Rimac Technology said: "Rimac Technology is developing a scalable cell-to-pack integration technology for solid-state pouch cells, designed to meet and exceed the requirements the automotive industry is expected to set over the coming decade. A wide range of integration solutions is currently being evaluated and tested in parallel on functional battery segments, covering thermal management, swelling management, cell integration and system-level design. Some of these solutions are oriented towards maximum energy density and reduced space and weight, while others are oriented towards delivering performance. The work starts from vehicle-level requirements and aims to improve every aspect of the battery design by reducing complexity, combining functions and reducing weight. It does so with cost in mind, while still delivering state-of-the-art charging times and power output. Once validated at vehicle level, the solution is expected to deliver significant weight savings, improving driving efficiency and extending range. OEMs could then choose between more energy on board at the same weight, a smaller and lighter battery for the same range, or any combination in between.” A Clear Pathway to Full-Scale Battery Packs and In-Vehicle Testing According to Rimac Technology's current development roadmap, the functional battery segment currently in development is planned for display at CES 2027, with the full-scale functional battery pack identified as a development milestone for the second half of 2027. Subsequent targets include in-vehicle and public-road testing in the second half of 2028.These stages will progressively expand the scope of validation, from assessing integration concepts in a functional battery segment to a full-scale battery pack, followed by vehicle installation and road testing to evaluate system performance in an automotive environment. At the Paris Motor Show, the companies will present the concept mockup stage of the collaboration and outline the next steps in functional hardware development and integration validation. By combining cell technology with battery systems engineering, ProLogium and Rimac Technology will continue to advance next-generation battery integration technology development from concept design toward automotive applications. artigo.texto: ABB Broad industrial charger portfolio According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Industrial Battery Charger market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global industrial battery charger market is a critical enabler of the energy transition, providing the power conversion backbone for grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) and heavy-duty industrial electrification. Unlike consumer chargers, industrial battery chargers must manage high-power AC/DC conversion, grid-code compliance, and safety certification, making them high-value components embedded in bankable energy projects. Demand is bifurcating: standardized, cost-optimized chargers for containerized BESS versus customized, feature-rich systems for grid-support and harsh industrial environments. The competitive landscape pits diversified power-electronics giants against specialized OEMs with deep application engineering. Procurement is dominated by sophisticated buyers—BESS integrators, EPC firms, and utilities—who prioritize total cost of ownership and long-term service over upfront price. Supply chain resilience, particularly for SiC/GaN semiconductors and magnetics, remains a key concern. Regulatory frameworks and grid codes are primary product drivers, mandating advanced functionalities like fault ride-through and frequency regulation. As the market evolves through 2035, chargers will become intelligent grid-edge assets, with software-defined controls enabling active grid management. This report provides a structured analysis of market size, segmentation, demand drivers, competitive dynamics, and regional outlook, offering actionable insights for manufacturers, integrators, investors, and policymakers navigating this rapidly evolving landscape. The baseline scenario for the industrial battery charger market through 2035 anticipates robust expansion, underpinned by the accelerating deployment of grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) and the electrification of heavy-duty transport and industrial processes. As renewable energy penetration rises, the need for flexible, grid-compliant charging infrastructure becomes paramount, driving demand for advanced chargers capable of bidirectional power flow, grid-forming capabilities, and seamless integration with energy management systems. The market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8.2% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 220 (2025=100). Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the largest market, driven by China's dominance in BESS manufacturing and deployment, while North America and Europe will see strong growth supported by policy incentives and grid modernization initiatives. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa will emerge as opportunistic markets, albeit from a smaller base. Key risks include supply chain bottlenecks for specialized semiconductors, regulatory delays, and the potential for technology shifts that could disrupt incumbent product architectures. However, the long-term trajectory remains positive, with chargers increasingly viewed as strategic components in the energy transition. Grid-scale BESS represents the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for industrial battery chargers. As utilities and independent power producers deploy massive battery arrays to store excess renewable energy and provide grid services, the demand for high-power, grid-compliant chargers surges. These chargers must manage bidirectional power flow, support grid-forming capabilities, and comply with stringent interconnection standards. The shift toward longer-duration storage and hybrid projects further amplifies charger requirements, as does the need for seamless integration with energy management systems. Demand-side indicators include renewable capacity additions, battery storage procurement targets, and grid stability mandates. These applications require robust, high-power chargers capable of delivering rapid charging cycles and managing large battery capacities. By 2035, this segment will see significant growth, with chargers becoming more integrated with fleet management systems and renewable energy sources. Bandyopadhyay said NVVN also intends to commission an additional 500 MWh of capacity during the current financial year. The plans are part of the government’s scheme to support the development of 3,000 MWh of battery energy storage capacity through different modes. The comments were made on the sidelines of the 18th India Coal Summit, organised by the Indian Chamber of Commerce in New Delhi. NVVN is involved in developing large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) across the country as India expands its electricity storage infrastructure. A BESS uses batteries, either individually or more commonly in groups, to store electricity generated by power plants. The stored electricity can subsequently be supplied to the grid when demand rises or when renewable generation is unavailable. Battery storage systems are increasingly being used to help utilities manage peak electricity demand and improve grid reliability. They can store power during periods of lower demand or high renewable energy generation and release it during peak-demand periods, supporting the integration of intermittent sources such as solar and wind power. India is scaling up its BESS ecosystem through policy support and capacity additions as it seeks to strengthen the power grid and accommodate a growing share of renewable energy. NVVN’s planned projects are expected to contribute to the government’s broader effort to establish utility-scale storage facilities and improve flexibility in electricity supply. artigo.texto: - Energy - 2 min read India's battery energy storage sector set for 91% growth to 302GWh by FY32E: Nuvama Cumulative BESS capacity could rise to 302 GWh from 6.3 GWh, driven by renewable integration and falling costs, creating growth opportunities for domestic manufacturers. India's Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) sector is projected to register a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 91 per cent between FY26 and FY32E, according to a recent report by Nuvama. The expansion reflects a critical infrastructure cycle designed to support renewable integration, grid balancing, and round-the-clock power requirements across the country. The report noted that cumulative capacity will surge from 6.3 GWh to 302GWh over the same period, with annual additions climbing from 5.7GWh in FY26 to 56 GWh by FY32E. The report noted that the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) estimates national BESS demand at 236 GWh by FY32 and 1,840 GWh by 2047. "We estimate annual BESS additions to rise from 5.7 GWh in FY26 to 56 GWh by FY32E, taking cumulative capacity from 6.3GWh to 302GWh (91 per cent CAGR) over FY2632E," the report said. "With 89 per cent of current requirements met through imports, falling battery costs, alongside a likely ALMM-like framework, could accelerate adoption, localisation and domestic capacity growth. Although Li-ion occupies 98 per cent of the BESS market, sodium-ion technology and China+1 themes are an opportunity for India," the report added. Manufacturing economics reveal distinct margins across end-markets, with commercial, industrial, and retail segments yielding spreads of $18 to 23 per kilowatt-hour, corresponding to EBITDA margins of 17 to 20 per cent. By contrast, the utility segment records spreads of $8 per kilowatt-hour and an EBITDA margin of 9 per cent. "Our analysis shows attractive cell-to-pack manufacturing economics with materially differentiated spreads across end-markets," the report noted. "Even with low spreads of USD8/kWh (EBITDA margin 9 per cent) for the Utility segment, our calculation and channel checks indicate a one-to-two-year payback." The report also highlighted that while returns for an integrated BESS facility yield a modest internal rate of return of 12 per cent, domestic production maintains a distinct cost advantage through capital expenditure of $80 million per gigawatt-hour, coupled with production-linked incentive support of ₹181 billion for 50 GWh and competitive labour expenses. Cell-to-pack configurations demonstrate an internal rate of return of 31 per cent. "We believe with policy support, localisation and scale, integrated BESS could open up export-led growth," the report noted. Financially, BESS integration is estimated to contribute 17 to 60 per cent to company revenues by FY28. Premier presents an opportunity of ₹103 billion, representing 60 per cent of its projected FY28 revenue, while Vikram is positioned for a 54 per cent revenue uplift. "Despite early battery ambitions and potential BESS addition of 17-60 per cent to FY28E revenue, most listed solar/BESS players' earnings are yet to capture meaningful BESS contribution," the report stated. "At 17x FY27E EPS, solar/BESS trades at a 77 per cent discount to battery chemicals and a 64 per cent discount to battery IPP peers. As capacity ramps up, we believe BESS could emerge as a strong driver of earnings upgrade and valuation re-rating," the report said.

artigo.texto: Harrisburg, Pa. — The president of Concerned Citizens of Montour County was among the speakers at a state Capitol rally on Oct. 6, where organizers say more than 250 people from across Pa. called on Gov. Josh Shapiro and legislators to impose a moratorium on data center development. “All they have to fight with is money,” said Sam Burleigh, president and co-founder of the Montour County group. “We have collective voices, elective powers, constitutional laws, and home field advantage. Together we can beat them! Unite and fight!” Burleigh has also previously spoken at meetings focused on Muncy and Gregg townships' proposed data centers. The rally in the Capitol Rotunda was organized by the Better Path Coalition, No False Climate Solutions PA, and 30 partner organizations. Speakers addressed concerns including surveillance, affordability, impacts on health, the environment, and agriculture, threats from artificial intelligence to intellectual property, and the future being left to children. Speakers during the event criticized legislators for what participants described as “putting polluters before people via data center deals that were brokered outside of the public’s view.” The rally closed with speeches on what organizers called the state government’s failure to enforce Pa.’s Green Amendment, Article 1, Section 27 of the state constitution. “Once again, our elected officials are leaping before they look to do the bidding of an industry,” said Karen Feridun, co-founder of the Better Path Coalition and No False Climate Solutions PA and the rally’s emcee. “Governor Shapiro claims to have changed his position on data centers, but his recent Executive Order implementing his GRID initiative is all about making sure data centers are built, not taking the break the public is demanding to decide what role, if any, hyperscale data centers and generative AI should play in Pennsylvania.” Stuart Day of Ohio Valley Allies, who described himself as a Pa. farmer and investigative journalist, compared the expansion of hyperscale data centers to the shale-gas boom. “I believe AI and the infrastructure supporting it represent a transformative moment in human history — and decisions of that magnitude demand deliberation, transparency, and meaningful public participation. This development should not be foisted upon communities and landowners without independent economic and environmental analysis, strong oversight, enforceable protections, and an honest accounting of who receives the benefits and who carries the costs. Rural Pennsylvania has heard promises of salvation from outside industries before; we should have learned by now that something this consequential demands caution, wisdom, and a process with real teeth,” Day said. Hilary Flint, program director at Center for Organizing, said more than 40,000 people have joined the Pennsylvania Data Center Resistance Facebook group. “People understand that projects of this scale will shape their communities for decades, and they are saying no. This movement is growing, it is organized, and we will keep showing up because communities deserve more than a seat at the table. They deserve the power to say no to what gets built in their own backyards,” Flint said. The rally also launched a fall campaign of letters from specific groups of residents explaining why signers oppose data center development. The letters will be delivered to Gov. Shapiro, state legislators, and the winners of the upcoming election. Josephine Gingerich, health advocacy outreach coordinator at Physicians for Social Responsibility PA, led a delegation to Gov. Shapiro’s office to deliver a letter from 80 health professionals. Letters from faith leaders, artists and other creatives, and parents and guardians are open for signatures at bit.ly/NoDataCentersPA, with letters from other groups being planned. Maya van Rossum, founder of Green Amendments For The Generations and the Delaware Riverkeeper, said residents “have a true and enforceable right to pure water, clean air, and healthy environments” under the state constitution. “We are offended when our governor, legislators, or local officials throw out our environmental rights — the rights specifically respected in our state constitution’s declaration of rights — as a throwaway talking point. Our environmental rights are clear and enforceable here in Pennsylvania. When our governor, legislators, or local officials try to ignore or evade them, we will stand up and defend them.” Other speakers listed by organizers included representatives of the Phoenixville Liberation Center, March on Harrisburg, the Delaware Riverkeeper Network, Make the Road PA, Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living, and the Intertwined faith community.

artigo.texto: This electric vehicle company has fallen sharply from its all-time high as competition, weak financial performance, and continued cash burn weighed on the stock. The company is now focusing on improving volumes, expanding its product portfolio and scaling battery manufacturing to support its turnaround. With a market capitalisation of Rs. 16,254 cr, the shares of Ola Electric Mobility Ltd closed at Rs. 35.12 per share, up from its previous close of Rs. 34.50 per share. The stock made a high of Rs. 158 per share in Aug 2024, trading at a discount of 78% from that level. The stock has gone through a major de-rating Ola Electric’s sharp correction from its all-time high reflects a significant reset in investor expectations. Investors initially valued the company on the assumption that it could rapidly scale its electric two-wheeler business and establish a strong leadership position in India’s EV market. However, weaker-than-expected volumes, persistent losses, cash burn, and rising competition have led to a substantial stock de-rating. Also Read: Empower India Shares Jump 30% in 5 Trading Sessions: Here’s What’s Driving the Rally The company’s financial performance has also remained under pressure. While Ola has started showing some sequential improvement in deliveries, the recovery has not yet translated into meaningful revenue growth or profitability. This has made investors increasingly focused on whether the company can build a sustainable business model rather than simply increase sales volumes. Deliveries have improved, but revenue remains under pressure Deliveries nearly doubled quarter-on-quarter to approximately 39,200 units, while orders rose to around 44,000 units. The improvement suggests that the company’s recent product launches, pricing initiatives and efforts to strengthen its distribution network are beginning to support volumes. However, revenue remained a major concern. Q1FY27 revenue declined 45% year-on-year to Rs. 455 crore, highlighting the impact of lower realisations and the company’s earlier weakness in volumes. At the same time, the net loss narrowed to Rs. 336 crore from Rs. 500 crore in Q4FY26. Although the sequential improvement is encouraging, the company still needs a sustained improvement in revenue, gross margins and operating profitability before the turnaround can be considered established. Competition has intensified sharply Ola’s biggest challenge is no longer simply expanding the electric two-wheeler market, but defending its position within it. Established manufacturers such as TVS Motor and Bajaj Auto, along with EV-focused players such as Ather Energy, have strengthened their presence in the segment. The competitive pressure has affected Ola’s market share and forced the company to rethink its sales strategy. It is expanding its product portfolio, increasing distribution and moving toward a larger network of dealer-operated outlets. The objective is to improve customer reach while reducing the cost and capital intensity associated with an entirely company-operated retail network. The key question for investors is whether Ola can sustain its recent improvement in deliveries while rebuilding its market position without relying excessively on discounts or sacrificing margins. New products could help Ola regain volumes Product launches remain central to Ola’s recovery strategy. The company has been expanding beyond its premium positioning and targeting a broader customer base with products such as the S1Z. A wider product portfolio could allow Ola to address different price segments and increase its addressable market. Technology is another important part of the strategy. Ola is increasingly focusing on its own battery technology and has been integrating its Bharat Cell LFP technology into its products. The company has also received BIS certification for its 46100 LFP cell, which is an important step toward commercialising its indigenous battery technology. If these products achieve better cost efficiency, reliability and scale, they could help Ola improve competitiveness while reducing dependence on externally sourced battery technology. Battery manufacturing could become a long-term differentiator Ola’s battery strategy is potentially one of the most important parts of its long-term business model. The company is expanding its Gigafactory and moving toward greater vertical integration, with the objective of manufacturing critical battery components in-house. The company has also secured the full five-year Advanced Chemistry Cell Production Linked Incentive window through CY2031, potentially making it eligible for incentives of up to Rs. 7,240 crore. This could significantly support the economics of its battery manufacturing operations if Ola can achieve the required production scale and manufacturing yields. However, battery manufacturing also brings execution risks. The company must demonstrate that it can achieve consistent yields, scale production efficiently, and commercialise its cells at competitive costs. Therefore, the Gigafactory could become either a major competitive advantage or an additional source of capital expenditure and cash burn, depending on execution. Fresh capital provides additional financial flexibility Ola has continued to raise capital to support its operations and growth plans. The company recently approved a Rs. 1,000 crore rights issue, following the Rs. 780 crore QIP completed in June. The proposed use of the rights proceeds provides some indication of management’s priorities. The company plans to use around Rs. 350 crore for debt repayment, while proposing approximately Rs. 400 crore for organic growth. Founder and CEO Bhavish Aggarwal also said he will subscribe to his entitlement. The fundraising provides Ola with additional liquidity at a time when the business is still loss-making. artigo.texto: For many Indian businesses, the climate journey begins with a simple exercise: measuring their carbon footprint. But as India’s carbon market takes shape, knowing your emissions is only the starting point. A more important question then emerges: What do these numbers mean for business and what should we do next? India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) is moving from framework development towards implementation. Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity (GEI) targets have been notified for energy-intensive sectors, and the compliance mechanism now covers 490 obligated entities across sectors1. For businesses, this means carbon is no longer just a number to measure and report at the end of the reporting cycle. It needs to be understood in the context of how the business operates and where there is scope to improve. Figure 1: Sector Covered Under CCTS CCTS: From Emissions to Performance Under the CCTS compliance mechanism, obligated entities are required to meet GEI targets. This means a company’s emissions are considered in relation to its output or production, rather than simply looking at how much it emits in total. Take a simple example. A company increases production, so its total emissions also go up. But if production grows faster than emissions, it is emitting less for every unit it produces. The opposite can happen too, emissions may come down, but if production falls even more, emissions per unit can increase. That is why total emissions alone do not tell the whole story. How Should Businesses prepare for CCTS? - Know Where You Stand The first step is to determine whether the company or its relevant facilities fall within the notified CCTS compliance mechanism. For covered entities, the management should know: - Notified target for its sector - The relevant baseline period - The applicable unit of production - Current emission intensity This should become a regular management metric rather than something reviewed only during reporting. - Build a Reliable Emissions Baseline A company cannot manage what it cannot reliably measure. Businesses should establish an emissions baseline covering relevant Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, while assessing material Scope 3 categories where relevant. For CCTS-covered entities, particular attention should be given to the data required for calculating and monitoring GEI performance. The data should be accurate, consistent, traceable and supported by appropriate records. - Identify What Drives Emission Intensity Once the baseline is established, the next question is: what is driving our emissions? Figure 2: Factors Influencing Emission Intensity Identifying these drivers helps companies move from simply reporting an emissions number to identifying where intervention is possible. - Identify Reduction Opportunities The objective should not be to reduce emissions simply because a target exists. Companies should understand which interventions can improve both carbon performance and business efficiency. Potential areas may include: Figure 3: Potential Areas for Emission Reduction The right combination will depend on the company's sector, technology, production process and economics. - Understand the CCTS Gap Companies should establish a clear view of their position: Figure 4: Understanding the CCTS GAP This can help management assess whether existing measures are sufficient or whether additional interventions may be required. For an obligated entity, the assessment also provides an indication of whether the company is likely to outperform its notified GEI target or face a shortfall. Entities that perform better than their notified GEI targets may be eligible to earn Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs). On the other hand, an entity that falls short of its target may need to purchase CCCs from the market and surrender them against its compliance obligation, in accordance with the applicable provisions of the scheme. - Strengthen MRV and Verification Readiness The CCTS framework includes a Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system, with annual verification of GHG emissions data and an ecosystem of Accredited Carbon Verification agencies. Companies should therefore ensure that: - Emission calculations are documented - Data sources are clearly identified - Methodologies and emission factors are consistently applied - Supporting records are maintained - Responsibilities for data are clearly assigned - Internal review and controls are established - Data can be traced back to source records The CCTS Readiness Checklist Before the compliance cycle becomes deadline-driven, management should be able to answer: Figure 5: CCTS Readiness Checklist From CCTS Compliance to Carbon Strategy This is where CCTS preparation needs to move beyond compliance and become part of the company’s broader carbon strategy. The biggest risk for businesses is to treat CCTS as a box-ticking exercise, limited to determining applicability, submitting data and meeting a notified target. Such an approach may address the immediate compliance requirement, but it does not help the business understand what is driving its emission intensity or how its performance can be improved. The real value of CCTS lies in using emission-intensity data to identify practical opportunities across operations, technology and investment planning. It can help companies assess energy efficiency, process performance, technology choices, capacity utilization and decarbonisation options in a more structured manner. Figure 6: CCTS Preparation Journey Starting early gives companies the time to understand the factors influencing their emission intensity, assess technically and economically viable reduction measures, and establish reliable data, monitoring and verification systems. artigo.texto: CATL expands Seres battery capacity: what it means for Contemporary Amperex Technology stock Published on 10/13/2026 at 09:01 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Key points in brief - CATL agreed with Seres on October 11, 2026, to expand dedicated battery capacity to more than 20 GWh annually. - The October 11 agreement adds 10 to 12 GWh of annual pack capacity at Seres' Chongqing plant. - Second-quarter 2026 revenue reached CNY 147.8 billion, while net income was CNY 22.5 billion. - The Shenzhen quote was CNY 288.71 on October 13, 2026, 1.24 percent above the 52-week low. Contemporary Amperex Technology stock was quoted at CNY 288.71 on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on October 13, 2026 at 2:45 p.m. CST, as CATL expanded its battery partnership with Seres. The October 11 agreement adds 10 to 12 gigawatt-hours of annual pack capacity and takes dedicated capacity at Seres' Chongqing plant above 20 gigawatt-hours, according to East Asia Brief on October 11, 2026. What 20 GWh means for CATL The Seres project places CATL battery assembly directly inside the vehicle plant. The expansion adds 10 to 12 GWh of annual pack capacity, while the agreement gives CATL a five-year supply framework running through August 2027, East Asia Brief reported. The operating model also locks CATL into Seres' Aito vehicle range, whose cumulative deliveries equipped with CATL batteries have exceeded 1.2 million units, according to the same October 11 report. For CATL, the value is production visibility rather than a disclosed order amount because the companies did not publish construction costs or a commissioning date. Recent results show scale CATL reported CNY 147.8 billion of revenue and CNY 22.5 billion of net income for the second quarter of 2026. Revenue rose 57 percent from CNY 94.2 billion in the second quarter of 2025, while net income increased 37 percent from CNY 16.5 billion, according to Simply Wall St. The comparison also shows the pressure behind the capacity push: second-quarter profit growth trailed revenue growth by 20 percentage points. Simply Wall St reported that the second-quarter profit margin was 15 percent, down from 18 percent a year earlier, while earnings per share exceeded analyst expectations by 2.1 percent. Three dated operating milestones On July 25, 2026, CATL reported second-quarter revenue of CNY 147.8 billion and net income of CNY 22.5 billion. On September 22, 2026, its Debrecen factory began trial production after the company had produced 537,000 battery modules at the site. On October 11, 2026, the Seres agreement lifted the Chongqing plant's planned dedicated capacity above 20 GWh, with each event covered by Simply Wall St and East Asia Brief. Next results come into view CATL's board is scheduled to meet on October 20, 2026, to consider third-quarter results for the nine months ended September 30, according to Futubull. The company is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 results on October 21, 2026, according to Simply Wall St. Stock stays near its yearly low The Shenzhen quote of CNY 288.71 on October 13, 2026 stood 1.24 percent above the 52-week low of CNY 285.17 and 38.33 percent below the 52-week high of CNY 468.75. CATL's market capitalization was CNY 1.3 trillion on that date, giving the Seres expansion a market setting defined by scale and a wide distance from the yearly high. The continuously updated company information is available through the Market report Shanghai Composite. artigo.texto: by Wedan Emmanuel Gnibga & Andrew A. Chien Datacenter (DC) power demand is rapidly growing to support AI workloads. With increasing pressure to reduce water consumption, DC cooling power can be up to 30% overall DC power, reducing IT power capacity. Cooling is especially power-demanding during hot periods, which often coincide with peak grid loads and insufficient renewable generation, increasing costs and carbon emissions. Exacerbating the problem is growing compute power density. Rack power densities have grown from under 20kW (2010) to more than 120kW (today), and could reach 1MW (2029). Conversely, cooling and power distribution are not scaling in density, so their space use grows in proportion. This limits DC scalability and lifetime. We explore the benefits of augmenting DC cooling with cold Underground Thermal Energy Systems (Cold UTES), a technology with no water consumption, well-suited to water-stressed regions. Cold UTES can store thermal energy in underground formations (e.g., natural reservoir or shallow rock) during off-peak times and release it to cool DCs during peak periods. Results show this can increase IT capacity by 9.8% across regions, and improve cooling power efficiency, reducing on-peak power use (e.g., 44.4% in Texas), operational carbon emissions (e.g., 10.4% in Arizona), and cooling costs (e.g., 3.4% in Arizona). Cold UTES can improve DC scalability, extending DC lifetime from one to three generations (2 to 6 years).

artigo.texto: A expansão de setores de alta tecnologia pode não produzir oportunidades de trabalho na mesma proporção dos investimentos anunciados na Tailândia. O alerta é de Tanit Sorat, vice-presidente da Confederação de Empregadores do Comércio e da Indústria da Tailândia. Segundo ele, data centers são altamente automatizados, empregam poucos especialistas em tecnologia da informação e, em muitos casos, recorrem a profissionais estrangeiros. Esses empreendimentos também demandam grandes volumes de eletricidade e água para refrigeração. No primeiro semestre de 2026, os pedidos de investimento cresceram 73% em um ano, para 1,47 trilhão de bahts, distribuídos por 1.299 projetos. O setor digital respondeu por 1,12 trilhão de bahts, impulsionado por inteligência artificial e data centers. Principais fatos e números - Pedidos de investimento somaram 1,47 trilhão de bahts no primeiro semestre de 2026. - O valor representou crescimento anual de 73%, segundo o Conselho de Investimento da Tailândia. - Foram registrados 1.299 projetos no período. - O setor digital respondeu por 1,12 trilhão de bahts. - Até 75% das peças, materiais e equipamentos para data centers precisam ser importados. - Data centers empregam poucos especialistas por serem altamente automatizados. Por que isso importa para empresários e investidores O volume de capital abre oportunidades para fornecedores de energia, refrigeração, infraestrutura digital e formação técnica. Entretanto, a elevada automação e a dependência de componentes importados limitam o efeito imediato sobre empregos e indústria local. Empresas também devem considerar a pressão de longo prazo sobre eletricidade e água, além da possível necessidade de contratar especialistas estrangeiros. Os dados disponíveis mostram forte intenção de investimento, mas não informam quanto será efetivamente executado, quantos postos serão criados nem em que prazo. Essa incerteza exige cautela ao projetar demanda, capacidade produtiva e retorno econômico.

artigo.texto: Intelligent Flow Measurement Has Become Essential for Next-Generation Data Center Cooling As AI workloads drive higher rack densities and greater thermal demands, data center liquid cooling is becoming an increasingly important part of modern facility design. But moving from traditional air cooling to liquid-based architectures also creates a greater need to understand exactly what is happening inside critical cooling loops. This Ask the Expert explains why flow measurement for data centers is becoming essential to cooling performance, efficiency, and uptime. It explores how chilled water flow monitoring, combined with temperature and other operational data, can provide greater visibility into cooling system performance and help operators make more informed decisions about energy and water use. The discussion also examines magnetic flow meters, which are ideally suited for many liquid cooling applications and can deliver accurate measurements without introducing pressure loss. It provides insight into installation considerations, commissioning challenges, piping constraints, and the importance of measurement accuracy and repeatability as facilities scale. For teams designing, building, or operating next-generation infrastructure, understanding the role of flow measurement is becoming an important part of optimizing the cooling systems that support high-density computing. Discover how flow data can support both building management systems and data center infrastructure management (DCIM) platforms, providing greater visibility across increasingly complex AI data center cooling environments.

artigo.texto: Data centers may soon require special-use permits to build in Lawrence after a vote by the Lawrence-Douglas County Planning Commission on Sept. 21. The commission voted 6-1 to recommend that the Lawrence City Commission require that developers receive a special-use permit before building data centers in industrial zoning districts within city limits. The Lawrence City Commission voted on July 14 to pass a two-year moratorium on data center development. Drew Bealby, a city planner, told planning commissioners that, in addition to restricting data center construction, the moratorium directed planning staff to research data centers and gave them time to write policies, such as special-use permit requirements, to regulate data centers once it’s over. City commissioners will review the research before considering a ban. Previously, the development code allowed data center development without review by the planning or city commissions. For a special-use permit, projects must be presented to both commissions. The approval process allows commissioners to set approval conditions and consider potential impacts on surrounding neighborhoods. It also requires public comment. “I think we have terrifically bright people [in Lawrence], if we will just listen to you,” Commissioner Charlie Thomas said in an interview with the Kansan. “And any time we cut the people out of the process, I think we have done a disservice to any regulations that we write, so this will give people many chances to have input, and that’s what we need.” This change would require a special-use permit for data center development in Lawrence’s industrial districts, in addition to the mixed corridor and commercial center districts, which already require a special-use permit for data centers. Bealby said this change will not affect the moratorium overall. Instead, commissioners may approve a moratorium exception for data center projects approved for a special-use permit on a case-by-case basis. Data centers that are powering artificial intelligence’s growth are an issue for American communities. These issues prompted 17 members of the public to voice their concerns to the commission. Most supported a complete ban, carrying signs that said “full ban now,” “we need water” and “listen to your people.” Many told the commission that the proposed changes aren’t restrictive enough. Some described how a data center would affect local water, electricity and agriculture; others spoke about AI's growing power and its potential use in military and surveillance operations. One public commenter, Jeremy Rothe-Kushel, co-host of the podcast “The Antedote,” compared AI and data centers to nuclear weapons and nuclear weapons sites. He said U.S. adversaries may soon treat AI as a weapon and, therefore, treat data centers as military targets. “I hope we don’t go there as a world,” Rothe-Kushel said. “But we do not yet have international law, let alone treaties, like we did in terms of nuclear weapons, yet.” Rothe-Kushel said in an interview with the Kansan that data centers aren’t always bad for a community, but Lawrence needs to study how to scale and site them properly and design them with minimal ecological impacts. Dominique Sexton, member of the Coalition for Collaborative Governance, said AI will negatively impact American society and already affects children’s lives. “I mean, we don’t even understand the consequences of AI with data centers,” Sexton said in an interview with the Kansan. “We see it tied to the military-industrial complex. We see it tied to ICE in the way that it’s dehumanizing our neighbors. And these are all consequences that these young kids are growing up [with] as their normal experience. And I just worry so much about that.” Commissioner Gary Rexroad voted against the special-permit measure, arguing that the restrictions would be too broad and only large data centers should be restricted. He said he worried the measure would create an undue burden on businesses’ small data centers that handle business functions. “I really feel like this application in front of us tonight is immature,” Rexroad said. Commissioner Jane Eldredge said the measure will “provide the opportunity to learn what we need to regulate, what we don’t need to regulate.” Bealby said businesses’ small data centers used for their own operations are considered a secondary use of the property. Therefore, they will likely be exempted from the moratorium. Thomas said he knows a data center when he sees it, and waiting longer to pass restrictions is risky. “The unintended consequences of not doing this tonight, of not approving this, I think places this community more at risk,” Thomas said. artigo.texto: Mercado global de carregadores de bateria industriais: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de carregadores de bateria industriais até 2035: implantação de BESS em escala de rede e eletrificação de veículos pesados impulsionam o crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Carregadores de Bateria Industriais, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de carregadores de bateria industriais é um habilitador essencial da transição energética, fornecendo a base de conversão de energia para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em escala de rede e para a eletrificação industrial pesada. Diferentemente dos carregadores de consumo, os carregadores industriais precisam gerenciar conversão CA/CC de alta potência, conformidade com códigos de rede e certificação de segurança, o que os torna componentes de alto valor incorporados a projetos de energia financiáveis. A demanda está se bifurcando: carregadores padronizados e otimizados em custo para BESS em contêineres, de um lado, e sistemas personalizados e ricos em recursos para suporte à rede e ambientes industriais severos, de outro. O cenário competitivo opõe gigantes diversificados da eletrônica de potência a fabricantes especializados com profunda engenharia de aplicação. As compras são dominadas por compradores sofisticados — integradores de BESS, empresas de EPC e concessionárias de energia —, que priorizam o custo total de propriedade e o serviço de longo prazo em vez do preço inicial. A resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos, especialmente para semicondutores de SiC/GaN e componentes magnéticos, continua sendo uma preocupação central. Estruturas regulatórias e códigos de rede são os principais indutores de produto, exigindo funcionalidades avançadas como suportabilidade a afundamentos de tensão e regulação de frequência. À medida que o mercado evolui até 2035, os carregadores se tornarão ativos inteligentes na borda da rede, com controles definidos por software que viabilizam a gestão ativa da rede. Este relatório oferece uma análise estruturada do tamanho de mercado, da segmentação, dos indutores de demanda, da dinâmica competitiva e das perspectivas regionais, com insights acionáveis para fabricantes, integradores, investidores e formuladores de políticas que navegam por esse cenário em rápida evolução. O cenário-base para o mercado de carregadores de bateria industriais até 2035 prevê expansão robusta, sustentada pela implantação acelerada de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em escala de rede e pela eletrificação do transporte pesado e de processos industriais. Com o avanço da participação de energias renováveis, a necessidade de infraestrutura de recarga flexível e compatível com a rede torna-se primordial, impulsionando a demanda por carregadores avançados capazes de fluxo bidirecional de energia, recursos de formação de rede e integração perfeita com sistemas de gestão de energia. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de 8,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 220 (2025=100). Esse crescimento não é apenas volumétrico; reflete uma mudança em direção a carregadores de maior valor, definidos por software, que atuam como ativos inteligentes na borda da rede. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico continuará sendo o maior mercado, impulsionada pelo domínio da China na fabricação e implantação de BESS, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão forte crescimento, apoiadas por incentivos de política pública e iniciativas de modernização da rede. América Latina e Oriente Médio e África surgirão como mercados de oportunidade, ainda que a partir de uma base menor. Os principais riscos incluem gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de semicondutores especializados, atrasos regulatórios e a possibilidade de mudanças tecnológicas que perturbem as arquiteturas de produto estabelecidas. Ainda assim, a trajetória de longo prazo permanece positiva, com os carregadores sendo cada vez mais vistos como componentes estratégicos da transição energética. Indutores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Indutores de Demanda - Expansão acelerada das implantações de BESS em escala de rede para integrar energias renováveis e aumentar a estabilidade da rede. - Eletrificação de veículos pesados (ônibus, caminhões, equipamentos portuários), que exige carregadores industriais de alta potência. - Códigos de rede rigorosos que exigem funcionalidades avançadas como suportabilidade a afundamentos de tensão, regulação de frequência e capacidade de formação de rede. - Crescimento dos investimentos industriais em resiliência, com energia de reserva e microrredes, especialmente em operações remotas ou críticas. - Queda dos custos da eletrônica de potência e das baterias, melhorando a economia dos projetos de infraestrutura de recarga industrial. - Incentivos governamentais e metas de descarbonização que promovem o armazenamento de energia e a mobilidade elétrica. Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de semicondutores especializados de alta potência (SiC/GaN) e componentes magnéticos, gerando volatilidade nos prazos de entrega. - Custos iniciais elevados e processos complexos de qualificação, sobretudo para conformidade com códigos de rede e certificação de segurança. - Falta de protocolos padronizados e de interoperabilidade entre diferentes arquiteturas de BESS e de carregadores, o que aumenta a complexidade de integração. - Escassez de mão de obra de engenharia com experti

artigo.texto: Por que baterias portáteis podem pegar fogo em aviões? Entenda os riscos após caso na Índia Incêndio em carregador externo levou avião da IndiGo a fazer pouso de emergência na Índia; baterias de lítio podem sofrer superaquecimento e provocar chamas intensas Por O Globo — Nova Deli Atualizado Um voo da companhia aérea indiana IndiGo precisou ser desviado para Hyderabad, na Índia, neste domingo (11), depois que uma bateria portátil pegou fogo dentro da cabine. O dispositivo estava guardado em uma bagagem no compartimento superior do avião, que seguia de Delhi para Chennai. A tripulação conseguiu controlar as chamas com extintores, e a aeronave pousou em segurança. Segundo a companhia, o voo 6E 6115 foi desviado após a detecção de fumaça proveniente do dispositivo eletrônico de um passageiro. Os passageiros desembarcaram em Hyderabad e seguiram viagem em outra aeronave. Veja o momento: O que faz uma bateria portátil pegar fogo? Os carregadores portáteis, conhecidos como power banks, utilizam baterias de íons de lítio, que armazenam grande quantidade de energia em pouco espaço. Quando danificadas, superaquecidas ou submetidas a falhas internas, essas baterias podem entrar em um processo chamado fuga térmica, no qual a temperatura aumenta rapidamente e desencadeia uma reação em cadeia. O fenômeno pode provocar chamas intensas, fumaça e liberação de gases tóxicos, dificultando o combate ao incêndio. Quais são as regras para transportar carregadores em aviões? As regras variam conforme o país e a companhia aérea. No Reino Unido, a Autoridade de Aviação Civil (CAA) estabeleceu, a partir de 27 de março de 2026, novas exigências para o transporte de baterias de lítio e carregadores portáteis. Pelas orientações do órgão, os dispositivos devem permanecer na bagagem de mão, protegidos individualmente quando não estiverem em uso. Também não devem ser recarregados a bordo nem utilizados para carregar outros aparelhos durante o voo. O limite estabelecido é de dois carregadores por passageiro. O caso na Índia ocorre após outro incidente semelhante no mês passado, quando um voo que partia da Holanda em direção ao Caribe precisou retornar após suspeita de incêndio envolvendo uma bateria portátil. Os episódios reforçam a importância de seguir as regras de segurança e verificar as restrições específicas da companhia aérea antes de embarcar.

artigo.texto: CARLOS MASTRANGELO APONTA DISPUTA POR EQUIPAMENTOS COM DATA CENTERS E ADOÇÃO DE NOVAS TECNOLOGIAS COMO DESAFIOS DO MERCADO DE FPSOs Considerado um dos pioneiros na disseminação mundial do uso de plataformas do tipo FPSO, Carlos Mastrangelo escreveu, em parceria com o também experiente executivo Jorge Mitidieri, o livro “FPSO: Legado Offshore”. A obra aborda desde as escolhas técnicas que moldaram o mercado de navios-plataformas até os atuais desafios operacionais e as tendências futuras. Em entrevista ao Petronotícias, Mastrangelo analisou os fatores que pressionam o mercado de unidades de produção offshore, como a disputa por equipamentos com setores como os de data centers e aviação, e as incertezas que afetam as decisões de investimento em projetos de petróleo e gás. O executivo também discutiu os impactos da adoção de novas tecnologias, como a inteligência artificial, e defendeu o planejamento de longo prazo e a atuação do governo para evitar sobrecargas na cadeia brasileira de fornecedores e ampliar a participação nacional nos projetos. Qual foi a proposta da obra e por que considera importante olhar para o passado ao pensar no futuro da indústria? O título FPSO: Legado Offshore pode dar a impressão de que se trata de um livro de história, voltado ao passado. No entanto, essa não é a proposta. A obra busca compreender o presente com base nos acontecimentos anteriores, de modo a projetar o futuro. A palavra “legado” está relacionada justamente ao que deixamos para as próximas gerações, oferecendo referências para que possam pensar no futuro. Para projetar o futuro, seja na vida pessoal ou nas empresas, é preciso conhecer o passado. As histórias se repetem e, infelizmente, os erros também. O livro aborda diversos aspectos dessa relação, incluindo a influência da inteligência artificial nos projetos. Por exemplo: existe um discurso politicamente alinhado de que a IA contribuirá para reduzir o número de pessoas a bordo e substituir atividades realizadas no mar. Essa redução de pessoal se concretizou em outras etapas da evolução tecnológica? No livro, fazemos um regaste histórico do que aconteceu na indústria ao longo dos anos. No início da década de 1990, surgiram as primeiras unidades com sistemas digitais no Brasil, enquanto essa transformação também começava a ocorrer em outras partes do mundo. Os computadores passaram a permitir a substituição dos sinais mecânicos de pressão por sinais elétricos, por exemplo. A expectativa inicial era simplificar os processos e aumentar a eficiência na leitura dos dados de campo. Imaginava-se que, no futuro, seria possível reduzir o número de pessoas a bordo. Ao longo do tempo, porém, embora o perfil do trabalhador embarcado tenha mudado, também houve uma tendência de aumento do efetivo a bordo, por diversos outros motivos. O livro aborda essa questão em detalhes. Inicialmente, o uso de IA pode demandar um acréscimo de demanda de atividades que hoje são executadas por pessoas que já trabalham a bordo das plataformas. Portanto, existe uma preocupação de que aconteça o mesmo que ocorreu no passado: estressar as unidades de produção por conta das novas demandas. Em síntese, a proposta da obra é relacionar o presente aos acontecimentos do passado, compreender as reações dos especialistas e abordar diferentes temas, sempre com uma perspectiva voltada também para o futuro. Falando do mercado de maneira geral, quais são hoje os principais desafios do setor que dificultam a chegada de um projeto à decisão final de investimento? A situação é desfavorável porque, de um lado, a cadeia de suprimentos enfrenta preços elevados em um mercado pressionado. Essa pressão decorre não apenas da demanda, mas também da concorrência com projetos de desenvolvimento mais simples. Um exemplo são os grandes data centers, que competem diretamente com os projetos de águas profundas. Esses empreendimentos utilizam as mesmas máquinas de geração de energia empregadas nos grandes FPSOs. Ao mesmo tempo, quem desenvolve um projeto de upstream precisa realizar estudos de viabilidade, avaliar os investimentos e estimar os prazos de retorno, considerando diferentes cenários de rentabilidade futura e a imprevisibilidade natural do negócio. Além das incertezas relacionadas ao reservatório, que são inerentes à atividade, existem as incertezas externas a ele, que também precisam ser consideradas na análise de viabilidade dos projetos. Além dos data centers, que outros setores disputam os mesmos equipamentos? A indústria da aviação também utiliza máquinas que concorrem com as demandadas pelo setor de petróleo e gás. Há ainda a disputa por chips, painéis elétricos e outros equipamentos. Trata-se de uma concorrência que envolve diversos segmentos. As grandes instalações de gás natural liquefeito (GNL), com pacotes de até US$ 20 bilhões, também fazem parte desse cenário de disputa por recursos e equipamentos. Nesse contexto, a cadeia de suprimentos precisa apresentar propostas firmes às operadoras, considerando os preços atuais e as condições de um mercado pressionado. Do outro lado, as operadoras precisam avaliar seus projetos com base nesses custos atuais, mas considerando receitas futuras cujo valor ainda é desconhecido. Falando agora sobre conteúdo local, como a cadeia brasileira de fornecedores pode ampliar sua participação e conquistar novos negócios no contexto atual? Tenho propriedade para falar sobre conteúdo local porque, entre 2005 e 2006, saí do Brasil para os Estados Unidos para desenvolver o projeto do primeiro FPSO naquele país. Na época, ainda não havia um roteiro regulatório ou técnico definido, e existiam diferentes caminhos possíveis. Uma das primeiras questões que tivemos de analisar foi a Jones Act, uma lei americana da década de 1920 que regulamenta a cabotagem entre portos dos Estados Unidos. artigo.texto: NEW DELHI: India and the European Commission on Monday discussed continuing technical engagement on recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms and auditing (MRV) systems. Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal met with Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union, European Commission, in New Delhi, the Power Ministry said in a release. Both sides expressed willingness to continue technical engagement on recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms; monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems; and capacity building. An MRV system is an accounting process that measures climate actions, quantifies GHG emissions, and confirms reductions. The two sides agreed to strengthen cooperation and continue dialogue on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies, and other areas of mutual interest. Discussions focused on India's carbon market development, the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and opportunities for enhanced technical cooperation. The secretary highlighted India's progress under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including notifying emission intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units and developing the domestic carbon market. He also highlighted India's progress in increasing the share of non-fossil sources in its electricity generation capacity, noting that non-fossil sources account for 308 GW of the country's total installed capacity of 558 GW. The EU side appreciated India's progress in developing its carbon market and shared updates on CBAM implementation. The global market for Advance Battery Technologies is entering a phase of accelerated commercial scaling, driven by the limitations of conventional lithium-ion in safety, duration, and material criticality. This report analyzes the market for next-generation electrochemical energy storage beyond standard lithium-ion, including solid-state, advanced lithium variants, flow batteries, metal-air, and sodium-ion chemistries. The market is bifurcating into distinct technology pathways: solid-state and advanced lithium for high-energy-density mobility; flow and metal-air for long-duration stationary storage; and sodium-ion for cost-sensitive, high-safety applications. Commercial viability is shifting from cell-level $/kWh to total cost of ownership and levelized cost of storage, incorporating cycle life, safety systems, and balance-of-plant requirements. Supply chain bottlenecks have moved from raw material extraction to novel material synthesis and specialized manufacturing equipment, creating higher barriers than conventional gigafactory scaling. System integration complexity and multi-year qualification timelines are critical constraints, favoring players with deep testing resources and strategic partnerships. Procurement is moving from component-centric to performance-centric models, especially in stationary storage, where utilities and IPPs seek guaranteed performance. Geographic specialization is crystallizing, with IP and R&D in advanced economies, pilot-scale demonstration in regulatory-supportive markets, and GWh-scale output in regions with industrial policy. The forecast horizon 2026-2035 points to robust growth, with demand driven by grid modernization, renewable integration, and electrification of transport. The baseline scenario for the Advance Battery Technologies Market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 18.5%, reaching a market index of 545 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is supported by accelerating deployment of grid-scale energy storage, where flow and metal-air batteries are gaining traction for long-duration applications, and by the commercialization of solid-state batteries in premium electric vehicles. Key risks include qualification delays, raw material price volatility, and competition from continued lithium-ion cost reductions. However, the fundamental drivers of safety, duration, and material diversity remain strong, positioning advanced battery technologies for sustained growth through 2035. The electric vehicle sector is the largest end-use for advanced battery technologies, driven by the need for higher energy density, faster charging, and improved safety. Currently, conventional lithium-ion dominates, but solid-state and advanced lithium variants are entering pilot production. Through 2035, as these technologies achieve commercial scale, they will enable longer range and shorter charging times, accelerating EV adoption. Demand-side indicators include EV sales volumes, battery pack energy density targets, and charging infrastructure build-out. The shift to solid-state will be gradual, starting with premium vehicles and expanding to mass-market models as costs decline. Key mechanisms include the replacement of liquid electrolytes with solid ones, enhancing safety and energy density, and the use of lithium-metal anodes. This transition will reduce reliance on graphite and cobalt, diversifying supply chains. Major automotive OEMs are investing heavily in solid-state battery development, often through partnerships with specialized firms. The sector's growth will be supported by government mandates phasing out internal combustion engines and consumer demand for better performance. Current trend: Rapid adoption of solid-state and advanced lithium batteries in premium and mid-range EVs. Major trends: Solid-state battery commercialization for premium EVs, Advanced lithium-ion with silicon anodes for increased energy density, Integration of battery management systems with fast-charging networks, Partnerships between automakers and battery developers, and Government incentives for EV adoption and local battery production. Representative participants: Tesla, Toyota, Volkswagen, QuantumScape, Solid Power, and SES AI. Through 2035, as renewable penetration increases, the need for long-duration storage will surge, supported by government auctions and utility procurement. artigo.texto: Um relatório global põe as baterias abaixo das turbinas a gás de pico no custo da energia. No Brasil, a corrida dos data centers por conexão já começou, e o primeiro leilão de baterias do país está marcado para 2 e 4 de dezembro. As baterias de quatro horas ficaram mais baratas que as turbinas a gás de ciclo aberto em todos os 43 mercados onde a Wood Mackenzie comparou as duas tecnologias. A conta é o custo nivelado da energia, o LCOE: o preço médio de cada megawatt-hora ao longo da vida da usina. O relatório saiu em outubro de 2026. “A mudança econômica é decisiva e está se ampliando”, disse Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, analista principal da Wood Mackenzie. Ele aponta dois motores. De um lado, faltam turbinas a gás e o combustível oscila. Do outro, a produção de baterias cresce. O que o estudo mede, e o que ele não mede A manchete que circulou fala em “data centers”, mas o relatório trata de custo de geração de pico, e não de um data center específico. A Wood Mackenzie compara uma bateria de quatro horas com uma turbina a gás de ciclo aberto. É o tipo de usina que as distribuidoras ligam só nas horas de maior consumo. - Energia renovável perde ritmo no Brasil com cortes de geração e incerteza para investidores - Áustria teve 43.300 tickets em 10 minutos para disputar R$ 215 milhões de subsídio solar que paga R$ 838 por kWp, enquanto no Brasil painel novo já paga 60% do Fio B - Usina solar de Indiana instalou 20 mil painéis por dia com 1.800 operários em 18 meses e está prestes a operar - Agricultor de Illinois tem 10 torres eólicas na fazenda e recebe cerca de R$ 600 mil por ano, mas no Nordeste os relatos vão de R$ 600 a R$ 2 mil por mês por torre A bateria não gera energia. Ela guarda a que veio do sol, do vento ou da rede e devolve na ponta. Por isso a conta fecha melhor onde a geração solar é barata para carregá-la. Segundo o mesmo relatório, a solar com seguidor é a fonte nova mais barata em 43 dos 48 mercados. O pano de fundo é a fila das turbinas. Conforme o TechCrunch, citado pelo site Mezha, quem monta os maiores data centers tem comprado as turbinas disponíveis. As turbinas a gás de ciclo aberto levam de dois a quatro anos para chegar. A fila das de ciclo combinado vai até o início dos anos 2030. Quanto custa a bateria hoje O custo global de referência de um projeto de bateria de quatro horas caiu 27% em 2025, para US$ 78 por MWh, de acordo com o levantamento de fevereiro da BloombergNEF, citado pelo TaiyangNews. A China puxa a média para baixo. O custo de lá é mais de 55% inferior ao do resto da Ásia-Pacífico, que fica em US$ 134 por MWh. Para a América Latina, a Wood Mackenzie projeta queda de 42% no custo das baterias em escala de rede até 2060. O Brasil não aparece, nos textos abertos sobre o relatório, entre os 43 mercados citados. O relatório completo não está público, então a Wood Mackenzie é lida aqui pelos resumos da imprensa especializada. O Brasil: data centers entram na fila da rede O lado brasileiro já tem número. Em 6 de outubro, o primeiro processo competitivo de acesso à transmissão, o PNAST, alocou os 228 MW que sobravam em quatro pontos de conexão de São Paulo. Os três vencedores são data centers: Pahlavan One, Pahlavan Three e Digital DC Brasil, informou o Canal Solar. Sete projetos disputaram, somando 451 MW. Sobraram 223 MW de pedidos sem espaço na rede. Nesta temporada, o ONS cadastrou 367 empreendimentos de geração e consumo, com mais de 20 GW em solicitações. Quem olha o consumo vê o motivo. O Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2036, divulgado em 8 de outubro pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia e pela EPE, estima que os data centers saltem de 3 TWh para 30 TWh em 2036, segundo a Agência Eixos. O consumo total do país vai de 702 TWh para 979 TWh no mesmo período. A conta própria: o consumo cresce 277 TWh (979 menos 702) e os data centers respondem por 27 TWh desse aumento (30 menos 3). Dá cerca de 9,7% de toda a expansão vinda de um único setor. E as baterias no Brasil? O mesmo plano estima que o sistema precise de 9,2 GW de armazenamento em dez anos: 7,2 GW em baterias e 2,0 GW em hidrelétricas reversíveis. Os primeiros leilões de baterias estão marcados para dezembro, com início de fornecimento em agosto de 2028. Há um limite de rede. Em coluna no Canal Solar, Roberto Valer lembra que o leilão recebeu 296 GW de baterias cadastradas, mas nem todas cabem. A nota técnica do ONS de 30 de setembro lista 373 barramentos candidatos. Só 315 têm margem de 30 MW, o mínimo para habilitar um projeto. Quem paga pelas baterias? A Aneel abriu consulta pública, aberta até 9 de novembro, sobre como dividir o custo do leilão de baterias. Pela proposta da área técnica, eólicas, solares e nucleares podem responder pela parcela máxima do encargo, enquanto térmicas e hidrelétricas pagariam percentuais menores. A micro e minigeração distribuída fica fora da base inicial, informou a Cenário Energia. A metodologia final só sai depois do leilão. Quanto desse encargo chegaria à conta de luz do consumidor ainda não foi calculado em nenhum documento aberto, e por isso não há número honesto para dar aqui. O que fica para o leitor Três pontos para acompanhar: a consulta da Aneel até 9 de novembro, o leilão de baterias de 2 e 4 de dezembro e a consulta pública do PDE 2036, aberta até 6 de novembro. A comparação mundial entre baterias e turbinas a gás de pico dá o cenário de custo. Quanto ela vale para o Brasil depende do leilão de baterias e do desenho do encargo.

artigo.texto: EnergyPathways plc (AIM: EPP), a UK-based energy transition firm, has completed a placing raising £1.75 million by issuing shares at 5.75 pence each to a sole institutional investor who requested exclusive participation. This fundraising, initially announced on 28 September 2026, will support the advancement of the company's MESH Long Duration Energy Storage project and provide additional working capital. Trading of EPP's existing ordinary shares was scheduled to resume at 7:30 a.m. on 13 October 2026 following the closure of the Capital Access Window linked to the placing. Key Points - EnergyPathways plc (AIM: EPP) focuses on the UK energy transition and the MESH Long Duration Energy Storage project - Raised £1.75 million through placing 30,434,782 new ordinary shares at 5.75p each with a single institutional subscriber - New shares expected to be admitted to AIM at 8:00 a.m. on 15 October 2026, bringing total voting rights to 282,134,998 - Investors should monitor developments on MESH asset acquisitions, institutional partnership talks, and the forthcoming Energy Independence Bill £1.75 Million Placing Finalized with Single Institutional Subscriber at 5.75p Per Share EnergyPathways confirms the successful closure of the fundraise announced on 28 September 2026, issuing 30,434,782 new ordinary shares at 5.75 pence each exclusively to one institutional investor. The new shares will rank equally with existing ordinary shares in all respects, including entitlement to dividends and distributions declared after issuance. Admission to AIM remains conditional and is anticipated at 8:00 a.m. on 15 October 2026. Post-admission, EPP’s total issued ordinary share capital will be 282,134,998 shares with no treasury shares held. Utilizing Proceeds to Acquire Assets and De-Risk MESH Project The £1.75 million raised will be allocated to accelerating the MESH project and funding working capital. EnergyPathways plans to acquire critical assets such as land, existing pipelines, and technical data to further de-risk the MESH project ahead of institutional and strategic partner investments, with active discussions ongoing. The UK Government has designated MESH as a project of "national significance," aiming to become the UK’s largest Long Duration Energy Storage project with a 300 MW, 55 GWh capacity, and storage duration exceeding 100 hours. MESH Project Aims for Hydrogen Production by 2029 and LDES Operations by 2031 The MESH initiative integrates compressed air energy storage with natural gas and hydrogen storage. Hydrogen production is targeted to commence between 2029 and 2030, with Long Duration Energy Storage operations expected from 2031 to 2032, contingent on government policy, approvals, and financing. The project could offer gas and hydrogen storage equivalent to six days of the UK’s national gas supply. Notably, wind power curtailment costs surpassed £1.5 billion last year and are projected to exceed £8 billion by 2030, underscoring the critical need for multi-day storage solutions beyond the capabilities of battery technologies. Trading Resumption and Regulatory Outlook on AIM The Capital Access Window that opened on 28 September 2026 has now closed. Trading in EnergyPathways’ existing ordinary shares was expected to recommence at 7:30 a.m. on 13 October 2026. Cairn Financial Advisers LLP serves as the company’s nominated adviser, with Fortified Securities and SP Angel Corporate Finance LLP acting as joint brokers. Investors should be aware that the MESH project timeline is subject to policy developments under the upcoming Energy Independence Bill, which represents a significant regulatory factor and project risk highlighted by the company.

Here's a map of single-copy locations. URBANA — There aren’t a lot of topics where one can expect unanimous agreement from the Champaign County Board, said board member John Farney. However, there may be at least one issue where the board’s 21 members can find consensus. “The county board is pretty unified in all things related to data centers right now — very cautious, very much in favor of having strong regulations, very much in favor of transparency,” Farney said. In that vein, two items related to this topic will be discussed at tonight’s committee-of-the-whole meeting: an ordinance prohibiting nondisclosure agreements and a resolution against property-tax incentives for hyperscale data-center developments. No final action will be taken during the meeting. “These are all commitments that we have made,” said board member Emily Rodriguez, who chairs the data-center activities task force. “We are not interested in anything that dodges taxes, for example. That’s something we all agree on on the data-center task force. We also all agree that nondisclosure agreements are bad governance and that folks should be embarrassed to sign them, and data centers should not ask that of local governments.” The proposed ordinance against NDAs states that such agreements have “become an issue with other units of government in local and national news.” If approved, the ordinance would prohibit county board members and county employees from entering into NDAs regarding county business — in any situation, not just instances where data-center developers are involved. As for the other piece of legislation, the proposed resolution would prohibit “the negotiation of tax-abatement agreements, payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements and other concessions for the development and construction of hyperscale data centers within Champaign County.” “No data-center applications have yet been submitted to the county for rural Champaign County, but rumors and public outcry have prompted the need for a formal position,” the resolution states. The two proposals come after the village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data center project in “a rural area west of Champaign” that falls within Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency. Farney, who wrote the resolution against tax incentives for hyperscale data centers, sent a draft to the board’s policy and finance committee chairs on Oct. 5. “And like a half-hour later, somebody texted me the article that says, ‘Hey, Mahomet’s saying they’re backing off,’” he said. “But I wanted to get that out there right away for the county to actually be able to do something immediately. We don’t have to go through the same processes that we do for the zoning ordinance change in order to put a policy in effect for tax breaks for developments. And so I wanted to have something on record.” When asked how payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements work, Farney said it’s his understanding that data-center developers sometimes offer to make payments to communities while also entering into agreements for long-term property-tax abatements or reductions. Farney said that such agreements end up “being a benefit to the developer and not to the taxing bodies within the area as far as collecting the full value of property taxes.” “Basically, what I’m saying is, if you want to build a data center here, then you’re going to have to do it by our ordinances, which are going to be very stringent when the data-center task force gets done with their work,” he told The News-Gazette. “You’re also going to have to play by the rules that are in place for every other taxpayer in the county, as far as the county’s portion of the tax bill goes. And so we’re not going to give any incentives for data centers. If they can make it, they’re gonna make it on their own.” It’s his hope that other governments and taxing bodies will enact similar policies and form a united front. Champaign County currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with “at least 10,000 square feet of processing area”; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county also created the data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. A previous statement from Leslie Farmer, Clean Cloud Energy’s director of environmental and permitting, indicated that the company may still be considering the project, just not in partnership with Mahomet. “Clean Cloud Energy has decided not to seek annexation into the village of Mahomet following discussions with village leadership,” she said. “We respect Champaign County’s ongoing review of data-center regulations and will evaluate our project’s development in accordance with the framework established by the county.” Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Communications between the village and Clean Cloud Energy included multiple drafts of a proposed redevelopment and annexation agreement. Both Farney and Rodriguez said that if a municipality annexes an unincorporated area, that land would no longer be subject to the county’s moratorium or zoning regulations on data centers. “I was very surprised to hear that Mahomet was in those discussions, knowing that the county was working on a data-center ordinance,” Farney said. “...
