artigo.texto: CATL's capital play is eerily similar to that of NVIDIA. Earning 240 million yuan per day, CATL still believes its battery business is not large enough. After investing 5 billion yuan in June this year to become the second-largest external investor of Deepseek, CATL was recently revealed to have once again led a new round of financing of nearly 100 billion yuan for DeepSeek. This is just the tip of the iceberg of CATL's cross-sector investments. Since 2026, CATL has poured in more than 100 billion yuan, covering AI large models, data centers, HVDC power supply and energy storage systems, and even extended its reach to nuclear fusion. Zeng Yuqun, founder of CATL, once stated his ambition bluntly: to build the "four pillars and eight beams" of the new energy era, and the battery is only one of the pillars; some capabilities cannot be cultivated internally quickly, so the gaps will be filled through mergers and acquisitions. This makes the "Ning King" increasingly similar to NVIDIA in the new energy era. In the AI industry, NVIDIA takes GPUs as the fulcrum, on the one hand investing in model, cloud computing and application companies to expand computing demand and technical cooperation; on the other hand, it closely binds key customers and embeds its computing platform into the entire AI industrial chain. CATL is also taking batteries as the fulcrum, extending its capabilities to computing power, electricity and energy infrastructure through investment and mergers and acquisitions. Transforming from a power battery supplier to the underlying platform of the new energy industry may be a historic opportunity for CATL. Striving for upstream and downstream layout There is a famous scene in the history of China's new energy vehicles: Zeng Qinghong, then chairman of GAC Group, publicly complained that "all car companies are working for CATL". Wu Kai, chief scientist of CATL, immediately complained in response that the company was only "struggling on the edge of profit", pointing the finger at the skyrocketing prices of upstream battery raw materials. Neither car companies nor battery manufacturers were willing to take the blame, and the problem finally fell on a piece of "stone". Key raw materials such as lithium carbonate are important variables affecting the cost of power batteries. However, the mining industry is a typical strong cyclical industry, with prices fluctuating sharply along with the supply and demand cycle. Back in 2022, lithium prices soared all the way, pushing the profit contradictions of the entire industrial chain to the forefront. Perhaps having suffered enough from the pain of "no mines in hand", CATL has accelerated its expansion to the upstream. Through self-construction, equity participation, joint ventures and acquisitions, it has invested in lithium mica projects in Yichun, Jiangxi, spodumene projects in Sichuan, copper and cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, nickel mines in Indonesia and lithium mine projects in Africa, trying to grasp the resources that affect battery costs in its own hands as much as possible. After 2023, as lithium prices went down, CATL's mining investment also shrank to some extent. In April this year, the company announced its plan to establish Times Resource Group with a registered capital of 30 billion yuan to integrate its mining assets under its banner. On the other hand, by taking shares in Jiangxi Shenghua, a subsidiary of lithium iron phosphate supplier Fulin Jinggong, Hunan Yuneng, a phosphate cathode material supplier, and investing in Xinmai Semiconductor, a power management chip supplier, CATL is also strengthening its ties with the supply chain. In the upstream, CATL and NVIDIA do not use the same set of strategies — in the face of manufacturing oligarchs such as TSMC and SK Hynix, NVIDIA mostly uses orders, advance payments and joint development to lock in production capacity; while CATL, facing the more scattered mining and material links with greater cyclical fluctuations, relies more on equity plus long-term agreements. However, when optical communication becomes the new bottleneck of AI clusters, NVIDIA has also begun to invest in Coherent and Lumentum. This means that although their "toolkits" may not be the same, the two chain leaders are highly consistent at their core: The real hegemony of the industrial chain is not only to master the links that others cannot bypass, but also to ensure that you do not have to rely on others that you cannot bypass. If investing in the upstream is to solve the problem of neck sticking and ensure that batteries can be manufactured stably, then making moves in the downstream is to solve the market demand. Power battery is a capital-intensive and not fully standardized business. From production line construction, equipment procurement to commissioning and ramp-up, huge amounts of funds need to be invested in advance; different car models have different requirements for cell specifications, battery pack structure, fast charging and thermal management. If a production line is misaligned, the cost will be huge. To this end, CATL has successively invested in car companies such as AVATR, BAIC New Energy, Zeekr, IM Motors, Neta and Chery. In 2021, it directly contributed 770 million yuan to become the second largest shareholder of AVATR; in addition to equity investment, it also established joint venture battery companies with SAIC, GAC, Geely, Changan, Dongfeng (note: later withdrew) and other car companies, and explored the "factory in factory" cooperation model with Seres. These capital relationships allow CATL to enter the vehicle R&D, procurement and production systems earlier, increase the probability of its batteries being selected, and also raise the cost for car companies to replace suppliers. artigo.texto: Unwilling to pay the "CATL tax" any longer, Li Auto, Xiaomi and Leapmotor start to develop and produce batteries on their own. On October 9, Li Xiang, founder and CEO of Li Auto, warmed up for the 2026 Li Auto i6 on Weibo. Among the six major upgrades, the most notable one is the self-developed ultra-fast charging large battery with 96 kWh capacity and a CLTC range of 780 km. The battery replacement adjustment targets Li Auto's best-selling model. Li Auto delivered more than 120,000 units of the i6 in the first half of this year, contributing over 50% of its total sales. The latest announcement from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology shows that the manufacturers of the two battery assemblies for the 2026 Li Auto i6 are both Shandong Li Auto Battery Co., Ltd., with cell suppliers being Sunwoda and CALB. For the 2025 i6, the battery suppliers were CATL and Sunwoda. This shift means CATL has withdrawn from Li Auto's main selling model. Li Auto is far from the only new energy vehicle enterprise that has replaced CATL's batteries, chosen to cooperate with other manufacturers or develop batteries independently. On September 4, Xiaomi released its Longjia Battery, announcing strategic cooperation with CALB and Sunwoda Power, which will be equipped on all models of the Pengcheng series. On September 16, Leapmotor announced at its Huzhou Technology Day that it has achieved 100% independent R&D of battery cells. Shortly after, He Xiaopeng, Chairman of Xpeng Motors, stated at the G9L launch event: "Starting from this year, Xpeng will develop and produce all its batteries on its own." Jointly defining batteries with second-tier battery manufacturers, independently developing and producing battery cells, or only manufacturing battery packs. Despite different paths, leading new car-making forces have collectively written "independent R&D" into their strategies. In the past, except for BYD which operates a fully self-contained system, almost all automakers' battery budgets flowed to CATL. The phrase "equipped with CATL batteries" used to be a major selling point at press conferences. Today, however, "de-CATL" has become the most consistent collective action taken by automakers this year. Automakers and CATL: The Competition for Consumers Has Arrived In mid-September, the official website and App of Li Auto i6 stopped accepting online orders. An offline store salesperson revealed to Tech Planet that the available units that can still be delivered are basically the versions equipped with Sunwoda batteries. During the National Day holiday, a salesperson of Li Auto i6 said that the CATL battery version is basically unavailable for purchase. However, he also told Tech Planet that the most frequently asked question from customers entering the store during the National Day period is "Is the new version's battery still made by CATL?" Automakers have chosen to develop batteries independently or replace suppliers, but consumers' perception has not changed for the time being. In the past few years, the advertising slogan "When buying an EV, choose CATL" has appeared more and more frequently on TV, stadiums, elevators and mobile phone screens. This repeated anchoring of consumer psychology has turned a component brand hidden under the car chassis into the "default option" for Chinese consumers when purchasing electric vehicles. On September 17, Nielsen IQ released the *2026 Global New Energy Vehicle Consumer Research Report*, pointing out that power batteries have become a key decision-making factor for consumers when selecting and purchasing vehicles. The most obvious reflection of consumers' trust in CATL is a conclusion that 40% of Chinese respondents said they will not choose a vehicle that is not equipped with CATL batteries. Specifically, 37.1% of Chinese consumers stated directly that they will give up buying their favorite model if it does not use CATL batteries. The votes cast by consumers are finally reflected in CATL's financial statements. Data from SNE Research shows that in the first seven months of this year, CATL's global power battery usage increased by 26.6% year-on-year, and its share rose from 38% in the same period of the previous year to 39.9%. In the first half of 2026, its net profit reached 43.284 billion yuan, which is more than the total net profit of 15 mainstream listed domestic vehicle enterprises combined. When it comes to specific car purchase decisions, this perception is influencing consumers' choices. Many consumers started to look at other brands after learning that Li Auto i6 had a facelift; a consumer who planned to replace his existing vehicle said that the safety of a battery requires long-term verification by the owner, and he "does not want to be a guinea pig". However, some consumers said that replacing CATL's batteries is not unacceptable, and the key factor is the price. "If Li Auto offers a sincere price, we may consider it." Consumers' obsession does not come out of nowhere. CATL's total installed capacity in 2025 was 464.7 GWh, with a global market share of about 39%. It has profound accumulation in technology, production capacity and brand, and is the preferred supplier for most high-end models. As for CALB, the new battery supplier for Li Auto i6, although it is the fastest-growing dark horse in recent years, its global installed capacity in 2025 was about 44.4 GWh, with a market share of about 5.3%, which is far behind CATL. artigo.texto: Blockchain to underpin credibility; Korea Exchange to handle early trading Credits split by host-country approval status; developing nations to join governance 3 trillion won overseas construction fund to support project wins abroad South Korea will formally launch the Global Verified Carbon Market, or GVCM, next year — a marketplace where greenhouse gas reduction credits generated overseas can be issued and traded. Key information will be recorded on a blockchain to boost reliability, and the government is also reviewing the possibility of issuing credits as digital assets in the future. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il unveiled the detailed GVCM implementation plan Monday at a meeting of ministers on external economic affairs held at Government Complex Seoul. The GVCM is a market framework designed to enhance the credibility of overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects and promote international trading of the resulting credits. The government is renaming the initiative from "Global Voluntary Carbon Market" to "Global Verified Carbon Market," reflecting a broader scope that goes beyond voluntary corporate emissions cuts to also support countries in meeting their nationally determined contributions, or NDCs, and complying with emissions regulations. The centerpiece of the plan is a system for managing the issuance and trading of carbon credits in a way that ensures their integrity. Key data — including the project operator, host country and region, unique identification number, reduction methodology and volume — will be recorded on a blockchain. Full records will be stored in a conventional database, while only core information is written to the blockchain, balancing management efficiency with data reliability. Initially, credits will be issued through standard electronic means and traded on a Korean voluntary carbon market exchange that Korea Exchange is building. The government plans to draw on its experience operating the emissions trading system to establish a solid trading foundation and build market participants' confidence. Down the line, the government will consider issuing credits in parallel as digital assets, taking into account the scale of credit issuance and trading, the legislative progress of a basic digital assets act and overall market confidence. Officials noted that the existing exchange framework imposes constraints on round-the-clock trading and participation by individuals and foreign investors due to operating hours, eligible participant rules and foreign exchange regulations. However, the government said it would also take into account the varying levels of digital asset legislation and regulatory readiness among participating countries. Credits will be classified as either "GVCM A" or "GVCM NA" depending on whether the host country has approved the international transfer of the reduction outcome. Approved credits are intended for use in meeting the investing country's NDC targets, complying with regulatory frameworks such as the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, known as CORSIA, and supporting ESG activities. Non-approved credits will be directed toward ESG activities that contribute to the host country's own emissions reduction goals. Credits can later be upgraded to approved status if the host country grants a corresponding adjustment. The government is also reviewing whether GVCM credits could be used within South Korea's emissions trading system and greenhouse gas target management scheme. Doing so would require meeting conditions beyond credit reliability, including corresponding adjustments under the Paris Agreement and eligibility criteria for domestic project operators. Consultations with relevant agencies on CORSIA compatibility will also continue. The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee and a secretariat. The board, in which member countries participate, will set policy direction; the technical oversight committee will decide whether to issue credits; and the secretariat will handle issuance and management. Developing countries, where most reduction projects take place, will be able to join the board and nominate technical committee members, ensuring their views are reflected in operations. The government will work with related ministries and the Global Green Growth Institute to secure participating countries and identify reduction projects that pair developing-country development needs with South Korean technology. Examples cited include nature-based projects such as mangrove forests, agricultural waste management, methane capture and energy efficiency improvements. The government will also discuss converting reduction outcomes from World Bank and Green Climate Fund projects into GVCM credits. It plans to pursue the signing of letters of intent at this year's 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, with participating countries and the issuing body to be established next year as the project structure is finalized. The meeting also discussed external economic risk assessment and response measures, a review of economic deliverables from recent summits, and plans to develop a dedicated industrial complex in India for South Korean companies. Lee said South Korea's economy has maintained solid export momentum despite a challenging external environment, providing a foundation for growth. "The current account surplus reached $46.11 billion in August, extending a streak of 40 consecutive months of surplus and demonstrating overall stability," he said. He added that the government would respond to external uncertainties as a unified economic team and turn the challenges into new growth opportunities. "We will prepare without fail so that the tasks discussed today translate into tangible results on the ground," he said. artigo.texto: Key credit data to be recorded on blockchain; Korea Exchange to handle early trading Credits classified by host-country transfer approval; developing nations to join governance The South Korean government plans to formally launch the Global Verified Carbon Market, or GVCM, next year. Key information on carbon credits — which represent greenhouse gas reduction outcomes — will be recorded on a blockchain, and the government is also reviewing the possibility of issuing the credits as digital assets. Credits will be classified based on whether the host country of an overseas reduction project has granted transfer approval, broadening their use from voluntary corporate carbon-reduction activities to regulatory compliance. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il unveiled the detailed GVCM implementation plan at the 274th Council of Ministers on External Economic Affairs at the Government Complex Seoul on Monday. The government aims to secure participating countries this year and move into full operation next year, including establishing a credit issuance body and advancing individual projects. The GVCM is a framework designed to boost the credibility of international carbon markets and invigorate the trading of verified emission reductions. To reflect its intent to cover both voluntary and compliance markets, the government is renaming the initiative from "Global Voluntary Carbon Market" to "Global Verified Carbon Market." Central to the plan is how carbon credits are recorded and issued. Key data — including the project operator, the country and region where the project is located, a unique identification number, the emission reduction methodology, and the volume of reductions — will be stored on a blockchain. Full records will be kept in a conventional database, with the blockchain serving to verify the integrity of core information. In the early stage, credits will be issued through conventional electronic means and traded on a Korean voluntary carbon market exchange to be built by Korea Exchange. The plan draws on Korea Exchange's experience operating an emissions trading platform to build trust among market participants. The government will later consider issuing credits in parallel as digital assets, taking into account credit issuance and trading volumes, the legislative progress of a basic digital assets law, and market confidence in digital assets. Under the existing exchange framework, round-the-clock trading and participation by individuals and foreign investors are constrained by operating hours, eligible participant rules, and foreign exchange regulations. However, the government said it will take into account each participating country's position, given that digital asset legislation varies across nations. Credits will be divided into two categories: "GVCM A," which has received transfer approval from the host country, and "GVCM NA," which has not. Approved credits are intended for use in regulatory compliance — such as meeting a country's nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement or satisfying requirements under CORSIA, the international aviation carbon offsetting and reduction scheme — as well as for ESG activities. Non-approved credits will be directed toward ESG activities that contribute to the host country's own emission reduction goals. Credits in the non-approved category can be converted to approved status if the host country subsequently grants corresponding adjustment approval. The government is also reviewing whether GVCM credits could be used under South Korea's domestic emissions trading scheme and greenhouse gas target management system. Doing so would require meeting conditions related to credit credibility, corresponding adjustments under the Paris Agreement, and eligibility criteria for domestic project operators. Consultations with relevant agencies will also be pursued to enable use under CORSIA. The issuance body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee and a secretariat. The board, in which member countries participate, will set policy direction; the technical oversight committee will decide whether to issue credits; and the secretariat will handle issuance and management. Developing countries, where most emission reduction projects take place, will be able to join the board and recommend expert committee members, ensuring their views are reflected in operations. The government will work with related ministries and the Global Green Growth Institute to secure participating countries and identify reduction projects that combine developing-country development needs with South Korean technology. Examples cited include nature-based projects such as mangrove forest restoration, agricultural waste management, methane capture and energy efficiency improvements. The government will also discuss converting emission reductions generated through World Bank and Green Climate Fund projects into GVCM credits. It plans to pursue the signing of letters of intent at this year's 31st UN Climate Change Conference of the Parties, and to finalize participating countries, establish the issuance body, and flesh out the project structure next year. fact0514@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: ■ Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) announced on the 12th that a team led by Professor Song Hyun-gon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at UNIST and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at KAIST has developed an electrolyte that can extend the lifespan of lithium metal batteries. In theory, lithium metal batteries can almost double the capacity of the battery itself, but there is a problem in that lithium metal reacts unnecessarily with the electrolyte, causing the usable capacity to plummet. The research team mixed two solvents that had been considered unsuitable for lithium metal batteries, ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL), in a 3:7 ratio and added a small amount of additives that stabilize the lithium salt and the electrode protection layer, thereby creating a high-performance electrolyte. A high-nickel cathode battery using the developed electrolyte was charged up to 4.5 V at 25℃ and, even after 150 charge–discharge cycles, maintained about 80% of its initial capacity. Batteries using conventional carbonate-based electrolytes fell below 80% of their initial capacity after only about 50 cycles. Gas generation caused by electrolyte decomposition and the dissolution of nickel from the cathode were also reduced. With an initial coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average coulombic efficiency of 99.35%, the study confirmed that the combination of the two solvents is effective in reducing lithium loss during the charge–discharge process. ■ POSTECH announced on the 12th that the "Center for Communication and Public Discourse" has been selected for the education-linked program of the "2026 Humanities and Social Sciences Research Institute Support Project" organized by the National Research Foundation of Korea, and will receive more than KRW 1.9 billion in research funding, including indirect costs, over six years. The selected project is titled "Future Narrative Literacy Education Model: Development and Dissemination of an AI–XR–Game Linked Multidisciplinary Curriculum for Science and Technology-focused Universities." The principal investigator is Professor Kim Jin-hee of the Division of Humanities and Social Sciences, and researchers from six fields—literature, cognitive science, science and technology studies, communication studies, economics, and arts—will participate. The research team defines future narrative literacy as consisting of three domains: "narrative and cognition," "science and technology," and "social institutions," and plans to develop a multidisciplinary curriculum that links these areas. POSTECH is the first science and technology-focused university to develop a future narrative literacy education model. The team intends to apply the developed education model to both formal and informal education within POSTECH and then spread it to local communities and other universities, thereby expanding the foundation for communication and education on science, technology, and future society. ■ KAIST announced on the 12th that it will hold the "2026 KAIST Tech Fair" on the 13th in conjunction with "KES 2026 (Korea Electronics Show)" at COEX in Seoul. At this event, six promising commercialization technologies and products and services from four faculty startup companies will be presented, and consultations will be held for technology transfer and joint research. From the 13th to the 16th, the "KAIST Special Pavilion" will be operated in Hall A at COEX. Corporate representatives and visitors can explore promising commercialization technologies and products and services from faculty startup companies in the Special Pavilion and receive information on KAIST's technology commercialization support programs. On the first day of the event, from 1:30 p.m. on the 13th, a technology transfer briefing session will be held at the KES Stage in Hall B at COEX. KAIST researchers will directly introduce six promising technologies and explain applicable industrial fields and commercialization potential. Each presentation will consist of 15 minutes of technology introduction and 5 minutes of Q&A. A one-on-one technology transfer consultation session will also be operated at the KES Lounge in Hall B at COEX. KAIST will connect pre-registered companies with its researchers to support discussions on technology adoption, joint research, follow-up technology development, and commercialization strategies. Four faculty startup companies, including Daim Technology and Airtours, will participate in the KAIST Special Pavilion to showcase their key products and technologies and conduct on-site consultations with companies, investors, and industry representatives. In addition to the faculty startup zone, the Special Pavilion will feature a space introducing promising commercialization technologies, a promotion area for the Institute for the Value Creation of Technology, and a "Brand KAIST" zone. Companies wishing to participate in the technology transfer briefing session or consultations can pre-register via the KAIST TLO website, and inquiries related to the event and participation can be directed to the KAIST Institute for the Value Creation of Technology. * KAIST TLO website link: https://tlo.kaist.ac.kr/ * Institute for the Value Creation of Technology contact: T. 042-350-2978 E-mail: iptc@kaist.ac.kr

artigo.texto: South Korea to Fully Launch GVCM International Carbon Market Next Year, Review Digital-Asset Credit Issuance Summary - The government said it will begin full operations of the international carbon market GVCM next year and issue credits divided into 'GVCM A' and 'GVCM NA'. - The government said it plans to record key information, including project operators and emissions reductions, on the blockchain and build a trading market using the Korea Exchange (KRX). - The government said it will also discuss issuing carbon credits in digital-asset form in the future and converting project results from the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) into GVCM credits. Forecast Trend Report by Period South Korea plans to fully launch its international carbon market next year and is also reviewing a plan to issue carbon credits in digital-asset form. The government discussed detailed measures for the Global Voluntary Carbon Mechanism, or GVCM, at a ministerial meeting on external economic affairs on Oct. 12, Seoul Economic Daily reported. GVCM is a market for trading greenhouse-gas reduction credits. Credits will be issued as either "GVCM A" or "GVCM NA," depending on whether the host country approves the project. Approved credits can be used to meet national greenhouse-gas reduction targets, or NDCs, and to comply with international aviation rules. Unapproved credits would be used for companies' voluntary environmental activities. To bolster trust in trading, the government plans to record key information such as project operators and emissions reductions on a blockchain. It also plans to build a trading market using the Korea Exchange, or KRX, and is reviewing the future issuance of carbon credits in digital-asset form. The government plans to secure countries interested in participating this year and set up an issuing body next year to flesh out the project. It will also discuss converting emissions-reduction results generated by World Bank and Green Climate Fund projects into GVCM credits. artigo.texto: Appeal for major energy storage system rejected - Published Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed. Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year. The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire. In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location". A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, external. Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway. The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this. The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it. These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations. Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked. Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater." Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment". Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy. The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand. "They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated. artigo.texto: Report Overview In 2025, the Global AI Data Center GPU Market was valued at USD 7.4 billion. The market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 18.5% during 2026–2035, reaching approximately USD 40.4 billion by 2035. North America dominated the global market in 2025, accounting for more than 37.7% of the total market share and generating approximately USD 2.8 billion in revenue. The data center build-out for AI drives this growth. The IEA reported that global data center power use will roughly double from 415 TWh in 2024 to about 945 TWh by 2030. That equals just under 3% of all power used in the world. The IEA also expects power use in accelerated servers, which run mostly on GPUs, to grow 30% each year. Power use in regular servers will grow only 9% each year. Accelerated servers will cover almost half of the net rise in data center power demand. Each new AI facility needs dense GPU clusters, so higher power demand points straight to higher GPU spending. A regular data center draws 10 to 25 MW. A large AI facility can draw more than 100 MW. North America region hosts the biggest cloud and AI model builders. The IEA found that the United States and China together will make up nearly 80% of global data center power growth to 2030. Berkeley Lab, part of the US Department of Energy, projects that AI data centers will drive more than 40% of US power demand growth through 2030. Key Takeaways - The Global AI Data Center GPU Market reached USD 7.4 billion in 2025 and will reach USD 40.4 billion by 2035. grow at a CAGR of 18.5% from 2026 to 2035. - Graphics Processing Units lead the Product Type segment with a 24.3% share. - Inference leads the Function segment with a 71.2% share. - Cloud leads the Deployment Mode segment with a 62.3% share and is also the fastest-growing sub-segment. - Information Technology and Telecom leads the End User Industry segment with a 33.9% share. - North America leads with a 37.7% share and USD 2.8 billion in revenue. By Product Type Graphics Processing Units dominate with 24.3% due to mature software support across AI workloads. Accelerator Cards are growing fastest as buyers want more speed for each watt and each rack. NVIDIA posted record quarterly Data Center revenue of $62.3 billion in the fourth quarter, up 75% from a year earlier. Cloud firms and large companies add plug-in cards to their current servers to raise output without building new halls. Fast links between chips also push this shift. NVIDIA’s Data Center networking revenue jumped 142% as NVLink connections spread across GB200 and GB300 systems. These links let many cards work as one large engine. Server makers now design around dense card setups, which keeps demand for accelerator cards rising quickly. By Function Inference dominates with 71.2% due to daily use of live AI apps. Inference holds the largest share because every chatbot reply, search answer, and code suggestion runs on inference chips. Microsoft says its AI business passed $37 billion in annual revenue run rate, up 123%. Each new user adds steady, round-the-clock compute load. Training is growing faster as model builders race to release larger and smarter models. The IEA projects that electricity use in accelerated servers will grow 30% per year, against only 9% for regular servers. Training runs drive much of that power demand because they keep thousands of chips busy for weeks at a time. By Deployment Mode Cloud dominates with 62.3% due to hyperscaler spending on rented GPU capacity. Cloud leads because most firms prefer to rent GPU power rather than buy costly hardware. Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 capital spending reached about $115.95 billion, up 79.6%. In one quarter, roughly two-thirds of its $31.9 billion capex went to short-lived assets, mainly GPUs and CPUs. Cloud is also the fastest-growing mode, because buyers can scale up in hours instead of waiting months for chips. Microsoft Cloud revenue hit $54.5 billion in one quarter, up 29%. Pay-as-you-go pricing lets startups and mid-sized firms test AI without high upfront costs. The spending plans stay large. Microsoft expects to invest roughly $190 billion in calendar 2026, including about $25 billion linked to higher component prices. On-premises setups still serve banks and defence users with strict data rules. Even so, cloud keeps winning new workloads because of its speed and flexibility. By End User Industry Information Technology and Telecom dominates with 33.9% due to large data centre and network ownership. IT and telecom firms lead because they own and run most of the world’s data centres. The IEA puts data centre power use at about 415 terawatt hours in 2024, roughly 1.5% of global electricity. That demand has grown 12% a year over the past five years, mostly driven by tech and telecom operators. Healthcare and life sciences are growing fastest as hospitals and drug makers put AI into daily work. The US FDA list covers 1,357 AI-enabled medical devices cleared or approved through December 2025. Imaging, drug discovery, and genomics all need heavy GPU compute to train and run their models. Large funding moves add to this demand. NVIDIA announced commitments worth $1 billion to build US capacity for research in fields including healthcare. As more medical tools reach approval, hospitals and research groups will keep buying GPU capacity. artigo.texto: Chinese battery makers are losing some of their biggest competitive advantages in the US as rising freight costs and import tariffs erode their price edge. Energy storage system (ESS) battery prices in North America were 20% higher than factory prices in China in September and also exceeded prices in Europe. With US import duties of up to 40.9% adding to the cost, Chinese cells are becoming less attractive to American buyers. South Korean battery makers with local production facilities are positioned to gain market share. According to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence's Q3 2026 Battery Cell Price Review, released on October 9, the CIF North America price of Chinese 314-ampere-hour (Ah) lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells reached $61.99 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September. That was $10.37, or 20.1%, above the ex-works (EXW) China price of $51.62 per kWh. The CIF Europe price for the same cells was $59.18 per kWh, $2.81 below the North American price. CIF prices include the cost of the goods, insurance and freight to the destination, but exclude US import tariffs. The price relationship between North America and Europe reversed in September. In July, the North American price was $64.99 per kWh, below Europe's $67.11. Prices declined in both regions in August, but diverged the following month. North American prices rose 3.3% month on month in September, while European prices fell 4.8%. Rising freight costs were a key factor in the reversal. Higher shipping costs on routes from China to the US have weakened the price advantage of Chinese cells by the time they reach North American customers. US import duties pose an additional challenge. Applying a tariff rate of up to 40.9% to the North American arrival price of $61.99 per kWh would raise the cost to approximately $87 per kWh. That is nearly 70% above the $51.62 per kWh factory price in China. Even if Chinese manufacturers cut their cell prices, US buyers could still face higher procurement costs. For a 1-gigawatt-hour (GWh) ESS project, every $10-per-kWh increase in battery prices adds $10 million to procurement costs. This shift could benefit South Korean battery makers with manufacturing facilities in North America. LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On are converting or using local production capacity to manufacture LFP batteries for ESS applications as electric vehicle (EV) demand weakens. LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI are expanding their US ESS LFP battery production capacity, with annual capacity expected to exceed 50 GWh by the end of 2026 and in the second half of 2028, respectively. They are also supplying complete, containerized ESS solutions developed in-house to renewable energy engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies and ESS system integrators (SIs). Their customer base is expanding to include global hyperscalers operating artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Chinese battery makers' price competitiveness in the US could weaken further. China ended export tax rebates for battery products and introduced a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries effective September 1, narrowing manufacturers' room to cut prices. These changes could also put pressure on Chinese suppliers' competitiveness in Europe. Major Chinese battery makers have already begun raising prices. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. (CATL), EVE Energy and REPT BATTERO raised prices for EV and ESS batteries starting in July. ESS system integrators also increased product prices by 5% to 30%. In September, CATL raised prices for its 280Ah ESS cells by 1.1% and its 314Ah cells by 2.0%.

VOLTRICELL opens in a new tab is a brand-new suite of materials designed to optimize battery manufacturing processes and improve the performance of today’s battery and emerging sodium-ion, silicon-anode and solid-state battery technologies. It is Dow’s first material platform designed specifically for supporting optimal electrochemistry inside the cell. As battery technologies continue to evolve, manufacturers face growing pressure to improve energy density, extend cycle life, increase charging speed and scale production across multiple chemistries and manufacturing approaches. VOLTRICELL brings together Dow's growing portfolio of battery cell materials under a unified platform designed to support innovation across electrodes, separators, coatings and battery cell packaging applications. The portfolio includes binders, dispersants, rheology modifiers, surfactants and specialty additives that can be selected and combined to help support performance, manufacturability and scalability. "In the battery industry, there are a multitude of chemistries and cell manufacturing strategies in play and under development for the future," said Joel McDonald, Global Technical Director for Dow MobilityScience. "Battery manufacturers need materials partners that can evolve with their technology roadmaps. Through VOLTRICELL™, we can help customers innovate with confidence, leveraging Dow’s broad toolbox to support today's cell chemistries and the next generation of energy storage." By combining deep materials science expertise with application development capabilities and global technical support through its global MobilityScience Studiosopens in a new tab, Dow helps battery manufacturers accelerate innovation from cell design to system-level integration. artigo.texto: A gigante russa de tecnologia da informação Yandex, chamada de Google da Rússia, diz que um data center da empresa nos arredores de Moscou foi atacado por um drone ucraniano. A Yandex anunciou domingo que foi danificada a infraestrutura do data center, situado na região de Vladimir, e que as suas atividades foram completamente interrompidas. O grande jornal russo Kommersant noticiou no mesmo dia que não estavam disponíveis para usuários alguns serviços da Yandex, como de solicitação de táxis e de entrega de refeições. Segundo o periódico, também ficaram parcialmente indisponíveis serviços mantidos pela Yandex no Cazaquistão e no Quirguistão — nações da Ásia Central que têm estreitos laços com a Rússia. É o terceiro ataque ucraniano a instalações pertencentes à gigante russa de tecnologia. Na quinta-feira, foi atacado um data center da Yandex em Ryazan, na região central da Rússia, e na sexta-feira, outro na região de Kaluga, vizinha a Moscou. A mídia ucraniana noticiou quinta-feira que o presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, fez menção a um plano para revidar ataques lançados pela Rússia a data centers situados na Ucrânia.

artigo.texto: Mixing Two Unsuitable Solvents Nearly Triples Lithium-Metal Battery Life [Reading Science] UNIST, KAIST Maintain 80% Capacity After 150 High-Voltage Charge-Discharge Cycles Identify "Cooperative Solvation" Principle That Weakens Lithium-Ion Binding Mixing two solvents considered unsuitable for lithium-metal batteries instead nearly tripled battery life. When used separately, the solvents bound lithium ions so strongly that they interfered with charging and discharging. But when combined, they became more likely to release the lithium ions. A South Korean research team has extended the life of next-generation batteries using an approach that overturns conventional wisdom about electrolyte design. Performance comparison of lithium metal batteries using a cooperative solvation electrolyte. Their charge-discharge cycle life was approximately three times longer than that of batteries with conventional electrolytes, and lithium was found to deposit evenly on the anode surface. Gas generation and electrolyte consumption were also greatly reduced, improving battery stability. Provided by the research team. View original image Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) said on October 12 that a joint research team led by Professor Song Hyeon-gon of its Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering and Professor Seo Donghwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) had developed an electrolyte that extends the charge-discharge life of lithium-metal batteries by about three times. The findings were published in the international journal ACS Nano on August 11. Unlike the widely used lithium-ion batteries, lithium-metal batteries use lithium metal instead of graphite as the anode. They have attracted attention as next-generation, high-capacity batteries because they can store more electrical energy at the same weight. However, lithium metal reacts unnecessarily with the electrolyte during charging and discharging, causing capacity to decline rapidly. This problem becomes more severe when batteries are charged at high voltages to store more energy. A reversal for two unsuitable solvents...reducing lithium loss The research team mixed two solvents, ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL), in a 3:7 ratio, then added a lithium salt and a small amount of an additive to create a new electrolyte. Both solvents were considered difficult to use in lithium-metal batteries because they bind strongly to lithium ions. During charging, lithium ions must shed the surrounding solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode surface. But when solvents hold the lithium ions tightly, this process does not proceed smoothly. Lithium then deposits unevenly, and side reactions with the electrolyte reduce battery capacity. When the team mixed the two solvents, the results were contrary to expectations. As the solvent molecules attracted one another, their hold on the lithium ions actually weakened. This allowed the lithium ions to shed the solvent molecules more easily and deposit evenly on the anode surface. The team named this effect "cooperative solvation." Solvation is the process in which solvent molecules surround lithium ions. The term describes how two types of solvents influence one another to regulate their bonds with lithium ions. Experiments confirmed the performance improvement. The developed electrolyte recorded an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. Coulombic efficiency indicates how much of the lithium deposited during charging can be recovered during discharging. A higher value means less lithium is consumed during charge-discharge cycles. Three times longer life even with high-voltage charging...further validation needed for commercialization The research team tested the developed electrolyte in batteries with high-nickel cathodes and compared their performance. When charged to 4.5 V at 25°C, the batteries retained about 80% of their initial capacity even after approximately 150 charge-discharge cycles. By contrast, batteries using a conventional carbonate-based electrolyte fell below 80% of their initial capacity after about 50 cycles. Under the same conditions, the charge-discharge life was therefore about three times longer. The team also confirmed reductions in gas generation caused by electrolyte decomposition and in the dissolution of nickel from the cathode. UNIST researchers (from left): Professor Song Hyungon and researcher Hong Jingi. Photo courtesy of UNIST. View original image The study is significant because it improved battery performance using combinations of commonly used solvents, without relying on expensive fluorinated solvents or highly concentrated lithium salts. However, 150 charge-discharge cycles remain limited for applications in electric vehicles or energy storage systems (ESS). Further validation is needed to determine whether the performance can be maintained during long-term use, across a range of temperatures, and under fast-charging conditions. First author and researcher Hong Jin-gi said, "Mixing two solvents with strong bonding forces to weaken their bonds with lithium ions is a new design principle that overturns conventional wisdom about electrolyte design." He added, "It could also be used to improve electrolyte performance in commercial lithium-ion batteries, in addition to lithium-metal batteries." Government Moves to Establish 'Global High-Integrity Carbon Market' The government plans to establish the Global High-Integrity Carbon Market (GVCM), an international market where greenhouse gas reductions achieved in developing countries are issued as carbon credits and traded internationally. The initiative aims to build a foundation for international carbon trading that will enhance the credibility of emissions reductions and allow Korean companies to use credits earned by participating in overseas reduction projects for regulatory compliance and environmental, social and governance (ESG) management. On the 12th, the government discussed detailed plans for the GVCM at a meeting of foreign economic ministers held at the Government Complex Seoul, chaired by Lee Hyungil, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy. The GVCM is an international carbon market being developed to address credibility issues raised in existing international carbon markets. The government plans to build a framework covering everything from identifying and supporting emissions reduction projects to issuing and trading credits and establishing cooperation among countries, with the aim of increasing the market's credibility. The international carbon credit market is projected to grow to $7 billion-$35 billion by 2030 and $45 billion-$250 billion by 2050. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il speaks at the inaugural Emergency Economic Headquarters Meeting and Ministerial Meeting on Economic Affairs at Government Complex Seoul in Jongno-gu, Seoul, on Oct. 1, 2026. Photo by Cho Yongjun. View original image Credits Classified by Host-Country Approval...Usable for ESG and Regulatory Compliance The GVCM's core feature is to classify credits according to whether the country hosting an emissions reduction project authorizes their transfer. Credits approved for transfer by the host country will be classified as "GVCM A," while those without approval will be classified as "GVCM NA." GVCM A credits are intended for use in meeting the investing country's national greenhouse gas reduction target and for regulatory compliance, including under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). They may also be used for corporate ESG activities. GVCM NA credits are intended for corporate ESG activities, and may be converted to GVCM A if the host country subsequently approves the corresponding adjustment. Approval from the host country is required to use emissions reductions achieved overseas for domestic or international regulatory compliance. When emissions reductions are transferred to the investing country, they may be counted toward the reduction targets of the investing and purchasing countries. Without approval, however, the reductions are in principle counted toward the host country's national reduction target. The government plans to specify in the operating rules an obligation for participating countries to make efforts to approve credit transfers. The scope of credit use will also be expanded beyond voluntary markets to include compliance markets. The government will consider linking the credits with the domestic emissions trading system and the greenhouse gas target management system, assessing whether they meet requirements for credit credibility, corresponding adjustments under the Paris Agreement, and business participation under domestic laws and regulations. Overseas, it will consult with relevant agencies to enable the credits to be used for regulatory compliance, including under CORSIA. Blockchain technology will also be introduced to ensure credit credibility. Key information, including the project operator, the country or region where the project is carried out, a unique identification number, the reduction methodology, and the volume of reductions, will be recorded on the blockchain, while the complete dataset will be stored in a conventional database. The aim is to prevent double counting of emissions reductions and greenwashing during trading, while improving the security of records. Initially, credits will be issued through conventional electronic processes. The government plans to use the Korea Exchange as the trading platform. It believes the Korea Exchange can help secure the confidence of market participants, given its experience operating an emissions trading exchange since 2015. However, constraints related to operating hours, eligible trading participants, and foreign exchange regulations limit the possibility of 24-hour trading and participation by individuals and foreign investors. The government has therefore left open the possibility of issuing digital assets alongside the existing system in the future. Issuing Body to Include Developing Countries...Identifying Overseas Emissions Reduction Projects The GVCM's governing body will consist of a board, a technical supervisory committee, and a secretariat. The board, made up of member countries, will set policy direction and oversee the technical supervisory committee. The technical supervisory committee will decide whether to issue credits, and experts nominated by developing countries will be able to participate so that the needs and policy positions of host countries are reflected. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), an international organization, will temporarily serve as the secretariat, and the government plans to establish a separate secretariat after the GVCM's official launch. artigo.texto: 12.10.26 – By NewsIP Bureau – New Delhi – India and the European Union discussed carbon market development, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and technical cooperation during a bilateral meeting in New Delhi on October 12, 2026. Pankaj Agarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Power, met Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union at the European Commission, to exchange views on carbon pricing frameworks and implementation-related developments. The discussions covered India’s domestic carbon market initiatives, the EU’s CBAM framework and opportunities to strengthen cooperation on monitoring, reporting, verification and capacity building. Also Read: Ministry of Power clears up to 654 MW electricity export to Nepal During the meeting, Agarwal highlighted progress under India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including the notification of emission-intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units. The initiative forms part of the country’s efforts to develop a domestic carbon market. He also outlined the expansion of non-fossil energy capacity in India’s electricity sector. Non-fossil sources account for 308 GW of the country’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW, according to the figures presented during the meeting. These developments provided context for the exchange on carbon pricing and climate-related policy frameworks. Also Read: Power Minister Boosts Morale at NHPC’s J&K Sites The European Commission side acknowledged India’s progress in carbon market development and shared updates concerning CBAM implementation. Discussions also addressed the potential for technical engagement on the recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms and the development of monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems. Capacity building was another area identified for cooperation. These subjects are relevant to understanding how carbon pricing approaches are assessed and implemented, while the meeting provided an opportunity for both sides to exchange information on their respective policy developments. Also Read: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: Key Developments Both sides agreed to continue dialogue and strengthen cooperation on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies and other areas of mutual interest. The proposed continued engagement will cover technical issues, including carbon pricing mechanisms, MRV systems and capacity building. The meeting reflects an ongoing exchange between India and the European Union on carbon market policies and implementation approaches. No specific agreement on formal recognition of either side’s carbon pricing mechanism was announced in the information provided.

artigo.texto: St. Petersburg’s existing zoning rules prohibit standalone data centers, according to an Oct. 9 memo from Planning Director Derek Kilborn to Mayor Ken Welch explaining how a new Florida law relates to the city’s regulation of the facilities. The city’s land development code does not list data centers as a permitted use or special exception, and uses that are not listed are presumed prohibited unless they are similar enough to an approved use to qualify. Kilborn found no basis for treating data centers as an existing permitted use, including under the classifications for utility plants and substations. His determination follows the passage of Senate Bill 484, signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis on May 7, which preserves local governments’ authority to regulate facilities with substantial electricity and utility demands. The law also prevents large-load customers from being treated as electric substations under a state provision governing substation approvals, a distinction relevant to the city’s existing zoning classifications. To determine whether an unlisted use qualifies, St. Petersburg’s zoning code relies on the American Planning Association’s land-use classification system and the North American Industry Classification System. Kilborn wrote that neither provides a clear basis for treating data centers as similar to an existing permitted use. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. The new state law defines large-scale data centers as facilities with an anticipated monthly peak electrical load of at least 50 megawatts, calculated using the highest average load over a 15-minute interval. St. Petersburg’s determination also covers smaller standalone data centers that fall below that threshold. The restriction does not apply to data centers that serve as ancillary parts of otherwise permitted businesses, allowing supporting data infrastructure to operate alongside an approved primary use. Kilborn’s memorandum does not propose any changes to the city’s zoning code.

artigo.texto: Nearly 4 million abandoned US oil wells could become underground batteries, with geothermal heat boosting storage output by 9.5% Abandoned oil wells may hold a second life as underground energy storage — and a Penn State study suggests trapped geothermal heat could make the whole system 9.5% more efficient. Renewable energy is growing fast — but the grid still goes dark when the wind dies and the sun sets. Solving that problem has sent engineers searching for new ways to store power at scale, from massive battery farms to pumped-water reservoirs. The answer, according to a new Penn State study, may already be in the ground. Across the United States, nearly 4 million depleted oil and gas wells sit largely forgotten — rusting relics of the fossil fuel era. Researchers now believe that infrastructure could be repurposed into something the clean energy transition urgently needs. Regions built around oil and gas extraction — western Pennsylvania, parts of Texas, Appalachia — face real economic disruption as fossil fuel production declines. A grid problem hiding in plain sight Renewable energy’s central weakness isn’t generation — it’s timing. Solar panels produce power at noon; demand peaks at dinner. Wind turbines spin through the night when most of the grid is asleep. That mismatch between supply and demand is one of the biggest structural challenges of the clean energy transition. Energy storage is the obvious fix, but storing electricity at grid scale is harder than it sounds. Battery farms help — they’re just expensive and limited in capacity. Pumped-water reservoirs work well where geography cooperates, which isn’t everywhere. Compressed-air energy storage, or CAES, offers another path. During periods of low demand, excess electricity compresses air and pushes it underground. When demand rises, that pressurized air drives turbines to generate power. It’s a proven approach in principle, but building the infrastructure needed to make CAES commercially viable has kept most projects on the drawing board rather than in the ground. What Penn State researchers discovered The Penn State team, led by Arash Dahi Taleghani — a professor of petroleum and natural gas engineering — proposed a way to change that equation. Their study, published in the Journal of Energy Storage, describes a geothermal-assisted CAES system built around depleted oil and gas wells. The key insight is thermodynamic. Deep underground, rock formations retain significant natural heat, and when compressed air is stored in those hot environments, its temperature rises. Higher temperature means higher pressure, and higher pressure means more energy stored in the same space. Using numerical modeling and simulation, the researchers quantified the effect: placing CAES systems in abandoned wells significantly increased air temperature, boosting efficiency by 9.5% over conventional CAES. “Without taking advantage of the geothermal setup, you could not get enough encouraging numbers,” Taleghani said. That efficiency gain, combined with cost savings from reusing existing wells, is what makes the economics potentially viable. Nearly 4 million wells — already in the ground The scale of America’s abandoned well problem becomes, in this context, an unexpected asset. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates approximately 3.9 million depleted oil and gas wells across the United States. Most sit idle — already drilled, already cased, already connected to the surface. Reusing those wells eliminates one of CAES’s biggest cost barriers. For an industry weighing whether a project pencils out, that upfront savings could tip the calculation. Pennsylvania illustrates both the opportunity and the urgency. State regulators estimate hundreds of thousands of orphaned and abandoned wells within its borders alone. Many are improperly plugged or structurally compromised, and when that happens, they can leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas — into the atmosphere and groundwater alike. Two problems, one solution Sealing a leaking well and converting it into an energy storage asset aren’t competing goals. They’re the same action. “If we use existing wells, we are basically hitting two birds with one stone,” Taleghani said. “First, we are sealing these wells. That stops any potential leaks. And then if we are repurposing these wells for energy storage, we are still using the infrastructure that is in place in these communities.” The social dimension matters too. Regions built around oil and gas extraction — western Pennsylvania, parts of Texas, Appalachia — face real economic disruption as fossil fuel production declines. Repurposing existing infrastructure could preserve technical jobs and keep communities tied to the energy sector rather than left behind by it. This research is part of Penn State’s Repurposing Center for Energy Transition, known as ReCET, and was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy. What comes next The 9.5% efficiency figure comes from modeling and simulation — no real-world pilot has been built and tested yet. The gap between a promising simulation and a functioning commercial system is significant, and worth being clear-eyed about. Challenges remain across several dimensions. Regulatory frameworks for underground energy storage in repurposed wells don’t fully exist. Each candidate well would need structural integrity assessments before it could be safely pressurized, and scaling the concept to a network capable of meaningfully supporting the grid is a separate engineering problem entirely. But if those hurdles can be cleared, the potential payoff is substantial. A validated system could simultaneously accelerate clean energy storage deployment and begin cleaning up nearly four million sources of legacy pollution — the kind of practical convergence that tends to attract serious investment. You can learn more about this discovery here: Penn State. “Reusing old oil and gas wells may offer green energy storage solution.” ScienceDaily

artigo.texto: The handwritten warning was left at an Amazon data center construction site in suburban Virginia: A dozen pipe bombs scattered throughout the building would explode in the next half hour. Officers rushed to the scene as workers dropped their tools and fled. Bomb-sniffing dogs prowled every corner of the site. That April 22 message in the city of Manassas, authorities soon confirmed, was an empty threat – the latest in a string this year that has rattled the state and communities across the nation. As thousands of new data centers have been built to fuel the booming artificial intelligence industry, escalating public resentment against both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself is roiling small towns and suburban communities from coast to coast, a CNN investigation has found. Police have been called into action to investigate dozens of threats to data centers, from bomb claims etched on bathroom walls to online incitements to “use bullets on city council members” to suggestions that protesters should “unalive” pro-development officials, according to a CNN review of more than 100 police reports filed since last year. Aside from rare cases like an Indianapolis council member whose home was sprayed with gunfire, those threats have rarely led to actual violence – but they’ve eaten up hundreds of hours of police time, alarmed workers and inflamed communities already on edge over the projects. That rising outrage has also inspired a growing police crackdown, including federal agencies tracking data center protests and local cops questioning vocal activists, and even filing criminal charges against critics that have later fallen apart in court. The police records as a whole paint a vivid picture of a national backlash against the rise of data centers and AI reaching a boiling point at a moment when the debate has become a key issue threading party lines ahead of the midterm elections. They also show growing concern among law enforcement agencies about extremist groups at opposite ends of the political spectrum hopping on the anti-data-center bandwagon. “Anti-technology extremist narratives appeal to a broad array of ideological movements – including anarchists, environmental extremists, and white supremacists – creating a common target between otherwise opposing movements,” Colorado state officials warned in an April bulletin for police agencies. A similar California memo warned in June of “a broad range of threat actors… mobilized by AI-related grievances.” Still, some people who have been charged with making threatening comments insist they’re not extremists and do not actually wish violence upon anyone. Rather, they say they were driven to take dramatic action by rising electricity bills, environmental worries or fears of AI. “I’m not really political,” Anthony Hinojosa, an Illinois man arrested in February over an alleged data center threat, told an investigator who interrogated him, according to police recordings. “I feel like we don’t have a vote.” But elected officials say the reports show how the battle over data centers and AI is entering dangerous territory, where they’re fearing for their lives just for doing their jobs. Minneapolis council member Michael Rainville was left pleading in an August letter to his constituents for a more peaceful dialogue over the issue. “Please stop the threats against me and my family,” he wrote. ‘Terroristic threats’ In early February, police in Troy, Illinois fielded multiple calls about ominous statements on a community Facebook page. At the time, the city had been debating whether to clear the way for a roughly 200-acre data center that backers said could create hundreds of jobs. Like similar proposals around America, the once-anodyne pitch had become hugely contentious. Views of data centers have soured significantly this year. Nearly nine in 10 Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of these facilities, a CNN poll conducted by SSRS found in September. Amid that debate, Troy officials confronted a tirade on Facebook: “My hypothesis is no one would want to be shot at so just start shooting the people involved and it’ll never be built,” Hinojosa, a 33-year-old lawn-care businessman, commented beneath a post about the proposed data center. When a user asked if he was really suggesting violence, Hinojosa responded, “for sure,” screenshots of his posts show. Later that day, officers knocked on his door. “You’re being placed under arrest for making terroristic threats,” an officer said. “I think people are taking things out of context,” Hinojosa told the authorities. He said he had been upset about the proposed data center’s potential strain on electricity and water supply, but he insisted he would not hurt anyone and his words had been misconstrued. “Over a misunderstanding you are literally going to ruin my life,” he said. “It just feels like the mayor of Troy and the city council, they’re just not really listening to the public.” Hinojosa, who described himself in police recordings as a moderate Republican, now faces felony charges for intimidation and harassment through electronic communication. He has pleaded not guilty. His lawyer declined comment, citing an upcoming trial. Hinojosa’s case is one of about 70 among the police reports CNN reviewed that include allegations of threats, intimidation or planned attacks – a collection showing a striking range of anger at AI infrastructure that at times has spilled into serious claims of potential violence. Dozens of additional police reports detail other security concerns, including scuffles at county meetings, calls for police patrols at local officials’ homes and confrontations with data center staff. artigo.texto: BYD has unveiled its new Atto 8 at the Paris Motor Show, a large seven-seat electric SUV capable of charging its battery from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes using the manufacturer’s latest charging technology. The Atto 8 will sit at the top of BYD’s European SUV range, above models such as the Atto 3 and Sealion 7. Measuring just over five metres long, it will compete with large electric family SUVs such as the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90. Two versions have been announced, both featuring a large 115kWh battery. The rear-wheel-drive ‘Design’ model produces 456hp and offers a claimed driving range of up to 405 miles on a single charge, while the more powerful ‘Excellence AWD’ produces 764hp and has a range of up to 374 miles. The all-wheel-drive model can accelerate from 0-62mph in 4.6 seconds, compared with eight seconds for the rear-wheel-drive version. Rapid charging The Atto 8 will be the first BYD model in Europe to use the manufacturer’s second-generation Blade Battery, introducing its new Flash Charging technology. BYD claims the battery can be charged from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in nine minutes, when connected to a compatible charger. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, the manufacturer says a 20% to 97% charge can be completed in 12 minutes. These figures are considerably faster than the charging times currently offered by most electric SUVs, although achieving them will require access to BYD’s dedicated Flash Charging network. BYD plans to install 3,000 Flash Charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027. It has not yet confirmed how many will be located in the UK. Seven seats and plenty of equipment The Atto 8 has three rows of seats, with a 270-litre boot when all seven seats are in use. Folding the second and third rows increases luggage space to 1,960 litres, while an additional 136-litre storage compartment sits beneath the bonnet. Inside, both versions feature a 16-inch infotainment touchscreen with Google built-in, a ten-inch digital instrument display and a head-up display. Standard equipment includes leather upholstery, a panoramic glass roof and heated, ventilated and massaging seats in both the front and middle rows. Other features include three-zone climate control, wireless smartphone charging and a small refrigerated compartment that can also be used to keep food and drinks warm. The rear-wheel-drive model comes with a ten-speaker sound system, while the all-wheel-drive version gets a 21-speaker setup. When is it arriving? The BYD Atto 8 is expected to go on sale in European markets during the first three months of 2027. UK pricing, specifications and a customer delivery date have yet to be confirmed.

artigo.texto: Company Establishes Pilot Line in South Korea, Preparing 30MWh Sample Tests for North American Customers LG Energy Solution is accelerating the development of sodium-ion batteries as a potential next-generation growth driver, expanding its battery portfolio beyond conventional lithium-ion technology. The company has established a pilot production line in South Korea and is preparing to validate its technology with North American customers, positioning itself for an early entry into the emerging sodium-ion energy storage system (ESS) market. According to battery industry sources on Oct. 13, LG Energy Solution has established a sodium-ion battery pilot line at its Ochang Energy Plant in North Chungcheong Province. The company is currently conducting vehicle tests involving 12-volt and 24-volt batteries and plans to carry out sample testing for approximately 30 megawatt-hours (MWh) of sodium-ion ESS batteries with North American customers by the first half of 2027. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium instead of lithium as a key raw material, offering the potential for lower production costs and improved thermal safety. One of the technology's main advantages is the abundance and accessibility of its raw materials. Sodium is estimated to be approximately 1,200 times more abundant than lithium in the Earth's crust and can also be extracted from seawater, potentially reducing dependence on geographically concentrated supply chains. Sodium-ion technology also offers promising low-temperature performance. According to the performance figures cited in the industry, certain sodium-ion batteries can retain more than 90% of their charge capacity at temperatures as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius, although actual performance varies by cell chemistry and design. LG Energy Solution is pursuing a commercialization roadmap targeting 2027, initially focusing on automotive auxiliary batteries, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and stationary energy storage systems. The company eventually aims to expand into affordable electric vehicles as improvements in energy density make the technology suitable for a broader range of applications. It also plans to work with South Korean materials suppliers to establish a domestic sourcing network and strengthen its supply chain competitiveness. Competition is intensifying as other South Korean battery manufacturers advance their own sodium-ion development programs. Samsung SDI is developing UPS solutions for AI data centers and stationary ESS products using its proprietary technologies, with more detailed mass-production plans expected in 2027. SK On is also expanding its ESS development efforts, targeting completion of sodium-ion battery prototypes in 2027 and commercialization in 2028. Stationary energy storage is emerging as a promising initial market for sodium-ion technology because space and weight constraints are generally less demanding than those for electric vehicles. Although sodium-ion batteries typically have lower energy density than lithium-ion alternatives, their potential cost advantages and low-temperature performance could make them attractive for fixed-site applications. The South Korean government is also seeking to accelerate the commercialization of next-generation battery technologies. At a recent event, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs and the minister of climate, energy and environment pledged support for emerging technologies, including sodium-ion batteries, as part of the government's ambition to lead the next-generation battery market by 2035. Competition from Chinese manufacturers remains a major challenge. CATL, the world's leading battery manufacturer, unveiled a sodium-ion ESS product in June and announced plans for cumulative shipments of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) by the end of 2026. An LG Energy Solution representative said the company aims to establish a leading position in the emerging market by securing key technologies and supply chain capabilities at an early stage. The company's progress in customer validation, production readiness and cost competitiveness will be critical to determining how quickly sodium-ion batteries can become a commercially viable addition to its existing portfolio.
