artigo.texto: Lithium Metal Battery Lifespan Extended Threefold — South Korean Researchers Overturn Electrolyte Design Convention South Korean researchers have developed an electrolyte technology that extends battery lifespan by nearly threefold by blending two commercial solvents previously deemed unsuitable for lithium metal batteries due to their strong lithium-ion binding properties. The approach resolves the rapid capacity degradation that occurs during high-voltage charging without relying on expensive specialty solvents or high-concentration salts. Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) announced the findings on the 12th. The research was published in the August 11 issue of ACS Nano, an international journal in the nanoscience field. Unlike commercial lithium-ion batteries that use graphite anodes, lithium metal batteries employ lithium metal as the anode, theoretically enabling nearly double the capacity. They have been regarded as a key technology for extending electric vehicle driving range and increasing the capacity of energy storage systems (ESS). However, lithium metal undergoes unwanted side reactions with the electrolyte during charge-discharge cycles, sharply reducing lifespan — a problem that worsens under high-voltage charging conditions. 'Cooperative Solvation' Overturns Conventional Design Principles The research team focused on ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL). Both solvents had been excluded from lithium metal battery design because of their strong binding affinity for lithium ions. During charging, lithium ions must shed surrounding solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode surface. When solvents bind lithium ions too tightly, this process is impeded, causing uneven lithium deposition and capacity loss through side reactions with the electrolyte. The team inverted the conventional approach by mixing the two solvents at a 3:7 weight ratio and adding a lithium salt along with a small amount of electrode protective film stabilizing additive. The result defied expectations. Strong intermolecular forces — including hydrogen bonding between EC's hydrogen atoms and SL's oxygen atoms — emerged between the solvents, paradoxically weakening each solvent's individual binding affinity for lithium ions. The team characterized this phenomenon, in which the two solvents mutually influence each other to modulate lithium-ion binding and anion interfacial accessibility, as "cooperative solvation." Hong Jin-ki, the first author of the study, explained: "Mixing two strongly binding solvents to actually weaken their interaction with lithium ions represents a new design principle that overturns conventional electrolyte design wisdom. Beyond lithium metal batteries, this approach could be applied to enhance electrolyte performance in commercial lithium-ion batteries as well." Performance Validated Under High-Voltage Conditions Performance verification results were confirmed quantitatively. The new electrolyte achieved an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. Coulombic efficiency measures how much of the lithium deposited during charging can be recovered during discharge — higher values indicate less lithium is consumed during charge-discharge cycles. When applied to a high-nickel (NCM811) cathode battery and tested at 25°C with charging up to 4.5V, the battery retained approximately 80% of its initial capacity after 150 charge-discharge cycles. Compared with the conventional carbonate-based electrolyte, which fell below 80% capacity after roughly 50 cycles, the new electrolyte extended cycle life by approximately threefold under the same capacity retention standard. Note: Coulombic efficiency figures for the conventional electrolyte were not disclosed by the research team. Gas generation from electrolyte decomposition and nickel dissolution from the cathode material were also suppressed. This indicates that the major factors accelerating battery degradation under high-voltage charging conditions were simultaneously controlled. Professor Song Hyun-kon stated: "We improved electrolyte performance using commercial solvents without relying on expensive fluorinated solvents or high-concentration salts. We expect this will help extend the operational life of high-capacity lithium metal batteries for ESS and electric vehicle applications." Additional Validation Needed for Commercialization The study is significant in that it improved battery performance using only combinations of low-cost, commercially available solvents. However, 150 charge-discharge cycles remains a limited benchmark for real-world EV or ESS applications, as EV batteries typically require cycle lives in the thousands. Further validation is needed to confirm performance retention under long-term use, diverse temperature conditions, and fast-charging environments. The research team expects the technology can be extended beyond lithium metal batteries to high-voltage lithium-ion batteries and various next-generation battery systems, including sodium-ion and potassium-ion batteries. The research was supported by the Korea Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology (KEIT) under South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, and the National Research Council of Science & Technology (NST).

artigo.texto: China's Solid-State Battery Stock Frenzy Cools as Companies Rush to Clarify They Have No Such Business Shidai Wanheng (600241.SS), which had locked in the daily limit-up for five consecutive trading sessions, issued an urgent announcement after market close on October 9, explicitly stating that the company's products are not involved in solid-state batteries. The clarification directly targets the core concept driving this round of market speculation—yet the company had issued risk warnings in the prior three trading days without making any mention of its solid-state battery business status. According to Shidai Wanheng's announcement, the company's lithium battery products are small-power cylindrical ternary lithium batteries primarily used in small electric tools, with the 1865 and 1450 models as its mainstay products. Its nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) battery products are mainly applied in personal care, consumer goods, and electric tools. The company's existing main products and production lines remain unchanged, and its fundamental production and operations have not undergone material changes, with production currently organized on an order-by-order basis. Zizhu High-tech, which had also hit the daily limit-up for four consecutive sessions, issued a clarification announcement the same day. The company stated that as of now, its aluminum-plastic film products for lithium batteries and solid-state battery-related business remain in an early stage of exploration and R&D, and there is considerable uncertainty over when these products can achieve commercialization and contribute stable, scalable revenue. This round of solid-state battery concept speculation was ignited by the release of a heavyweight industrial policy on September 28. Seven agencies—including China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Transport, the Ministry of Commerce, the State Administration for Market Regulation, the National Energy Administration, and the National Railway Administration—jointly issued the 15th Five-Year Plan for New Battery Industry Development. This is China's first national-level special plan for the battery sector, explicitly setting targets for initial scaled application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, long-life lithium batteries achieving 15,000 charge cycles, and leading enterprises reaching PPB-level defect rates, while continuing to build out lithium battery standards systems and advancing standards development in key areas such as all-solid-state batteries and sodium batteries. The plan also, for the first time, elevates new batteries from a "component" positioning to "the foundational layer of multi-domain electrification and the new energy system," meaning the battery industry's service boundaries will expand significantly from new energy vehicles to emerging pillar sectors including energy storage, the low-altitude economy, and intelligent robotics. Catalyzed by the policy, China's A-share battery supply chain rallied against an overall weak market on October 9. More than 4,100 stocks fell across the market that day, with 13 hitting limit-down, yet the solid-liquid battery index surged 3.80% to lead all sectors, the lithium cathode index rose 3.65%, the power battery index gained 3.29%, and the solid-state battery index climbed 2.50%. At the individual stock level, China's Keheng Co. hit the 20% limit-up, Fengyuan Chemical rose 10% to notch a second consecutive limit-up, Tinci Materials gained 10%, and Guibao Science & Technology soared 14.71%. Heavyweight leaders also performed strongly: CATL (300750.SZ) surged as much as 4.85% intraday with turnover exceeding 9.1 billion yuan (approximately $1.4 billion); Ganfeng Lithium (002460.SZ) rose 4.23%, EVE Energy (300014.SZ) gained 2.91%, and BYD (002594.SZ) advanced 2.50%. On the capital flow front, the solid-state battery sector saw net inflows of 5.089 billion yuan (approximately $761.9 million) in super-large orders, marking a fourth consecutive day of net inflows, with institutional and northbound Stock Connect funds entering aggressively. Market analysts noted this indicates the current rally is not short-term speculative trading by hot money, but rather structural positioning by trend-following capital. From a commercialization standpoint, technological breakthroughs among leading players are accelerating. Public information shows CATL has completed a 1GWh all-solid-state pilot line, with laboratory sample energy density reaching 500Wh/kg, targeting a pilot line yield rate above 90% by the fourth quarter and planning small-batch production by 2027. BYD's sulfide-based all-solid-state single cell has achieved energy density of 400Wh/kg, with a prototype vehicle achieving a combined range exceeding 1,218 kilometers under CLTC conditions, and the battery has passed the full suite of automotive-grade safety tests at CATARC. Gotion High-tech (002074.SZ) has broken through 400Wh/kg energy density with its Jinshi all-solid-state battery, with its 0.2GWh pilot line achieving yield rates above 90% and already commencing vehicle road testing, while the 2GWh mass production line design is essentially complete, targeting small-batch vehicle installation before the end of 2026. CITIC Securities believes that solid-state battery industrialization is accelerating continuously, projecting global solid-state battery shipments to exceed 700GWh by 2030, of which all-solid-state batteries will account for over 200GWh. China's semi-solid-state batteries have already achieved mass production, establishing a competitive advantage over Europe, the United States, Japan, and South Korea. However, a clear disconnect has emerged between secondary market capital preferences and industrial fundamentals. artigo.texto: South Korea to Launch International Carbon Market Next Year with Blockchain-Based Credit Issuance South Korea will fully launch an international carbon market next year for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits. The plan involves issuing reduction credits as carbon credits, trading them on the Korea Exchange, and enabling their use for corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities as well as national emissions reduction target compliance. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il presided over a meeting of economy-related ministers at the Government Complex Seoul on the 12th, where the government finalized the "Detailed Implementation Plan for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)." The GVCM is a market for issuing and trading carbon credits generated from overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The government has now specified the operational framework based on the roadmap announced in December last year. The core of this plan lies in ensuring credit credibility and activating trading. The government has decided to apply blockchain technology to data management. A dual-track approach will be adopted: core information such as project operators, reduction volumes, unique identification numbers, and reduction methodologies will be recorded on the blockchain, while remaining data will be stored in conventional databases. The intent is to apply the technology selectively to core information rather than uploading all data to the blockchain, thereby securing both management efficiency and stability. Credits will initially be issued in standard electronic form and traded on South Korea's voluntary carbon market exchange. Going forward, the government plans to consider parallel issuance in digital asset form, taking into account issuance and trading volumes, the status of digital asset legislation, and market confidence. The market's name has also been changed from "Global Voluntary Carbon Market" to "Global Verified Carbon Market." The change reflects the intent to encompass regulatory markets as well, based on the judgment that the previous name could give the impression that credits were only usable in voluntary markets. Credits are divided into two categories depending on whether the host country grants transfer authorization. "GVCM A" credits, which have received authorization, can be used for both regulatory compliance—such as fulfilling investor countries' Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) or the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA)—and ESG activities. "GVCM NA" credits, which have not received authorization, are limited to corporate voluntary environmental activities. However, GVCM NA credits can be converted to GVCM A status if the host country subsequently grants corresponding adjustment approval. The government is also reviewing options to link the GVCM with South Korea's domestic emissions trading scheme or greenhouse gas target management system, provided that credibility requirements, corresponding adjustments under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and domestic legal participation conditions are met. The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat. The board, composed of member countries, will determine policy direction and oversee the technical oversight committee. The technical oversight committee will decide on technical matters such as credit issuance, with expert members recommended by developing countries able to participate in issuance decisions. The secretariat will handle issuance, management, and registry operations. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is currently serving as interim secretariat, with a separate secretariat to be established upon official launch. The government is also prioritizing participation from developing countries. Governance has been designed so that developing countries can reflect their needs in operational processes and gain experience in carbon market operations. The approach respects participating countries' sovereignty when establishing operational regulations, emissions baseline setting, and sustainable development guidelines. Project sectors will be identified based on participating countries' development needs and South Korea's technological competitiveness. Examples include nature-based solutions such as mangrove forest restoration, agricultural waste treatment, methane capture, and energy efficiency improvements. The government is also in discussions with international organizations including the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to convert reduction volumes generated from existing reduction projects into GVCM credits. International carbon markets are gaining attention as a means to achieve national greenhouse gas reduction targets. This comes as major Paris Agreement parties anticipate difficulty in meeting their 2030 NDCs through domestic reduction efforts alone. However, the lack of standardized international market criteria has led to ongoing controversy over credit credibility and actual reduction effectiveness. The government has taken note of the international carbon market's growth potential. According to MSCI projections, the carbon credit market is expected to grow to $7 billion–$35 billion by 2030 and $45 billion–$250 billion by 2050. The government's assessment is that, as the boundary between voluntary and regulatory carbon markets weakens internationally, credits usable in both markets must be developed. The government plans to collaborate with GGGI to leverage networks such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable (APCMR) to secure participating countries. artigo.texto: SERES expands CATL in-plant capacity layout and ramps up overseas charging infrastructure SERES Group and CATL signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement in Chongqing on October 10, under which the two sides will advance construction of the second phase of the battery pack "plant-within-a-plant" at SERES' super factory, and extend cooperation to supercharging, battery swapping, battery services, and overseas markets. The AITO brand will continue to equip all models with CATL batteries over the long term, while AIVA plans to adopt a battery-swap model and become a key brand for SERES' overseas business expansion. Under the agreement, CATL will continue to increase investment in Chongqing, and SERES and CATL will strengthen local industrial synergy, deepening cooperation in areas including battery safety, supply chain coordination, and global ecosystem collaboration. The two sides will also jointly promote AITO's entry into Europe, the Middle East, and Central Asia, and explore a battery service system covering the full vehicle lifecycle. One of the core projects under this cooperation is the battery pack production line located inside SERES' super factory. CATL's first-phase project began production on June 30, 2025, comprising two CTP 2.0 high-end battery pack production lines primarily supplying localized power battery systems for flagship models such as the AITO M9 and M8. This marked CATL's first adoption of the "plant-within-a-plant" model and its first production base in Chongqing. The second-phase project is planned for annual capacity of 10–12 GWh; once completed, combined first- and second-phase annual capacity will exceed 20 GWh. The "plant-within-a-plant" model places battery pack manufacturing directly inside the vehicle production base. Battery cells are integrated into vehicle-ready battery packs, which then enter the vehicle assembly process nearby, helping to shorten transport distances and improve coordination efficiency among battery pack supply, vehicle production scheduling, and delivery. The two sides can also coordinate on the same production site for model refreshes, battery specification adjustments, and changes in vehicle production capacity. Although the production line is located inside SERES' factory, battery pack manufacturing remains CATL's responsibility. This means SERES is bringing the supply link even closer to the vehicle production site while continuing to leverage the manufacturing capabilities of a specialized battery company. Unlike full in-house development and manufacturing, this arrangement separates the production location from the manufacturing entity, reflecting the automaker's trade-offs across different stages of the battery business. Note: The above capacity figures are planned data; cumulative delivery figures were disclosed by CATL and relevant partners. AITO is the primary focus of the existing cooperation between the two sides. The brand, jointly launched by SERES and Huawei in 2021, has equipped all models with CATL batteries since its inception, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million units. When the first-phase production line began operations in June 2025, its installed base exceeded 700,000 vehicles. As the installed base grows, the battery supply relationship no longer covers only new-vehicle assembly but will also extend to diagnostics, maintenance, and technical support during vehicle use. This agreement brings supercharging networks and battery services into the scope of cooperation, signaling that both sides are extending their partnership from the manufacturing end to after-sales and charging infrastructure. Overseas business adds a new application scenario to the relationship. SERES and CATL jointly participate in building the AIVA brand. Saidou Technology, which owns AIVA, was formerly Chongqing Landian Technology under SERES. After completing a capital increase of approximately 6.671 billion yuan (approximately $996.8 million) in 2026, Chongqing local state-owned capital became the largest shareholder, with SERES as the second-largest shareholder and CATL holding approximately 9.89% through its subsidiary Wending Investment. The AIVA brand was unveiled in June 2026 and, under current plans, will adopt a battery-swap model, positioned as one of SERES' main brands for overseas expansion. According to earlier reporting by LatePost, its first production model, the ME7, is planned to debut within 2026, with pre-orders expected to open in early 2027. The battery-swap model requires alignment among vehicle products, battery specifications, swap facilities, and operational services. After vehicles enter a new market, in addition to sales channels, there must be synchronized arrangements for battery turnover, maintenance, swap station construction, and ongoing operations. Since launching its battery-swap service brand EVOGO in 2022, CATL has been advancing battery swapping as large-scale infrastructure from the end of 2024, introducing standardized "Choco-SEB" swappable battery blocks. As of the end of June 2026, CATL had built 2,000 Choco-SEB swap stations covering 31 provinces and 180 cities in China, and was jointly building a "super-swap shared network" with multiple automakers including Changan, Chery, GAC, and SERES. AIVA plans to connect to this existing public battery-swap network. CATL's participation in AIVA's battery-swap and overseas business means its cooperation scope will extend further from battery manufacturing to charging infrastructure and service systems. SERES places AIVA in an important position for overseas expansion, while CATL provides support in battery supply, battery-swap technology coordination, and market infrastructure. For both sides, whether overseas business can advance smoothly depends not only on vehicle sales but also on whether local charging networks can be built in sync with product launches. artigo.texto: Seres Deepens Partnership with CATL as AITO Cumulative Deliveries Surpass 1.2 Million Units Chinese new energy vehicle manufacturer Seres (09927.HK) announced the signing of a long-term strategic cooperation deepening agreement with battery giant CATL (03750.HK), with both parties further consolidating their strategic partnership in areas including battery safety, supply chain coordination, and global ecosystem cooperation. Following the announcement, Seres' share price rose more than 4% in early trading on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Under the agreement, Seres' AITO brand has been equipped exclusively with CATL batteries across its entire lineup since the brand's inception, with cumulative deliveries surpassing 1.2 million units to date. Building on this milestone, AITO will continue to use CATL batteries across all models on a long-term basis, with cooperation spanning core areas including the expansion of "plant-within-a-plant" production capacity, the construction of a supercharging energy replenishment ecosystem, and the acceleration of global expansion. The signing ceremony was held in Chongqing on October 10, attended by Seres Group Chairman Zhang Xinghai and CATL Chairman Robin Zeng. Cooperation Focuses on Three Key Areas The deepening agreement clarifies both parties' continued commitment to the Chongqing production base. The Phase II "plant-within-a-plant" project for premium battery packs at Seres' super factory will be accelerated, while both parties will also deepen cooperation in supercharging, battery swapping, and battery services, jointly exploring innovative pathways for new energy vehicle energy replenishment ecosystems. On the global expansion front, both parties will work together to expand into overseas markets. The agreement also specifies that CATL will continue to increase investment in Chongqing, supporting the city's efforts to build a trillion-yuan premium intelligent connected new energy vehicle industrial cluster. Capital Market Reaction Seres' share price rose more than 4% in early trading on the first trading day following the announcement, with gains narrowing to 2.84% at HK$34.74 (approximately $4.4) as of press time, with trading volume of HK$13.6042 million (approximately $1.7 million). Market observers noted that the deepening cooperation between Seres and CATL helps stabilize the AITO brand's battery supply chain, particularly in premium battery pack capacity expansion. The "plant-within-a-plant" model effectively shortens supply chain distances and reduces logistics costs, which carries positive implications for Seres' gross margin improvement. Industry Background Seres and CATL have a long-standing cooperative relationship. The AITO brand, jointly developed by Seres and Huawei as a premium intelligent electric vehicle brand, has used CATL batteries across its entire lineup since launch, with both parties establishing deep ties at the battery technology and supply chain levels. The timing of this agreement coincides with intensifying competition in China's new energy vehicle market. As competitors such as BYD and Xiaomi continue to expand market share, battery supply stability and cost control have become critical competitive factors for automakers. Seres' decision to deepen its strategic cooperation with CATL at this juncture is being interpreted by the market as an important move to secure supply chain safety and enhance long-term competitiveness. Chongqing, as Seres' key production hub, has been actively promoting the development of the intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry in recent years. CATL's continued investment in Chongqing also aligns with the local government's policy objective of building a trillion-yuan industrial cluster.

artigo.texto: Bilhões de dólares foram investidos em centros de dados. De acordo com o relatório "Asia Pacific Data Centre Investment Landscape 2026" da Cushman & Wakefield, o valor total dos ativos de data centers operacionais na região Ásia-Pacífico (APAC) deverá ultrapassar US$ 950 bilhões até 2030. Para acomodar o crescente número de projetos, a APAC precisará de mais de US$ 280 bilhões em novos investimentos. Ainda há um espaço significativo para crescimento, visto que a região da Ásia-Pacífico representa mais de 60% da população mundial , mas atualmente possui apenas cerca de 22% da capacidade total global de data centers. A capacidade da região deverá aumentar 2,7 vezes até 2030. Atualmente, 26.455 MW de capacidade estão em desenvolvimento, em comparação com 15.135 MW em operação. A maior parte do capital permanece concentrada nos grandes mercados de data centers. Aproximadamente 77% da demanda total de investimentos na região da Ásia-Pacífico até 2030, equivalente a US$ 215 bilhões, deverá ser destinada ao Japão, Malásia , Austrália, Índia e Indonésia. Nessa onda de investimentos, o Vietnã ainda não está entre os líderes em termos de escala, mas é cada vez mais reconhecido como um destino promissor no cenário regional de infraestrutura digital. De acordo com a Cushman & Wakefield, o Vietnã atualmente apresenta a maior escassez de data centers na região da Ásia-Pacífico, com aproximadamente 1,4 milhão de pessoas por MW de capacidade operacional. Enquanto isso, a demanda por serviços digitais e computação em nuvem continua a crescer rapidamente. O custo de construção de um centro de dados no Vietnã varia atualmente de US$ 5,7 milhões a US$ 8,7 milhões por MW, com uma média de cerca de US$ 7,2 milhões por MW. O Vietnã também ocupa o segundo lugar na região da Ásia-Pacífico em termos de retorno sobre o investimento. O mercado analisado pela Cushman & Wakefield é dominado principalmente pelos dois "motores" de Hanói e Cidade de Ho Chi Minh, com aproximadamente 73 MW de capacidade operacional atual e mais 137 MW projetados para serem fornecidos até 2030. A diferença entre a capacidade existente e a demanda futura está começando a atrair projetos de grande escala. Will Tran, Diretor de Negócios Industriais e de Escritórios no Vietnã da JLL, observa que o mercado está entrando em uma nova fase, onde os motores de crescimento vêm cada vez mais de indústrias de alta tecnologia, em vez de indústrias tradicionais com uso intensivo de mão de obra. No Norte, as indústrias de eletrônica, equipamentos elétricos, alta tecnologia e engenharia de precisão continuam em expansão. Enquanto isso, o Sul atrai crescente interesse em áreas de alta tecnologia, pesquisa e desenvolvimento, produtos farmacêuticos, centros de dados e logística moderna. Espera-se que os centros de dados, em particular, se tornem uma nova força motriz, à medida que a inteligência artificial (IA), a computação em nuvem e a economia digital aumentam a demanda por infraestrutura de dados. Esse segmento também possui requisitos específicos em relação à energia, infraestrutura técnica e conectividade, abrindo assim outra via para o desenvolvimento de imóveis industriais no Vietnã. De fato, essas oportunidades começam a se refletir na escala dos fluxos de capital para a cidade de Ho Chi Minh. Recentemente, o Comitê Popular da cidade de Ho Chi Minh decidiu arrendar quase 4,5 hectares no Parque de Alta Tecnologia de Ho Chi Minh (bairro de Tang Nhon Phu) para a Starmason Joint Stock Company, a fim de desenvolver um complexo de data center de grande porte. O projeto tem um investimento total de 480,2 milhões de dólares, construído em fases, com capacidade de computação de até 90 MW. Ainda no Parque de Alta Tecnologia da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh, a Evolution DC VN HCMC Joint Stock Company arrendou mais de 49.500 m² de terreno para investir em um centro de dados com um capital total de 508,7 milhões de dólares, implementado por um consórcio de três investidores de Singapura : Hathor, Frontier e Evolution. Fluxos de capital ainda maiores estão sendo direcionados para diversos projetos em andamento ou propostos. O complexo de data center e IA do campus SGI-HCM, no Parque Industrial Tan Phu Trung, investido pela Kinh Bac Urban Development Corporation (KBC) em colaboração com a Accelerated Infrastructure Capital (AIC) e o VietinBank , tem um investimento total projetado de aproximadamente US$ 2,1 bilhões. Um novo megacentro de dados para IA foi proposto pela G42, Microsoft, FPT, Viet Thai e VinaCapital, com um investimento total de aproximadamente US$ 2 bilhões. Os investidores continuam a refinar o plano e a pesquisar possíveis locais para a implantação. É necessária uma nova geração de infraestrutura industrial. De centros de dados de escala relativamente pequena, o mercado agora testemunha o surgimento de complexos que abrangem dezenas de megawatts, com investimentos que variam de centenas de milhões a bilhões de dólares, e profundamente integrados à IA. Essa mudança de escala impõe uma demanda diferente ao setor imobiliário industrial: a infraestrutura deve ser preparada adequadamente para acomodar esse influxo de capital. Diferentemente das fábricas convencionais, os centros de dados exigem um fornecimento de eletricidade muito grande e contínuo. Os sistemas de backup, as telecomunicações e a conectividade de dados também devem atender a altos padrões de estabilidade. É nesse ponto que os centros de dados criam novas exigências para o setor imobiliário industrial. O Sr. Nguyen Tuan Anh, Vice-Diretor Geral do Grupo KN Holdings, afirmou que, embora anteriormente um terreno limpo fosse uma vantagem competitiva crucial, atrair projetos de alta tecnologia exige agora que os desenvolvedores de parques industriais preparem infraestrutura especializada para cada setor. artigo.texto: Regarding “Data centers are hot. We should use Lake Michigan to cool them” (Oct. 6): I think the idea of cooling coils under Lake Michigan for data centers has merit. Of course, a thorough environmental assessment would need to be done prior to moving forward. And with one reservation, the idea of data centers occupying former industrial sites in Chicago is also attractive. But what about the impact regarding electrical usage? Does Chicago have the capacity to support possibly multiple data centers? What impact would there be on residents’ electric bills if this were to go forward? While this is good news, there are still a few hurdles to get over before the city leaps forward. — Tom Canning, Homer Glen Cooling proposal’s flaws Regarding Joe Holberg’s op-ed, his mayoral candidacy, math knowledge and business ownership are impressive. But should he be promoting vast, expensive projects such as coolant loops “miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom” of Lake Michigan to cool data centers? Holberg addresses the concern that this cooling loop plan for data centers might “cook the lake.” He writes that “setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool” wouldn’t change the pool’s temperature. He misunderstands heat exchange parameters with that inelegant comparison — a sealed, insulated thermos is not comparable to a metallic coil. He states without evidence that “we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact.” Tell that to the fish. Taking his inexact idea of heat exchange even further, hot data centers “should have windows.” As every Chicago resident without air conditioning knows, opening windows does not satisfy the need to cool, and it would only add to atmospheric heat. He must know the heat has to go somewhere, as he quixotically writes “climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year.” While seeming to minimize or disregard the impact of data centers on humans and the environment, Holberg spends several paragraphs addressing the saving of money. Normally, when I read commentary supporting the building of these projects, there seems to be an unbalanced emphasis on money, including arguments for creating jobs and adding to local tax bases. Does money have an overriding importance? What is the effect to our neighborhoods and communities, to our noise and pollution levels, to our air and water quality? Midway, Holberg proposes “a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it.” Perhaps he should have opened with that. — Patrick Comer, Clarendon Hills More study is needed Joe Holberg’s op-ed contains sufficient information to earn further review and consideration. I was initially concerned about a few of the points, including that miles of coil in Lake Michigan would “not even marginally increase the temperature” of the lake. He saves himself by suggesting a study. Opening and closing windows to take advantage of Chicago weather vicissitudes seems simplistic, so it, too, needs deep study. More information about Toronto and Cornell University is intriguing and ought to provide a few clues. Although touting Cornell University’s prowess is gutsy, if not a welcome “first step”-like program. — Terrance W. Gainer, Wheaton Who committed these crimes? Regarding the story “Aldermen advance $261M police misconduct settlement” (Oct. 6): There is a proposed settlement to resolve 16 lawsuits filed against the city of Chicago by people who claim that they were victims of police misconduct by a former Chicago detective and that they were convicted of crimes they did not commit. Dozens of men have been issued certificates of innocence. Important questions come to mind: If the plaintiffs did not commit these crimes, who did commit the crimes? Have these investigations been reopened? Has anyone new been charged with or convicted of the crimes in question? Don’t the victims and their families deserve fresh investigations to identify the real perpetrators? — John Mulvey, Chicago Helping Chicago’s seniors Why do millions of budgeted 2026 funds go unspent while low-income seniors continue to struggle to access help for critical home repairs and modifications? A group of Chicago community organizations — including Housing Opportunities and Maintenance for the Elderly (H.O.M.E.), Access Living, North Branch Works, Mothers Opposed to Violence Everywhere (M.O.V.E.), Illinois Anti-Foreclosure Coalition, Light Up Lawndale, Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago and Northside Community Resources — sent a letter on Sept. 1 to Mayor Brandon Johnson and housing leaders in his administration and in the City Council calling for an explanation. We are still waiting. Approximately $6.3 million in unspent 2025 funds associated with the city’s Home Repair Program is being carried over into the next budget. At the same time, approximately $28 million in federal Community Development Block Grant funding is identified for administrative costs, including about $20.8 million carried over from 2025 and a new allocation of $7.3 million. This is not just about looking at numbers in a budget. This represents a disconnect between available resources and the urgent needs of Chicago’s most vulnerable residents. In 2025, the city folded the Small Accessible Repairs for Seniors (SARFS) program into a general Home Repair Program. SARFS provided safety and accessibility repairs to many senior households yearly. artigo.texto: Nas colinas de Águas de Santa Bárbara, um município de cerca de 7 mil habitantes no interior de São Paulo, o Patria Investimentos está testando uma nova tese climática para o seu Reforest Fund. O Patria entrou no mercado de capital natural olhando para uma das apostas mais recorrentes da transição climática: o carbono. Acabou encontrando uma oportunidade menos óbvia – e bem mais saborosa: o avocado. É na região centro-oeste do estado de São Paulo que a gestora está investindo cerca de R$ 100 milhões para produzir a fruta, ainda pouco conhecida dos brasileiros. O projeto combina produção agrícola, restauração ambiental e geração de créditos de carbono. O Patria comprou duas fazendas que juntas somam mil hectares, e fechou uma parceria com a Jaguacy, que é um dos maiores produtores e exportadores brasileiros da fruta e vai tocar a operação. Hoje o Brasil produz pouco mais de 60 mil toneladas do abacate Hass, uma variedade criada na Califórnia há um século e que reina no avocado toast e nas saladas dos americanos. Boa parte da produção nacional é voltada para a exportação. O Reforest Fund foi desenhado para combinar diferentes fontes de capital – e diferentes interesses. De um lado estão investidores que olham para a agenda de restauração, biodiversidade e descarbonização. De outro, o capital mais tradicional, que precisa enxergar retorno, risco e previsibilidade de receita. “Ao longo do desenho do fundo, a pergunta era quanto da exposição ao mercado de carbono queríamos ter. É uma solução relevante, porque muitos dos esforços de descarbonização passam pelo mecanismo de offset. Mas o mercado tem se desenvolvido de uma forma que exige soluções mais customizadas. A gente sabia que o avocado preenchia essa lacuna,” disse Pedro Faria, sócio do Pátria e co-CEO da vertical de high growth. O fundo nasceu com a meta de mobilizar R$ 2 bilhões — e já chegou perto disso. Na primeira rodada, anunciada pelo Patria em 2025, foram captados R$ 100 milhões com a Desenvolve SP, a agência de fomento do Governo de São Paulo; David Vélez, o fundador do Nubank; Teresa e Candido Bracher, reconhecidos ambientalistas; e o Enseada, o family office dos Larragoiti. Mais recentemente, o fundo atraiu novos investidores – entre eles a Vale – e chegou a R$ 160 milhões. No momento, o Patria está em negociações com investidores institucionais internacionais. Outra frente de captação vem de instrumentos de capital catalítico – que aceitam maior risco, menor retorno ou prazos mais longos . No início do ano, o fundo foi um dos sete selecionados na chamada pública de mitigação climática que vai destinar R$ 4,3 bilhões em aportes do BNDESPar. Nessa frente, o veículo pode receber até R$ 500 milhões. Além disso, o Patria também vai acessar recursos do Fundo Clima e do terceiro leilão do Eco Invest. Os recursos do capital catalítico funcionam como uma espécie de colchão para atrair investidores. “O capital catalítico passa a ser uma camada de proteção. Nesse modelo, o dinheiro que pode ser ‘perdido’ é utilizado antes dos recursos do investidor tradicional,” disse Faria. A lógica adotada é que cada investidor também possa enxergar uma porta de entrada diferente para o mesmo ativo. Para uma empresa com metas de descarbonização e restauração, o projeto entrega atributos ambientais. É o caso da Vale, que entrou no fundo para acessar os créditos gerados pelo sequestro de carbono. Já para um investidor financeiro, a produção agrícola e a receita associada aos créditos ajudam a compor a equação de risco e retorno. “No nível da operação é um arranjo agroflorestal, no nível do fundo é um arranjo multifacetado de investidores entrando em cotas,” disse o executivo. Foi nesse desenho que o avocado ganhou espaço. Estima-se que o mercado global da fruta movimente cerca de US$ 20 bilhões por ano. O Brasil ocupa hoje a sétima posição entre os produtores, mas, na visão de Faria, tem condições para avançar bastante. “Quando você olha a questão de custo, competitividade e acesso a dinheiro, não há nenhuma razão para que o Brasil não esteja entre os três maiores produtores mundiais de avocado.” Para o Patria, os mercados europeu e asiático são o foco para a exportação. Em 2025, Japão e Chile passaram a importar a fruta do Brasil. A parceria com a Jaguacy, que cultiva 1200 hectares de avocado e atende clientes como Carrefour e Pão de Açúcar, garante não só a operação das fazendas como também o acesso à infraestrutura de processamento e aos canais de distribuição. A região de Águas de Santa Bárbara escolhida não foi por acaso. As propriedades estão em uma área de solo fértil, altitude adequada e disponibilidade de água, mas que também passou por ciclos de agricultura, pecuária e monoculturas que degradaram parte do território. O cultivo será feito em sistema agroflorestal, combinando as fileiras de avocado com espécies nativas, que protegem as árvores frutíferas contra potenciais danos causados pelo vento. Dos quase 1 mil hectares, a previsão é plantar cerca de 100 hectares neste semestre. A primeira colheita virá em quatro anos. O projeto também servirá como laboratório para o que pode vir depois. O Patria já identificou café e cacau como próximas culturas a serem desenvolvidas e vê espaço para levar o modelo a outros biomas. Para Faria, as mudanças climáticas estão tornando a produção de alimentos uma questão cada vez mais estratégica para o capital. A demanda global cresce, enquanto eventos climáticos mais frequentes aumentam o risco de choques de oferta. É essa combinação que transforma a agricultura resiliente em uma tese de investimento: produzir mais, restaurar áreas degradadas e, ao mesmo tempo, construir cadeias de alimentos menos vulneráveis às mudanças do clima. O avocado do Patria deverá ganhar mesas mundo afora. O carbono, por sua vez, fica como crédito para o planeta.

artigo.texto: With participation confirmed from 24 African countries and 45 countries globally, CMAS 2026 will bring together more than 100 speakers, over 50 investors, buyers and financiers, 20 African governments and more than 40 project developers in Kigali from 13 to 15 October. The diversity of participation reflects growing engagement with African carbon markets from governments, project developers, financiers and credit buyers. The international presence will bring African policymakers and projects into direct contact with organisations active across carbon markets globally. For Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance & Stakeholder Engagement for the Government of Nigeria, the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 represents an opportunity for continental participants to play a central role in determining how the market develops. “This gathering of the leading players in African carbon markets represents a continental ownership in driving the future of carbon markets shaped by Africans, for the benefit of Africa.” Investor and buyer participation will add an important commercial dimension to the gathering. Dedicated Investor Roundtables will provide focused opportunities for capital providers, buyers and project developers to engage directly, while meetings across the summit will allow participants to identify potential partnerships and areas for further engagement. More than 40 project developers and project representatives working across sectors including nature-based solutions, agriculture, waste, clean cooking and carbon removals will also participate, providing investors and buyers with direct exposure to projects from across the continent. For Maggie Kinyanjui, Sourcing Manager, Africa, Climate Impact Partners, greater engagement between project developers, buyers and investors is essential to building a stronger African carbon market. “Africa should not just participate in carbon markets. We should help shape them. The opportunity is to build a market that attracts capital, rewards integrity and ensures that value reaches the countries and communities delivering climate impact.” The timing also coincides with an active period for international carbon markets. These discussions will take place at a time when key international carbon market rules and mechanisms continue to evolve. The Article 6.4 Supervisory Body, which oversees the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, is holding its 23rd meeting this week in Bonn, immediately ahead of CMAS 2026. Amy Rhoades, Chief Communications & Engagement Officer, Carbon Standards, says meaningful engagement across the carbon value chain is critical to the growth of credible carbon removal solutions on the continent. “Africa isn’t waiting for global carbon markets to mature; it’s actively building them. At Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we’re not just sponsoring a conference, we’re engaging the policymakers, entrepreneurs, and buyers who are building the carbon removal ecosystem in Africa. That engagement is the future of credible CDR and that’s why Carbon Standards is in Kigali.” Against that international backdrop, discussions in Kigali will provide an opportunity for African governments and market participants to consider what developments in the global market mean in practice for the continent, while investors, buyers and project developers explore opportunities for greater cooperation. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and African Development Bank (AfDB) as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. With the summit now days away, Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director, says the breadth of participation has been particularly encouraging. “The real opportunity lies in bringing decision-makers, financiers, buyers and project developers into the same room. Those conversations can help unlock investment, strengthen project pipelines and accelerate the partnerships needed to scale African carbon markets.” The scale and diversity of participation heading to Kigali reflect a market increasingly attracting attention from governments, investors, buyers and project developers alike. As these groups come together over three days, the focus will shift from market ambition to the partnerships and transactions needed to move implementation forward. CMAS 2026 takes place from 13 to 15 October 2026 at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda.

artigo.texto: NBC’s comedy show “Saturday Night Live” mocked “Shark Tank” investor Kevin O’Leary and his plans to build the massive Stratos data center in Utah — with a fake O’Leary calling it “the most evil name of all time.” “All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God’s untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job,” actor James Austin Johnson said Saturday night from the show’s “Weekend Update” desk, wearing a bald cap to impersonate O’Leary, aka “Mr. Wonderful.” “Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who’s to say?” Johnson’s O’Leary continued in a calm voice echoing the real O’Leary’s cadence. “But on the flip side, it’s going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that’s great.” Anchor Colin Jost then noted that most Americans don’t want data centers near them, and Johnson’s O’Leary agreed, saying, “that’s why I’m building one in Utah.” He held up a map of Utah, with the Stratos site in Box Elder County ringed with a red target zone, which he said would be the area affected by noise and water pollution. “You have to understand — I don’t live there,” he said. Jost countered that other people do live there. “You’re missing the point,” the fake O’Leary replied. “That’s not real to me. … Those are Sims.” Johnson’s O’Leary then referenced one of the real O’Leary’s “Shark Tank” failures: “When I missed out on Scrub Daddy, I learned a very valuable lesson, which is I’m going to destroy the world.” Jost asked about the defamation lawsuit O’Leary is facing from activists protesting the Stratos project. The fake O’Leary noted that “yes, I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid Communist super-agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they’re not doesn’t mean they aren’t.” Last month, the real O’Leary’s lawyers filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that no “reasonable viewer” would have taken his claims that China funded his opposition as fact. Johnson’s O’Leary concluded the three-minute skit with another observation based on the real O’Leary’s “Shark Tank” experience: “When I missed out on Bombas socks, I could have gotten mad. But instead I made a decision: I’m going to make the future go away. And we’re doing just that in Utah.” Utahns by an overwhelming margin, 76%, don’t want more data centers built in the state, according to a survey released this month by Utah State University’s Community and Natural Resources Institute.

artigo.texto: Words by Oliver Milman photographs by michael hauptman Our world is already beset by a climate crisis, galloping biodiversity loss, and a plague of plastic that has reached nearly every waterway and mountaintop. It may be unfortunate timing, then, that another—and perhaps final—environmental frontier is now rapidly coming into view: space. A slew of industrial projects designed for Earth’s orbit or other celestial bodies are currently underway. Some, like mining the moon for helium or reflecting sunlight back to Earth after dark with giant mirrors, remain out-there aspirations that may never materialize. Others are moving more quickly. Some of the world’s wealthiest people are determined that even if they cannot yet colonize other planets, they will soon be able to encircle our own with fleets of space-based data centers. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin has applied to the Federal Communications Commission to launch 51,600 data centers, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX has even grander ambitions—a constellation of 1 million facilities, with testing set to begin next year. Google on October 1 launched Project Suncatcher, its orbital data center initiative exploring how to power AI in space, into low Earth orbit. The prospect of banishing data centers to space may appeal to people on Earth who abhor their explosive growth and decry their ravenous use of energy and water. In the United States, the issue has become so politically toxic that living next to a data center polls even worse than residing beside a nuclear plant. Musk has said space-based data centers will prove “ridiculously better” than their terrestrial counterparts. “Elon (Musk) and others in the industry are like, ‘Let’s take the data centers that no one likes in your backyard—it seems like there’s a lot of consensus on that—and put them into space where they won’t bother anyone,’” Jared Isaacman, administrator of NASA, said in August on the Pod Force One podcast. Isaacman has said separately that while countries like China escalate their space ambitions, the U.S. can win the “space race for sure, but the AI race, too.” The potential environmental payoff is substantial. The Department of Energy projects that data centers could account for as much as 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, driven largely by the growth of AI. A large terrestrial data center can require around 100 megawatts of power and around 200,000 gallons of water a day for cooling, according to the Government Accountability Office. Moving some of that computing into orbit could, in theory, reduce the need for new power infrastructure, freshwater, and land on Earth. In sun-synchronous orbit, satellites could also receive near-continuous sunlight, allowing them to generate solar power without the nighttime interruptions affecting solar farms on the ground. Space could also shift one of the most resource-intensive parts of computing: cooling. Rather than consuming freshwater to carry away heat, an orbital data center would use large radiators to release that heat into space, though cooling in a vacuum remains technically difficult. For proponents, the appeal is that networks of solar-powered satellites could eventually take on some of the computing now driving the construction of energy- and water-intensive facilities on Earth. Whether that produces a net environmental benefit depends on what it takes to manufacture, launch, maintain, and ultimately dispose of them. But some experts are more wary. “Many issues occur with data centers in space that wouldn’t happen on Earth,” said Daniel Capper, a professor of philosophy at the Metropolitan State University of Denver and a proponent of space environmentalism. Even if the daunting cost and logistics of launching data centers into orbit can be overcome, adding 1 million large structures to low Earth orbit raises uncomfortable questions about energy, debris, and what happens when those structures eventually fall back to Earth. “A land-based data center can’t fall on your head. If one falls in this way, upon a city or in the ocean causing a tsunami, we are in big trouble.” Space-based data centers would be roughly the size of a tennis court, with only a fraction of the area housing computing equipment. The rest would be devoted to shielding the hardware from radiation, dispersing heat, and generating power. Should large, 5-gigawatt data centers make it into orbit, the solar arrays required to power them would also be sprawling—measuring more than six square miles, according to Starcloud, a company developing space-based data centers. All of that would require hundreds of rocket launches, generating additional emissions while adding large satellites to a band of space already cluttered with human-made debris. Around 30,000 pieces of tracked debris currently hurtle through orbit at roughly 10 times the speed of a bullet, posing a threat to satellites and other infrastructure we depend on for everyday functions such as GPS. “We have already entered a period of unstable debris growth in low Earth orbit; the amount of stuff in orbit will continue to grow even without human intervention,” said Cole Donovan, an advocate for the Stand Up for Science group who previously worked for the U.S. government on a new “air traffic control” system for various space actors. Satellites are equipped with automated collision-avoidance systems, but adding another million large objects could increase the risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical chain reaction in which collisions create more debris, which in turn triggers further collisions until parts of orbit become impossible for new missions. “We are already at the beginning of Kessler syndrome; if it gets extreme we will have to remain grounded,” said Capper. artigo.texto: Peugeot is looking to bring back the spirit of its iconic RCZ coupe with the Peugeot RCZ Vision, a futuristic electric sports car concept that combines French design, advanced battery technology and a renewed focus on driving pleasure. Positioned as a successor to the original Peugeot RCZ, produced between 2009 and 2015, the RCZ Vision previews the brand’s vision for high-performance electric mobility. It introduces Peugeot’s new “Feline Future” design language while showcasing technologies intended to shape the company’s next generation of vehicles. The concept’s headline specifications include 500 horsepower, up to 600 km (373 miles) of range and a targeted energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km. It also features a solid-state battery developed with Factorial Energy and a 1,000-volt electrical architecture designed to deliver exceptionally fast charging. Peugeot has not presented the RCZ Vision as a conventional production-car launch. Instead, it serves as a design and technology manifesto, offering a glimpse of what future Peugeot models could look like. Peugeot RCZ Vision Revives an Iconic Coupe The original Peugeot RCZ became one of the French automaker’s most distinctive modern models thanks to its sculpted bodywork, low roofline and characteristic double-bubble roof design. Although production ended in 2015, the coupe has since developed a following among enthusiasts and collectors. The RCZ Vision revisits that heritage with a more futuristic interpretation. Its proportions combine a low, wide stance with muscular bodywork, a compact-looking glass cabin and flowing surfaces intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency. The concept also introduces Peugeot’s “Feline Future” design philosophy, built around five principles: freedom, courage, elegance, inner force and instinct. Together, these ideas aim to create a car that looks powerful without appearing unnecessarily aggressive. At the front, ultra-slim lighting elements reinterpret Peugeot’s signature three-claw light design. An illuminated emblem, a distinctive RCZ graphic and intricately detailed air intakes give the concept a dramatic appearance. The rear continues the same minimalist approach, with integrated three-claw lighting and an active spoiler that remains hidden when the car is stationary and deploys while driving to improve aerodynamic performance. Peugeot has also retained the original RCZ’s distinctive double-bubble styling, reinterpreting it with slimmer, seemingly floating roof arches. The glass-bubble concept extends across much of the vehicle, creating a light and futuristic silhouette. 500 HP and Up to 373 Miles of Electric Range Beyond its styling, the Peugeot RCZ Vision showcases an ambitious electric powertrain concept. Peugeot targets 500 horsepower and a driving range of up to 600 km, equivalent to approximately 373 miles. The company also cites energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km on the WLTP combined cycle, although the figure is marked as subject to confirmation. If achieved in practice, that combination would make the RCZ Vision an especially efficient proposition for a high-performance electric sports coupe. Its final range and consumption would, however, depend on the production specification, driving conditions and other factors. The concept is based on an architecture derived from Stellantis’ STLA One platform concept, designed to accommodate next-generation technologies and different battery solutions. A key highlight is the solid-state battery developed in collaboration with Factorial Energy. Solid-state batteries are attracting interest across the automotive industry because their potential advantages include higher energy density, reduced packaging requirements and improved charging performance. In the RCZ Vision, the battery is paired with a 1,000-volt electrical architecture. Peugeot targets a charging time of just 10 minutes to increase the battery’s state of charge from 10% to 80%. These figures describe the concept’s intended capabilities rather than verified performance from a production vehicle. Nevertheless, they illustrate Peugeot’s ambition to combine sports-car performance with more efficient energy use and shorter charging stops. Hypersquare Steering and Brake-by-Wire Technology The RCZ Vision is also a showcase for Peugeot’s next-generation driving technology, particularly its Hypersquare steering control and electronic vehicle-control systems. Hypersquare replaces the conventional round steering wheel with a distinctive rectangular control featuring four circular openings. The layout places key functions within easy reach, allowing the driver to keep their hands on the steering control. Combined with steer-by-wire technology, Hypersquare eliminates the traditional mechanical connection between the steering control and the front wheels. Instead, electronic systems manage steering inputs and adjust the steering ratio according to vehicle speed. At low speeds, the system is designed to make parking and tight manoeuvres easier by reducing the amount of steering input required. At higher speeds, the steering response is adjusted to provide greater stability and smoother control. The concept also introduces brake-by-wire technology, replacing the conventional hydraulic connection between the brake pedal and braking system with electronic control. Peugeot says this approach can improve braking precision and integrate regenerative braking more effectively, helping recover energy during deceleration. The RCZ Vision additionally previews Level 2++ automated-driving capabilities, including a hands-free function available on demand in city and highway environments. The precise operating conditions and availability of these features have not been detailed for a production vehicle. Importantly, Peugeot says the production version of Hypersquare will also feature in the next-generation Peugeot E-208, indicating that at least part of the technology is intended to extend beyond the concept itself. artigo.texto: UK bespoke raw materials company Avocet Materials Group is developing specialist lithium-ion battery components in Cheshire for high-performance applications including Formula One (F1), aerospace, defence, electric vehicles and energy storage, as it expands its advanced manufacturing and research capabilities. The family-owned business has established a 29-strong manufacturing and R&D operation in Holmes Chapel, producing components it says were previously manufactured only in Asia. It exports 99% of its battery products to international markets including China, Japan and the US. At the heart of its technology portfolio are lead tabs, small but critical metal components that connect a lithium-ion battery cell to an external circuit. Their properties can affect battery weight, conductivity and reliability, making precision manufacturing essential for demanding applications. One of Avocet’s innovations is Flyweight, a bimetallic lead tab designed for pouch cells and used in F1 battery applications to reduce battery system weight. The company is also developing DryTab, a next-generation surface technology that has secured government backing through the DRIVE35 programme. Avocet moved from specialist metals distribution into manufacturing during the Covid-19 pandemic. Supported by a £1.4m Innovate UK grant through the Advanced Propulsion Centre and further investment, it now operates through three businesses: Avocet Precision Metals, Avocet Battery Materials and Avocet Research Centre. Kieren Hall, CEO, said: “When you think that five years ago we didn’t manufacture anything, what we’ve achieved is pretty remarkable. We’ve built a manufacturing operation from scratch, developed our own technology and we’re now making specialist components for lithium-ion batteries in Cheshire for some of the most demanding applications in the world. “We’re exporting 99% of our battery products and selling into countries with some of the biggest battery industries in the world, including China and Japan. For a business of our size to be competing internationally at that level is something we’re incredibly proud of.” Turnover has grown from £1.5m to £3.5m, with sales increasing by around 25% this year. To support further expansion, Avocet is working with Made Smarter North West on manufacturing systems and digital infrastructure. The company has secured a £13,000 grant towards a £75,000 enterprise resource planning system, scheduled to go live in January 2027. The system will integrate operations across the business and support productivity and capacity growth. Avocet is also exploring automated inspection technology and artificial intelligence to improve manufacturing efficiency and decision-making as it develops its battery technology portfolio. artigo.texto: Baterias já são mais baratas que turbinas a gás de data centers Relatório da Wood Mackenzie mostra que baterias de 4 horas custam menos que turbinas a gás em todos os 43 mercados analisados. A tendência deve se acelerar. Existe um consenso quase universal de que a inteligência artificial vai consumir quantidades absurdas de energia nos próximos anos. O debate, até agora, girava em torno de qual fonte supriria essa demanda. Um novo relatório da consultoria Wood Mackenzie traz uma resposta que pode surpreender: baterias de armazenamento já são mais baratas que as turbinas a gás usadas por boa parte dos data centers no mundo. A conclusão vale para todos os continentes e cada um dos 43 mercados analisados pela consultoria. Baterias com duração de quatro horas custam menos que turbinas de ciclo aberto a gás natural. E a tendência é de divergência crescente: o custo da eletricidade armazenada em baterias deve continuar caindo, enquanto o da geração a gás tende a encarecer nas próximas décadas. Por que as turbinas a gás ficaram tão caras A explicação passa diretamente pela corrida da IA. Desenvolvedores de data centers voltados para inteligência artificial têm comprado qualquer modelo de turbina disponível no mercado, pressionando preços para cima. O efeito é mais agudo nas turbinas de ciclo aberto, que são mais simples de fabricar, porém menos eficientes e mais caras de operar. Essas turbinas costumam ser usadas por concessionárias como plantas de pico, acionadas em momentos de alta demanda. Quando o preço desses equipamentos sobe, o custo repassa para toda a cadeia elétrica. Mesmo sendo mais simples, turbinas de ciclo aberto agora levam de dois a quatro anos para serem entregues. As de ciclo fechado, mais eficientes, têm filas que se estendem até o início da década de 2030. O resultado: os preços de novas usinas a gás natural dispararam em praticamente todas as categorias. Como mostramos em nossa cobertura sobre infraestrutura tecnológica, a demanda por energia dos data centers já pressiona tarifas elétricas nos Estados Unidos e em outros mercados. Solar é a energia nova mais barata do mundo O relatório da Wood Mackenzie traz outro dado relevante: a energia solar já é a forma mais barata de nova geração em todos os mercados analisados. Inclusive na América do Norte, apesar das tarifas de importação e restrições comerciais que pressionam o setor. Nos Estados Unidos, projetos solares em escala de concessionária (utility-scale) estão relativamente protegidos no curto prazo. Cerca de 168 gigawatts em capacidade se beneficiam de cláusulas de proteção (safe-harbor provisions) que mantêm créditos fiscais para projetos já iniciados ou concluídos antes do fim de 2027. Na prática, isso significa que boa parte da expansão solar americana já contratada não será afetada pelas oscilações regulatórias atuais. Quem acompanha o impacto de políticas energéticas nos mercados financeiros sabe que essa previsibilidade regulatória é decisiva para a alocação de capital em infraestrutura. O mapa global da transição energética em data centers Os números regionais reforçam a tese de que a transição é estrutural, não conjuntural. No Oriente Médio e na África, baterias de quatro horas devem ser 33% mais baratas que turbinas de pico a gás até 2035, deslocando a geração a gás por questões puramente econômicas em cada mercado da região. Na China, os custos de armazenamento de energia são 55% inferiores aos dos países vizinhos. Isso dá à indústria chinesa uma vantagem competitiva significativa na corrida pela infraestrutura de IA, um ponto que frequentemente escapa ao debate focado apenas em chips e modelos de linguagem. “Essa mudança econômica é decisiva e está se ampliando”, afirmou Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, analista principal da Wood Mackenzie, no comunicado que acompanha o relatório. O que isso significa para a infraestrutura de IA A consequência prática é profunda. Até agora, grande parte dos projetos de data centers para IA vinham sendo planejados com geração a gás como pilar energético. Empresas como Microsoft, Google e Amazon fecharam contratos bilionários envolvendo usinas nucleares e a gás para garantir fornecimento estável. Com baterias mais baratas e tempos de entrega menores que os das turbinas, a equação muda. Baterias de quatro horas não substituem geração de base, é verdade. Elas são ideais para cobrir picos de demanda, exatamente o papel que as turbinas de ciclo aberto desempenham. Nessa função específica, a competição já está decidida em termos de custo. Para investidores que acompanham o setor de tecnologia e infraestrutura digital, o sinal é claro: os próximos data centers provavelmente terão mais baterias e painéis solares do que turbinas a gás. Isso altera a dinâmica de investimento em toda a cadeia, dos fabricantes de células de lítio às concessionárias de energia. O gás natural perde espaço, mas não desaparece É importante contextualizar. O relatório da Wood Mackenzie não decreta o fim do gás natural na geração elétrica. Turbinas de ciclo fechado, mais eficientes e capazes de operar como geração de base, seguem relevantes. O que muda é a lógica das plantas de pico: onde antes se instalava uma turbina simples para cobrir momentos de alta demanda, agora faz mais sentido econômico instalar baterias. No mercado americano, a demanda por gás natural deve se estreitar na próxima década, segundo a consultoria. Não por regulação ambiental, mas por economia pura. Quando a alternativa limpa é também a mais barata, a transição deixa de depender de subsídios ou vontade política. O dado mais revelador do relatório talvez seja esse: a virada não é projetada para o futuro. Ela já aconteceu. Em todos os 43 mercados analisados, sem exceção, armazenar energia em baterias custa menos que gerar com turbinas a gás de ciclo aberto. A pergunta agora é a velocidade com que o mercado de data centers vai absorver essa realidade. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. CATL, SERES Deepen Strategic Partnership On October 10, 2026, CATL and SERES Group signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement in Chongqing. All AITO-branded vehicles have been equipped with CATL batteries since the brand's launch, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million vehicles. The two companies will continue their full-range battery partnership and deepen cooperation in three areas: Production capacity: Accelerate Phase II construction of the battery plant within SERES' super factory, with planned annual capacity of 10–12 GWh. Combined annual capacity for Phases I and II will exceed 20 GWh once completed. Charging services: Cooperate on fast-charging networks and battery services to build a full-lifecycle service system. Global expansion: Jointly explore overseas markets in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. Geely Galaxy ZJ700 Hits Market On October 10, 2026, Geely officially launched the Galaxy ZJ700, its first AI-powered all-terrain SUV, offering six variants. Built on Geely's GTA new-energy off-road architecture, the SUV combines advanced driver assistance, off-road capability and premium comfort. Its Qiankun H7 driver-assistance system uses a Thor-U chip delivering 700 TOPS of computing power. The sensor suite includes a 192-line LiDAR, three millimeter-wave radars, 11 high-definition cameras, 12 ultrasonic radars and two wading radars. The vehicle supports highway and urban Navigation on Autopilot (NOA), point-to-point parking navigation and multi-scenario automated parking assistance. Power comes from Geely's Leishen EM-T off-road hybrid system, combining a 2.0TD off-road hybrid engine with electric motors. Key performance figures include: Combined power: 830 kW Battery capacity: 47.14 kWh Pure electric range: 305 km Combined range: 1,770 km Fast charging: 10% to 80% in 10 minutes, with 6C charging support Wading depth: 800 mm Additional off-road features include mechanical differential locks and dual-chamber closed air suspension with CCD continuously variable damping. The SUV also supports a minimum turning radius of 3.36 meters and a "Waltz Turn" maneuver. GEENER, Wolfspeed Ink Deal Wolfspeed and GEENER recently signed a memorandum of understanding in Hangzhou to cooperate on silicon carbide (SiC) power modules. GEENER will prioritize Wolfspeed's SiC bare dies for integration into its next-generation power module platform, initially targeting applications such as main inverters for new-energy vehicles. Wolfspeed will leverage its established 200 mm SiC production lines to develop bare dies that meet or exceed GEENER's performance requirements, while providing stable supply and commercial support. The two companies will jointly engage with leading Chinese automakers on high-voltage electric vehicle platforms, aiming to secure vehicle design wins. The partnership combines Wolfspeed's SiC chip technology and manufacturing capacity with GEENER's expertise in module design, packaging and reliability validation. Beyond electric vehicles, the companies also see potential applications in AI data centers, where reliable power modules and stable supply are increasingly important.

artigo.texto: User-side energy storage is critical to low-carbon energy deployment across residential, commercial, industrial and transportation sectors, driving rising demand for energy-storage technologies featuring high energy density and safety. Tin-based anodes represent promising candidates for high-energy-density flow batteries, owing to their high theoretical specific capacity, high solubility, dendrite-free deposition behaviour, and the potential for four-electron transfer. Nevertheless, the conversion of Sn4+ to metallic Sn proceeds via two sequential electrochemical reactions: Sn4+/Sn2+ and Sn2+/Sn0. The Sn4+/Sn2+ conversion suffers from high reorganization energy, sluggish reaction kinetics and poor reversibility, which restricts access to the full four-electron capacity. To tackle this challenge, a research team led by Prof. LI Xianfeng from the Dalian Institute of Chemical Sciences (DICP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with Prof. CHEN Shengli from Wuhan University, has developed a coordination-structure modulation strategy to boost the kinetics and reversibility of tin redox reactions, realizing highly reversible four-electron transfer. The study was published in Nature Chemistry on Oct. 9. The researchers incorporated iodide ions into a highly soluble tin tetrachloride (SnCl4) electrolyte to build a coordination environment comprising both SnCl62- and SnI62- species. SnI62- reduces the reorganization energy for Sn4+/Sn2+ electron transfer, enabling faster and more reversible redox reactions, whereas SnCl62- preserves the high solubility of tin salts within the electrolyte. This mechanism sustains continuous four-electron transfer from Sn4+ to Sn0 via the Sn2+ intermediate state. Using this strategy, the potential gap between the Sn4+/Sn2+ redox peaks narrowed from 978â¯mV under a chloride-dominated coordination environment to 97â¯mV in the iodide-containing system. The team also detected reduced charge-transfer impedance, indicating improved electrochemical kinetics. To assess the strategy in practical battery hardware, the researchers paired the highly reversible Sn4+/Sn0 anode with a Br-/Br2 cathode to construct a Sn-Br flow battery. At a current density of 40â¯mAâ¯cm-2, the battery delivered an energy efficiency of 89â¯%. The anode electrolyte attained a volumetric capacity density of 227 Ah L-1, corresponding to an energy density of 205 Wh L-1. The researchers further scaled up the technology and demonstrated its performance in a kilowatt-scale stack. The stack maintained stable operation for over 1â¯000â¯hours, highlighting the promise of this coordination-engineering approach for developing high-energy-density flow batteries.

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania launches interactive data center permit tracker amid environmental concerns PENNSYLVANIA (WHP) — Pennsylvania has launched a public map that will allow the public to track proposed data centers that are seeking environmental permits. The data center tracker is operated by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). The interactive map shows the locations of proposed data center projects in the Commonwealth and includes a list of environmental permits for each project and their status. Data centers have continued to be a point of contention in Pennsylvania, including as a talking point in the debate between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Shapiro started off the debate saying he's been listening to concerns of the people, and after doing so, drafted the "strictest guardrail in the nation" for data centers. He said it is important to protect air and water and that it must include local benefits. Meanwhile, Garrity discussed individual cases where people are fighting against data centers in their own backyard. Over the weekend, the Swatara Township Board of Commissioners approved community benefits agreements for a pair of proposed data centers. RELATED | Swatara Township approves community benefits plan for data center projects The types of permits and/or authorizations often associated with large-scale data centers include: - Earth disturbance and stormwater management - Wetland and waterway encroachment - Storage tanks - Air quality - Sewage facilities planning - Clean water To track the status of a permit authorization, use the DEP's permit tracker.
