artigo.texto: - Aito will continue using CATL batteries across its lineup, with total annual capacity set to exceed 20 GWh after a joint project is completed. - The companies will also collaborate on supercharging networks and battery services, and jointly pursue markets in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement with Seres (HKEX: 9927) to expand battery production capacity for the automaker's Aito brand and extend their partnership into charging services and overseas markets. The companies signed the agreement on Saturday in Chongqing, where Seres is headquartered. Aito will continue using CATL batteries across its lineup over the long term, reinforcing their existing supply relationship. Aito has used CATL batteries in all its models since the brand's inception, and cumulative deliveries have surpassed 1.2 million vehicles, the Chinese battery giant said in a statement. Capacity expansion is a key part of the agreement. The companies will accelerate construction of the second phase of their "plant-in-plant" project at the Seres plant, with planned annual capacity of 10 to 12 GWh. Once the second phase is completed, combined annual capacity across both phases will exceed 20 GWh. CATL said the companies aim to improve supply chain resilience and competitiveness by concentrating production at the site. The expansion builds on their model of producing batteries within an auto assembly plant, integrating battery system production with Aito vehicle manufacturing at the same site. On June 30, 2025, CATL began operating 2 CTP (cell-to-pack) 2.0 battery pack production lines at the Seres plant, providing a local supply of battery systems for Aito vehicles. The project marked CATL's first production base in Chongqing and its first use of the "plant-in-plant" model. The latest agreement will expand that manufacturing footprint. Beyond capacity expansion, the companies will collaborate on supercharging networks and battery services to build a service system covering the full battery lifecycle. They will also jointly pursue overseas markets including Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, according to CATL's statement. The announcement did not disclose the agreement's duration or when the second phase would begin operations. It provided no details on the models or implementation plans involved in the overseas cooperation. Seres also recently renewed its Aito partnership with Huawei, another key partner. The companies signed a new 5-year cooperation agreement in Shenzhen on September 30 to jointly develop the Aito business. Under arrangements announced on October 1, Huawei and Seres will jointly establish a dedicated Aito team and continue developing brand-specific operations to strengthen the brand and improve customer service. For CATL, the agreement further cements its long-term supply relationship with Aito. The company remains the world's largest EV battery supplier. CATL's global EV battery installations reached 333.0 GWh in the first 8 months of this year, up 25.2% from a year earlier, giving it a 39.4% market share, according to data released on October 2 by South Korean market researcher SNE Research.

artigo.texto: BYD Explores 1,500kW Ultra-Fast EV Charging for Pakistan Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer BYD is in talks to introduce its cutting-edge 1,500kW ultra-fast charging technology in Pakistan. These discussions are ongoing with Mega Motor Company, a local automotive player, as BYD assesses the viability of deploying this advanced charging system within the country’s evolving infrastructure. Next-Generation Charging Technology BYD’s new charging platform integrates the second-generation Blade Battery with its FLASH Charging technology, capable of delivering up to 1,500kW through a single connector. This allows compatible EVs to recharge from 10% to 70% battery capacity in just five minutes, and reach up to 97% in nine minutes under optimal conditions. Even in cold climates of -30°C, the system can charge a vehicle from 20% to 97% within 12 minutes. However, these ultra-fast charging speeds are limited to vehicles designed specifically for BYD’s new battery and charging system. Existing BYD models available in Pakistan may not achieve such rapid recharge rates, as actual performance depends on a vehicle’s battery design and maximum supported charging power. Strategic Growth and Local Production In addition to technology deployment, BYD is planning to expand its footprint in Pakistan through a local assembly facility scheduled to commence operations in the latter half of 2026. The plant is expected to produce approximately 25,000 vehicles annually, with scalable capacity to double production as demand grows. BYD Vice President Liu Xueliang emphasized that the availability of local infrastructure and stakeholder feedback will shape the decision to launch the ultra-fast charging network. “The rollout depends largely on local readiness and future vehicle plans,” Liu noted, signaling a cautious but optimistic approach. Significance for Pakistan’s EV Market As Pakistan gradually embraces electric mobility, the introduction of high-capacity charging stations could alleviate major obstacles such as long charging times and limited infrastructure. These improvements may accelerate EV adoption by providing more convenience for consumers and encouraging investment in the sector. By exploring this technology and establishing local manufacturing, BYD is positioning itself as a leading player in Pakistan’s burgeoning EV landscape, which could contribute to cleaner transportation and reduced reliance on fossil fuels. While no official timeline has been confirmed for either the ultra-fast charger rollout or vehicle production start, these developments mark a potential turning point in Pakistan’s electric vehicle ecosystem.

artigo.texto: In Bessemer, Alabama, a secrecy pact with the developer of a proposed $14.5 billion data center didn’t just keep city officials quiet. It required them to destroy records. In Salem, Oregon, a city council member learned of her city’s nondisclosure agreement only when the public did. In Pine Island, Minnesota, officials knew about a project for two years before residents heard a word. One resident told lawmakers the democratic process there had been “hijacked by big tech.” These aren’t isolated lapses. That’s how the artificial intelligence boom is being built: deals negotiated behind closed doors, with elected officials contractually barred from telling constituents what enterprise is coming, how much electricity and water the facility will consume, and what tax breaks it will get. The AI train has left the station. Secrecy is a choice, and it’s the wrong one. When University of Mary Washington sociologist Eric Bonds filed public records requests across Virginia, the nation’s data center capital, he found nondisclosure agreements in 25 of 31 localities. Why would any official sign away the public’s right to know? Towns and states are competing for these investments, and a developer that doesn’t get its secrecy can take its billions elsewhere. Red and blue states alike have signed. And the pushback is just as bipartisan: Republicans and Democrats in Congress have joined forces on a bill to ban the agreements. What do these contracts hide? Sometimes just the business’s name. In Spotsylvania County, Virginia, an agreement with Amazon kept the company’s water use confidential. Residents drink from that same public system, yet they couldn’t find out how much Amazon would draw from it. The industry’s argument isn’t frivolous. Once landowners learn a data center is the buyer, prices soar, Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition told Spotlight PA. Fair enough, for a land deal. That doesn’t require hiding a facility’s water and power use from the people who will live beside it. Microsoft said in March that it would end its nondisclosure agreements with local governments. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman has since written that the company “ no longer use(s) nondisclosure agreements with the government agencies” it works with. Distrust breeds backlash: Garman counts more than 100 data center moratoriums under consideration nationwide. In Monterey Park, outside Los Angeles, 88% of voters banned data centers outright. Ending nondisclosure agreements only lets us see the bill. It doesn’t decide who pays it. That’s settled piecemeal, by utility commissions, county boards and water agencies, each with its own rules. Government often approves a data center with the same scrutiny as a shopping mall, by zoning boards never designed to handle infrastructure of national consequence. We’ve done this before. America didn’t build the interstate highway system by letting every county haggle over asphalt. It set national standards and built one network. The AI build-out deserves the same. Ohio offers a start. When data center demand outran central Ohio’s grid, regulators required large new facilities to pay for at least 85% of their expected power, for up to 12 years, whether they use it or not. The rules weeded out speculative projects, let new hookups resume, and aim to keep households from paying for power some server farm has reserved. Manufacturers have challenged it in court. However, it answers the question nondisclosure agreements never do: Who pays? California has gone further. Laws by San Diego state Sen. Steve Padilla and others order regulators to set separate electricity rates so data centers, not households, cover their grid upgrades, and require developers to report projected power demand when seeking local permits. Pima County, Arizona, went after the secrecy itself, capping nondisclosure agreements at two years and requiring disclosure at least 90 days before any county vote. Now, take these models national. Permit server farms like power plants. Before any council or county board approves a land sale, rezoning or tax break, require developers to disclose power, water and incentives. And make data centers pay. The servers are coming either way. What’s still up for a vote is whether Americans get to see the deal, and whether they’re the ones stuck paying for it.

artigo.texto: Ucranianos usaram drones para atingir três dos maiores data centers da Yandex, provocando quedas de serviço que revelam fragilidades na estratégia digital russa. Como começou a campanha de drones russos contra a Ucrânia? Em setembro passado, a Rússia iniciou uma série de ataques aéreos contra infraestruturas críticas ucranianas, incluindo centros de dados e redes de telefonia móvel. O objetivo declarado era interromper comunicações e limitar o acesso à internet em Kiev, afetando cerca de cem mil residências. Esses ataques faziam parte de um plano maior que também visava a rede elétrica, ferrovias e até blocos residenciais. Qual foi a reação da Ucrânia aos ataques russos? Como resposta direta, a Ucrânia passou a mirar instalações russas que sustentam serviços digitais essenciais. Em outubro, drones ucranianos atingiram um data center da Yandex na região de Sasovo, ao sudeste de Moscou, danificando equipamentos que hospedam dois dos três supercomputadores usados para treinar o modelo de IA YandexGPT. Que importância têm os supercomputadores da Yandex? Os dois sistemas afetados – batizados de Chervonenkis e Lyapunov – são baseados em gpus nvidia a100, reconhecidas pela alta performance em tarefas de aprendizado de máquina. O Chervonenkis registra cerca de 29,4 petaflops, ocupando a posição 101 no ranking Top500 de supercomputadores, enquanto o Lyapunov oferece 20,0 petaflops, posicionando‑se em 161. Essa capacidade permite à Yandex desenvolver modelos de linguagem avançados, aproximando‑se do que empresas como Google e Microsoft oferecem. Por que a infraestrutura russa parece vulnerável? Especialistas ligados ao círculo pró‑Kremlin, citados por pesquisadores independentes como ChrisO_wiki, alertam que a economia digital da Rússia está excessivamente centralizada. A maioria dos serviços de nuvem, busca e IA está concentrada em poucos data centers controlados por gigantes como a Yandex. Quando esses pontos críticos são atingidos, o efeito dominó pode comprometer desde serviços de streaming até plataformas de pagamento. O que o modelo descentralizado da Ucrânia oferece? A Ucrânia tem investido em soluções distribuídas, com provedores menores e redes peer‑to‑peer que dificultam a interrupção total. Essa arquitetura resiliente pode se tornar um exemplo para outros países que buscam reduzir a dependência de grandes provedores e melhorar a segurança nacional. Quais são as possíveis consequências para os usuários russos? - Interrupções temporárias em serviços de busca, mapas e assistentes virtuais da Yandex. - Impacto nas plataformas de e‑commerce que dependem da infraestrutura de nuvem da empresa. - Risco de atrasos nas atualizações de modelos de IA, prejudicando a competitividade da Rússia no mercado global. - Pressão para que o governo russo invista em redundância e diversificação de provedores. Como a comunidade tech brasileira deve interpretar esse conflito? Para os profissionais e entusiastas de tecnologia no Brasil, o episódio serve como alerta sobre a importância da arquitetura distribuída. Empresas que ainda dependem de um único provedor de nuvem podem considerar estratégias de multi‑cloud ou edge computing para mitigar riscos semelhantes. Além disso, o caso evidencia que a guerra digital pode ser tão decisiva quanto os combates tradicionais, influenciando políticas de segurança cibernética em todo o mundo. O que ainda não está claro sobre os danos aos supercomputadores? Até o momento, não há informações oficiais sobre o grau de comprometimento dos chips Nvidia A100 dentro dos sistemas Chervonenkis e Lyapunov. A complexidade de reparar ou substituir esses componentes pode levar semanas, e a Yandex ainda não divulgou um plano de recuperação detalhado. Para ficar no radar Os próximos dias serão críticos para observar como a Rússia reagirá a esses ataques. Se a estratégia de retaliação incluir novas ofensivas cibernéticas ou reforço de defesas físicas, o cenário digital da região pode mudar rapidamente. Enquanto isso, profissionais de TI no Brasil podem usar o caso como estudo de caso para reforçar a importância de arquiteturas resilientes e de um planejamento de continuidade de negócios robusto.

artigo.texto: BYD has launched its brand-new Festive Edition Sealion 7 SUV in India, which is priced at Rs. 50.60 lakh ex-showroom. The new edition is based on the premium trim and is limited to 150 units. BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition The ultra-limited Festive Edition (150 units) was specifically introduced to capitalise on the Indian festive shopping season. It offers high-end buyers exclusivity through a unique Tan and Black interior treatment, maintaining momentum for a model that has quickly become one of BYD India's top sellers. Interior and Exterior Features The Sealion 7 festive edition features an 82.56 kWh Blade Battery and a rear-mounted electric motor that delivers 230 kW (308 hp) and 380 Nm of torque. The electric SUV can accelerate from 0 to 100 kmph in 6.7 seconds and has a claimed driving range of 567 km under the NEDC testing cycle. The Electric SUV is equipped with BYD's Cell-to-Body (CTB) technology, which integrates the battery pack into the vehicle's structural architecture. The festive edition also features torque adaptation control, which manages torque delivery based on traction conditions. These features were already seen in the premium model. The car comes with a 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen infotainment system, quilted Nappa leather seats, and a panoramic glass roof with an electric sunshade. It also comes with a dual-tone cabin treatment. It has 11 airbags and a five-star Euro NCAP rating. Other attributes include a DYNAUDIO system, ventilated front seats, driver's memory seats, a 360 camera, an ADAS suite, a panoramic glass roof, a powered tailgate, double-glazed glass, and a 12-speaker system. The Sealion 7 measures 4,830 mm in length, 1,925 mm in width, and 1,620 mm in height, with a 2,930 mm wheelbase. The cargo capacity is 500 litres at the back, expandable to 1,789 litres, and the frunk holds 58 litres. The Sealion 7 Festive Edition extends that approach, bringing a distinctive Tan & Black interior to the premium variant in a limited run for the festive season. At its core, it retains the technology, safety and performance that define the Sealion 7, while offering customers a differentiated expression of the model. Its biggest strengths are the Blade Battery, premium interior, 308 bhp performance and extensive equipment. The main point to remember is that this special edition is essentially the existing Premium variant with a different cabin colour scheme.

artigo.texto: Data center boom puts Republicans in a bind before midterm elections A year ago, there weren't many voters talking about data centers. Now, the massive facilities being built to satisfy the enormous computing needs of the AI boom have become one of the most explosive issues of the 2026 midterms, and their construction is opening a divide between the Trump administration and Republicans running in state and federal races this fall. When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, most data centers were being built in blue states. But by 2025, 68% of data centers online were in red states. Now, 75% of data centers under construction and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly Republican states, according to new data from Cleanview Research, an independent energy market intelligence company tracking data center development. "Red states have more of a history of accepting large, energy intensive, infrastructure projects — even those that might have detrimental effects on communities," said Chris Millay, a data center analyst at the macroeconomic consultancy Greenmantle. He also points to the relative lack of environmental regulation and the availability of open land as reasons rural states are receiving more investment. President Trump sees the AI race as critical to the economy and national security, and he's one of data centers' biggest boosters. At a recent Ohio rally, he said of data centers, "We want them … look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio — you can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." He has repeatedly dismissed public opposition to data centers, posting on Truth Social that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." Mr. Trump has also resisted regulation, though he has called on developers to give back to local communities through education, lower taxes, job creation and energy cost protections. Red states may be hosting most of the boom, and increasingly, communities living next to data centers are pushing back. People who live near data centers have reported concerns about their property values, noise, higher energy bills and resource depletion. Meanwhile, calls for moratoriums are spreading through communities across the country. Overall, opposition to data centers outweighs support by 30 points, with polls showing the majority of Republicans oppose the construction of data centers near them. "It's such a consensus issue it's really impossible to take the other side," said Millay. "When voters see a politician who supports data centers, they think, 'Well, how am I going to trust him with my job?'" Some of the president's closest allies have begun to break with him on the issue. In Texas, which has the most data centers under construction, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott has paused environmental permits and grid connections for new data centers. Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa. In Texas' tight Senate race, the Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers. He has also said they should be held criminally liable if they power AI chatbots that endanger children. Data centers seem to be the single issue where Democratic and Republican candidates sound nearly identical. In Ohio, Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in a press release, "I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers." Her GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, has gone further. He vowed to "issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio," and to keep that pause in place until lawmakers pass his "Ohioans-First" law, which would require data centers to provide free electricity to surrounding residents. A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that data centers are a weak point for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, with voters favoring his opponent by an 11-point margin on the issue. Campaigns have spent $45 million this year on ads that mention data centers — most of them in opposition — according to AdImpact. In Georgia, where candidates have spent nearly $13 million on ads mentioning data centers — more than any other state — the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, is sticking with Mr. Trump. While the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, is calling for a temporary moratorium on construction, Jackson says the decision should be left up to local officials. Jackson made the case for data centers at a recent press conference, saying he wanted "to educate people on the benefit if they want [a data center]." Some counties, he said, expect they "will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in." Effingham County, where OpenAI plans a $20 billion data center, has pledged to use some of that revenue to cut homeowners' property taxes. Because most of the next wave of data centers is largely planned in states Mr. Trump won in 2024, the choices Republican candidates make, siding with voters or with the president, could decide whether those projects are paused, made more expensive or even canceled.

artigo.texto: For luxury electric cars, longer range often comes with a familiar compromise: a bigger battery adds weight. Solid-state technology could help ease that trade-off by storing more energy without requiring a heavier pack. BYD’s upcoming Yangwang executive sedan brings that possibility into the ultra-luxury conversation. Spotted testing in China, the roughly 5.5-meter (about 18 feet) vehicle combines coach doors and imposing proportions with reports that it could carry solid-state batteries. BYD has not confirmed that specification. While its appearance draws comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom, the battery question connects it to a broader development effort. BMW and Mercedes-Benz are already using electric sedans to investigate how advanced cells perform beyond the laboratory. What changes inside the battery? The difference begins with the electrolyte, which allows lithium ions to move between electrodes during charging and discharging. Conventional lithium-ion cells typically use a liquid electrolyte. All-solid-state designs replace that liquid with a solid material. This change can support electrode materials such as lithium metal, potentially increasing the energy stored for a given battery weight. For an electric car, that could mean longer range without simply adding more battery mass. Mercedes-Benz identifies higher energy density as a key benefit of its solid-state development work. More from Transportation See All Safety is another potential advantage. According to the US Department of Energy, solid electrolytes are less prone to leakage when damaged, although a complete battery’s performance still depends on its materials and construction. None of these possibilities establishes the Yangwang sedan’s range or charging speed. Those figures require confirmed specifications and testing. How Yangwang supports BYD’s luxury push Yangwang occupies the highest tier of BYD’s lineup, above Denza, and showcases technologies such as the company’s quad-motor e4 platform. The upcoming sedan extends that role into the executive segment. Its long wheelbase, boxy profile and coach doors introduce styling associated with established luxury flagships, giving BYD’s technological ambitions a more traditional exterior. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing described it as “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” The combination suggests a strategy built around luxury design and technological differentiation. A solid-state battery could strengthen that positioning, but its inclusion remains unconfirmed. What road tests actually demonstrate BMW announced in May 2025 that an i7 prototype near Munich was testing Solid Power’s all-solid-state cells. Engineers are examining cell expansion, pressure control and temperature management, with BMW acknowledging that further development is needed for a competitive complete battery system. Mercedes-Benz demonstrated another step in August 2025. An EQS prototype fitted with Factorial lithium-metal solid-state cells traveled 1,205 kilometers (748.8 miles) without recharging. Mercedes reported 25 percent more usable battery energy with comparable pack size and weight. These were development results, rather than specifications for a car available to buyers. Such tests show progress while revealing the engineering work still involved. For BYD, the next step is confirmation of what powers its flagship, followed by evidence that the battery can deliver alongside the luxury experience.

artigo.texto: Moscou, Rússia, 13 de outubro de 2026 – TASS – A gigante russa do setor de tecnologia Yandex teve a infraestrutura de seu centro de dados gravemente danificada na região de Vladimir, nas proximidades da capital Moscou, após um ataque direcionado promovido por drones ucranianos. A ofensiva registrada no domingo (11) forçou a paralisação completa das operações na unidade afetada, resultando no bloqueio instantâneo e na indisponibilidade de serviços populares da plataforma, como aplicativos de transporte por aplicativo e entregas de refeições. Os impactos do ataque transpassaram as fronteiras nacionais e atingiram nações vizinhas da Ásia Central, como o Cazaquistão e o Quirguistão, onde usuários relataram instabilidade e interrupção parcial no funcionamento de diversos ecossistemas digitais da empresa. O bombardeio representa o terceiro ataque coordenado contra instalações estratégicas da empresa tecnológica em poucos dias, após unidades no centro da região de Ryazan terem sido atingidas na quinta-feira (8) e outra instalação na região de Kaluga ter sido alvo na sexta-feira (9). As incursões táticas ucranianas integram uma estratégia deliberada de retaliação contra a infraestrutura de dados russa em resposta aos contínuos bombardeios efetuados contra centros de tecnologia e processamento de informações na Ucrânia. artigo.texto: South Korea plans to launch the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) in 2027 to facilitate trading in carbon credits generated by overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The system will classify credits according to host-country approval, use blockchain to record key project information and rely on the Korea Exchange (KRX) for trading. The government is also considering digital-asset-based credit issuance and links with its domestic emissions trading scheme. Key Overview - Launch target: 2027. - Market: Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM). - Trading platform: Korea Exchange (KRX). - Credit categories: GVCM A and GVCM NA. - Technology: Blockchain-based records of key project and emissions-reduction information. - Future options: Digital-asset issuance and possible links with South Korea’s domestic emissions trading scheme. - International cooperation: Participation by other countries and potential conversion of selected World Bank and Green Climate Fund project outcomes into GVCM credits. South Korea Prepares to Launch an International Carbon Market South Korea is preparing to establish an international marketplace for carbon credits generated through overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects, with full operations targeted for 2027. The initiative, called the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM), is designed to support the issuance and trading of credits while addressing concerns about the credibility and consistency of carbon markets. The government discussed the detailed implementation plan at a ministerial meeting on international economic affairs on 12 October 2026, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il. Under the proposed system, verified emissions-reduction outcomes from overseas projects will be converted into carbon credits that can be traded through the Korea Exchange. Depending on the relevant approvals, the credits could support corporate environmental activities and certain regulatory obligations, including national climate targets. The initiative represents a move beyond a market limited to voluntary corporate offsetting. The government has replaced the earlier name, Global Voluntary Carbon Market, with Global Verified Carbon Market to reflect the broader intended uses of eligible credits. Two Credit Categories Will Determine How Credits Can Be Used A central feature of the framework is the distinction between credits approved for international transfer by the host country and those without that approval. Credits classified as GVCM A will be eligible for specified compliance uses, including contributions towards the investing country’s nationally determined contribution (NDC) and compliance with international aviation requirements under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). They may also support corporate environmental, social and governance activities. Credits classified as GVCM NA will initially be restricted to voluntary corporate environmental activities. Their permitted uses could expand if the host country subsequently grants the required transfer approval. This distinction matters because approval by the country hosting a carbon-reduction project affects whether the resulting credits can be used towards international climate commitments. It also provides a basis for separating credits intended for voluntary claims from those eligible for specified compliance purposes. The two categories of carbon credits are therefore central to the proposed market’s structure and the conditions under which buyers can use the credits they acquire. Blockchain Records to Support Credit Credibility South Korea plans to use blockchain technology to strengthen the traceability of carbon credits. Key information, including project operators and emissions-reduction volumes, will be recorded on the blockchain to help establish a more transparent record of the credits issued. The system is intended to improve confidence in transactions in a market where the credibility of claimed emissions reductions has been a longstanding concern. Better access to project information can help participants track the origins and reported outcomes of credits. The government also plans to use the Korea Exchange as the trading platform. The approach combines blockchain-based information management with an established exchange infrastructure for trading the credits. However, blockchain records alone cannot guarantee that a project has delivered the emissions reductions it claims. The effectiveness of the framework will also depend on project assessment, reliable measurement and verification, and compliance with the applicable approval requirements. Context is everything. This remains under review rather than a confirmed feature of the initial launch. The government will need to consider the relevant legal framework, market conditions and the reliability of the proposed infrastructure before deciding how digital-asset issuance might operate. It is also examining whether GVCM credits could be linked to the domestic emissions trading scheme and greenhouse gas target management system, subject to the necessary conditions. Such a link could create additional uses for eligible credits, although the proposal has not yet been confirmed as an operational arrangement. artigo.texto: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centers Finnish authorities have ordered work to stop at two planned Google data centre sites following concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. The projects in Muhos and Kajaani are part of Google‘s €13 billion investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago as its largest single investment in Europe. Finland’s Supervisory Agency said work at one site had been carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment. Preparatorywork included removing trees and topsoil, building roads and storage areas, and altering ditches. Google acknowledged it had “fallen short” of its own standards and said it would follow the authorities’ guidance. The company behind the projects has been ordered to explain how it intends to proceed, with officials warning that enforcement action could follow if requirements are not met. artigo.texto: EnergyPathways plc (LSE:EPP) has raised £1.75 million through a share placing with a single institutional investor to support the development of its MESH long-duration energy storage project and provide additional working capital. The UK energy transition company issued the new shares at 5.75 pence each, with the proceeds intended to fund further project development activities, including the potential acquisition of land, pipelines and technical data associated with MESH. The placing involves the issue of 30,434,782 new ordinary shares, which are expected to be admitted to trading on AIM on 15 October 2026. Following admission, EnergyPathways will have 282,134,998 ordinary shares in issue, with the newly issued shares representing approximately 10.8% of the enlarged share capital. The company also confirmed the closure of its Capital Access Window following completion of the fundraising process. Trading in its existing ordinary shares is scheduled to resume on 13 October 2026. EnergyPathways said the additional funding will allow it to progress work on MESH, a proposed integrated energy storage development designed to combine compressed air, natural gas and hydrogen storage infrastructure. The company intends to use part of the proceeds to acquire assets and technical information considered necessary for advancing the project through its development stages. These acquisitions are intended to reduce project development risks and support future discussions with institutional investors and strategic partners regarding potential financing arrangements. MESH has been designated as a project of national significance by the UK Government, according to the company. The proposed development is designed to store surplus electricity generated by wind farms and make energy available when required, using a combination of long-duration storage technologies and associated gas infrastructure. EnergyPathways is targeting a power capacity of approximately 300 megawatts and an energy storage capacity of 55 gigawatt-hours, with the proposed system designed to provide more than 100 hours of storage. The company believes the project could contribute to reducing the amount of wind-generated electricity that is curtailed when supply exceeds demand or transmission capacity. Management also expects the proposed infrastructure to provide additional flexibility to the UK electricity system by enabling stored energy to be dispatched during periods of lower renewable generation. The project includes plans for natural gas and hydrogen storage facilities, alongside infrastructure intended to support future hydrogen production and energy supply.

artigo.texto: Lexington extended its temporary ban on data center construction. Mercer County rejected regulations that would allow hyperscale data centers. And a Carroll County ethics board is looking into dealings surrounding a proposed hyperscale data center. As local governments in Kentucky are weighing and making decisions on potential hyperscale data centers, some Kentuckians came to Frankfort to tell state lawmakers that they need to do more to regulate large data centers — not put that burden on local governments. Just a few months away from when state lawmakers meet again in Frankfort, catch up on the latest data center news in this round-up as reported by the Lantern and other news outlets from around Kentucky. Kentuckians tell state lawmakers to act More than 60 people from across the state, ranging from Pike County to Daviess County, came to a committee room earlier this month to lay out a number of concerns they have about hyperscale data center proposals and their potential impacts on electricity ratepayers, rural land and the state’s natural resources. The gathering was for a “listening session” on data centers organized by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, who is preparing legislation on data center regulations for when the GOP-controlled state legislature meets again next year. Rep. Josh Bray, R-Mount Vernon, the vice-chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, is also preparing legislation on data centers. A few of those speakers told the state lawmakers at the meeting that local governments shouldn’t be expected to regulate data centers on their own. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth,” said Diane Floyd of Mercer County. Local government decisions Meanwhile, local governments including Mercer County have been hearing public commentary and taking votes on whether to regulate hyperscale data centers or allow them at all. The Mercer County Fiscal Court through a unanimous voice vote in late September rejected proposed regulations that would have allowed the placement of hyperscale data centers next to a coal-fired power plant. Opponents of the regulations argued the land near the power plant was also relatively close to Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, a historic site preserving structures of the Kentucky Shakers religious community. In Kentucky’s second-largest city of Lexington, the city council voted to move forward with potential data center regulations and also a temporary ban, or moratorium, on data center construction in the city through October 2027, according to public radio station WEKU. In Carroll County, Kentucky Public Radio reported in late September that frustrated community members have filed local ethics complaints arguing that several city council members for the Carroll County seat of Carrollton should have abstained from votes to sign land deals with a prospective hyperscale data center because of conflicts of interest. Carroll County is home to two proposed large data centers, one of them by Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, which is also building a hyperscale data center in West Louisville. Other communities, including the Christian County seat of Hopkinsville, are moving forward with proposed data center regulations, or, in the case of the Scott County seat of Georgetown, looking at an outright ban on hyperscale data centers.

artigo.texto: A migração da inteligência artificial corporativa para sistemas agênticos está mudando a proporção entre componentes nos data centers. Na avaliação da AMD, a arquitetura tradicional, que costumava operar com um processador central para cada quatro ou oito GPUs dedicadas à inferência, caminha para uma razão próxima de 1:1 — e, em cenários de alta concorrência, a demanda por CPU pode superar a das GPUs. O motivo, conforme a empresa, é que a IA agêntica não depende apenas do modelo de linguagem rodando no acelerador. Segurança, middleware, repositórios vetoriais, orquestração, APIs e gestão de memória exigem uma camada robusta de processamento central. Quando a CPU é subdimensionada, as GPUs ficam ociosas à espera de dados, o que amplia a latência e encarece a operação. A AMD defende que a métrica de avaliação passe a ser a capacidade de vazão por rack considerando limites energéticos, de espaço e de refrigeração, e não o desempenho de componentes isolados. Para a fabricante, o avanço dos projetos-piloto para a produção em larga escala depende de um ecossistema equilibrado de CPUs e aceleradores, com conectividade de baixa latência, para sustentar o retorno sobre o investimento. artigo.texto: Nobody wants a data center in their backyard. So a developer from Natick came up with a novel idea: Sink a data center under the ocean off Downeast Maine, and harness the motion of the extraordinarily strong tides there to power it. He says it’s a solution that could neutralize some of the main objections to data centers — they use up too much fresh water and energy, and they release too much heat. “Tidal currents are free, continuous, and completely predictable, unlike wind or solar,” said developer Louis Wolfson. “And the ocean naturally cools things without touching a single drop of drinking water.” But it turns out people don’t like underwater data centers either. Though the idea at this point is little more than “an idea on a bar napkin,” as the Eastport city manager put it, opposition is building fast. In August, the City Council announced a 180-day moratorium on data center development. The council and the local port authority are opposing the project. And a group of residents has organized — Eastport Residents for Healthy Oceans — in part around their concern that if the developer gets an initial permit for a study, it could be harder to stop the project. They and others say the bay just feels too precious and fragile to risk. Already, thanks to the rapidly warming waters of the Gulf of Maine, species are being stressed and pushed north to cooler water. Some species — like one commonly called the flat periwinkle — are already gone. Others — like green crabs — were brought here in larger numbers by warming waters. “I don’t think anybody’s for it,” said Jared Hagan, a co-owner of Picnic, a coffee shop in Eastport. The concept first surfaced in February, when Wolfson, a Needham real estate developer and lifelong Cape Cod surf-caster, put forward a proposal with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for a preliminary permit to construct a 15-megawatt underwater data center powered by the tides. The tides off Eastport are some of the strongest in the continental United States, often gaining some 20 feet between high and low tide. The preliminary vision includes a roughly 80-foot-wide, 11-foot-tall frame made of marine-grade reinforced concrete that would be sunk to the seafloor. Inside would be 40-foot long cylinders with steel-pressured hulls. The project would be powered by up to 50 turbines for generating tidal energy and connected to land by 1.5-mile subsea cable to a facility on Kendall Head. Data centers on land have become the rare point of agreement in the United States — residents in red and blue states alike oppose them, and dozens of projects have been delayed or canceled as a result. High on the list of concerns are energy usage, high water demands, and heat. Recent research led by a team at the University of Cambridge found that AI data centers on land can increase the nearby land surface temperature — between 2.7 and 4.3 degrees Fahrenheit, on average. In theory, that’s why moving a data center off the land, and into the water, could help. Much of the energy used for data centers comes from the need to constantly cool the servers by circulating fresh, cool water around the structure. Placing a data center underwater — particularly in a place with constant, massive tides, Wolfson says — could solve that problem. And the concept isn’t just theoretical. In 2015, Microsoft sank a small prototype of an underwater data center off the coast of California, running it for three months before hauling it out for assessment. Three years later, it launched the real thing off the coast of Orkney, an archipelago off mainland Scotland. “It was a totally new concept,” said Jason Schofield, managing director of Green Marine, an Orkney-based marine services company that was contracted to install the data center and remove it at the project’s completion. He said the project was a huge success. Installation was fast and easy. The data center had one-eighth the failure rate of a comparable land-based one. When Schofield went to remove the data center, he said crabs and other marine life were present on the ocean floor; photos of the shipping-container sized structure were covered in algae, barnacles, and sea anemones. But Microsoft’s track record with Project Natick doesn’t seem to mean much in Eastport. Like many locals, Elijah Brice, a 24-year-old lobsterman, worries about how a sunken data center could affect marine life in Passamaquoddy Bay, where he tends some 800 lobster traps. The tides there are “just such a crazy physical force,” Brice said recently, taking a quick break from the boat house he’s building. When he heads into the waters off Kendall Head, he said he brings heavy gear, including a 100-pound anchor, but still, it’s hard to keep it from moving. “You could probably put a 100-ton excavator or some, like, massive machine on the bottom, and the tide would roll that around until it’s crushed like a little Tonka truck.” He worries that force that strong could damage the data center and pollute the waters. Even without that, he wonders what any generated heat would do to lobster and other species in the area. Wolfson, the project’s developer, said he respects these kinds of concerns, but it’s still early in the process. What he’s looking for at this point is a permit that would allow him to spend two years figuring out if a plan is even feasible by conducting baseline environmental studies and silt-scour engineering, which would let him know how the tides affect the silt-beds and the seafloor. “We should have done a better job early on making it clear that this is a quiet, early study, not construction,” he said. “The concerns about fishing, sound, and the harsh water are all fair points, and they’re what the multiyear study is meant to figure out.” He’s excited enough about the possibilities of tide-powered data centers that he has also proposed an underwater AI data center in Upper Cook Inlet, Alaska, the stretch of water just below Anchorage that boasts among the greatest t

artigo.texto: Utex to Build 20 GWh Battery Storage Facility in Maharashtra ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Utex New Energy, a Pagariya Group company, has announced a 20 GWh battery energy storage system assembly plant in Nagpur, Maharashtra, in partnership with ENcore Systems. - Why it matters: The facility will provide a significant domestic supply chain boost for BESS developers, featuring automated production lines capable of handling 628 Ah cells. - Watch: The phased rollout, starting with an initial 5.5 GWh capacity, as the company scales toward its 20 GWh target over the next two years. Background and Context The push for grid-scale energy storage in India has reached a critical inflection point, with the nation’s energy storage pipeline now exceeding 110 GWh. As renewable energy penetration increases, the demand for battery energy storage system (BESS) solutions for grid balancing and peak demand management has surged. Addressing this manufacturing gap, Utex New Energy, a Pagariya Group company, has signed a strategic agreement to establish a large-scale battery energy storage system assembly plant in Nagpur, Maharashtra. Key Details The project is structured in two distinct phases to ensure operational efficiency and technical precision. The initial phase will launch with an annual assembly capacity of 5.5 GWh. Utex New Energy plans to scale this footprint to a total of 20 GWh within the next one to two years. The facility will leverage advanced technology through a partnership with ENcore Systems, focusing on fully automated production lines. These lines will be equipped with high-precision robots supplied by Germany-based KUKA, capable of handling battery cells with capacities of up to 628 Ah. To maintain rigorous quality standards, the plant will utilize a Manufacturing Execution System (MES) integrated with SAP systems. This digital infrastructure will provide real-time oversight of production output, quality control, and operational performance, ensuring full traceability throughout the manufacturing cycle. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and renewable energy developers, the localization of high-capacity battery assembly is a significant development. With India adding 8.2 GWh of battery energy storage in the first half of 2026 alone—a massive increase compared to previous years—the availability of domestically assembled, high-capacity cells will likely reduce lead times and logistics costs for large-scale storage projects. The ability to handle 628 Ah cells positions this facility to support the next generation of high-density storage requirements. What Happens Next As India continues to integrate variable renewable energy, the role of storage becomes paramount. With Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Maharashtra currently leading the storage landscape, the addition of a major assembly hub in Nagpur strengthens the regional supply chain. Stakeholders should monitor the commissioning of the first 5.5 GWh phase, as it will serve as a bellwether for the scalability of large-scale BESS manufacturing in India. This investment reflects the broader trend of the India renewable energy sector shifting from project deployment toward vertical integration and domestic manufacturing self-sufficiency.

artigo.texto: Cleveland City Council is preparing to extend the city’s moratorium on data centers for another three months. Council Member Brian Kazy said he plans to introduce legislation on Monday to continue the pause. Passed this summer, the moratorium was meant to give City Hall time to draw up regulations for the centers, which have become central to the artificial intelligence boom. Kazy, the chair of council’s Utilities Committee, convened a trio of public meetings on the topic. Council members also toured two local data centers, he said. He took away from the hearings that most people oppose the “hyperscale” centers that require large amounts of energy to power AI. He drew a distinction between those centers and small and medium-sized facilities that form part of the infrastructure of the internet. Now the city needs 90 more days “to assure that we get this thing right,” Kazy told Weekly Chatter. Democrats try to rock the southwest suburbs Strongsville is a Republican stalwart in strongly Democratic Cuyahoga County. But Democrats hope to unseat the suburb’s longtime County Council representative this fall. Council Member Mike Gallagher faces a Democratic opponent for the first time since 2010, when he originally won his seat with 59% of the vote. Democrats have already flipped the other two GOP seats on the 11-member council. Democratic challenger Courtney Scheff, an attorney and former prosecutor, has the support of County Executive Chris Ronayne, who has accused Gallagher of trying to “thwart progress.” A critic of the administration, Gallagher has embraced Ronayne’s opposition. Despite Ronayne’s support, Scheff told Weekly Chatter that she “absolutely” could serve as a check on the Democratic executive. Asked about the county’s budget troubles, she suggested consolidating programs and holding down department spending. Scheff said she wouldn’t have voted for a new building department the county created last year, for instance. Both candidates emphasized their ability to reach across the aisle. The Republican-leaning district reaches beyond Strongsville to include North Royalton, Berea, Olmsted Falls and Olmsted Township. President Donald Trump won the district by about 5 percentage points in 2024. Can a down-ballot Democrat win there? Scheff argued that, nationwide, voters are tiring of Trump and the GOP-controlled Congress. “Whether that translates into the district, I don’t know,” she said. “But I believe it will. I think that people are kind of fed up with the same old thing over and over again.” Rainbow Terrace family goes to court The estate of Cordale Sheffield, the man who died from burns he received in last year’s explosion and fire at Rainbow Terrace, has brought a wrongful death lawsuit over the blast. Sheffield’s estate is suing Enbridge Gas, the owner of the apartment building and others. Attorneys for the estate focused on a gas line at the site, writing that it was decades old. The suit also cites a finding by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio that, after the blast, Enbridge removed pipes in such a way that they “could not be leak tested.” An investigation by the City of Cleveland pointed to a gas leak as the likely fuel for the explosion but said the ultimate cause was “undetermined.” A spokesperson for Enbridge declined to comment on the suit but wrote in an email, “Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragic event, particularly the Sheffield family.”

artigo.texto: Car changing is a big deal The new BYD Atto 8 is a large electric SUV which features the brand’s Flash Charging technology, and it also has up to 775hp. News editor Jamie Edkins is here to tell you all about it. Charging times are one of the main sticking points for long-distance electric car drivers. As someone with no way of charging at home, I find sitting in a car park for half an hour at a time to top up gets tiresome after a while, but BYD may have the answer to all of our prayers. It’s called Flash charging, and it’ll feature on the newly-revealed BYD Atto 8 as well as cars from its Denza luxury spin-off brand. It’s essentially a super high-powered charger which can get you back up on the road in as little as five minutes. Remember, you can buy a brand new or used car right here on Carwow. And you can sell your car, too. We’re here to help you through every step of your car-changing journey. New BYD Atto 8: batteries, range and Flash Charging The fastest chargers on offer in the UK right now top out at 480kW, but BYD has developed its new Flash Charging technology which can deliver up to 1,500kW from a single connector. In the BYD Atto 8, this means you can charge its 115kWh battery from 10-70% in just five minutes. 10-97% can also be achieved in nine minutes. Consumer writer Siobhan Doyle has tested BYD’s Flash Charging on the Denza Z9 GT, and she managed to get that car from 10-80% in six minutes and 28 seconds, while a full charge took eight minutes and 57 seconds. That car has a larger 122kWh battery compared to the BYD Atto 8 as well, so it’s certainly impressive. The fastest-charging electric car on sale right now is the Xpeng G6, and that car takes 12 minutes to go from 10-80%. BYD’s new tech cuts this time in half. There will be two versions of the BYD Atto 8 on offer. Both use a 115kWh battery, but the basic rear-wheel drive car gets 462hp and 405 miles of range. You can also get an all-wheel drive model with a whopping 775hp, but the added performance cuts your range down to 374 miles. New BYD Atto 8: interior and technology The Atto 8 will be BYD’s largest electric car, going up against other seven-seaters such as the Kia EV9 and Skoda Peaq. The interior is pretty standard fare for a Chinese EV. You get a large 15.6-inch screen in the middle, very few physical buttons and a tall centre console with a couple of wireless charging pads near the front. That screen features Google-based software, so you can have Google Maps and Google’s voice assistant without having to pair your phone to it. You can also get a temperature-controlled centre console which cools to minus six degrees, or warms up to 50 degrees. The front and outer middle row seats get heating, ventilation and massage functions as well. With all seven seats in place, you get 270 litres of boot space. This is almost 30 litres down on the Skoda Peaq, and it’s over 60 litres less than you get in a Kia EV9. You do get a 136-litre front boot though, beating the Peaq by almost 100 litres and the EV9 by 46 litres. When can I buy the new BYD Atto 8? The BYD Atto 8 will arrive in showrooms in early 2027, but BYD hasn’t said how much it’ll cost yet. artigo.texto: A senior Iranian official says Tehran finds the latest U.S. response to a proposal to end the war “insufficient” and warns of attacks on regional data centers and cables if fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country’s longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance with elections weeks away. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. Iran says latest US response is ‘insufficient’ The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States “insufficient” as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along. The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency. Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear. Iran’s delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation. Rezaei also threatened “cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region” if intense fighting breaks out again. Meanwhile, the Guard’s navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be “identified as hostile,” according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran’s proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday. Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu’s long-running corruption trial. Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022. Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing. Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes A projectile struck the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday’s attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis’ military spokesperson, urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously” about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace. The attacks have marked a major escalation in the war between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before. Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee. “Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes,” Abed said. Israel’s military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers. One year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes. Netanyahu wants probe into ‘NAZA’ documentary Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the new documentary “NAZA,” in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza. Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells “a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel” and its military. The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose view of the war in Gaza differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territory has grown. Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue. Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling Lebanon’s army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater. It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was “directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank” and called it “a flagrant violation of existing understandings.” An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident. Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March.

artigo.texto: Drones ucranianos derrubam centro de dados do "Google da Rússia". Um ataque com drones desativou o grande centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir, na Rússia, na manhã de 11 de outubro (horário local), interrompendo mais de 80 serviços. Segundo a mídia russa, o centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir teve que interromper temporariamente suas operações, causando ampla interrupção em mais de 80 serviços, incluindo plataformas digitais e ferramentas de IA. Este é o terceiro ataque à infraestrutura de servidores da Yandex em quatro dias. Anteriormente, os alvos estavam localizados nas regiões de Ryazan e Kaluga. Especificamente, em 8 de outubro, drones ucranianos atacaram um centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo (Ryazan), causando um incêndio e forçando seu desligamento completo, desativando a infraestrutura de servidores usada pela Russian Railways (RZhD), pela rede MegaFon e por diversas agências de notícias. No dia seguinte, 9 de outubro, drones atacaram outro centro da Yandex em Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. A Yandex confirmou que vários módulos de hardware foram desativados. Você também pode gostar O Centro de Vladimir foi projetado para acomodar até 2.880 racks de servidores, representando um dos principais centros de processamento da Yandex. Após as explosões, a Yandex confirmou que as operações em seu centro de dados em Vladimir foram temporariamente suspensas. O incidente afetou diversos aplicativos para o consumidor, incluindo a assistente de voz Alice, o Yandex Music, a ferramenta de videoconferência Telemost e o Yandex Smart Home. Os sistemas empresariais hospedados na Yandex Cloud também sofreram interrupções nos serviços de computação, armazenamento e gerenciamento de banco de dados, incluindo Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL e ClickHouse. Além disso, ferramentas e interfaces de programação de IA, como a API YandexGPT, SpeechKit e Vision OCR, também foram afetadas. A interrupção se estendeu além dos aplicativos principais da Yandex e afetou plataformas de comércio de terceiros na Rússia e em países vizinhos. Usuários relataram falhas de conexão ao acessar aplicativos de bancos, transporte por aplicativo e varejo. Segundo o prefeito Vladimir, ataques com drones danificaram subestações locais, derrubando a rede elétrica da cidade. Na manhã do mesmo dia, aproximadamente 80% do fornecimento de energia elétrica nas áreas afetadas já havia sido restabelecido. Você também pode gostar O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que seus sistemas de defesa aérea interceptaram 479 drones ucranianos em 16 regiões, incluindo Vladimir, Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk e Rostov. Especialistas militares ucranianos observam que o bloqueio sistemático de centros de dados e redes de comunicação corporativas interromperia a logística, a governança corporativa e prejudicaria as capacidades de comando digital da Rússia.

artigo.texto: Newswise — David Adams is an Associate Professor of Public Administration in the College of Humanities and Social Sciences who is an expert on data centers. CSUF News recently caught up with him to discuss water, energy, data centers, the government’s role in greenlighting data centers, and long-term impacts. CSUF News: What’s your research about? Adams: A lot of my research has been in oil and gas and energy infrastructure. I’ve been focused on that for a while, as well as water. My initial dissertation research focused on institutional collaboration in watersheds across the country and how people come together to improve water quality. I just published a book on that in May 2026 with Jonathan Fisk and John Morris, Navigating Water Quality Outcomes in American Watersheds (Cambridge University Press). I also have studied energy—oil and gas infrastructure. You are in the public administration division. How does this relate to oil and gas? Adams: I’m wondering how government agencies maintain legitimacy, achieve their goals, and serve every community fairly. Legitimacy means the public seeks their work as not just legal, but also important and valid. What’s the topic of your latest research? Adams: Data centers. A few of us working together on this research have come to realize that data centers are really similar to oil and gas infrastructure. The public initially sees a benefit in the build-out of a data center. If a new oil field is taken over by a gas company that comes in there, it builds out all the infrastructure, and there are a lot of jobs right away. Then, once it’s built or once the oil companies move on, the jobs go away. So [for energy companies], what’s still there is just the producing ground where the benefit is not local but spread out everywhere, while the cost is really local. Data centers are similar; they’re put in one spot by a multinational corporation whose dollars are everywhere. The people living in that area are getting some benefit from the build-out, but the costs are borne locally, and those benefits are spread across all of us. We’re all benefiting when there is a new data center put in the middle of the Sonoran Desert, right? Our phones work faster; we’re able to do cool, flashy things [on our computers]; we’re able to talk on Zoom. But the costs are really on the environment right there locally in Arizona, where the data centers operate. Quantify the data center story for us. What’s the scale of data center construction in the US? Adams: There are 7,000 data center buildings operating, proposed, or under construction across the country, and about 2,100 operating right now, on roughly 1,400 sites, as of September 1. Some of these are single buildings. Some of them are 30 buildings across 190 acres of land. What are the initial perceived benefits of data centers for cities? Adams: Cities and counties like the fact that the data center is a new source of tax revenue is coming in, but it’s not like it’s a factory that is going to require workers, apartment buildings, neighborhoods, new street maintenance and new school capacity. It’s just a new building that’s producing tax dollars and paying land rent. It’s great revenue. You don’t have to fund increased road pressure, but you don’t have to absorb new capacity of the schools to handle the students. [The city] is just getting more money. And the downside of data centers? Adams: The “down the road” risk for data centers for these communities is the same one we see with the abandoned and orphaned oil wells. The infrastructure is going to be stranded eventually, because the technology is going to move on. In the meantime, the environmental costs are local. A big campus can use as much electricity as a small city, and many data centers cool their servers with water, often in places like Arizona that are already short on it. When a data center switches to air cooling to save water, it uses more electricity, so some of that water use just moves to the power plant. Who makes the decision to approve a data center? Which governing body/bodies? Adams: The governance is so fragmented. There are so many different governments that are involved: state, local, special district, commissions. Tucson is a really interesting case. A developer with Amazon Web Services as its customer wanted to build a data center there. They went into the county and got a bunch of land. But the city said they couldn’t have access to water. Then they redesigned it to cool with air, so they didn’t need the city’s water. They then went to the Arizona Corporation Commission, the state utility regulator, and just asked for access to electricity. So the Commission approved the power deal. This was in contrast to the city, where the public showed up with signs and picketing and the council voted no. But the Commission said yes, and the county had already sold them the land. So what happened? The fences go up, the bulldozers come in, and all the public is standing there at the fence saying, “Look, we said no, why are you building these things?” And the whole thing was a mismatch of institutions. This is just one case in Arizona. There could be 15 different governments involved, and the public could be arguing with the wrong government. You have your own database on data center growth. What sort of information are you tracking? Any interesting trends? Adams: I really do have a huge database that I’ve gathered. I have gone out and searched maps to find where data centers are located. What I found so far is that the data centers are following the fiber. Where the internet cables already are, which is typically in more affluent areas, better educated, more money, that’s where these things are being located. They’re following that because that’s the best location for it because it’s the easiest access to connect to the infrastructure . What else? Adams: They’re also following the energy. artigo.texto: BYD has unveiled the all-electric Atto 8 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, expanding the flagship SUV’s international line-up alongside the existing plug-in hybrid (PHEV) version. The EV variant also marks BYD’s debut of ultra-fast ‘Flash Charging’ technology, which can charge its 115kWh battery from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. Meanwhile, the PHEV version continues with a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine paired with either a 19kWh or a 35.6kWh battery. - Gets a 115kWh battery pack with a claimed WLTP range of up to 653km - ‘Flash Charging’ tops up the battery from 10-70 percent in 5 minutes - Exterior and interior design is similar to those of the PHEV version BYD Atto 8 EV powertrain details EV version is available in both RWD, AWD guises and supports ‘Flash Charging’ The BYD Atto 8 EV is offered with a 115kWh battery pack powering either a rear axle-mounted electric motor (RWD) or a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) setup. The RWD version puts out 462hp and 365Nm, and does a 0-100kph run in a claimed 8 seconds. It has a claimed WLTP range of 653km. The AWD version has a combined output of 775hp and 775Nm, and does a 0-00kph run in just 4.6 seconds (claimed). It has a claimed WLTP range of 602km. The headline, however, is ‘Flash Charging’ support, a first for any BYD, which can recharge the battery pack from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. This charging technology can top up the battery from 0 to 70 percent in just five minutes. In extremely cold temperatures as low as -30deg C, when charging power is drastically reduced, it takes only 12 minutes to charge from 20 to 97 percent. The BYD Atto 8 PHEV, meanwhile, continues with a 148hp 1.5-litre turbocharged 4-cylinder petrol engine paired with either a 19kWh or a 35.6kWh battery. The smaller battery has a FWD setup with 275hp output, while the larger battery has an AWD setup with a combined output of 481hp. BYD Atto 8 EV exterior design Save for new alloys and missing tailpipe, the EV’s exterior design mimics the PHEV’s Save for more aerodynamic alloy wheels and a missing tailpipe, the Atto 8 EV looks identical to the PHEV version. Up front, it gets a blanked-off grille with matrix LED headlights and a curved LED DRL bar, and a black section on the lower portion of the bumper with functional air inlets to cool the internals. A LiDAR sensor can also be seen on the roof. In profile, it sports black alloy wheels with aerodynamic inserts, flared wheel arches and slim roof rails. There’s a chrome strip on the front fender extending to the front doors and a black portion on the lower section of the doors. At the rear, it gets 'infinity knot' LED taillights with an illuminated BYD logo in the centre, and a roof-mounted spoiler. BYD Atto 8 EV interior and features 7-seater SUV gets dual digital screens, panoramic glass roof and 3-zone AC The interior design of the Atto 8 EV is identical to the PHEV. The dashboard continues with a 10.25-inch digital driver’s display, a 15.6-inch infotainment touchscreen and a 3-spoke steering wheel, thankfully with physical buttons and scrollers. The dashboard features slim air vents and a lot of soft-touch leather elements. It gets 7 seats in a 2+2+3 configuration, with a 270-litre boot space like the PHEV. However, it has a 136-litre frunk (boot space under the hood), which is unique to the EV version. The first and second rows feature heated, ventilated, and massaging seats. Other features include a panoramic glass roof, 3-zone climate control, a 21-speaker DiSound audio system, dual 50-watt wireless phone chargers and a front refrigerator that can cool to -6deg C and warm to 50deg C. Internationally, the BYD Atto 8 EV locks horns with the Kia EV9, Skoda Peaq and Hyundai Ioniq 9.
