artigo.texto: Wood Mackenzie: Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas Peaking on Cost Across 43 modeled markets, four-hour battery storage costs less than open-cycle gas turbines. Wood Mackenzie details cost trajectories for solar, wind and storage by region. Wood Mackenzie says its latest global report on levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) shows four-hour battery storage is cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where both technologies were modeled. According to the firm, gas turbine shortages and fuel volatility are raising peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing is pushing storage costs down. On the financing side, Lydian Energy and Infranity closed a $300 million credit facility for energy storage. The report covers Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Africa. Middle East, Africa and China lead on costs In the Middle East and Africa, utility-scale solar already stands at an LCOE of $37/MWh. The cost of four-hour storage is forecast to fall a further 33% to $80/MWh by 2035, which would place it ahead of gas peaking in every gas market in the region. China remains the global benchmark, with storage costs more than 55% below the Asia Pacific average excluding China. "This economic shift is decisive and widening," said Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie. He said gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are driving up peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing continues to push storage costs down. He noted that a similar transformation has already reshaped baseload economics. Company Wood Mackenzie: company profile Solar dominates baseload generation According to the report, single-axis tracker solar is the lowest-cost new-build technology in 43 of the 48 modeled markets, with onshore wind leading in five. In Saudi Arabia and the UAE, the most competitive markets, solar LCOE is on track to fall below $20/MWh by 2033. In Latin America, solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the lowest-cost generation technology in 2026, with average costs expected to fall 38% by 2060. Brazil, Chile and Mexico hold a structural advantage tied to their solar resources and high capacity factors. The regional average onshore wind LCOE is expected to fall nearly 21% by 2030, from $73/MWh to $58/MWh, as Chinese manufacturers intensify price competition and larger turbines lift yields. Grid-scale storage LCOE is forecast to fall 42% by 2060, and offshore wind would approach combined-cycle gas turbine parity only in the early 2040s. Asia Pacific: sharp regional gaps In Asia Pacific, utility-scale solar remains the most cost-competitive source, but regional disparities are stark. In 2026, solar generation in the highest-cost market is more than 200% more expensive than in the lowest, a gap expected to widen to 250% by 2030. Onshore wind costs range more than six times between the cheapest and most costly markets in the region. China posts a benchmark grid-scale storage LCOE more than 55% below the rest of Asia Pacific average of $134/MWh. That average is expected to fall to $92/MWh by 2036, but Japan, Australia and the Philippines would remain at a premium because of import duties, elevated installation costs and domestic manufacturing policies. Outside China, offshore wind costs remain under near-term pressure, with declines expected from the early 2030s. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 % Europe: battery capex turns upward In Europe, solar PV remains the cheapest power technology, with fixed-tilt LCOE forecast to fall 22% by 2060, despite a 14% capex increase in 2026 driven by higher module costs. Onshore wind capex is declining at an average annual rate of 2.5% through the rest of the decade, after which rising capacity factors become the main LCOE driver, with costs of $60/MWh by 2060. Battery storage turnkey capex rose about 2%, the first increase in three years, as cell prices rebounded around 10% from their 2025 low on stronger demand and higher lithium prices. Capex is forecast to fall 12% by 2031, before the pace moderates, with lithium prices expected to roughly double in 2029.

artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Announces a Two Hundred Million Dollar Reduction in the Amount of Sales that May Be Made under the Sales Agreement Providing for Its Current ATM Offering LAS VEGAS , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it has amended the At-the-Market ("ATM") Issuance Sales Agreement (the "Agreement"), dated June 18, 2026, by and between the Company and Spartan Capital Securities, LLC, as sales agent (the "Agent"), reducing the aggregate amount that may be sold pursuant to the Agreement from Three Hundred Million Dollars ($300,000,000) in shares of the Company's Class A common stock, par value $0.001 per share (the "Common Stock") to One Hundred Million Dollars ($100,000,000), including the shares of Common Stock that have been sold pursuant to the Agreement through an amendment to the Agreement (the "Amendment"). The Company has sold 121,827,841 shares of Common Stock and raised approximately $49.8 million in gross proceeds, or approximately $0.41 per share, pursuant to the ATM. "Based on our current capital plans, we do not believe the additional $200 million of ATM capacity is currently necessary," said Will Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data. "Reducing the size of the ATM reflects our commitment to disciplined capital management while preserving financial flexibility to support our AI data center strategy. We believe that our equity is significantly undervalued and this $200 million reduction will limit the dilution to our equity and is in the best interests of our stockholders. Our focus remains on deploying capital prudently and building long-term value through the buildout of our Michigan AI data center (the "Facility") to initially support the 20 megawatts of critical compute capacity of our neocloud customer. It is our intention to augment the Facility buildout costs with debt financing and preliminary estimates on the existing buildout indicate that the Facility will support project debt financing between $100 million to $150 million." The Company may evaluate capital markets options in the future as appropriate and in the best interests of the Company and its stockholders. This press release shall not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy, nor shall there be any sale of shares of the Common Stock in any state or other jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or other jurisdiction. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). artigo.texto: Flex Expands Prefabricated Modular Data Center Portfolio to Accelerate AI Factory Deployment Integrated solutions combine power, compute and cooling to speed deployment by up to 50% News summary - Introduces AI Modules that integrate power, compute and cooling in prefabricated modular solutions to accelerate AI factory deployment by up to 50% - Enables faster deployment of next-generation AI infrastructure through factory-built, integrated systems - Strengthens Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure portfolio, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom Solutions International, Inc. (Axiom), in the first quarter of calendar 2027 SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Flex (NASDAQ: FLEX) today announced an expanded portfolio of prefabricated modular data center solutions designed to accelerate deployment of next-generation AI factories. The portfolio includes new AI Modules that integrate power, high-density compute and advanced liquid cooling into pre-engineered, factory-built systems, enabling customers to reduce deployment timelines by up to 50% compared with traditional construction approaches. The expanded portfolio is part of Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure (CPI) segment, which Flex plans to separate into Axiom, an independent publicly traded company, in the first quarter of calendar 2027. "Meeting the demands of AI infrastructure at scale requires more than incremental improvements. It requires rethinking how power, compute and cooling work together as a system," said Chris Butler, expected Chief Technology and Strategy Officer at Axiom. "Our system-level approach brings these critical technologies together with advanced manufacturing to simplify integration, accelerate deployment and deliver AI factories at scale." As AI infrastructure grows in scale and power density, data center operators face increasing complexity across power delivery, cooling, compute integration and deployment. Addressing these challenges requires a more integrated approach to designing and deploying the critical infrastructure that supports next-generation AI factories. The Axiom AI Modules integrate critical AI infrastructure into pre-engineered, factory-built systems, including: - 800 VDC Power Rack: Delivers high-efficiency power conversion and distribution for next-generation 800 VDC AI infrastructure and high-density compute. - Advanced cooling distribution units (CDUs): Provide liquid cooling to efficiently manage the increasing heat generated by power-intensive AI workloads. - High-density IT racks: Integrate AI servers, networking and high-speed interconnects to support next-generation AI compute at scale. By shifting complex infrastructure integration from the data center site to a controlled factory environment, the Axiom AI Modules are assembled, integrated and tested in parallel with site development. This approach reduces on-site complexity and helps customers bring AI capacity online faster. Flex is actively building prefabricated modular solutions for hyperscalers across its global footprint, including more than three million square feet of dedicated data center infrastructure manufacturing capacity in the U.S. With deep expertise across power, compute, cooling and systems integration, Flex has the scale and capabilities to support rapid AI infrastructure deployment across regions. artigo.texto: Oklahoma currently has 64 data centers operating or in progress. Editor’s note: This story was updated on 10/12/2026 with new information from the U.S. Data Center map. Our Data Center Info Hub features an interactive map, data center profiles, frequently asked questions, and a form to ask us your questions about data centers in your area. Data centers have become a central issue in Oklahoma’s midterm elections, with gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei (R) saying he supports them with guardrails, and Democratic nominee Cyndi Munson promising a day-one moratorium. Related Story: Mike Mazzei and Cyndi Munson share their stances on Oklahoma data center development Driven by affordable land, access to power, and growing demand for cloud and AI services, companies ranging from global tech giants to regional providers are expanding their presence in Oklahoma. According to the US Data Center Map, data as of Oct 2026. https://dcmap.us, Oklahoma has: - 64 data center projects overall - 34 operational data centers - 6 data centers under construction - 20 data centers planned - 2 paused data center projects - 2 inactive data centers Below is a running list of data center projects across the state. This article will be updated as new facilities are announced, approved, or completed. Claremore Project Mustang (Approved) Project Mustang is an approved data center development at the Claremore Industrial Park by Beale Infrastructure. Plans call for multiple data center buildings and office space, with power supplied by Grand River Dam Authority and water and wastewater services provided by the City of Claremore. City leaders say the property is already zoned for industrial use and that the developer would pay for required infrastructure upgrades. The Claremore City Council approved plans Monday, May 18, for “Project Mustang.” Claremore City Hall reached standing-room capacity during the meeting, with dozens of people waiting outside and rotating in to comply with fire code limits. Public comment lasted nearly two hours before the council voted on the proposal. Related Story: Claremore approves Project Mustang data center plan The agreement allows Beale Infrastructure to seek a 25-year ad valorem tax exemption for each phase of the project. Company representatives said the development would still contribute more than $250 million toward Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. Some residents have raised concerns about water usage, environmental impacts and transparency. City officials and the developer say the project would not raise taxes or utility rates and could bring long-term investment and jobs. Muskogee County Google Data Centers (Summit and Council Hill) (Early Development) Google plans to build two new data center campuses near Summit and Council Hill as part of a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma. The facilities are expected to support Google’s cloud and AI services, including Search, Maps and Google Cloud. The company says the projects will be paired with clean energy agreements expected to add hundreds of megawatts of renewable power to Oklahoma’s grid. Construction timelines have not been released. Related Story: Google to build two data centers in Muskogee County as part of $9B Oklahoma investment In April, OG&E announced that it will power the Muskogee data centers as well as a data center coming to Stillwater (see below) “OG&E is pleased to support Google and together advance growth in our home state, ensuring our current customers benefit from data center expansion that meets the technology needs of the 21st century economy at some of the lowest rates in the country,” said Sean Trauschke, Chairman, President and CEO of OGE Energy Corp. “This unique agreement is a model for future data center partnerships and forms the basis for a new large-load tariff that OG&E will submit in the coming weeks that protects our current customers from bearing the costs of this growing demand and Oklahoma’s goals for economic growth.” Core Scientific (Under Construction) Core Scientific has partnered with Port Muskogee to develop a 100 MW high-performance computing (HPC) data center in Muskogee at 1525 W 43rd St S . Scheduled to become operational in 2026. A second Core Scientific data center is planned for Muskogee at 4800 S 24th St W. Oklahoma City American Tower EDC Oklahoma (Planned) American Tower EDC Oklahoma is a construction-ready edge data center* development located at 1309 Northeast 122nd Street in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. According to American Tower, the facility would be on 83.5 acres and provide 4MW of capacity. The American Tower EDC Oklahoma company says that zoning has been approved and that the facility can be ready in 18 months once a customer signs an anchor lease. *An edge data center is a smaller, decentralized facility positioned near the source of data generation. Cerebras Systems operates a 10-megawatt data center in Oklahoma City in partnership with Scale Datacenters. The facility supports large-scale AI computing and uses a closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus - 3 Data Centers (Under Construction) The CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus is planned to be an expansive location with a total capacity of 200MW covering at least three data centers. The project was set to break ground at the end of 2025; however, its construction appears to have been impacted by OKC’s data center moratorium. It is planned for the area near 2000 S Council Rd. Cogent Data Center (Operational) The Cogent Data Center in Oklahoma City is 5,294 square feet of colocation space designed for 42U cabinets. The Cogent data center is what’s known as a “carrier hotel,” meaning that it has equipment, space, and/or bandwidth available for rental to retail customers. artigo.texto: TI unveils new ADC to enable nanosecond-level telemetry and minimize downtime in AI data centers As AI workloads increase in volume and complexity, Texas Instruments is delivering the essential solutions needed to power, monitor and optimize AI data centers News highlights: - TI's ADC34DSO75 is the industry's highest performance 3 gigasamples per second ADC, enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution – thousands of times faster than what current solutions offer. - The LMI800PS is the industry's first 800V isolated hot-swap controller, replacing a complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection. - The LMK6B is a bulk acoustic wave-based oscillator that delivers best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio. SAN JOSE, Calif. , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Texas Instruments (TI) (Nasdaq: TXN) debuted the first analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to enable 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution. As AI workloads rapidly increase, data center operators face significant challenges around power instability, inadequate real-time monitoring and signal degradation, all of which can lead to costly downtime. TI is addressing these challenges through its new ADC device and other analog solutions designed to tackle the challenges of scaling artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructures. Demonstrations on display in TI's booth, No. E45, at OCP include: - Real-time nanosecond-level telemetry: TI's ADC34DSO75 is the industry's highest performance 3 gigasamples per second (GSPS) ADC, enabling 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution – thousands of times faster than what current solutions offer. Existing monitoring solutions often fail to detect the nanosecond-level power-rail glitches that cause costly, unplanned downtime in data centers. By combining ultra-high-speed sampling with advanced on-chip digital signal processing in a small form factor, the ADC34DSO75 detects and captures transient fault events in real time. As the industry's first solution to offer fully remote, event-based telemetry, the device eliminates the need for on-site debugging and oscilloscopes. By providing continuous, high-resolution monitoring of low-voltage, high-current power rails, the ADC34DSO75 helps data centers minimize downtime – which can cost operators hundreds of thousands of dollars an hour – while optimizing grid power efficiency. This compact, efficient solution offers hyperscalers unmatched remote diagnostic capabilities at a fraction of the size and cost of conventional monitoring methods. - Reliable high-voltage power delivery: The LMI800PS is the industry's first 800V isolated hot-swap controller, replacing a complex discrete solution requiring five integrated circuits with a single high-density package that delivers in-rush current and power path protection. The integration of an isolated bias supply and PMBus telemetry reduces board area by more than 60% and simplifies high-voltage designs. The LMI800PS enables safe power insertion and fast fault isolation, meeting safety standards with 5kVrms reinforced isolation and more than 8mm creepage. This prevents a single load failure from disrupting the shared power bus and maximizes data center stability. Supporting both ±400V and 800V distributions, the device provides a scalable solution for diverse rack architectures, accelerating the deployment of high-efficiency power systems required for next-generation AI infrastructures. - Ultra-low jitter signal integrity: The LMK6B is a bulk acoustic wave (BAW)-based oscillator that delivers best-in-class jitter performance and power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR). As data center transmission rates approach 3.2Tbps, the margin for timing error shrinks significantly, and even minute jitter can increase bit error rates and cause system instability. The LMK6B provides industry-leading jitter performance of 9.6fs at 625MHz, ensuring reliable performance and preserving signal integrity for next-generation, AI-driven networking infrastructures. "As AI workloads drive massive scale, the need for real-time visibility and architectural stability has never been greater," said Karthik Vasanth, vice president and general manager for TI's Data, Converters and Clocks business unit. "By delivering industry-leading solutions for high-speed telemetry, advanced power protection and precision timing, TI is enabling hyperscalers and operators to design the next generation of AI data centers with optimized performance and minimal downtime." More details Also at OCP, TI Power Electronics Engineer David Reusch will present "800V Data Center DC/DC Design Considerations, Topology Comparisons and Trade-Offs," on Oct. 15 at 2:45 p.m. in room 230A. See ti.com/ocp for more information. For more information on the ADC34DSO75, read the technical article "The power glitches AI data centers can't see." At our core, we have a passion to create a better world by making electronics more affordable through semiconductors. This passion is alive today as each generation of innovation builds upon the last to make our technology more reliable, more affordable and lower power, making it possible for semiconductors to go into electronics everywhere. Set us as preferred California has always hidden the true price of progress somewhere beyond the horizon. The water arrives from a distant river. The electricity crosses a mountain range. By the time the benefits reach us, the damage has been assigned elsewhere. Now the future is arriving in windowless buildings. Data centers are rising from industrial corridors and farmland with the appetite of cities. They pull electricity by the hundreds of megawatts. Inside, servers build fortunes. Outside, residents open their utility bills and wonder what will remain. Before California approves another facility, every host community deserves an answer: What will this project make better here? Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven laws that begin to make the hidden costs visible. Until those are in effect, a company could arrive with the appetite of a city and quietly leave its bill for wires and water with people who never asked for it. Now utility regulators must reckon with what it takes to serve that appetite. The rates and connection terms are meant to make new users shoulder their share of the grid and the electricity it must supply, instead of loading those costs onto a family studying its bill. Regulators must now make that promise real. The water, too, must come into the open. Data centers are water guzzlers, using huge volumes for cooling. Before construction, a developer must show where that water will come from, how the facility will fare in drought and who will pay for the new pipes. After the servers begin to hum, estimates must give way to actual water use. State planners will gain an account of energy consumption and efficiency. A town needs numbers it can see. And the project can no longer pass under a blanket environmental exemption. A quicker path through court is reserved for facilities that meet demanding conditions on clean power, water and protection of ratepayers. In California, speed must be earned. These laws draw a floor beneath the bargain. They do not guarantee that a neighborhood gains something lasting from the land, power and water it commits. California should establish a “community benefit standard” for every new data center and major expansion. Protect the resources of the place. Pay every cost the project creates. Then deliver a public benefit that residents can see, measure and enforce. The first requirements are obligations, not generosity. Developers must disclose projected electricity demand, water consumption, emissions, noise and infrastructure needs. That includes drought, extreme heat and nearby projects. Households cannot pay for capacity reserved by a corporation that may never use it. No company should receive applause for obeying environmental law. Efficient cooling is not a community gift when the machinery is necessary to run the servers. A research grant cannot excuse an unacceptable water plan. Public benefits cannot purchase permission to pollute a neighborhood or drain an aquifer. Only after those tests are met does the additional bargain begin. Each major project should fund at least one substantial technology program tied to an identified public need. Residents and public agencies would help choose the priority. California should measure what changes, not what gets announced. One developer might finance advanced water reuse with a local district beyond what is required to address its own demand. The compact would state how much freshwater demand must be eliminated, how savings will be verified and who will operate the system. Buying equipment would not count. Producing verified water savings would. Another facility might guarantee computing capacity to California hospitals and universities studying rare diseases, cancer or wildfire behavior. The agreement would specify secure access, support and computing hours, and bind the tenant. Researchers would receive usable capacity, not whatever remains after commercial customers finish. A third project could finance batteries and controls that keep a clinic, cooling center or water system operating during an outage. The equipment must serve the public in an emergency. Backup power reserved for company servers would not qualify. Every project must still provide a direct local benefit. A statewide research program may supplement that commitment, but it cannot replace it. The compact would name beneficiaries, funding, responsible parties, milestones and penalties for failure. Its duties would survive a sale or tenant change. Independent verification would report delivery, not spending. If one method underperforms, the agreements between data centers and communities should permit another. The obligation itself remains. Contribution levels should reflect project size. Small facilities could pool resources. Large campuses could not divide themselves into smaller applications to escape responsibility. Broader innovation contributions should be legally sound and separate from required mitigation. Projects with unacceptable impacts should be rejected or relocated. Those meeting environmental standards and securing credible, enforceable benefits deserve coordinated reviews and clear timelines. The Legislature has drawn the line against making families pay for the servers that power someone else’s fortune. The industry can meet that line by showing, in public and before construction, how it will protect the grid and water system. Then it can show what it will build for the people living outside its walls. For too long, California has sent the rewards of progress in one direction and the damage in another. If our communities are asked to power the future, that future must also power them. Dean Florez is a former California Senate majority leader, representing portions of the Central Valley. artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) has published results in all three waves of the Global Battery Alliance (GBA) battery passport pilot, a record the Chinese battery maker says no rival has matched. The latest round covered cell producers with nearly 80% of global capacity, ahead of a full certification scheme due in early 2027. The pilot is building a shared method to track, measure and verify the environmental, social and governance (ESG) record of a battery over its life. CATL’s entry this year reported ESG data for every stage of supply, from mining and refining through materials, cells and packs. That breadth matters as passports move from trial to obligation. EU rules will require digital passports for electric vehicle batteries from February 2027, giving suppliers with verified upstream data an edge with European automakers. CATL joined at the GBA’s first proof of concept in January 2023, and in the second wave sought separate passports for its Shenxing and cell-to-pack batteries, with results checked by an independent auditor. It also says its core operations are carbon neutral and targets a carbon-neutral value chain by 2035. In a statement, Dennis Pan, Head of Sustainable Development at CATL, said: “The GBA Battery Passport pilot program provides an effective methodology for the industry to monitor, quantify and demonstrate ESG performance across the battery value chain. It helps the industry better prepare for future sustainability risks and challenges.” Source: CATL

artigo.texto: A Finnish battery startup facing sustained accusations from industry rivals that its technology is overstated or outright fraudulent has released new independent test data showing its solid-state cells deliver more than their rated capacity at temperatures that would degrade or destroy a conventional lithium-ion battery. Donut Lab, which has previously claimed its cells can charge in minutes and offer high energy density, commissioned a second evaluation by VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, the country’s state-run research institute. The results, published by Donut Lab this week, focus specifically on thermal performance, examining how the battery behaves at 80°C and 100°C, temperatures at which standard lithium-ion cells begin to suffer serious performance loss and pose safety risks. Standard lithium-ion batteries are very sensitive to heat, with an upper operating temperature limit of typically around 60 to 70 degrees Celsius. High temperatures increase the risk of damage to battery cells and shorten their service life. High temperatures can also cause accelerated reactions inside the cell, and in the worst case, the risk of thermal runaway increases significantly. The Donut Battery does not use flammable liquid electrolytes, the component most responsible for thermal runaway in conventional cells. That difference in architecture is what VTT’s tests were designed to quantify under real thermal stress. The methodology was straightforward. Engineers placed the cell on an aluminium profile, secured a steel plate on top to apply light pressure and reduce hot spots, then measured capacity in stages at each temperature. At 176°F, the battery delivered about 110% of its rated capacity, showed better efficiency than at room temperature, and the cell showed no visible changes after the test. At 212°F, the battery used roughly 107% of its capacity and recharged back to 4.15 volts with the same capacity as at room temperature. Although the pouch lost vacuum at that temperature, the active materials remained fully functional. The efficiency gain at elevated temperatures is explained by basic electrochemistry. Heat reduces the internal resistance of a cell, which in turn reduces the voltage drop during discharge, allowing more of the stored energy to be extracted as usable output. In a liquid-electrolyte battery, that benefit is overwhelmed by accelerating degradation chemistry. In Donut Lab’s solid-state design, the degradation mechanism is largely absent, allowing the efficiency benefit to dominate instead. “The battery’s full capacity was utilised with excellent results at both 80 and 100 degrees Celsius, and it was possible to discharge it at a 1C discharge rate at 80 degrees and a 0.5C discharge rate at 100 degrees without any increase in temperature. The battery’s properties did not change even at 100 degrees, and it functioned normally when recharged, which demonstrates the convincing performance of the Donut Battery even in extremely hot conditions. This confirms that the battery is exceptional not only in terms of performance but also in terms of safety,” said Ville Piippo, CTO at Donut Lab. The results carry practical implications beyond the laboratory. Batteries that tolerate extreme heat without cooling system support could reduce the weight, complexity, and cost of thermal management in electric vehicles, particularly relevant for markets in desert climates where ambient temperatures routinely exceed the operating ceiling of conventional packs. Industrial applications including grid storage, aerospace, and military systems have similarly been constrained by the thermal sensitivity of existing battery chemistry. The tests also represent a deliberate shift in how Donut Lab is managing its public credibility. After bold claims generated skepticism rather than investment interest, the company is now building its case incrementally through third-party data published openly, letting the numbers do the work that press releases could not. For automakers in the US and companies focused on energy storage, having batteries that can handle extreme heat is absolutely essential. Batteries that can endure high temperatures not only lessen the strain on cooling systems but also enhance safety in sweltering regions like Arizona, Texas, and Nevada. Whether the technology proves durable at manufacturing scale remains the central unanswered question, but on the narrow question of what the cells do under extreme heat, the independent record now says they perform better than anything currently in mass production.

artigo.texto: SC Senate candidates clash over data center expansion in debate COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - During Sunday’s debate in South Carolina’s heated U.S. Senate race, data centers became a big point of contention for all three candidates. Republican Sen. Darline Graham, along with challengers Dr. Annie Andrews and Kasie Whitener, were asked Sunday if they supported data center moratoriums and if they’d support federal regulations. Andrews, the Democratic challenger, pushed Graham on her stance on data centers. “She [Graham] thinks we need to all get with the program and build data centers faster and faster,” said Andrews. “So why does ‘Data Center Darline’ think we need to do that? Because data center companies and AI companies have spent millions to prop up her campaign.” Graham fired back. “Since we’re name-calling here. obviously, you don’t know my stance on data centers. I’m concerned about data centers too, but let me be clear here: I think there needs to be community involvement when it comes to data centers,” the senator responded. Whitener, running as a Libertarian, said she feels local communities need to have a voice when it comes to building new data centers in their area. “It is a local issue,” Whitener said. At least six Midlands communities have voted to temporarily pause data center development, with others also doing so across the state. More South Carolinians are raising concerns about possible impacts of those data centers, including water consumption and higher energy bills. “These data centers are being built in communities’ backyards without any community input,” said Andrews. Andrews said her data center plan includes a two-year moratorium. Graham criticized the proposal, citing national security concerns and what she argued is a growing threat from China. “Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country because in two years, China is going to be so far ahead, we’re going to be in so much trouble,” said Graham. Whitener doubled down on her stance. “Your community should be talking to one another and figuring out what’s best for you, and again you don’t need the government’s permission to do that,” Whitener said. Meanwhile, South Carolina state lawmakers are set to reassess statewide regulations on data centers when they return for the next legislative session in 2027. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Celestica apresenta o switch de óptica coempacotada DS6005 para data centers de IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Celestica apresentou o DS6005, um switch para data centers totalmente refrigerado a líquido, que oferece capacidade de até 102,4 Tbps por meio de óptica coempacotada, em um comunicado da empresa datado de 12 de outubro de 2026. O sistema é baseado no chip de switch Tomahawk 6 – Davisson, da Broadcom, e a Celestica o está apresentando no OCP Global Summit 2026, em San Jose, realizado de 12 a 15 de outubro de 2026. A empresa, sediada em Toronto, descreveu o DS6005 como um sistema de comutação por óptica coempacotada (CPO), projetado para atender aos requisitos de densidade de largura de banda, consumo de energia, latência e alcance das redes de data centers de IA de próxima geração. A Celestica afirmou que o switch foi desenvolvido especificamente para redes de ampliação vertical e horizontal de IA e aprendizado de máquina, e que reduz o consumo de energia e a latência, além de melhorar a eficiência e a confiabilidade dos clusters de IA de próxima geração. Gavin Cato, vice-presidente sênior e gerente-geral de soluções de portfólio e engenharia de plataformas de IA da Celestica, afirmou que a infraestrutura de IA está impulsionando a demanda por largura de banda, enquanto o consumo de energia, o gerenciamento térmico, a latência e o alcance se tornam limitações cada vez mais importantes. “O DS6005 reúne óptica coempacotada, refrigeração líquida, módulos laser externos substituíveis em campo e gerenciamento de software compatível com CPO em uma plataforma compacta, projetada para ajudar os clientes a construir redes de IA escaláveis e eficientes em termos de energia”, disse Cato. Hardware e design do DS6005 O DS6005 posiciona seus mecanismos ópticos diretamente no encapsulamento do ASIC do switch, em vez de usar óptica plugável convencional no painel frontal. Segundo a Celestica, o design coempacotado tem como objetivo ajudar operadores de data centers a otimizar a densidade de largura de banda, reduzir a latência e melhorar a eficiência energética. A empresa informou que o equipamento conta com 64 portas de 1,6 TbE, que fornecem ao sistema capacidade de comutação de 102,4 Tbps, e que o gabinete de 1,5OU totalmente refrigerado a líquido, projetado para racks OCP ORv3, melhora a estabilidade térmica e a confiabilidade, ao mesmo tempo que aumenta a densidade geral do rack. O switch também é compatível com SONiC, o que, segundo a Celestica, permite acelerar a entrada em produção em uma arquitetura aberta e comprovada. A página do produto DS6005 lista uma CPU AMD Ryzen x86 ao lado do chip Broadcom TH6-Davisson. As 64 interconexões ópticas passam por 16x 4x conectores MMC-16, e o sistema também inclui uma porta 100GbE QSFP28, portas de console RJ45 e de gerenciamento GbE fora de banda, uma porta USB 3.0 Type A, uma porta USB-C de console e 16 interfaces ELSFP para módulos laser externos. O equipamento está em conformidade com a especificação de rack ORv3-HPR. Na página do produto, a Celestica afirmou que o switch reduz o consumo de energia dos links, oferece latência ultrabaixa e reduz a latência em comparação com a óptica com retimers. A página cita redes de ampliação vertical e horizontal de IA e aprendizado de máquina, computação de alto desempenho, modelos de IA de domínio para nuvens de fronteira e empresas e infraestrutura de nuvem em hiperescala como os tipos de implantação para os quais o sistema é otimizado. Silício Tomahawk 6 – Davisson da Broadcom A Broadcom anunciou, em 8 de outubro de 2025, que estava enviando o Tomahawk 6 – Davisson, seu switch Ethernet CPO de terceira geração, que descreveu como o primeiro do setor a oferecer capacidade de comutação habilitada por óptica de 102,4 Tbps. Para o dispositivo BCM78919, a Broadcom listou 16 mecanismos ópticos Davisson DR de 6,4 Tbps cada, largura de banda de 200 Gbps por link, módulos laser ELSFP substituíveis em campo e suporte a clusters de ampliação vertical com 512 XPUs, bem como a mais de 100.000 XPUs em redes de dois níveis, a 200 Gbps por link. Segundo a Broadcom, o chip está em conformidade com a norma IEEE 802.3 e é interoperável com os padrões 400G e 800G existentes. A Broadcom afirmou que o TH6-Davisson integra de forma heterogênea mecanismos ópticos baseados na tecnologia COUPE da TSMC com encapsulamento avançado de múltiplos chips no nível do substrato. A empresa relatou uma redução de 70% no consumo de energia das interconexões ópticas, um nível que descreveu como mais de 3,5 vezes inferior ao das soluções plugáveis tradicionais. Cato também fez uma declaração de apoio no comunicado de 2025, afirmando que a integração óptica, a eficiência energética e o desempenho do chip estavam alinhados à estratégia da Celestica para infraestrutura de IA e implantações de cargas de trabalho de próxima geração. Declarações de apoio e apresentação no Summit Manish Mehta, vice-presidente de marketing e operações da divisão Optical Systems da Broadcom, afirmou que transformar a óptica coempacotada de uma arquitetura avançada em um sistema pronto para produção exige colaboração nas áreas de silício, mecanismos ópticos, encapsulamento, design térmico, fabricação e integração de sistemas. Mehta disse que a engenharia de sistemas e a execução de plataformas da Celestica ajudaram a transformar a tecnologia da Broadcom em uma plataforma projetada para redes de IA de alta densidade. Sameh Boujelbene, vice-presidente de pesquisa do Dell’Oro Group, afirmou que as redes de IA estão deslocando o gargalo da computação para a infraestrutura física ao seu redor, na qual o consumo de energia, a densidade, o alcance e a complexidade da implantação são cada vez mais importantes. artigo.texto: Energy Dome Opens Piacenza Plant to Expand CO2 Battery Production Energy Dome, an Italian company focused on long-duration energy storage, has launched a production facility in Piacenza, Italy, as part of a push to scale up manufacturing of its CO2 Battery technology for projects worldwide. The site will produce essential components, among them the sizable domes that form part of Energy Dome's carbon dioxide-based storage systems. According to the company, the first dome made completely in-house has been sent to India for the 20 MW/160 MWh Kudgi project alongside state-owned utility NTPC. Manufacturing is also proceeding for the 20 MW/200 MWh Columbia Energy Storage Project in Wisconsin, United States, together with Alliant Energy. artigo.texto: A Yandex é a maior empresa de tecnologia da Rússia, oferecendo serviços como busca, transporte por aplicativo, comércio eletrônico, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial (IA). Sua plataforma Yandex Cloud – especializada em poder computacional, armazenamento de dados e ferramentas de IA – é atualmente utilizada por mais de um terço das maiores empresas da Rússia. O ataque de 11 de outubro teve como alvo uma instalação da Yandex na região de Vladimir, a cerca de 180 km a nordeste de Moscou. Essa instalação também abriga o Galushkin, um dos três supercomputadores da empresa usados para o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial. A Yandex anunciou no Telegram que o ataque danificou a infraestrutura do data center e forçou seu desligamento. “A infraestrutura do centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir foi danificada por um ataque de drone, e as operações no local foram completamente suspensas. Vários serviços da Yandex estão atualmente inacessíveis aos usuários”, afirmou a empresa. Não houve relatos de vítimas no ataque mencionado. As equipes de resgate e os engenheiros da Yandex trabalharam para avaliar os danos e restabelecer o serviço. A empresa também recomendou que os clientes de serviços em nuvem ativem seus planos de contingência para responder a incidentes semelhantes. Segundo relatos da mídia, o ataque forçou a Yandex Cloud a entrar em modo de emergência; a interrupção do serviço afetou bancos, plataformas de comércio eletrônico, serviços de entrega, aplicativos de varejo, farmácias, academias e o site do Aeroporto Pulkovo em São Petersburgo. Em uma atualização posterior, o Yandex afirmou que o acesso a alguns de seus serviços – incluindo a assistente virtual de IA Alice, Busca, Mapas, Táxi e E-mail – estava sendo gradualmente restaurado. Este é o terceiro ataque contra instalações da Yandex em quatro dias. Anteriormente, o centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo, região de Ryazan, foi severamente danificado em um ataque na noite de 7 de outubro, forçando seu desligamento. Outra instalação na região de Kaluga, a cerca de 150 km a sudoeste de Moscou, também foi danificada em um ataque com drone em 9 de outubro.

artigo.texto: The government is building an international carbon market that companies can use not only to trade voluntary greenhouse gas reduction credits but also to meet regulatory requirements, including national emissions targets. To that end, it will split the credit issuance system into two categories and begin full-scale operation of the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) next year. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung-il discussed the detailed implementation plan for the GVCM at a ministerial meeting on international economic affairs on the 12th. The GVCM is designed to spur trading in greenhouse gas reduction credits, whose credibility has been questioned because of a lack of internationally standardized criteria. The government fleshed out the operating framework based on a roadmap announced in December last year. Credits will first be divided into two types depending on whether the host country of a project has approved their transfer. Credits approved for transfer, designated "GVCM A," can be used to meet an investing country's nationally determined contribution (NDC) or to comply with regulations in the international aviation sector. Credits without such approval, designated "GVCM NA," will be used for companies' voluntary environmental activities. Their scope of use can be expanded if the host country grants approval later. The government will also review linking the credits to the domestic emissions trading scheme and the greenhouse gas target management system if certain conditions are met. In line with that shift, the market's previous name, the Global Voluntary Carbon Market, has been changed, with "Voluntary" replaced by "Verified." To improve the credibility of transactions, key information such as project operators and reduction volumes will be recorded on a blockchain. The government plans to build the trading platform using the Korea Exchange (KRX) and to consider issuing credits in the form of digital assets in the future. The government will secure participating countries this year and form an issuing body next year to flesh out the project. It will also discuss converting credits generated by greenhouse gas reduction projects of the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) into GVCM credits. The meeting also reaffirmed existing plans, including the creation of a 3 trillion won ($2.1 billion) overseas construction fund, follow-up negotiations on the South Korea-China free trade agreement (FTA), and an industrial complex in India dedicated to Korean companies. Lee said exports have maintained solid momentum, noting that the current account posted a surplus of $46.11 billion in August. He cited trade issues with the U.S., supply chain instability and the possibility of adjustments in artificial intelligence (AI) investment as external risks. "The government will respond to external uncertainties without wavering as one economic team and create new growth opportunities," Lee said.

artigo.texto: For many years, the price of both solid state drives (SSDs) and hard drives (HDDs) were decreasing in price. About a year ago, I bought a 5TB HDD for backing up my desktop and paid $130 through Amazon. Today, that same drive is $230. People throughout the tech industry have seen the doubling of pricing across the board when it comes to computer storage. And, like so many things in the world today, you can blame AI. While so many are protesting the creation of massive data centers around the country with worries over higher electricity bills and environmental concerns, a slightly more niche issue has emerged thanks to AI’s need for computing power. Hard drives, for portable external ones to replacements for your PC, are going way up in price as data center companies swallow up as much storage as they can get their hands on. The surge in demand has rippled across the technology industry and hit the hard drive market particularly severely, which is ironic considering speculation over the last decade was that the need for hardware like this would slowly disappear with a shift into the cloud. But, data centers have rapidly changed the math when it comes to storage. And hard drive prices aren’t alone. Since early 2025, the price of RAM, once a fairly inexpensive upgrade that has been declining in price for decades, is now through the roof. What cost less than $100 in some cases to upgrade in early 2025 now runs three to four times that, what the industry has dubbed RAMageddon. Some of this might feel like much ado about nothing in the grander scheme of AI’s potential risks to the world and humanity itself, but if you need to make what used to be a pretty easy and cheap upgrade to your computer or storage, suddenly like gas, eggs and virtually everything else, you are going to pay more. And, there really is no clear sign that things will slow down, No doubt manufacturers will begin to stabilize pricing as they produce more tech, but no one would blame them if they didn’t. AI’s rise is still a huge gamble and many people in the technology world have predicted that data centers may eventually be replaced by smaller and cheaper tech options. For now, it just means more money out of your pocket thanks to AI.

artigo.texto: A $410 million bet on Australia's biggest AI infrastructure IPO turned into a one-day stock rout for Maas Group, the industrial supplier caught holding Firmus equity nobody else wanted at the marketed price. Shares in Maas Group Holdings cracked as much as 30% in Sydney trading last Thursday. They closed down 22.4%, wiping out roughly A$517 million, or about US$340 million, in market value, then slid further on Friday and Monday. The trigger was the client it had quietly bet big on: Firmus, the Nvidia-backed AI data center operator, had just pulled its roughly A$7 billion ASX float. Investors refused to clear the offer even after the indicative price was cut from A$11 to A$8.25. StartupFortune covered the IPO withdrawal itself last week. What's new is who actually ate the loss, and it wasn't a hedge fund or a bank underwriter. It was a Dubbo-based construction and quarrying company that had piled A$410 million, including a A$300 million top-up in August, into a 3.2% stake in a business it also supplies through its JLE Group subsidiary. That's the uncomfortable mechanics of an AI infrastructure boom running years ahead of the capital markets built to fund it. Maas wasn't a passive financial investor chasing yield. It was a contractor who put real money into its own customer's growth story. Then it watched that customer's implied valuation collapse from almost A$44 billion to roughly A$33 billion in 48 hours of bookbuilding, before the whole deal got shelved entirely. The spark wasn't investor squeamishness about AI in the abstract. It was something far more specific: CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer said on a podcast that CDC's partnership with Firmus on Project Southgate was no longer going ahead. The project had been announced just last October as a plan to build up to 1.6 gigawatts of AI factories across Australia, with a potential A$73.3 billion in investment behind it. Two people involved in the IPO transaction said institutional orders started pulling out the next day. Firmus co-CEOs Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield pulled the $44 billion float on October 9 after bookbuilding stalled, with partner CDC Data Centres having already exited a $73 billion build-out only 2.5% complete. - nvidia backed AI data centre IPO withdrawn - Australian tech IPO cancelled after investor backlash The scale of the shortfall says everything. Project Southgate was supposed to scale toward 1.6 gigawatts by 2028. Firmus and CDC ended up deploying about 42 megawatts, about 2.6% of the original ambition, before calling it off. Boorer put it plainly: the two companies had made "other choices" about how to develop data centers that diverged from what CDC had envisaged. Layer that on top of Firmus's other problem and the IPO's failure looks less like bad timing and more like investors doing basic diligence. Only about 5% of the data center capacity Firmus has already sold to customers is actually built and running, well behind the roughly 25% completion rate at listed rival NextDC. Meanwhile Firmus is carrying close to $30 billion in debt against that unbuilt capacity. Two months before the float, a private funding round had priced the company at $10.5 billion. The IPO was asking the public market to pay more than three times that figure for a business that, by its own numbers, had delivered a fraction of what it had promised. Firmus says it will now chase private market capital instead, with a person involved in the process telling reporters a Nasdaq listing could follow down the line. The company declined to confirm that plan on record. Who's actually left holding the bag This is the part that should worry anyone watching the broader AI infrastructure trade, not just Firmus specifically. Banks and bond investors have spent recent months growing warier of data center debt generally, as the gap between promised AI compute capacity and physically delivered capacity widens across the sector. IREN is the AI data center firm serving a reported $9.7 billion Microsoft GPU cloud contract from its Childress, Texas campus. It raised $2.3 billion in convertible notes in December 2025 and arranged $3.6 billion of GPU financing in 2026 as it funded its buildout. Firmus's collapse is the clearest data point yet for what happens when that gap gets priced by a public market instead of a private one willing to take management's word for it. Maas Group's trading halt, imposed the morning after the IPO fell apart pending a "material announcement" about its contractual arrangements with Firmus, tells you how tangled supplier and investor relationships have become inside Australia's AI buildout. Maas isn't just exposed through its equity stake. JLE Group, its subsidiary, has construction and infrastructure contracts tied to the same Firmus campuses that are, by Firmus's own account, only 5% complete. A failed IPO doesn't just dent a balance sheet. It can slow or stall the actual construction pipeline that a supplier depends on for revenue. Frankly, the $340 million wiped off Maas in a single session is a cleaner measure of AI infrastructure risk than any valuation multiple Firmus or its bankers floated during the roadshow. Paper valuations can be marked up by a term sheet. A 22% single-day drop in a real, profitable industrial company's share price is money that doesn't come back just because the next funding round prices higher. artigo.texto: Meta has continued its PR blitz in support of its artificial intelligence push. On Oct. 8, the company published a new overview of data center myths as it works to counter negative sentiment around its massive infrastructure developments. In order to fuel its AI push, Meta needs to process increasing amounts of user data, which is why the company is spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build new data centers across the U.S. But the impacts on regions where these projects are being developed have been significant. Some regions have reported water contamination and impacted utilities, as well as damage to local infrastructure. Indeed, Time Magazine reported in July that only a third of Americans approve of the pace of data center development. Meanwhile, more than 300 cities, towns and counties have enacted bans or moratoriums on the construction of hyperscale data centers. Meta knows that this backlash could derail its AI push, which is why it’s been working to counter the negative reports about data center impacts with explainers from its own team about the main concerns with data center developments. In this latest iteration, creator Tom Shaw addressed three myths about data center development: - Regarding concerns about excess water usage and limiting water resources for local residents, Shaw said water usage for cooling Meta’s data centers is “permitted, metered, and counted in the local water plan, not carved out of it.” Shaw also said that many of Meta’s data center facilities use less water annually than an average U.S. golf course does in the same amount of time. - On power usage, Shaw said that Meta works with utility companies years before data center work begins in order to ensure that any new infrastructure is built and installed ahead of time with no impact to local supply. - Shaw also said that Meta’s data center developments create jobs in both the construction phase, and in the ongoing management phase. Shaw added that this often means Meta becomes the biggest employer in regions where data centers are installed. Meta is hoping that by addressing these concerns it can lessen community opposition and ensure that it can continue to build its massive data centers without facing negative public sentiment. Data center concerns have become a political issue, with some candidates using their support of, or opposition to, data centers in order to win support. U.S. President Donald Trump, however, has made his stance on data center development clear. As reported by ABC News, last month Trump said in a social media post: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." Yet, even with the president’s backing, Meta knows the negative impacts of its developments could have longer-term impacts for its business, which is why the company is working hard to counter concerns.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Electricity affordability, data center development and antitrust issues were top concerns voiced about the proposed NextEra Energy-Dominion Energy merger at a hearing held by the Virginia State Corporation Commission at the Fairfax County Government Center on Friday. - Most of the state and local officials who spoke at the hearing asked for the merger to be denied or allowed contingent on guarantees like Virginia Clean Economy Act compliance, data centers paying for infrastructure costs, and prohibitions on regulated utilities making campaign contributions. Local business and union leaders spoke in favor of the deal, citing job creation and the need to meet electricity demand. - Virginia Del. Irene Shin, D, who represents parts of Fairfax County, cited the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Sept. 23 letter to Dominion and NextEra calling their merger application incomplete and requesting more information on issues like rate impacts. “I'm surprised that the SCC has moved forward without doing the same,” she said, urging the commission to reject the merger. Dive Insight: The meeting was the second of two local in-person hearings in Virginia, with the first held Oct. 7 in Newport News. The SCC will also hear public testimony through telephonic hearings on Nov. 5, 9 and 10; the evidentiary hearing in the case begins Nov. 17. Under the case’s current 180-day review clock, the SCC is set to make a decision in the case in January. Virginia’s lieutenant governor, Ghazala Hashmi, D, said in a Tuesday report that she has concluded the merger is “not in the best interest of Virginians” following a five-city listening tour across the state. Gov. Abigail Spanberger, D, has not taken a definitive position on the deal but has called herself “skeptical” about it. In August, Spanberger filed with the SCC to be a respondent in the case. At the Oct. 9 hearing, Alexandria City Councilman John Taylor Chapman said, “Ultimately, our concern is that the creation of the nation's largest electric utility will put Alexandrians at risk of runaway utility costs with limited recourse. Utility costs have risen dramatically over the last several years.” Virginia Sen. Jennifer Boysko, D, whose statement was read by her chief of staff, Karen Harrison, did not speak for or against the merger but said she was concerned about ratepayer burden and “the lack of clear language in the merger proposal for ratepayer protection.” Boysko’s statement asked for a “clear commitment” to the VCEA. U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, D, said in his comments that he believes the proposed merger is “a bad deal for Virginians,” citing rising energy bills along with Dominion’s existing status as a monopoly utility. “This commission has a responsibility to protect Virginia ratepayers,” he said. “NextEra sees enormous profits to be made in Virginia, particularly with the explosion of data centers,” Vindman said. “That is crystal clear. Data centers need to pay their fair share. Virginia families should not have to subsidize corporate expansion through higher utility bills.” Don Slaiman, the political coordinator for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 26, which represents electrical workers in the D.C., area, said he had not planned to speak “because our unions are still negotiating with NextEra and Dominion.” Slaiman didn’t give his opinion on the merger, but said he felt the need to respond to the negative comments previous speakers had made about data center development. “If we did not have data centers to store this data and we reserved it to private service, we'd be using almost half of our grid instead of the 6% or 7% we're using now,” Slaiman said. “So unless you're ready to curb your own digital footprint, I would not admonish this industry so much, which has provided fantastic jobs for my membership.” State Del. Kirk McPike, D, whose district covers part of the city of Alexandria, said he is opposed to the merger unless there are “ironclad guarantees that costs will not increase for Virginia taxpayers, that large energy users like data centers will pay for their own infrastructure and energy usage,” that VCEA commitments are met in a timely manner “and that you'll never see the sort of corruption scandal that occurred in Florida occur here in Virginia.” NextEra agreed in June to pay a $150 million settlement over allegations that it lied about its involvement in political interference schemes in Florida. Shin’s comments also cited concerns about Florida Power & Light’s “Robo memo” which is filed in the SCC’s case docket but which the public has yet to review. Clean Virginia noted in a Sept. 2 motion to compel that the memo is titled, “Florida Power & Light Officers’ Potentially Unlawful Conduct Through Third-Party Consultants and Vendors.” SCC Chief Hearing Examiner Mathias Roussy ruled Oct. 2 in favor of the release of the Robo memo. Shin also said she has concerns about whether NextEra will commit to meeting Virginia’s clean energy goals if it acquires Dominion, saying previous responses from company representatives on the topic “[sounded] like a company laying the groundwork to walk away from the VCEA.” “When Dominion was asked about the VCEA, its executive vice president told the commission, ‘I am still your throat to choke,’ and that was a shocking thing for me to hear as a legislator,” she said. State Del. John McAuliff, D, who represents the 30th District in western Loudoun County and campaigned against data center development in 2025, expressed concerns about NextEra and Dominion's history of political contributions. “If we move forward with anything like this, we have to prohibit regulated utilities from making campaign contributions to the elected officials who oversee them,” McAuliff said.

artigo.texto: Estudo identifica como reduzir falhas em baterias de sódio Simulações computacionais mostram como ajustar eletrólitos para proteger áreas sensíveis das baterias e prolongar sua vida útil Baterias de íons de sódio despontam como uma alternativa viável às populares baterias de lítio, graças à maior abundância e distribuição de sua matéria-prima. No entanto, para melhorar seu desempenho, é preciso resolver um gargalo técnico: a formação de dendritos, estruturas que reduzem a vida útil e causam falhas de segurança no componente. Um estudo computacional realizado pelo Centro de Inovação em Novas Energias (CINE) mapeou esse processo em escala atômica, oferecendo orientações concretas para controlar o fenômeno e, dessa forma, melhorar o desempenho das baterias. As baterias de íons de sódio destinam-se a diversas aplicações, com destaque para o armazenamento de energia em larga escala, a integração de fontes renováveis às redes elétricas e a eletrônica portátil. Apesar de seu potencial, possuem densidade de energia menor que as baterias de lítio. Na prática, isso significa que precisam de mais volume e peso para armazenar a mesma quantidade de energia. Para superar esse desafio tecnológico, é fundamental compreender, em escala atômica, os mecanismos que regem as interações entre o ânodo —eletrodo em que os íons de sódio ficam armazenados durante a descarga da bateria— e o eletrólito —substância que permite o transporte dos íons de sódio entre os eletrodos. Cientistas do programa de Design Computacional de Materiais do CINE estudam um aspecto crítico dessas interações: a formação de uma camada muito fina na superfície do ânodo. Chamada de interface de eletrólito sólido (SEI, na sigla em inglês), essa camada se forma a partir da decomposição de componentes do eletrólito. Quando a SEI é de boa qualidade, protege o ânodo de reagir continuamente com o eletrólito e permite, ao mesmo tempo, a passagem de íons de sódio durante os ciclos de carga e descarga da bateria. Por outro lado, quando a SEI tem baixa qualidade, ela racha e cresce de forma irregular, favorecendo a formação de estruturas de sódio em forma de agulha — os dendritos —, que constituem uma das principais causas de falhas e riscos à segurança das baterias. A equipe do CINE se propôs a compreender os processos de formação da SEI em escala atômica. Esse objetivo só poderia ser alcançado com o uso de ferramentas computacionais, já que um estudo experimental seria inviável por causa da natureza ultrafina, quimicamente heterogênea e dinâmica da SEI. “Em nosso projeto, selecionamos alguns eletrólitos e um tipo de ânodo —o de sódio metálico— e simulamos como moléculas individuais dos eletrólitos interagem com esse ânodo”, detalhou Juarez L. F. da Silva, professor do Instituto de Química de São Carlos da Universidade de São Paulo (IQSC-USP) e coordenador do programa de Design Computacional do CINE, liderou a pesquisa. Inicialmente, os autores utilizaram simulações computacionais baseadas na física quântica para construir um modelo de uma superfície de sódio metálico com defeitos. “As superfícies reais desses ânodos nunca são perfeitamente lisas. Elas apresentam pequenos aglomerados de átomos em relevo e minúsculas cavidades onde faltam átomos”, explicou Tapasendra Adhikary, primeiro autor do artigo e pesquisador de pós-doutorado no IQSC-USP. Com esse modelo, a equipe simulou interações com 22 espécies químicas encontradas em eletrólitos de baterias. De acordo com Tapasendra, o objetivo foi compreender quais moléculas do eletrólito se fixam em cada local do ânodo e por quê, para projetar eletrólitos capazes de controlar a formação da camada SEI. Receita de bons eletrólitos Dessa maneira, a equipe conseguiu investigar como os componentes do eletrólito interagem, em escala atômica, com um ânodo de sódio com defeitos e como essas interações moldam os estágios iniciais da formação da SEI. “A descoberta fundamental é que essas irregularidades na superfície do sódio funcionam como pontos críticos de atividade química”, disse Tapasendra. Em outras palavras, o local em que uma molécula se fixa depende fortemente da geometria da superfície. Com base nos resultados, os autores formularam orientações concretas para desenvolver eletrólitos que promovam a formação de camadas SEI de boa qualidade. “Primeiro, deve-se dar preferência a sais que liberam fluoreto, uma vez que o fluoreto se liga com especial força aos sítios de defeito reativos e forma fluoreto de sódio — uma camada inorgânica resistente e muito eficaz em vedar esses pontos vulneráveis e bloquear o crescimento de dendritos”, sugeriu Tapasendra. A 2ª orientação consiste em combinar esses sais liberadores de fluoreto com solventes de carbonato cíclico para criar condições favoráveis à formação de uma camada protetora rica em fluoreto e carbonato nos pontos mais vulneráveis do ânodo. Além disso, os autores destacam a importância de desenvolver e testar formulações de eletrólitos levando em conta superfícies de eletrodos reais e imperfeitas, em vez de superfícies planas idealizadas. Isso porque a rugosidade da superfície determina onde e como a camada protetora se forma. Este texto foi publicado originalmente pela Agência Fapesp, em 7 de setembro de 2026. O conteúdo é livre para republicação, citada a fonte, e foi adaptado para o padrão do Poder360.

artigo.texto: Aurora neighbors call for removal of police chief, end to data centers in city During Monday's Aurora City Council meeting, neighbors called for a data center moratorium and for Aurora's police chief to be removed. City council unanimously passed an ordinance that will keep data centers from being built in some areas. It's a step toward limiting where data centers can be, not banning them entirely. The city of Aurora has nine existing data centers, with five in various stages of the development process. Many public commenters Monday spoke out against data centers. "We need a moratorium on all data centers!" one Aurora neighbor said, and was met with loud cheers from the audience. "I do not want this data center to be built near my home building this data center will affect all the creatures. Please don't build this data center, thank you," a young boy said on the record. City council voted unanimously to approve the first reading of an ordinance that would prohibit new data centers from being built in areas zoned "mixed-use office/institutional," where they could be located near schools, homes and assisted living facilities. It would not ban data centers citywide. While several commenters spoke directly in support of the ordinance, many Green Valley Ranch neighbors shared concerns about the proposed Trident data center that could move in near their homes. That area falls under different zoning, and it would not be impacted by the ordinance. "Reverse the A-D zoning; stop the Trident's data center," one woman said. Many in the audience cheered. There are currently no submitted development applications for data centers in "mixed-use office/institutional" zoned areas. City council will have its final vote on the ordinance on Oct. 26. If passed, the ordinance would likely take effect 30 days later. Throughout the meeting, dozens of community members stood with signs depicting the faces of Black men killed by police, demanding the removal of Todd Chamberlain as Aurora's police chief. Activists and community members staged a sit-in at the meeting. They said they won't leave city hall until officials agree to meet with them directly about their demand for new leadership in Aurora's police department, and make a termination plan for the police chief. They say it comes after their concerns over deadly police shootings and transparency have gone ignored. "We are tired of people being murdered by the Aurora Police Department," one activist said. "We will not leave this building until we have a termination date and strategy for Chief Todd Chamberlain," said MiDian Shofner, CEO of Epitome of Black Excellence and Partnership. Shofner said some council members indicated a meeting could take place after Monday's council meeting, but the demonstrators say they won't leave the building until there is a termination plan for Chamberlain. As of 10 p.m. Monday, the activists were still in the building. Aurora's leaders shared the following comments on the sit-in: Statement from Mayor Pro Tem Alison Coombs and Public Safety Committee Chair Rob Andrews, "We have reached out to all concerned parties and are actively working to schedule a meeting at the earliest opportunity." "We recognize and respect the importance of ensuring that every voice is heard, and we welcome the opportunity for open, honest, and constructive dialogue." "We remain committed to transparency, meaningful community engagement, and fostering an environment where residents feel comfortable expressing their perspectives, feedback, and concerns. We believe that listening to one another is essential to building trust and finding solutions that move our community forward." Statement from City Manager Jason Batchelor, "I welcome discussions with all community members on city issues and look forward to having a meaningful dialogue." "Crime in Aurora is down across every major category – murder, sexual assault, aggravated assault, robbery, burglary, larceny and motor vehicle theft. Total crime in Aurora is down 10% from this time last year and 38% from September 2024, when Todd Chamberlain was sworn in as chief." "In a recent community survey, nearly 74% of Aurora residents rated the job that APD is doing as fair, good or excellent. A similar survey at the start of the consent decree in 2022 had 57% expressing the same opinion." "The city of Aurora continues to make significant progress and improvements, including being in "substantial compliance" or "right track, 75-99% complete" on all mandates outlined in the state-mandated consent decree." "The city also continues to move forward with the Office of Public Safety Accountability, a city function that the city began contemplating before the consent decree process began in 2021. Applications for the Public Safety Accountability Manager closed in September and candidate review is underway. Community engagement, including a meet-and-greet with candidates, is planned as the process continues." "I stand behind the ongoing work and continuous improvement at APD."

artigo.texto: The Greek Ministry of Environment and Energy presented a bill of law setting detailed rules for the development of projects for data centers in the country. Greek authorities have witnessed a steep rise in interest in data centers. Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO or ADMIE) saw applications rise from 5 GW to 9 GW in just two months in the summer. The proposal for the new law is attempting to clarify the regulatory framework concerning the connections to the power network, as well as establish specific requirements. IPTO to handle requests above 10 MW When it comes to oversight, IPTO will have to include data centers in its ten-year development plan, separately from other large consumers. The operator is called to categorize availability at extra-high-voltage substations. They can be free, partially congested or fully congested. These estimations will be updated every two months to provide timely information to the market. As for the licensing process, IPTO will be responsible for data centers above 10 MW, with Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (HEDNO or DEDDIE) handling requests below that capacity. Projects won’t be allowed to be segmented into smaller parts for benefiting simpler regulations. Power must be 60% renewable Investors would be required to submit letters of guarantee for EUR 200,000 per MW, with a three-year duration. When ready, the operator would provide them with a three-year connection offer, at which point developers need to submit a report with the project’s technical features and a power supply agreement. Consumed electricity must be at least 60% renewable in origin. Data centers can connect directly to neighboring renewable electricity and energy storage facilities, or sign power purchase agreements (PPAs). Data centers above 200 MW would benefit from priority in their connection, although with certain caveats. The owner must establish that 80% of the electricity will come either from a distributed power producer, or from energy storage with a six-hour injection duration.
