artigo.texto: CATL Largest global volume According to Wood Mackenzie's newest outlook, the worldwide energy storage sector is entering a period characterized by both scale and complexity. The firm projects that cumulative capacity will exceed 7 TWh by 2035, while demand growth during 2026 alone will be near 30 percent. What matters more than the speed of expansion, however, is how the market is composed. China and the United States continue to hold the top two positions among national energy storage markets, but in 2026 Europe's yearly installations surpassed annual US energy storage capacity for the first time, claiming second place behind China. Government-led tenders remain the principal force in the utility segment, having cleared more than 80 GW of de-rated capacity worldwide, with India contributing the largest single share. Poland has emerged as the top emerging market globally, buoyed by capacity-market auctions and a grid lacking flexibility. Demand signals in mature utility markets are equally solid. Contracted offtake for storage has exceeded 130 GW, with utility power purchase agreements and tolling deals combined representing over three-quarters of all contracts signed, based on the firm's global offtake tracker. Within the residential landscape, the centre of gravity has moved southward. Australia has displaced Germany as the world's foremost residential energy storage market, with over half a million installations supported by its Cheaper Home Batteries subsidy, while the US market shrinks this year as tax credits grow less accessible. Wood Mackenzie forecasts commercial and industrial storage capacity as a separate category, and the breakdown reveals that industrial demand is substantially larger in certain regions. In the most recent market outlook update, Wood Mackenzie alters the way the utility energy storage market is measured. The utility segment is now divided into three parts — standalone, solar-paired and wind-paired — rather than one, since each is expanding for distinct reasons, at varying speeds and in different locations. Standalone projects continue to lead and will do so through 2035. Yet paired capacity is no longer negligible: nearly one-third of the storage anticipated to come online by 2035 will be located alongside a wind or solar plant. The revised breakdown reveals how dissimilar the regions are, owing to their differing policy and economic parameters. Europe is the most standalone-dominated market globally, with the vast majority of its utility pipeline unpaired. Nevertheless, it is also set for the quickest expansion in paired capacity, as deteriorating economics for standalone solar drive developers toward co-location. This positions Europe as the market most likely to move rapidly toward co-location as an economic remedy for stranded solar projects in markets such as Spain or Germany. The Americas occupy the opposite position. In the US, nearly half of utility storage additions are solar-paired — a legacy of the ITC pairing requirement in the early days and now poor solar capture rates in key markets like CAISO. That proportion is anticipated to decline as storage extends into lower solar-penetration states, where standalone economics perform better. Data centre-linked battery projects are also emerging in the US, though not all are paired with wind or solar: gas-plus-storage pairings are the new co-location favourites for emerging data center projects. Asia Pacific falls in between, with solar pairing the fastest-growing utility category, driven mainly by India, which has surpassed Australia as the region's largest utility-scale market. Regulatory changes are pivotal here: India's new rules will mandate that solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 incorporate co-located storage equal to at least 10 percent of capacity, increasing to a four-hour minimum duration from 2029. Aging storage assets will only begin to come offline and be replaced at scale after 2030, contributing 40 GWh of repowered capacity by 2035, led by the US, Japan and Germany. This marks the first indication of a market mature enough to require replacement, which has earned a reporting line in the latest energy storage outlook. Wood Mackenzie is holding a global energy storage outlook webinar on 3 November to examine which markets and segments are shaping the future of global energy storage. Anna Darmani serves as a research director on the Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables team, leading the EMEA energy storage team. She previously worked at EIT InnoEnergy, developing innovation and technology roadmaps and contributing to EU research and advisory projects. artigo.texto: Em outubro de 2026, drones ucranianos atingiram um centro de dados de inteligência artificial da Yandex, empresa russa frequentemente chamada de “o Google russo”, e tiraram a estrutura de operação, segundo a Ars Technica. A publicação Ars Technica não divulgou a data exata nem a localização da instalação atingida. Também não foram informados números sobre prejuízos financeiros ou quantidade de servidores danificados. A Yandex domina serviços de busca, mapas e plataformas digitais na Rússia, e expandiu sua infraestrutura para processamento de inteligência artificial. A empresa não se pronunciou publicamente sobre o incidente, segundo a Ars Technica. O ataque ao centro de dados de IA demonstra que a guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia passou a mirar a infraestrutura computacional que sustenta tanto a economia de guerra quanto sistemas de vigilância. A computação de alto desempenho se tornou um ativo estratégico. Diferentemente de alvos tradicionais, a neutralização de um data center de IA compromete a capacidade de processamento massivo de dados, essencial para logística, inteligência e monitoramento em tempo real. A Ars Technica destacou que o ataque representa um precedente em conflitos armados, ampliando o escopo de alvos para infraestrutura digital crítica. Segundo a Ars Technica, a paralisação do centro de dados interrompeu serviços associados à Yandex, mas a extensão do impacto sobre usuários e clientes corporativos não foi detalhada. O episódio consolida a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial como frente de batalha na guerra entre Rússia e Ucrânia, de acordo com a Ars Technica.

artigo.texto: Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) are two of the biggest spenders in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Each has a sprawling cloud computing business with far more demand than capacity, so they're spending unprecedented amounts of money to expand their data center footprints. For 2026, Amazon plans to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures, while Alphabet expects to lay out about $200 billion. Nearly all of that will go toward building out data centers. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » While I think both stocks are strong investments, I believe Amazon has far more to gain. But don't sleep on Alphabet, as it's growing at an incredibly fast rate. AWS is a major part of Amazon's overall picture The reason why I think Amazon has more to gain from its cloud computing investment is the position of Amazon Web Services (AWS) within Amazon as a whole. In Q2, AWS accounted for about 21% of Amazon's total revenue. However, AWS produced 60% of Amazon's operating profits. That's a natural result of the fact that e-commerce and retail generally are relatively low-margin businesses; AWS' operating margin is far higher. This magnifies the effect that revenue growth from AWS has on the overall company's profitability. So its net sales rose 20 year over year in Q2, but its operating income increased by 43%. As Amazon continues to invest big time in AWS, its added capacity will translate directly into impressive revenue growth and even larger profit growth. Likewise, Alphabet is benefiting from Google Cloud's growth, but not to the same degree. The company's core business is advertising from its Google family of products, and that already has a pretty strong operating margin. Companywide, Alphabet had an operating margin of 34% in Q2. Google Cloud did slightly better, with a 36% operating margin, but since it's already pretty close to the company's overall margin, it doesn't have the outsized effect on profits that AWS has on Amazon. But don't disregard Google Cloud, either. Google Cloud's revenue growth in Q2 was 82% year over year, while AWS's was 37%. That mismatch shows how Alphabet is rapidly expanding its cloud segment. However, it's doing so off a much smaller base. Amazon is the world's largest cloud infrastructure provider, with a 28% market share as of Q2. While No. 3 Alphabet is slowly cutting into that lead, it still accounts for just 15% of the market. Google Cloud booked $24.8 billion in revenue in Q2, while AWS booked $42.2 billion.

artigo.texto: On Maxxen Day 2026, Maxxen Energy opened its factory in Türkiye to the European energy storage industry and showed the most advanced BESS factory in Europe. Maxxen Day 2026 brought together more than 300 guests from 18 European countries and nearly 120 companies across the battery energy storage system (BESS) value chain. Discussions covered the technology landscape, market outlook and revenues, financing, risk management, as well as project development and scaling, according to Maxxen. Maxxen Day 2026 welcomed energy industry executives, investors, project developers, technology companies and business partners from all across the European continent, from the UK to Türkiye. In just nine months, the company has delivered more than 600 MWh across 20+ projects Maxxen Energy’s factory in Aydın, Türkiye, opened in December 2025. In just nine months, the company has delivered more than 600 MWh across 20+ projects, reaching nearly 5% of the European grid-scale BESS market. Maxxen believes this makes it the fastest-growing European BESS manufacturer ever. At the event, Maxxen also announced its membership in SolarPower Europe. Valiente: We are shaping the future of the industry, together Ruben Valiente, Managing Director of Maxxen Energy, said that on Maxxen Day it opened its factory in Türkiye to the European battery storage industry and showed what the company believes is one of the most advanced BESS factories in Europe. “We also believe Maxxen is the fastest-growing European BESS manufacturer ever, with more than 600 MWh delivered in just nine months. It was a privilege to host guests from all across the European continent, from the UK to Türkiye. Many told us it was one of the best industry events they had attended. None of this happens without people and culture,” he stressed. He thanked the Maxxen Energy team, and colleagues in Türkiye in particular, who work tirelessly and welcome everyone with great warmth. “As a European company, we are proud to contribute to Europe’s energy transition, and we look forward to doing so alongside our peers at SolarPower Europe,” Valiente added. The future of Europe’s energy storage market took centre stage Sessions explored the technology landscape, market dynamics and revenue outlook for Europe’s energy storage market. Panels looked at how to finance the investments needed to meet the growing demand for flexibility, and at the role of risk management and insurance in securing that financing, Maxxen said. Project developers shared what they learned moving from their first projects to large-scale portfolios, and the challenges of scaling. Sessions and panels featuring international companies including Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Wood Mackenzie, Clean Horizon, Solas Capital, Volteo Capital, Gresham House, Munich Re, Zagope, Luxera and Crowmie brought perspectives from across the BESS value chain. Guests saw the factory in action After the sessions, the programme continued with factory tours and product presentations. Guests followed the production of battery systems step by step and spoke directly with Maxxen’s engineering and technical teams. A networking gathering gave participants time to continue the conversation and build new business connections. On the second day, guests took part in a cultural programme showcasing the heritage of the Aegean region, Maxxen pointed out.

artigo.texto: Charlotte residents urge city to extend data center construction pause ‘I hope the council would do the right thing and go at least another year’ CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - As Charlotte leaders consider whether to extend a pause on new data centers, a group of residents in east Charlotte are urging the city to keep the freeze in place for another year. Cristopher Scalise, co-founder of STOP East Charlotte Data Center, lives about a mile from the site of a proposed 40,000-square-foot data center on Hood Road. “I wasn’t shocked to hear they wanted to put something up here, but I’m surprised at the scope of it and the size of it, right smack in the middle of a sea of residential properties,” Scalise said. The 150-day moratorium, which halts new data center development, expires Nov. 5. Scalise served on a city task force that studied data centers and potential concerns, including noise and water and energy use. He is now urging the city to extend the moratorium until it can develop policies to address possible harms. “I hope the council would do the right thing and go at least another year because, as we found on the task force, there is an enormous, enormous amount of work that still needs to be done,” Scalise said. “We’re not ready to move forward as a city on this issue.” This week, Scalise launched a webpage where residents can review timelines, key points and other research related to the first 75 day “learning period” during the moratorium. It can be accessed by clicking here. Though he is no longer on the task force, Scalise encouraged neighbors to stay involved and keep pressing elected officials for answers. “It needs to be consistent and loud,” he said. “And there needs to be this continual growth of a resistance movement that is putting constant pressure on elected officials to do the right thing for the right reason.” The City Council is expected to hold its final public hearing on a possible moratorium extension Monday night. A vote is anticipated in two weeks. Copyright 2026 WBTV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The Luxembourg meeting will test the bloc’s unity on climate policy and biodiversity goals as ministers prepare to negotiate on implementing global environmental commitments. Environment Council meets in Luxembourg on Monday as Europe prepares for key UN climate and biodiversity talks. European Union environment and climate ministers will gather in Luxembourg on Monday to debate the proposed overhaul of the bloc’s emissions trading system (ETS) and seek agreement on the EU’s negotiating positions ahead of two major United Nations summits on climate and biodiversity. The Environment Council meeting, scheduled for October 12, will open with a policy debate on the ETS review. The package was proposed by the European Commission on July 17, 2026, as part of efforts to implement the EU’s 2040 climate target. It is currently being examined by the Council’s preparatory bodies, and ministers will outline their views and priorities on key aspects of the proposal. The review also forms part of the “One Europe, One Market” roadmap. Ministers will then be invited to approve conclusions on preparations for COP31, the UN climate change conference scheduled for November 9-20 in Antalya, Türkiye, under the joint leadership of Türkiye and Australia. The EU’s main focus will be on implementing the Paris Agreement and delivering on commitments already made. They will also seek to adopt conclusions ahead of the UN biodiversity conference, COP17, to be held from October 19-30 in Yerevan, Armenia. The Yerevan summit will mark the first global review of collective progress towards the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its 2030 targets. Under other business, the Irish presidency and the Commission will brief ministers on the outcome of the UN desertification conference (UNCCD COP17), held this summer in Mongolia. The meeting comes as governments worldwide face growing pressure to turn climate and nature pledges into concrete action. How united the EU’s 27 member states appear in Luxembourg is likely to shape the bloc’s influence in the negotiating rooms in Yerevan and Antalya, where developing countries are expected to press for stronger finance and implementation support. The next Environment Council meeting is scheduled for December 11.

artigo.texto: Local Georgia Democrats presented a united front against data center development Monday morning when State Sen. Harold Jones issued statements in alongside other local Democratic Party representatives in a press event at a storefront campaign hub downtown. Jones emphasized a contrast between the positions of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms and her Republican opponent Rick Jackson regarding data centers projects popping up throughout the state. “The key is we do not want data centers for small communities. We do not want our electric bills to go up. We do not want Rick Jackson to profit from data centers as he has in healthcare,” said Jones, alluding to Jackson having declined going up against Bottoms in the Atlanta Press Club election debate also scheduled for Monday night. Speaking alongside Jones were Parin Amin, chair of the Columbia County committee of the Georgia Democratic Party, and Cathi Frederiksen, chair of the Georgia Democrats’ 12th Congressional District committee. All three speakers underscored Jackson’s investment in a data center development project in Texas. “Just listen to what the Texas residents say. It’s the same thing as people in Appling and Harlem. They said it’s sold out, that the community was not involved, the [nondisclosure agreements] kept it all quiet, and they forced it down at the very last minute,” said Amin, referencing the data center developments—two out of three that have thus far been approved by the Columbia County Board of Commissioners—that have sparked controversy for most of this year. “The first time most of us heard about it was at a planning and zoning meeting, and they came, they packed the house, but they didn’t listen to us. We can do much better than the self-enriching governor for Georgia.” Frederiksen, who also chairs the Georgia Democratic Rural Council, likewise referred to a $20 billion project by artificial intelligence company OpenAI to build a data center in Effingham County, Ga., signed off by that county’s development authority last year amid claims by county leaders that it could lead to eliminating the county’s property tax. “[Rick Jackson] needs to divest today. Not after the election, but today,” said Frederiksen. “Georgia is a hotbed for data center growth. Our next governor will make decisions about land, water, power bills, and who gets a seat at the table, those decisions will shape the state for generations. We cannot afford to have someone with millions invested in data centers making these calls.” Jones outlined candidate Bottoms’ plan for data center development in Georgia: to impose a statewide moratorium to make way, he says, for a thorough investigation into their potential ramifications, to eventually discern the best course of action to regulate data centers. “I think that’s the key, because when we talk about going back in January and all of a sudden now we’re just going to try to create these ordinances, we’re going to try to create these guardrails,” he said. “What we really need to do is study the issue a little bit more, and I think that’s what she is talking about for us to make an informed decision about what we should do from a state perspective, so I think her plan is a good common sense plan about how we ought to go about doing things.” The media conference comes amid Jackson’s scheduled appearance with Governor Brian Kemp Monday evening in a Republican rally at the Columbia County Exhibition Center in Grovetown, a stop along Jackson’s campaign tour. Skyler Andrews is a reporter covering general reporting with The Augusta Press. Reach him at skyler@theaugustapress.com.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen e chinesa Gotion aprofundam parceria em baterias Acordos preveem 3 joint ventures na Espanha, na Eslováquia e no Marrocos para ampliar a produção de baterias A unidade de baterias do Grupo Volkswagen, PowerCo SE, e a fabricante chinesa de baterias Gotion High-tech Co. Ltd. vão estabelecer 3 joint ventures na Espanha, na Eslováquia e no Marrocos para ampliar a produção de baterias. As empresas anunciaram os acordos em 28 de setembro. Em Valência, na Espanha, a megafábrica da PowerCo, atualmente em construção, será transferida para uma joint venture, na qual a PowerCo terá participação de 51% e a Gotion, de 49%. A unidade deverá se tornar o centro europeu de produção de baterias de LFP (fosfato de ferro-lítio) da Volkswagen, uma tecnologia de menor custo amplamente utilizada em veículos elétricos. Na Eslováquia, a fábrica de células de bateria da Gotion em Šurany será transferida para uma joint venture na qual a empresa chinesa terá participação de 51% e a PowerCo, de 49%. A parceria produzirá células LFP para veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. No Marrocos, as empresas estabelecerão uma joint venture para produzir materiais catódicos de LFP, com participação de 51% da Gotion e de 49% da PowerCo. A parceria é realizada enquanto a União Europeia avalia novas condições para investimentos estrangeiros em setores como o de baterias. De acordo com a proposta apresentada pela Comissão Europeia em março, investidores estrangeiros precisariam cumprir pelo menos 4 de 6 condições, incluindo limites à participação acionária estrangeira e exigências mínimas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento na UE e de aquisição de insumos localmente. A proposta continua em análise e ainda não tem um cronograma específico para implementação. Este texto foi publicado originalmente pela Caixin em 2 de outubro de 2026. Foi traduzida e republicada pelo Poder360 sob acordo mútuo de compartilhamento de conteúdo.

artigo.texto: The Poway City Council unanimously approved to ban large, third-party data centers used for artificial intelligence applications throughout the city. The ordinance approved by council members on a second reading Oct. 6 amends the Poway Municipal Code and the South Poway Specific Plan to prohibit data centers in all zones of the city. The ordinance states the city of Poway wishes to protect and preserve the public safety, health, welfare, resources and quality of development throughout the city through effective land use and planning. Mayor Steve Vaus said large-scale data centers “have very real impacts” when the item was introduced for a first reading on Sept. 15. “We are the first in the county to say no to AI data centers and I expect we will not be the last,” Vaus said during the Oct. 6 second reading of the item on the consent calendar. A staff report stated there is increasing evidence that these types of data centers use significant water and electricity and result in a strain on water and electricity infrastructure, and have an adverse impact on utility rates. Additionally, concerns include potential negative impacts on air quality, noise and increased fire risks. Vaus said banning AI data centers is a land use issue rather than a technology issue. There is a finite amount of land in the South Poway Business Park, he said. “Once that is consumed, we don’t get it back,” Vaus said. “AI data centers are simply not the highest and best use (of the land). “Local control means making these decisions before someone else makes them for us,” he added. Councilmember Anita Edmondson, who proposed the ban with Vaus, said the ban is not about entering philosophical debates over the merits of AI. Instead, her concern is with providing jobs, she said. “AI data centers are largely automated,” according to the staff report. “While they may result in temporary construction jobs, there is a lack of local, long-term jobs and economic growth provided when compared to traditional industrial, manufacturing and office uses that would otherwise be permitted in the city’s commercial areas, specifically including (the business park).” The data centers were identified in the staff report as computer servers that use high-density clusters of specialized accelerators such as graphics processing units and tensor processing units, and any associated data storage systems, for third-party entities that store, process, train or support AI applications. Speaker John Szlyk said data centers have high energy needs, the equipment needs to be cooled with large volumes of water, and they produce a constant humming noise. They also limit job growth because most of the jobs of these types of data centers are associated with maintenance of the facility, he said. Szlyk thanked the council for acting expeditiously to ban the AI data centers and requested that similar action be taken to lay down rules for pickleball courts in residential neighborhoods. Councilmember Christopher Pikus said banning AI data centers is about making the best use of limited land. Instead of an automated data center, the city could have businesses that hire people who live and shop in the community and contribute to its success, he said. “I want the business park to be a business park for everyone, not just a mausoleum for data storage,” Pikus said. “Ultimately, some proposal will come along. We have to get a regulation in place before someone drops a permit application on our desk.” Although Councilmember Jenny Maeda proposed placing a five-year moratorium on the development of AI data centers instead of a complete ban, the suggestion was not supported by the other council members.

artigo.texto: BISMARCK, N.D. (PSC) – The North Dakota Public Service Commission (PSC) will hold a public hearing on Friday, October 23, regarding a proposal to construct a battery energy storage system in Cass County, North Dakota. Harmony Storage, LLC (a subsidiary of Geronimo Power, LLC) is requesting a siting permit for a 200-megawatt battery energy storage system with a four-hour duration to store excess power. The project also includes associated inverters, transformers, underground cables and other ancillary facilities such as fencing, roads, storm water facilities and a Battery Management System. The project will connect to the Harmony Solar collector substation via underground collection lines. The estimated cost of the project is $249 million. The Project will be capable of storing surplus power from the Harmony Solar collector substation and the existing electric grid when production exceeds system demand (oversupply). If the grid has excess energy (e.g., during periods of low demand), this energy will be routed and stored by the project for later release. Developers say the project will enhance reliability and will be able to deliver surplus energy to the grid by storing low-cost, excess generation from the Harmony Solar Project and surplus power from the grid. The Project will then be able to discharge the stored energy into the grid at times of increased demand. The project would be located on approximately 9.73 acres within the 74-acre project area in Harmony Township and would be adjacent to the planned Harmony Solar Project, which has already been permitted by the Commission. The location is approximately 4.2 miles north of Mapleton, 7.4 miles northeast of Casselton and 10.3 miles northwest of Fargo. Details for the public hearing are as follows: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 10 a.m. Central Time in the Days Inn Hotel & Governorâs Waterpark, RV Park & Fitness Center 2050 Governorâs Drive Casselton, ND 58012 The hearing provides an opportunity for members of the public to contribute to the PSCâs official record. Any comments from members of the public must be received at a hearing to be part of the record. People with concerns or support/opposition for the project are encouraged to attend the hearing and present their information. Information received after the hearing will not be part of the official record and cannot be used as a basis for the Commissionâs decision unless certain additional procedures are followed.

artigo.texto: Equinix, a digital infrastructure and data center provider, has told w.media that it is finalizing a full incident response report in an effort to prevent a recurrence of a fuel leak that occurred at its NY2 data center facility in Secaucus, New Jersey, in September 2026. Equinix said it detected a leak from a storage tank outside the facility on September 11, 2026. It added that the leak was stopped and that it immediately engaged Clean Harbors, an environmental and industrial services provider, to begin remediation efforts. The company also notified the Secaucus Fire Department, New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP), and other agencies. “Our investigation found that a mechanical failure of two valves used as part of a routine filtration process for stored fuel caused the leak. We regret that this occurred and the concern it has caused the community. We are finalizing a full incident response report to prevent recurrence,” Equinix said in a statement to w.media. The company added that it has been a part of the Secaucus community since 2001 and is committed to rectifying the incident and maintaining the trust of its neighbors and local officials. Last week w.media reported that Congresswoman Nellie Pou, who represents the Ninth District of New Jersey, put pressure on NJDEP to provide answers about the fuel spill that had allegedly contaminated local waterways. According to Pou, this incident was the largest data center fuel spill on record in the state of New Jersey with as much as 5,500 gallons of fuel spilled during the incident. “I appreciate that NJDEP is working to investigate and address the spill. But NJDEP must provide a clear account of exactly what happened and what is being done to prevent another spill to ensure transparency and accountability,” the congresswoman said. NJDEP was given until October 9, 2026, to respond, but at the time of publication neither Pou’s office nor NJDEP had publicly confirmed that the deadline was met or that a report was submitted.

artigo.texto: City of Taylor moves forward with data center despite pushback from community TAYLOR, Texas - The city of Taylor is one step closer to getting another massive data center and power plant despite strong pushback from the community. City leaders say the deal gives them regulatory control and millions in potential revenue, but residents remain firm that they don't want these in their backyards. Data center coming to Taylor The backstory: The city of Taylor approved a development agreement for the "Taylor Technology Campus," formerly known as Project Mustang. The decision paves the way for big watt digital and powerhouse data centers to annex and develop a 664-acre campus at 3301 FM 112, east of city limits. The project is a 500-megawatt data center and a 750-megawatt natural gas-fired power generation facility. What they're saying: "Without an agreement, the land would remain in Williamson County, which has no zoning authority or ability to regulate noise, setbacks, water use or light pollution," said Daniel Seguin with the city of Taylor. Developers initially withdrew their zoning application last month. The city says it worked with the developers to make sure they’d meet regulatory standards. With the agreement, the land will be annexed into the city. "The agreement requires a 300-foot setback from the north, east and west property lines and a 700-foot setback from the south line to protect nearby homes. It limits noise to approximately 65 decibels, requires the site to meet dark site lighting standards and requires the two backup generators be tested," said Seguin. Some Taylor residents oppose the massive development The other side: While the city highlights the $28-million-dollar investment, residents made it clear they are against it. "It is very clear what we want. It's very clear that we don’t want this project, that we don’t want the gas plants, that we don’t want the data centers, that we don’t want all of this large revenue that's pouring in because we want our community, we want multifamily housing, we want intermediate housing we want small businesses," said resident Carrie D’Anna. "This isn't going to benefit anyone in Taylor. They say you can get the money, money sounds good, but we need to care about human lives, they should be more about human lives," said another resident. This isn't the first time residents have clashed over proposed data centers in Taylor. Last year, the city approved a separate 135,000 square foot data center on Carlos Parker Boulevard amid similar concerns regarding noise, light, water and air pollution. The Source: Information from the City of Taylor, Taylor residents, previous coverage and reporting by FOX 7 Austin's Jenna King

artigo.texto: 09/10/2026 O desembargador Rafael Paulo, do Tribunal Regional Federal da 1ª Região, determinou que a ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) conclua em 48 horas a análise de pedidos de medida cautelar relacionados ao acesso ao sistema elétrico de três data centers da Pahlavan. A empresa saiu vencedora da 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026, finalizada nesta semana, mas tenta desde já ter a garantia do aumento do montante de energia a ser usado da rede em 2029. A decisão, expedida na segunda-feira (6), ainda assegura que, até a deliberação da reguladora, não sejam adjudicadas propostas vencedoras na 1ª Temporada de Acesso de 2026 para conexão à rede na Subestação Replan, em São Paulo. Conforme a liminar, eventual capacidade remanescente do barramento na proporção dos montantes de uso de energia solicitados pela Pahlavan não poderá ser comprometida até a decisão da ANEEL. Segundo o desembargador, o restante do procedimento competitivo “prosseguirá regularmente quanto a todas as demais margens” e a determinação em questão não se trata de “reconhecimento de prioridade, reserva de capacidade ou autorização para contratação, energização ou incremento de carga”. Assim, os efeitos da liminar encerrarão após com deliberação da ANEEL, independentemente do resultado. A Pahlavan já tinha entrado com um primeiro pedido de cautelar na agência para ter a garantia do aumento do MUST (Montante de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão), que foi negado. Um recurso foi interposto na ANEEL em setembro, com novo pedido de cautelar, mas ainda não foi analisado pela reguladora. A empresa alega que seus três projetos de data centers são de grande porte, situados em Paulínia (SP), e que foram estruturados sob o regime anterior de acesso à transmissão, antes da Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão). No entanto, após o novo modelo, o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) apontou a inviabilidade dos incrementos de acesso pretendidos pela empresa. Os projetos entrariam em operação de forma escalonada, com uso da energia do sistema indo de 71 MW (megawatts) para 157 MW por unidade em 2029. Os empreendimentos já tinham portaria do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), atos autorizativos da ANEEL e pareceres de acesso e CUSTs (Contrato de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão) assinados. artigo.texto: A battery storage facility proposed for South Orange County won’t get built after residents spent years protesting the project, claiming it would be too close to homes and arguing it would pose too great of a wildfire risk. The company proposing the project officially withdrew their application last month after pressing pause on the facility as they looked for different site options. Compass Energy Storage, the company behind the proposal, withdrew their application to the California Energy Commission on Sept. 1. Their notice said the company wasn’t able to find a suitable location for the battery storage facility within their budget. “This notice is based on the inability to locate an alternative suitable site in proximity to the point of interconnect and due to changed economic conditions associated with the Project,” reads the notice, signed by Ricky Davis, vice president of Compass Energy. The project would have created a facility on 13 acres of land on the northern edge of San Juan Capistrano with lithium-iron-phosphate batteries connected to the energy grid to store excess power and release it back into the grid when necessary. These facilities — known as Battery Energy Storage Systems — are generally viewed by supporters as a positive step toward clean energy solutions since the batteries can help store and provide surplus energy, helping reduce the need for additional fossil fuel generation at high-need times. But similar facilities have also turned into fire hazards elsewhere within the state. A battery storage facility known as Moss Landing in California’s Monterey County ignited in January 2025, causing the evacuation of about 1,500 residents and complaints of health concerns like headaches, coughing and sore throats. There have also been multiple fires at battery energy storage facilities in San Diego County over the past few years, including at the Terra-Gen facility in Valley Center, the Gateway Energy facility in Otay Mesa and at the SDG&E facility in Escondido. Those facilities utilized an older battery technology, known as nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries, whereas the proposed Compass project would have used lithium iron phosphate batteries. A resident group known as BLESSIN — Ban Lithium Energy Storage Systems in Neighborhoods — spent years railing against the project proposed in OC, arguing the proposal would create a severe wildfire risk near schools and homes. During the Laguna Niguel City Council meeting on Oct. 6, Mayor Gene Johns commended several of the group’s leaders for successfully killing the project. “That was a 13-acre facility they were going to build — 1,500 feet away from homes here in Laguna Niguel,” Johns told members of the resident group during the meeting. “Because of your efforts, you put together a great group of people with great knowledge, and you fought a $80 billion worldwide company and showed them it was unsafe and it didn’t belong here.” Assemblymember Laurie Davies also attended the meeting to commend the community for their efforts. “These are community superheroes,” Davies said. “You came together and we were able to get the California Energy Commission to actually come here,” she said. “When they left, they said this was the most respectful community.” Tim Lineberger — spokesperson representing Engie North America, the parent company of Compass Energy — thanked the California Energy Commission and the community’s engagement in a Saturday email to Voice of OC. “While this specific project has been suspended, ENGIE remains committed to working with Orange County, local jurisdictions across California, and the CEC to advance clean, reliable, affordable, and safe electricity solutions for Californians,” Lineberger wrote. The San Juan Capistrano City Council voted multiple times to prohibit the construction of new commercial energy storage systems after the applicant previously submitted requests at the city level. After the city rejected the project, the applicant turned to the state instead, filing an application through the California Energy Commission, which had the power to bypass the city’s previous rulings and approve the project. A host of elected officials also spoke out against the project, including Supervisor Katrina Foley, Rep. Mike Levin, Assemblymember Diane Dixon and San Juan Capistrano city leaders. Cathleen Pryor, BLESSIN president, said the group supports clean energy but only when community members are engaged within the planning process to ensure safety for families and homes. “We support responsible clean energy development,” Pryor said. “At the same time, clean energy infrastructure must be carefully evaluated and appropriately located.” “Residents should never be excluded from decisions affecting the safety of their homes, animals, families, evacuation routes, open spaces and quality of life.” Angelina Hicks is the Voice of OC Collegiate News Service Editor. artigo.texto: Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas on Cost Globally, Says Report Wood Mackenzie finds four-hour battery storage cheaper than gas peaking across 43 markets worldwide. October 13, 2026. By EI News Network Four-hour battery energy storage systems (BESS) are now cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines (OCGTs) across all 43 markets where both technologies were modelled, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) report. The report attributes the shift to gas turbine shortages and fuel price volatility, which are raising gas peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing is driving storage costs down. In the Middle East and Africa, four-hour battery storage costs are estimated at USD 120/MWh in 2026 and are projected to decline by 33 percent to USD 80/MWh by 2035. The report said that storage is becoming more cost-competitive than gas peaking across every gas market in the region. Utility-scale solar remains the lowest-cost power generation technology in the Middle East and Africa, with single-axis tracker solar averaging USD 37/MWh in 2026. Its levelized cost is forecast to fall to USD 24/MWh by 2035. Solar costs in Saudi Arabia and the UAE are expected to drop below USD 20/MWh by 2033. China continues to set the global benchmark for grid-scale battery storage costs, with its levelized cost of storage more than 55 percent below the Asia Pacific regional average of USD 134/MWh. Manufacturing scale and integrated domestic supply chains are driving the cost advantage. Wood Mackenzie expects the Asia Pacific average to decline to USD 92/MWh by 2036 as competitively priced Chinese equipment influences regional markets. The report also found that single-axis tracker solar is the lowest-cost new-build generation technology in 43 of the 48 markets modelled, while onshore wind leads in the remaining five. Across Latin America, solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the cheapest generation option in 2026. Solar costs are projected to decline by 38 percent by 2060, while average onshore wind LCOE is expected to fall from USD 73/MWh to USD 58/MWh by 2030. In Europe, solar PV remains the most cost-competitive generation technology. However, battery storage turnkey capital expenditure increased by about 2 percent in 2026, marking its first annual rise in three years, as battery cell prices rebounded by around 10 percent from their 2025 lows. In North America, tariffs, trade restrictions and supply-chain constraints are putting pressure on solar costs. Meanwhile, growing electricity demand from data centres and constraints on gas-generation equipment supply are keeping thermal power investment costs elevated. Wood Mackenzie said that falling storage costs and competitive renewable energy resources are increasingly challenging the economic case for new gas peaking capacity. The report identifies battery storage as an increasingly important technology for integrating solar and wind generation and supporting power system planning. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Driven largely by the increased computing needs of artificial intelligence (AI), data centers are running out of power to grow. In the U.S., data centers are on track to consume as much as 12 percent of total U.S. electricity by 2028. Thirty percent of a data center’s total power draw comes from cooling the infrastructure. A new study looks at a way to ease that strain: pairing data center cooling systems with an emerging geothermal technology called Cold Underground Thermal Energy Storage (Cold UTES). Cold UTES stores cold water underground during off peak hours and draws it back up to meet cooling demand when it’s needed most. Unlike a conventional battery, it can hold that stored cooling capacity for weeks or even an entire season. To test the idea, Andrew Chien, the William Eckhardt Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science at the University of Chicago, and his University of Chicago co-author Wedan Emmanuel Gnigba modeled Cold UTES equipped data centers in three major U.S. markets: Virginia, Arizona, and Texas—regions chosen for their differing climates and grid conditions. Across the three sites, Cold UTES increased available IT power capacity by 9.8 percent. The biggest gains were seen in Arizona’s hot, dry climate, where capacity rose by 11 percent. “The key benefit of Cold UTES is that is enables data centers to make better use of their grid interconnection capacity, reducing pressure on the grid for power, and enabling AI companies to run more GPUs,” says Chien of the broader research effort behind the technology. “Given the more than $10 billion price tags on AI data centers, the 11 percent increase we have demonstrated could mean savings of billions of dollars. Cold UTES ability to create flexible cooling is a powerful new way to make and operate data centers.” The technology also improved cooling efficiency and eased pressure on space constrained equipment like rooftop dry coolers, the study finds, extending how long a facility can keep scaling before it outgrows its physical footprint. The research is part of a broader Cold UTES collaboration funded by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Geothermal Technologies Office, which also includes the National Laboratory of the Rockies, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and Princeton University. “With data center operators and grid planners racing to keep pace with AI-driven power demand, the findings point to underground cold storage as one option to accelerate AI capacity at lower cost and reducing the need to build new data centers and new power plants,” Chien says.

artigo.texto: Dar es Salaam – State Minister in the Vice President’s Office for Union and Environment Hamad Masauni has rejected an allegation that the government has handed forests to Saudi or Omani companies for carbon-credit trading, calling it false and pledging to leave public office if it is proved. Masauni was responding on October 11 to a claim attributed to CHADEMA Deputy Chairperson John Heche that forests had been given to the two Gulf states, which were collecting the proceeds. Speaking during a visit to inspect environmental conditions in Dar es Salaam, Masauni said: “If he can substantiate what he said, I will quit being a minister, quit Parliament and leave Chama Cha Mapinduzi.” The minister said carbon trading was not confined to forests or the transfer of title to land. He cited opportunities in clean energy, waste, agriculture, mining and forestry, and said the government had created an institution to regulate the sector. A carbon credit is a tradable unit representing a verified reduction, avoidance or removal of one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. In practice, a project developer may sell credits to companies seeking to compensate for emissions they have not yet eliminated, while the underlying land remains subject to Tanzania’s land and environmental laws. The 2022 Carbon Trading Regulations and national guidelines established the basic framework for project registration, approval, monitoring and benefit sharing. In 2025, Parliament gave the National Carbon Monitoring Centre a statutory mandate to register projects, verify and certify credits, manage transactions and promote international cooperation. The market extends beyond forests. The guidelines cover clean energy, waste, agriculture, industrial processes, forests and blue-carbon ecosystems such as mangroves, while requiring non-community projects to explain how local communities will participate and benefit. NCMC requires developers to establish land rights or community agreements, register their project, select a standard and complete baseline, monitoring and verification processes before selling credits. Masauni said in August that 117 projects had been registered by July, and announced four approved projects led by Burn Manufacturing, AP Energy Group with Sayari SA, Water Mission International Tanzania and Bridge Carbon Tanzania. The centre currently lists nine ongoing projects and 1.117 million credits issued, suggesting that the larger government figure includes projects at different registration or assessment stages. READ MORE: Carbon Credits Trading: A New Form of Africa’s Colonialism? Carbon Tanzania, a nature-based credit developer, and the Tanzania National Parks Authority are among the better-known players through a six-national-park project announced in 2023. Internationally, Tanzania also signed a June 2026 memorandum with Singapore on possible Article 6 cooperation under the Paris Agreement. The Chanzo could not identify a Saudi or Omani project that owns Tanzanian forests or receives national carbon revenues. The more direct Gulf connection, however, is a preliminary 2023 agreement with UAE-based Blue Carbon, reported as covering about eight million hectares of forest reserves. Saudi Arabia is also a significant regional buyer and marketplace builder. Its sovereign wealth fund and Saudi Tadawul formed the Regional Voluntary Carbon Market Company, which auctioned more than 2.2 million credits in Nairobi in 2023, most originating in the Middle East and Africa. The sector’s rapid growth has also prompted scrutiny. Then-Vice President Philip Mpango said in 2025 that limited public understanding and the dominance of a small number of brokers were barriers. At the same time, Maasai representatives and advocacy groups have raised concerns about consent, benefit sharing and grazing restrictions in proposed northern soil-carbon projects.

artigo.texto: First the city, now the county debates a data center temporary moratorium A narrow vote with four commissioners abstaining moves a proposed pause on data centers in unincorporated Shelby County to a second reading. MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Shelby County commissioners narrowly advanced a proposed temporary moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas outside city limits Monday, despite questions about whether a pause is necessary when no projects are currently identified in those areas. The measure passed its first reading in a 5-4 vote, with four commissioners abstaining. It must clear another vote and a third reading before the commission can make a final decision. Supporters argue the county should establish regulations before a data center developer proposes a project, while opponents have raised concerns about the county’s legal authority and whether a moratorium is the right approach. Commissioner Erika Sugarmon, who represents District 12 and introduced the ordinance alongside Commissioner Henri. E. Brooks, said the proposal is intended to give the county time to establish rules before data center development becomes a possibility in unincorporated areas. “The problem is if we don’t have anything in place and the data centers decide to move in... then there’s no such thing as ex post facto laws,” Sugarmon said. “That’s illegal. So if they move in, they come in without regulations.” Dr. Sugarmon emphasized that the goal is not to prevent data centers from coming to the county permanently, but to ensure rules are established before development begins. Other commissioners, like Commissioner Amber Huett-Garcia, who represents District 13, raised concerns about the county’s legal authority and the language of the proposed ordinance. Huett-Garcia is proposing an alternative focused on establishing regulatory guardrails rather than imposing a temporary moratorium. “I think we have citations incorrect about what our powers really are,” Huett-Garcia said. “And the attributed powers of city council are different from those of county government. So, I want us to clean this up at a minimum.” Huett-Garcia also pointed to infrastructure considerations, including the fact that unincorporated Shelby County does not have independent power and water infrastructure. Her proposal would focus on clarifying the county’s authority and determining what regulations it can establish for potential data center development. Some young residents who have followed the debate said they feel regulatory protections alone may not go far enough. Jasmine Bernard, a 17-year-old Shelby County resident, argued that the county should consider a moratorium and regulatory guardrails together rather than as competing options. “But if these guardrails and these extra ordinances mean that we will not be passing the moratorium, then we’re not actually solving the full issue, and we’re not getting to the root cause of what’s harming our communities,” Bernard said. “So we need guardrails and a moratorium. You can’t pick one or the other.” Hayden Wakefield encouraged residents to make their voices heard by contacting commissioners and representing their districts in the discussion. “I feel like if all of us spoke out and all of us represented each district, then they would listen to us more, and more things would be passed exactly like this,” Wakefield said. The proposed moratorium now moves to a second reading, where commissioners will have another opportunity to debate and vote on the measure before a final decision. The discussion comes as Memphis City Council considers its own temporary moratorium on data centers. Dr. Sugarmon said coordination between the county and city will be important because regulations adopted within Memphis could affect surrounding unincorporated communities. For now, commissioners must decide whether to pursue a temporary pause on data center development, establish regulatory guardrails or consider a combination of both approaches. The commission’s next vote will determine whether the proposed moratorium advances toward final approval. The Memphis City Council will vote on the municipal data center moratorium October 20. artigo.texto: A Yandex, empresa russa de tecnologia e inteligência artificial, informou neste domingo, 11 de outubro de 2026, que seu data center na região de Vladimir foi completamente desativado após um ataque com drones. A companhia garantiu que nenhuma pessoa ficou ferida, mas reconheceu que alguns de seus serviços ficaram indisponíveis para os usuários em decorrência do incidente. Essa instalação em Vladimir é a terceira a ter sua operação afetada em um intervalo de quatro dias. De acordo com a agência Reuters, a sequência de ataques compromete a infraestrutura digital da Yandex, que desempenha papel fundamental no avanço de projetos de inteligência artificial na Rússia. Na sexta-feira, 9 de outubro de 2026, drones ucranianos atingiram o data center localizado na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou, provocando paralisações parciais em sua operação. A companhia relatou que parte de sua capacidade de processar dados ficou suspensa temporariamente, gerando indisponibilidade de alguns sistemas. Um dia antes, na quinta-feira, 8 de outubro de 2026, outro ataque ucraniano desativou totalmente o data center da Yandex em Sasovo, ao sudeste de Moscou. Essa instalação abriga dois dos três supercomputadores utilizados para treinar e aprimorar os modelos de inteligência artificial da empresa, o que representa um golpe significativo à sua infraestrutura de pesquisa. A empresa alertou que a perda de capacidade em seus data centers pode prejudicar o funcionamento de serviços essenciais e atrasar o desenvolvimento de novos sistemas de IA. Até o momento, a Yandex não apresentou um cronograma para o restabelecimento completo das operações nas unidades atingidas. A série de ataques tem levantado dúvidas sobre a segurança dos demais data centers da companhia, espalhados por várias regiões do país. A Yandex ainda não detalhou quais contramedidas de proteção serão adotadas nem ofereceu uma previsão de quando as atividades poderão ser normalizadas em todas as suas instalações. Conhecida informalmente como “o Google da Rússia”, a Yandex oferece uma variedade de serviços digitais e lidera iniciativas de inteligência artificial no país. A empresa monitora atentamente o impacto desses incidentes para avaliar as consequências em sua operação diária e em seus projetos de pesquisa tecnológica.

artigo.texto: ULSAN — Korean researchers have developed an electrolyte technology that can triple the cycle life of next-generation lithium metal batteries by harnessing interactions between inexpensive commercial solvents. The approach addresses the rapid degradation that occurs during high-voltage charging without relying on costly specialty solvents or high-concentration salts. A joint research team led by Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) said on the 12th that it had developed an electrolyte that extends lithium metal battery life by exploiting the attraction between two commercial solvents. Lithium metal batteries are regarded as a next-generation high-energy-density option because they can deliver far greater capacity than commercial lithium-ion batteries that use graphite anodes. But their cycle life falls off sharply because lithium metal triggers unwanted side reactions with the electrolyte during charging and discharging, and the capacity loss becomes more severe under high-voltage charging conditions. The team solved the problem by mixing two solvents, ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL), at a weight ratio of 3 to 7 and adding a small amount of an additive that stabilizes the protective film. Both solvents had previously been excluded from lithium metal battery design because they bind lithium ions too strongly, hindering deposition on the electrode surface. When the two were combined, however, strong intermolecular attractions including hydrogen bonding formed between the hydrogen in EC and the oxygen in SL, which instead weakened the solvents' grip on lithium ions. The team identified this phenomenon — in which the two solvents influence each other to regulate lithium-ion binding and the interfacial accessibility of anions — as "cooperative solvation." In performance testing, the new electrolyte recorded an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. A battery with a high-nickel (NCM811) cathode retained about 80% of its initial capacity after 150 charge-discharge cycles in a 4.5-volt high-voltage environment. That is three times the cycle life of conventional carbonate-based electrolytes, which fell below 80% after about 50 cycles. Gas generation from electrolyte decomposition and nickel leaching from the cathode material were also suppressed. "We improved electrolyte performance using only commercial solvents, without depending on expensive fluorinated solvents or high-concentration salts," Song said. "This should help extend the service life of high-capacity lithium metal batteries for use in energy storage systems (ESS) and electric vehicles." Hong Jin-ki, the researcher who is first author of the paper, said the work represents "a new design principle in which solvents with strong binding forces are mixed to weaken their bonding with lithium ions." He added that it "can be extended not only to lithium metal batteries but also to commercial lithium-ion batteries and next-generation battery systems." The research was supported by the Korea Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology (KEIT) under the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy and by the National Research Council of Science and Technology (NST), and was published in ACS Nano, an international journal in the field of nanoscience.

artigo.texto: The Real Footprint of Trump’s Data Center Boom What the sprawling buildout means for energy, water, and land. Weeks ahead of high-stakes midterm elections, many Americans are revolting against the data centers being developed in their communities to power President Donald Trump’s artificial intelligence ambitions. About two-thirds of Americans oppose local data center construction, according to polls, and that resistance has been reflected in sweeping protests. In addition to concerns about the impact a new data center may have on jobs, local residents commonly cite the amounts of water, electricity, and land data centers consume and what that could mean for energy bills and the environment. Weeks ahead of high-stakes midterm elections, many Americans are revolting against the data centers being developed in their communities to power President Donald Trump’s artificial intelligence ambitions. About two-thirds of Americans oppose local data center construction, according to polls, and that resistance has been reflected in sweeping protests. In addition to concerns about the impact a new data center may have on jobs, local residents commonly cite the amounts of water, electricity, and land data centers consume and what that could mean for energy bills and the environment. Most controversial are the “hyperscale” data centers used by companies such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, which can dwarf the size of other facilities and have taken off amid the AI boom. Opposition has grown so fierce that at least 15 states are weighing moratoriums, while lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have aligned themselves with outraged locals. “We’ve finally found something that can unite the left and the right,” quipped Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin. Yet that backlash has done little to deter the Trump administration, which has championed data centers in its bid for global AI dominance. More than 1,500 data centers are now under development, adding to the 3,000 already operating in the country, according to the Pew Research Center. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump declared in a post on Truth Social in August. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” As tensions threaten to reach a fever pitch ahead of midterms, here’s what we know about data centers’ actual resource footprint. Power At a time of surging energy costs, national attention has focused on data centers’ power consumption, with half of Americans saying that they spell trouble for energy bills, according to Pew. Data centers accounted for 4.7 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption in 2024, up from 4.4 percent the year before, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. That share is set to surge in the coming years, though estimates range. Data centers could consume nearly 12 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030, according to Lawrence Berkeley. And by 2035, data centers could suck up so much energy that they make up about one-fifth of U.S. electricity consumption, according to BloombergNEF. So far, the data center construction frenzy has been largely concentrated in a handful of hot spots, with the biggest in Virginia, Texas, and California. But that is poised to spread as even more data centers are planned, including in Illinois, Georgia, Ohio, and Arizona. All of those forecasts point to a buildout unfolding at a speed and scale that states are ill-equipped for. “We’re looking at very rapid growth, and what’s been happening in recent years is very flat demand in the power sector,” said Lori Bird, an energy expert at the World Resources Institute. “So this is quite a reversal.” Texas offers a window into how such an expansion can strain local infrastructure—and ignite a political firestorm. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott once vowed to make the state the “epicenter of AI development,” and at least 248 new data center projects are planned, adding to the state’s existing 335. “There’s almost no muscle memory in the system to meet those growth rates,” said Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities at BloombergNEF, citing a scarcity of technicians, transformers, and transmission lines. “Therefore, you’re seeing this kind of scramble to try and get hands on as much power capacity to support your data center.” Demand has been relentless. Over the summer, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which operates the state’s grid, said it was considering about 474 gigawatts (GW) of interconnection requests—or over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand for the operator, according to the state officials; 90 percent of those new power requests are from data centers, ERCOT said. In August, Abbott directed state regulators to stop data center connections and ordered audits. “It’s insane,” said Rhodes, who said that the entire Houston area sees about 17 GW at peak demand. “Houston is about 17 gigawatts, and we’re seeing multiple Houstons’ [worth of] data centers trying to connect to the ERCOT system at a time.” The big question looming over the buildout, in Texas and beyond, is what this all means for consumers’ electric bills. The answer is, unsurprisingly, somewhat complicated. “It really depends on how much are you doing [and] does the system have the capacity to manage it,” said Bird, who said that it can be a benefit if you have a power system with excess generation available. “But what we’re seeing is that in a lot of these regions there’s not enough, and that they’re trying to move so quickly.” Gas turbine prices, for example, have spiked nearly 200 percent as a result of the data center expansion. As outrage has grown, Trump has said that corporations—not consumers—should bear the cost of the boom. And regulators, too, are scrambling to ease community tensions. artigo.texto: Three European Parliament groups oppose weakening ETS — Politico Europe In Brussels, Belgium, three major political groups in the European Parliament said they would oppose the European Commission’s proposal to weaken carbon emissions pricing rules. The Socialists and Democrats, Renew Europe and the Greens seek to preserve a more ambitious path toward net-zero emissions within the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), Politico reports. Dispute over the pace of reductions The position of these groups runs counter to the approach of the largest parliamentary group, the center-right European People’s Party, which generally supports the European Commission’s proposal. The main differences concern the linear reduction factor, a mechanism that determines the pace of the annual decrease in the number of emissions allowances. Under the current trajectory, the overall emissions cap for sectors covered by the ETS is to fall to zero around 2039–2040. The system covers, among others, electricity producers, steelworks and chemical plants. The proposal by Member of the European Parliament Peter Liese envisages moving this date into the 2040s, in line with the European Commission’s summer initiative. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. The Socialists and Democrats, Renew Europe and the Greens have submitted nearly identical amendments that provide for maintaining a higher reduction rate until the end of the next decade. According to Politico’s assessment, this would mean faster decarbonization of industry in Europe. Possible votes from right-wing groups Liese, who is leading Parliament’s work on the ETS revision, said he seeks to create the “broadest possible coalition,” which could include the European Conservatives and Reformists, the Greens and the Left. At the same time, Czech MEP Alexandr Vondra of the European Conservatives and Reformists group proposed cooperation with the EPP on condition of support for a more industry-friendly course, including slower progress toward net-zero emissions. According to the outlet, Polish, Spanish and Italian EPP representatives are dissatisfied with what they consider Liese’s proposal to be too favorable to climate goals. The Europe of Sovereign Nations group, which includes members of Germany’s Alternative for Germany, is seeking the complete abolition of the ETS. Patriots for Europe generally advocates a substantial slowdown of this policy, especially the planned ETS2 system. Their votes could potentially become one option for the EPP to support the reform.

artigo.texto: Cientistas dos EUA criam a primeira bateria inspirada no metabolismo humano: ela funciona com vitamina B2 e glicose Livre de metais pesados e totalmente biodegradável, a nova bateria de fluxo utiliza reações do nosso próprio organismo para armazenar energia renovável Pesquisadores da Universidade de Utah criaram uma inovadora bateria de fluxo inspirada no metabolismo humano para o armazenamento de energia limpa em larga escala. O dispositivo substitui metais pesados e compostos tóxicos por biomoléculas orgânicas e biodegradáveis: usa derivados de glicose no polo negativo e vitamina B2 no polo positivo para gerar eletricidade, reproduzindo a respiração celular e oferecendo uma alternativa sustentável às baterias convencionais de íon de lítio. Uma equipe da Universidade de Utah desenvolveu uma bateria de fluxo bioinspirada que utiliza biomoléculas totalmente orgânicas e biodegradáveis para armazenar energia limpa sem depender de metais pesados. O armazenamento de energia em grande escala é um dos maiores gargalos da transição energética. Baterias de íon de lítio convencionais são eficientes para eletrônicos e veículos elétricos, mas envolvem mineração tóxica e alto impacto ambiental. Para resolver isso, a resposta veio da própria biologia. Pesquisadores da Universidade de Utah, nos Estados Unidos, criaram uma bateria de fluxo bioinspirada que imita o metabolismo do corpo humano, utilizando vitamina B2 (riboflavina) e glicose para armazenar e liberar eletricidade de forma limpa e sustentável. Como funciona a bateria "metabólica"? As baterias de fluxo armazenam energia em eletrólitos líquidos contidos em tanques externos que passam por uma célula central onde ocorrem as reações eletroquímicas. No protótipo desenvolvido pela equipe, o processo é diretamente espelhado nas rotas metabólicas que as nossas células usam para extrair energia dos alimentos: - Anólito (polo negativo): Utiliza derivados de glicose, atuando como o "combustível" primário. - Católito (polo positivo): Utiliza flavinas modificadas com base na vitamina B2, que atuam como aceitadores de elétrons — um papel idêntico ao que desempenham no nosso organismo durante a respiração celular. artigo.texto: Power Integrations and Ideal Power Collaborate on Efficient, Always-On Solid State Circuit Breakers for 800 VDC AI Data Centers Collaboration addresses protection, control, and power conversion challenges in emerging 800 VDC AI Infrastructure SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 12, 2026-- Power Integrations (NASDAQ: POWI), the leader in high-voltage integrated circuits for energy-efficient power conversion, and Ideal Power Inc. (NASDAQ: IPWR), developer and provider of its innovative and widely patented B-TRAN® bidirectional semiconductor power switch, today announced a collaboration to deliver a solid-state circuit breaker (SSCB) solution providing fast, efficient, always-on protection that scales with the 800 VDC transition in AI data centers. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261012559063/en/ The companies will collaborate on a new architecture combining Power Integrations’ 1700 V InnoMux-2 power conversion ICs with Ideal Power’s B-TRAN® switches to deliver a self-powered, intelligent, ultra-fast SSCB. They have also demonstrated a working prototype and are working on a reference design. Rising voltages and rack power levels in AI data centers create a need for innovative approaches to circuit protection. Mechanical circuit breakers are too slow to protect sensitive rack equipment, while existing electronic breakers introduce losses, reducing system efficiency. Further, electronic breakers must be powered from the 800 V bus. In the next generation intelligent SSCB architecture, the InnoMux-2 IC converts 800 V into isolated power for gate-drive, control electronics, sensing, and auxiliary circuitry. Ideal Power’s B-TRAN® switch uses that intelligence to protect the 800 V power path to the AI computing load. The InnoMux-2 IC features 1700 V PowiGaN technology, which can operate from an 800 VDC bus with significant margin. The IC provides multiple independently regulated outputs instead of a conventional architecture with one isolated PSU followed by multiple DC-DC converters. The result is a highly efficient, self-powered protection solution that eliminates the need for an external auxiliary supply while enabling ultra-fast fault isolation. “As AI data centers move toward 800 VDC power architectures, the industry must address new challenges in power conversion, control, and protection at the system level,” said Chris Jacobs, senior vice president of marketing and product strategy at Power Integrations. “By combining Power Integrations' 1700 V InnoMux-2 IC with Ideal Power's innovative bidirectional solid-state circuit protection, we are helping enable intelligent 800 VDC power architectures that improve efficiency, resiliency, and scalability in next-generation AI data centers.” “High efficiency, ultra-fast fault interruption is essential for enabling the migration to 800 VDC AI data centers and energy infrastructure. Traditional protection methods are proving to be inadequate. Mechanical breakers are too slow, while previous semiconductor-based breakers have historically been disqualified by high power loss,” said David Somo, CEO of Ideal Power. “Power Integrations offers a unique combination of 1700 V GaN capability, multiple independently regulated outputs, high integration, and a compact solution footprint that is well suited to our 800 VDC solid-state circuit breaker architecture, which must meet demanding power efficiency requirements and strict mechanical constraints.” Resources For further information on Power Integrations, please visit the resource page on the web site. About Power Integrations Power Integrations, Inc. is a leading innovator in semiconductor technologies for high-voltage power conversion. The company’s products are key building blocks in the clean-power ecosystem, enabling the generation of renewable energy as well as the efficient transmission, conversion and consumption of power in applications ranging from milliwatts to megawatts in applications such as AI data centers, EVs and high-voltage direct current infrastructure. For more information, please visit www.power.com. About Ideal Power Inc. Ideal Power (Nasdaq: IPWR) is the developer and provider of its innovative and widely patented B-TRAN® bidirectional semiconductor power switch. B-TRAN® offers compelling advantages over conventional technologies and addresses the demanding standards of today’s solid-state circuit protection and intelligent power delivery systems. It features very low conduction losses that deliver improved power efficiency, thereby reducing energy consumption and providing cost savings. The unique bidirectional capability of B-TRAN® simplifies the design, control, and diagnostics of solid-state power solutions while enabling smaller, lower cost systems. B-TRAN® delivers compelling advantages for a broad spectrum of applications including solid-state circuit breakers, static transfer switches, battery disconnect units, and EV contactors that are widely used in data centers, industrial power systems, energy grid and storage systems, and electric vehicles and charging infrastructure. For more information, visit the Company’s website at www.IdealPower.com, on LinkedIn, on Twitter, and on Facebook.
