artigo.texto: Microsoft purchases over 600 acres in Woodward to build a data center In a residents-only community meeting Monday night, Woodward’s mayor and Microsoft representatives unveiled plans for the company to build a data center within city limits. More than 200 residents gathered in the auditorium of Woodward-Granger High School to hear details about the project and express their opinions. It comes as Microsoft purchased over 600 acres of land in Woodward late last week. The land was purchased from an independent seller, not from the city. It’s already zoned for industrial use, which includes data centers. Tempers flared within the meeting, with one person being escorted out by police as Microsoft officials and Mayor Todd Folkerts answered questions about the project. Many said they were frustrated at the lack of community involvement in the project. “Is this something that we get a vote on? I mean, something this big, the community should get to vote on instead of doing back-ended deals,” one resident said. Folkerts said residents would not get to vote on the matter, but city council would vote on negotiations between Microsoft and the city. Microsoft representatives said the project would bring dozens of jobs, increase the tax base, and would not impact utility costs for residents. Something Folkerts says is necessary. “I can safely say I have not seen a single one of you at a budget meeting when we try to balance a budget for this community,” he said to the crowd. “We have to find revenue sources for our community.” But frustrations extended beyond the data center. The meeting, which replaced the city’s regular city council meeting, was open to Woodward residents only. Attendees had to show proof of residency to get inside, and several people were turned away. Randy Evans, president of Iowa’s Freedom of Information Council, was one of the people turned away. He said requiring proof of residency goes against Iowa’s open meeting laws. “It runs counter to the openness that the public meetings all guarantee,” Evans told KCCI. “From my vantage point, it erodes the trust and confidence, and the respect for Woodward city government.” Microsoft said the building has not been designed, and doing so would take roughly two years before construction could even begin.

artigo.texto: Indiana utility regulators unanimously approved a plan for utility AES Indiana to build the solar, battery storage and electric line project needed to power a 390-megawatt Google data center project in Monrovia. At the Oct. 7 meeting, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission said the proposed project meets a 2025 state law that requires data centers and other large electricity users to cover 80% of costs reasonably assigned to it. The law also requires the plan to protect existing and future customers. The Monrovia project is the first data center filed under the new law. AES estimates the infrastructure investment at $1.3 billion. AES Indiana says Google will pay all of the costs. But the order says it is reasonable for existing customers to be assigned a share of the cost upgrades. The Citizens Action Coalition objected to this. AES Indiana says Google’s payments to the utility system will make up for customers’ costs. The Monrovia project, southwest of Indianapolis in Morgan County, will include two battery energy storage systems and a solar facility. The total project cost is $737.3 million. Commissioner Joby Jerrells said AES Indiana had testified that Google would pay for at least 100% of the costs under the requirement. “Not only does this agreement satisfy the statutory requirement, it exceeds it substantially,” Jerrells said. Regulators put their approval in a written order. It explains the energy project is designed to mainly serve large electricity customers, like the Google data center, while protecting current AES customers. Several groups joined the case, including the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, a consumer watchdog; Citizens Action Coalition, a nonprofit consumer advocate; the AES Indiana Industrial Group; and several residents of Morgan County. Brian A. Wright, an electric utility analyst with the consumer counselor’s office, testified that power line transmission upgrades wouldn’t be necessary without the data center’s energy needs. The office did not oppose the plan. “What we’re concerned about is a $74 million set of transmission upgrades that AES Indiana identified that it had to make specifically because this Google data center is being added to the grid,” Ben Inskeep, program director at Citizens Action Coalition, said. AES US Utilities CEO Gustavo Garaviglia said in testimony that Google will pay $32.3 million for direct connection facilities, while $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES’s transmission rate base and recovered in future retail rates. Bickey Rimal, vice president of consulting firm Concentric Energy Advisors, testified for AES that it wouldn’t be reasonable to assign all transmission upgrades to Google because the utility hadn’t done that with a customer in the past, and the upgrades would benefit all customers. The commission agreed. Inskeep said the data center, not the customer, should foot the upgrade costs. “We already have high bills here in Indianapolis,” he said. “We don’t need more rate increases caused by data centers to be added on top.” In a statement, AES Indiana President Brandi Davis-Handy called the approval “an important milestone.” The company has said that the partnership with Google protects existing customers. “None of those costs are shifted to existing AES Indiana customers,” it said. Google’s head of data centers in the Americas, Will Conkling, said that the company is paying for 100% of its electricity and any new infrastructure required to serve them. AES said the agreement will benefit customers by spreading fixed costs to more users and bring the cost per customer down, and that its modeling estimated about $770 million in savings during the term of the project. The contract with Google lasts at least 15 years, according to AES, and includes assurances that customers won’t get stuck paying for upgrades if Google scales back or leaves the project. AES also requested to keep certain information confidential, including portions of temporary, electric and construction service agreements and testimony. The Citizens Action Coalition raised concerns about that. The commission approved the request for confidentiality because the information includes trade secrets exempt from public disclosure under state law. A spokesperson for AES Indiana, Claire Rice, said in response to emailed questions seeking details about the agreements and what customer protections exist, that the company’s filings could be found in the case. “I want to clarify that the agreements are filed publicly with only certain competitively sensitive and confidential information redacted. The terms and details of the customer protection provisions and customer benefits have not been redacted,” she said. The electric, construction and temporary service agreements are filed as exhibits, but they include many redactions, including dollar amounts, rate schedules and timelines. The utility commission recently agreed to reconsider its June approval of a rate increase for AES Indiana. It will consider evidence related to the Monrovia data center project and the announced acquisition of AES’s parent company by BlackRock and other investors. The review will continue into 2027. artigo.texto: Solid-state lithium-metal batteries have long been heralded as the successor to the lithium-ion cells that have dominated the market since 1991. By replacing the flammable organic liquid electrolyte with a solid polymer electrolyte, these batteries promise improved safety, the possibility of using a lithium metal anode with a theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh per gram compared to 372 mAh per gram for graphite, and consequently higher gravimetric and volumetric energy density. Yet a stubborn obstacle has kept them out of commercial devices: the relatively low ionic conductivity of polymer electrolytes, which is typically addressed by incorporating highly dissociated lithium salts such as LiTFSI into a poly(ethylene oxide) host. Now, a team of researchers led by L. Fernandez-Diaz and M.C. Morant-Miñana, publishing in Results in Engineering, has shown that one of the most decisive factors in solid-state battery performance is not the chemistry of the materials at all, but something far more mundane: how long and how fast the electrode slurry is mixed. The composite cathode of a solid-state battery is a dense, non-porous blend of active material, conductive additive and a portion of solid electrolyte known as the catholyte. Unlike conventional lithium-ion cells, where a liquid electrolyte seeps into every pore, the solid-state version has no pore-filling liquid to rescue poor contacts. Every particle must touch its neighbour intimately, and both ions and electrons need homogeneous, percolating pathways through the electrode. The conductive additive in this study is Super C65, a carbon black from Imerys, which must form an unbroken electronic network threading through the cathode. The active material is carbon-coated lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, whose own carbon coating enhances intrinsic electronic conductivity and interfacial lithium transfer. The researchers were careful to distinguish between these two carbons: the factory-applied coating on the LFP particles and the C65 introduced during electrode processing behave very differently under the forces of mixing. To isolate the effects of processing, the team prepared slurries under dry-room conditions with a dew point below minus 60 degrees Celsius, using a bead mill to first dissolve LiTFSI in acetonitrile and then mix in high molecular weight PEO to form the catholyte. The LFP and C65 powders were dry-mixed in a planetary vacuum mixer at 200, 750 or 1500 revolutions per minute, and the resulting powder blend was then wet-mixed into the catholyte for 60, 120 or 180 minutes. Five slurries were produced in total, each cast onto carbon-coated aluminium current collectors and dried under vacuum. Crucially, the researchers deliberately skipped calendering, the mechanical compaction step common in electrode manufacturing, so that the morphological fingerprints left by the mixing process itself would remain visible in the finished electrodes. One of the study’s most elegant methodological contributions is the introduction of a relative viscosity parameter. Batch-to-batch variability in the PEO raw material, stemming from differences in molecular weight distribution, meant that absolute viscosity measurements could not be compared reliably across samples. By normalizing the slurry viscosity to the viscosity of the corresponding catholyte at the end of its own mixing, the team could decouple the true effects of mixing time and speed from uncontrolled fluctuations in the polymer feedstock. Validation experiments with four separate preparations, including three different PEO batches, confirmed that this normalization substantially reduced variability, offering a practical tool that other laboratories can adopt to make their slurry comparisons meaningful. The rheological results revealed a counterintuitive trend. Longer wet mixing times and higher dry mixing speeds both reduced slurry viscosity, and the researchers traced this not to further polymer degradation but to the progressive deagglomeration of the carbon black. Gel permeation chromatography showed that the PEO molecular weight decreased exponentially toward a plateau, with an apparent scission-rate constant of 7.49 times ten to the minus seven per minute, but since total mixing times stayed below the point where degradation becomes negligible, the viscosity drop had to come from elsewhere. As C65 agglomerates break apart, the number of carbon particles rises, promoting immobilization of polymer chains and reducing chain entanglement, a mechanism previously described by Hoffman and colleagues. More effective deagglomeration also increases interparticle volume, allowing more solvent molecules to occupy the spaces between carbon particles and thereby lowering the suspension viscosity. These rheological differences translated directly into electrode microstructure. Scanning electron microscopy of surfaces and argon ion-milled cross-sections, analysed with ImageJ, showed that longer wet mixing produced electrodes with lower porosity, higher active material loading and fewer surface lumps, because lower viscosity allows better particle rearrangement and compaction during drying. In the dry mixing series, the sample processed at 1500 rpm displayed the most homogeneous morphology, while the 200 rpm sample exhibited a highly cracked surface, suggesting that large C65 agglomerates weaken the mechanical integrity of the composite cathode and hinder uniform polymer distribution. Porosity values ranged from about 1.65 percent for the longest wet mixing time to nearly 3 percent for the mildest conditions, differences that proved consequential for transport properties. Electronic and ionic conductivity measurements told a more nuanced story. Reference pellets containing as little as 5 weight percent C65 achieved electronic conductivities of roughly ten to the minus two siemens per centimetre, confirming that this modest carbon fraction is sufficient for percolation. artigo.texto: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York. I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. artigo.texto: The ongoing festive season has brought a curated update to BYD’s electric SUV portfolio in India. The premium Sealion 7 is now available in an exclusive Festive Edition; however, this package does not introduce extra mechanical power or a new battery layout. Instead, BYD has focused its attention on elevating the cabin experience, offering this special edition in a strictly limited run of 150 units nationwide. The BYD Sealion 7 Festive Edition enters the market priced at Rs 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom). It is based directly on the high-spec Premium trim, which carries a sticker price of Rs 49.90 lakh, positioning this limited-run model at a premium of Rs 70,000 over the standard variant. What is new on the Sealion 7? The primary differentiator for the Festive Edition is found entirely within the interior. It introduces a sophisticated Tan and Black dual-tone theme that seamlessly accents the leather-appointed seats, layered dashboard, door cards, and the floating center console. The rest of the extensive equipment list is carried over directly from the high-end Premium trim. Core feature highlights include: - 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen - 10.25-inch driver display - Head-up display - Panoramic glass roof with electric sunshade - Ventilated front seats - Driver seat with memory function - Powered tailgate - 19-inch alloy wheels - 360-degree camera - 11 airbags - Level 2 ADAS - 12-speaker Dynaudio sound system - Dual-zone climate control - Double-glazed glass - All-LED lighting The SUV also gets leather upholstery, ambient lighting and auto-tilting ORVMs with memory function. On the exterior, the Festive Edition retains the identical styling cues, aerodynamic character lines, and 19-inch alloy wheels of the regular Premium variant, keeping changes strictly interior-focused. Battery and performance Under the skin, the Festive Edition uses the same 82.56kWh battery pack as the standard Premium model. This battery powers a rear-mounted permanent-magnet synchronous electric motor that puts out a healthy 308bhp and 380Nm of peak torque. BYD claims a 0-100km/h time of 6.7 seconds. The claimed range stands at 567km on the NEDC test cycle. The battery uses BYD’s Blade Battery technology and Cell-to-Body construction. The Sealion 7 also gets Intelligent Torque Adaptation Control, or iTAC, as part of its electric powertrain setup. The Festive Edition is offered only with the Premium specification. BYD has limited production to 150 units across India, making it a fairly small run. BYD Sealion 7 price in India What else from the brand? Beyond the core BYD lineup, the manufacturer is actively preparing to venture deeper into the ultra-luxury EV segment by introducing its premium sub-brand, Denza. Having officially teased its Indian entry, the luxury marque is widely expected to debut with two flagship models: the Z9 GT and the D9. The Denza Z9 GT is a high-performance electric shooting brake driven by a massive 122.5kWh battery pack and a triple-motor layout, generating a staggering 1,156hp and achieving a 0-100km/h sprint in just 2.7 seconds. Concurrently, the Denza D9 will cater to the executive segment as a large, ultra-luxurious electric MPV featuring a plush three-row, 2+2+3 seating configuration with individual rear captain’s chairs.

artigo.texto: A data center moratorium could once again be moving forward in Michigan City, but who controls the language is a topic of debate. The city council introduced, then tabled, an ordinance last month, to give the city’s planning department a chance to weigh in. But this week, council members announced a new ordinance, similar to the last one. It would suspend the approval of new data center developments, until the city adds regulations to its zoning ordinance or until July 31, 2028. It explicitly excludes both phases of Google’s current development. Council member Bryant Dabney said the pause would let city officials evaluate the Google project, before allowing more. “Not something that we heard happened in Texas or in Tennessee or wherever it may be. We’ll be able to get real data regarding noise, water usage, energy and so forth, from a data center right here in Michigan City,” Dabney said. But the sponsors of the original ordinance complained that they weren’t consulted about the new one. Council member Joseph Nelson called it disingenuous. "I worked my butt off for this, me and Nancy [Moldenhauer] and a lot of good people," Nelson said. "So, for you to come in and swoop and do this and not speak to me or Nancy about this, I do not appreciate that." Reaction from residents was mixed. While they want a moratorium, they had concerns with the way the ordinance was written and presented. Just Transition Northwest Indiana Executive Director Ashley Williams opposed letting the moratorium end as soon as new regulations are adopted. “It pauses just long enough to create an illusion of action while the planning department skates in an M-3 Data Center zoning district that we know it’s been working on behind the scenes, without public knowledge or input up until this point,” Williams told council members. Residents also voiced concerns about Google’s data center, including potential emissions from diesel generators and the storage of diesel fuel. Since the ordinance wasn’t filed in time for the council to take official action Tuesday, a formal first reading is scheduled for the next meeting.

artigo.texto: Jones holds Huntsville rally, calls for Medicaid expansion and data center regulation HUNTSVILLE, Ala. (WAFF) - Doug Jones held a rally in Huntsville Sunday as he seeks to become Alabama’s first Democratic governor since 2003, with 23 days remaining until the Nov. 3 midterm election. The former senator discussed issues he said are important to Alabama communities, including expanding Medicaid to help rural areas where hospitals have closed or are at risk of closing. Jones also called for stronger regulations on data centers, including limits on tax incentives and requirements to address their power and water use. Jones points to consistency Jones said his consistency in office should speak to voters. Voters in attendance said they are ready for the change Jones is talking about. Congressional candidate speaks at rally Andrew Sneed, the Democratic candidate for Alabama’s 5th Congressional District, also spoke at the rally. Sneed is facing incumbent Dale Strong in the Nov. 3 election. Sneed said people at the event were given the space to be heard. Jones and Sneed will both be on the Nov. 3 ballot. Tuberville rally set for Thursday Jones’ opponent in the governor’s race, Sen. Tommy Tuberville, will hold a rally Thursday. The Marshall County Republican Club is hosting the event, called “Liberty on the Lake.” Organizers say the event is free and open to anyone in the community who wants to hear from Tuberville. It will run from 4:30 to 6 p.m. Thursday at the Marshall County RSVP building on Highway 431. Strong has not advertised any upcoming campaign events on his social media pages or campaign website. artigo.texto: Um estudo publicado na revista científica Cambridge Prisms: Water estimou em 16,1 bilhões de litros por ano a pegada hídrica da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) na região metropolitana de São Paulo. O número soma água de refrigeração e de geração de eletricidade. O estudo, assinado pelo pesquisador Guangda Liang, analisou um conjunto de data centers com carga operacional de cerca de 550 megawatts na região. Mais de 46% da pegada hídrica é "água virtual" indireta, consumida na geração hidrelétrica que alimenta essas instalações, não na refrigeração direta dos servidores. Uma pergunta feita a uma IA, uma busca na internet ou um arquivo guardado na nuvem dependem de data centers, instalações que abrigam servidores e consomem recursos naturais para funcionar. Além de eletricidade, essas estruturas podem gastar água para controlar a temperatura dos equipamentos. Por que um data center precisa de água? Os servidores produzem calor durante o funcionamento, e as instalações usam sistemas de refrigeração que podem empregar água, ar ou outras tecnologias para evitar o superaquecimento. "Um data center utiliza água principalmente para resfriar os equipamentos, que geram muito calor durante a operação. Quanto maior o data center, mais calor ele vai gerar e mais água vai consumir", explica Diego Mota Siqueira, do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (INPE). Siqueira chefia o Serviço de Supercomputação (SESUP) do instituto. Publicidade O resultado do estudo veio de modelagem científica, com base em dados de infraestrutura, consumo energético e características dos sistemas hídricos da região. Não é uma medição direta da água consumida pelas instalações, e o próprio pesquisador pede cautela na leitura do número. "Essa resposta é muito relativa. De que tamanho de data center estamos falando? E de que tamanho de cidade? Isso vai determinar diretamente o impacto", afirma Siqueira. O debate ambiental soma-se a outro, econômico. Um data center de IA no Brasil pode valer R$ 25 bilhões e gerar 37 mil empregos, segundo levantamento recente. A fatura de energia também preocupa o setor. A energia necessária para alimentar data centers de IA já é um teste para a infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. O impacto de data centers sobre recursos naturais não é exclusividade brasileira. O boom desses empreendimentos já provocou protesto de moradores na Índia, em caso parecido. O que acontece agora Mesmo com a preocupação ambiental, o Brasil segue incentivando a instalação de data centers. O Senado isentou o setor de impostos por cinco anos, abrindo mão de R$ 5,2 bilhões em arrecadação como estímulo aos investimentos no país.

artigo.texto: St. Joseph City Council postponed vote on data center study contracts ST. JOSEPH, Mo. (KQTV) -- The St. Joseph City Council postponed two ordinances related to zoning and development guidelines for potential data center projects on Monday evening. The council postponed the ordinance after questions arose about whether the proposed consultants do business with data centers. One company recommended for a contract denied having business ties to data center development. "Any affiliation with data centers or data center developments was asked. I want to drill down on that with one company in particular that was mentioned," City Manager, Mike Schumacher said. During the meeting, several residents urged council members to consider how data center development could affect the community, with some also raising concerns about the proposed contract with GBA Inc. GBA Inc. provides turnkey data center services for handling the entire planning, designing, construction and maintenance process. The council is considering a contract with GBA Inc. for up to $42,440 to study data center development and recommend zoning changes and development guidelines. The review would address electric and water infrastructure, land use, environmental impacts, public services, costs and community concerns. "You're not gonna get accurate, fair information from somebody that makes their living building data centers," St. Joseph resident, Debra Miller said. "I opposed spending over $42,000 for a company that you can't trust is going to give you the best results that take in the consideration of the residents of St. Joe." The council is also considering a contract with Renew Missouri Advocates for up to $10,750 for community outreach and legal services related to data center development. The firm would also recommend zoning updates and potential changes to the city’s code of ordinances. One resident also urged the city to revise the ordinance language. "Please amend these bills and work toward that goal, and then I will say thank you for pursuing zoning restrictions, and regulations that protects the health, and well being of the citizens of St. Joseph," St. Joseph resident, Deb Ballin said. The council plans to review the language of both proposed ordinances before bringing them back for a vote at its next meeting. The council voted on a development plan for Bryan St. Joseph Apartments. The complex would be at 5408 N. Pointe Drive, behind the YMCA. The ordinance will allow the city to issue up to $40 million in bonds to help Bryan St. Joseph Apartments LLC build a 180-unit market-rate apartment complex. The project will receive property tax abatements on the improvements and a sales tax exemption on construction materials. The council voted to withdraw the request to add 55 parking spaces along Southwest Parkway between Fleeman Street and Mason Road. The school district requested the ordinance be withdrawn because they want to continue to evaluate the parking needs at Benton High School. The next city council meeting will take place on Monday, Oct. 26th, in the Council Chambers at City Hall.

artigo.texto: BYD reveals Atto 8 in new fully-electric iteration; previously PHEV only BYD has revealed the all-electric Atto 8 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The flagship electric SUV has up to 653km of claimed range and a new Flash Charging technology that can charge the battery from 10 to 97 percent in just nine minutes. New Delhi: BYD has expanded its flagship Atto 8 SUV lineup by introducing a fully electric version at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Joining the existing plug-in hybrid (PHEV) model, the new Atto 8 EV offers strong performance, a large battery pack, and the Chinese manufacturer’s latest charging technology. The biggest highlight is BYD’s new Flash Charging system, which makes its debut on the Atto 8 EV. The technology promises exceptionally short charging times, allowing the battery to gain a substantial amount of charge in just a few minutes. The electric SUV will be available in rear-wheel-drive (RWD) and all-wheel-drive (AWD) configurations, with the latter producing a combined 775hp. In terms of design, the electric version remains largely identical to its plug-in hybrid counterpart, apart from a few EV-specific changes. BYD Atto 8 EV: Battery, range and performance The BYD Atto 8 EV uses a 115kWh battery pack across both powertrain configurations. Buyers can choose between a single-motor rear-wheel-drive setup and a more powerful dual-motor all-wheel-drive version. The RWD variant produces 462hp and 365Nm of torque. BYD claims it can accelerate from 0 to 100 kph in eight seconds, while delivering a WLTP-certified driving range of up to 653km. The AWD model uses two electric motors to generate a combined output of 775hp and 775Nm. With the additional power and traction, the SUV can complete the 0-100 kph sprint in a claimed 4.6 seconds. However, its WLTP range is slightly lower at 602km. One of the most significant developments introduced with the Atto 8 EV is BYD’s Flash Charging technology. The system is designed to drastically reduce charging times, making longer journeys more convenient. As per BYD, the technology can replenish the battery from 10 to 97 per cent in just nine minutes. The manufacturer also claims that charging from 0 to 70 per cent takes only five minutes. BYD says the system can maintain impressive charging performance even in extremely cold conditions. At temperatures as low as -30 degrees Celsius, the battery can reportedly be charged from 20 to 97 per cent in approximately 12 minutes. These figures show the maker’s claimed charging capabilities. It is with actual charging times depend on factors such as charger compatibility, battery temperature and charging conditions. BYD Atto 8 EV: Exterior design The Atto 8 EV carries over most of its styling from the PHEV version. The most noticeable differences are the redesigned aerodynamic alloy wheels and the absence of an exhaust outlet. At the front, the electric SUV features a closed-off grille, matrix LED headlights and a curved LED daytime running light strip. The lower bumper incorporates black trim and functional air intakes intended to help cool the vehicle’s components. A LiDAR sensor is placed on the roof, indicating the presence of advanced driver-assistance hardware. The side profile of the Atto 8 EV features black alloy wheels with aerodynamic inserts, prominent wheel arches and slim roof rails. A chrome accent runs from the front fender towards the front doors, while black cladding covers the lower portion of the doors. At the back, the SUV gets distinctive infinity-knot-inspired LED tail lamps, connected by a design element incorporating an illuminated BYD badge. A roof-mounted spoiler completes the exterior styling. BYD Atto 8 EV: Interior and features On the inside, the Atto 8 EV shares its dashboard design and overall layout with the plug-in hybrid version. The cabin has a 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster and a large 15.6-inch touchscreen infotainment system. A three-spoke steering wheel houses physical buttons and scroll controls, while the dashboard incorporates slim air-conditioning vents and extensive soft-touch leather surfaces. The SUV offers a seven-seat configuration arranged in a 2+2+3 layout, with individual seats in the second row. Boot space sits at 270 litres, identical to the PHEV model. However, the fully electric Atto 8 benefits from an additional 136-litre front storage compartment, or frunk, made possible by the absence of a combustion engine. Comfort features include heating, ventilation and massage functions for both the first- and second-row seats. Other equipment highlights include a panoramic glass roof, three-zone automatic climate control and a 21-speaker DiSound audio system. The SUV also comes with two 50W wireless smartphone chargers and a front-mounted refrigerator capable of cooling its contents to -6 degrees Celsius or heating them to 50 degrees Celsius. artigo.texto: SACRAMENTO, Calif. — There are many issues Sacramento retiree Laureen Anderson said she is driven to speak out on, like reminding people to get out and vote early. Another she said are data center’s impacts on communities and the environment. “I’m very passionate about; I do not want data centers in our area,” Anderson said. “We don’t have enough water. It takes gallons and gallons of water every day to maintain it [a data center].” Anderson isn’t alone in her opposition. Several California communities have moved to temporarily pause or restrict new data center development. And beyond water consumption, there’s another concern, said Anderson. “Also, the electricity, that’s an issue too,” she said. The potential impact on electricity rates and who should pay for major grid upgrades are at the center of a California Public Utilities Commission review of an agreement between utility company PG&E and Google to connect a massive 250-megawatt data center in San Jose. The power needed for the center, sizeable to say the least, said assistant attorney at The Utility Reform Network, a utility watchdog organization, Elise Torres. “At 250 megawatts, it’s approximately the entire load of Marin County,” Torres said. “So that gives you a sense of the scale of just this one facility.” The commission has repeatedly postponed a vote on the agreement. One possible sticking point is a proposed requirement for Google to pay an additional upfront advance toward infrastructure costs, a first for data centers, said Torres. “My speculation is that Google and PG&A are both unhappy about the current provision in the draft resolution that requires Google to pay $600,000 per megawatt,” Torres said. That would amount to as much as $150 million, intended to protect other electricity customers from potentially being left with the costs of major grid upgrades. PG&E argues the upgrades were already planned, would move forward without Google, and would benefit thousands of homes and businesses. Google said the site will feature research and development facilities as well, and reports have noted the company said it will mainly use recycled water. The commission’s eventual decision could have implications well beyond this project, said Torres. “I personally think whatever they decide here, you know, will give us a big indicator of what they’re going to do in Rule 30,” Torres said. “And, will probably be the same standard they apply to exceptional case filings going forward.” Rule 30 is a broader set of proposed standards that the commission is considering for connecting large electricity customers to the transmission grid. Other environmental impacts Torres said he worries about are their potential to produce a large amount of e-waste, and also because they need so much energy, it may make it harder for the state to move away sooner from fossil-fueled power plants. As for Anderson, she said she’s not entirely opposed to data centers, but wants stronger oversight. “It really does need to be regulated, totally, totally regulated by the feds, by the state, by local [governments],” Anderson said. “They need to get together and regulate.” So, as she said, they truly can benefit every community that encounters them.

artigo.texto: Demand for data center labor is up, but can Indiana’s workforce growth match the pace? (Inside INdiana Business) - With large technology companies offering hefty wages and enticing incentives as a wave of data center developments washes across the state, now seems a good time to be a skilled tradesman in Indiana. But it’s a different story for contractors focused on wrapping up other projects. For them, the unprecedented number of data center projects and the benefits that come with them are becoming a hard-to-beat competitor. READ ORIGINAL REPORT HERE: Demand for data center labor is up, but can Indiana’s workforce growth match the pace? Several area industry leaders IBJ spoke with said Indiana’s current workforce might not be able to keep up with the rapidly rising demand for skilled electricians, pipe fitters and builders — even though national statistics show that labor numbers are growing steadily. Over the past decade, the number of construction workers in Indiana has increased by 37%, from 132,300 in August 2016 to 181,300 in August 2026, according to the latest federal labor statistics. And across the state, data center projects already under construction are employing thousands, with Google alone expected to employ about 5,000 workers daily across three sites. And they’re paying well — at least one data center project is reported to be paying workers $5,000-$6,000 a week. Major opportunities With the increased media and public attention on data centers over the past year or so, some might think they are a fresh concept, but that’s not necessarily the case. Data centers have existed for years. They are typically large facilities that support cloud computing and infrastructure for everyday internet uses. Advocates compare them to power plants or water treatment facilities. But in recent years, they have become more prominent and more controversial, likely because of the artificial intelligence boom. While supporters say data centers mean more economic development for communities and workers, opponents say the facilities’ staggering energy and water usage will strain local resources. According to the International Energy Agency, a conventional data center might have the capacity for 10 to 25 megawatts of power — which is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 10,000 to 25,000 homes. But a hyperscale, AI-focused data center can have the capacity of 100 megawatts or more, equivalent to about 100,000 households. Several large data center projects are already under construction in Indiana. For example, Meta is building a massive $10 billion, 1,500-acre data center campus at the LEAP Research and Innovation District in Lebanon. And Google is working on three data centers in the state: one in Fort Wayne, one in Morgan County and another in Michigan City. And three other projects were approved in Indianapolis before the City-County Council put a moratorium in place through the end of next year. While some of these facilities might only establish several dozen permanent jobs once complete, the size of the projects means building them will take years — and require lots of workers. Google’s projects, for example, are expected to support thousands of trade jobs daily, according to a spokesperson. In Fort Wayne, where Google is investing $847 million to build a 900-acre campus, about 3,000 workers are on site every day. The Morgan County project, which recently saw the topping out of its first building, has over 750 daily workers — 80% of whom are local and regional hires — and the company’s Michigan City data center is projected to have about 1,500 workers daily during “major construction phases.” (For reference, about 1,500 are still working on Indiana University Health’s new downtown hospital, according to recent IBJ reports.) In Lebanon, Meta’s project is expected to employ 4,000 skilled workers on site during peak construction. Once complete, there will be about 300 operational jobs. In Decatur Township in Marion County, Sabey Corp. was able to get a $4.3 billion, 1-million-square-foot data center project approved before Indianapolis put a moratorium in place. Economic development officials have called the project the largest private capital investment in the city’s history. The Indianapolis project would be the company’s largest data center development. Sabey Corp. CEO John Sabey told IBJ he expects the project to break ground in spring 2027, but that depends on when the company can get through the permitting process and resolve an ongoing legal challenge from several Decatur Township residents. Sabey said the company does not have exact figures, but he estimated the number of workers on site could reach 500 to 1,000, if not more, depending on when the project gets underway. David Peterson, the CEO and president of Indianapolis-based electrical contractor ERMCO, said data center projects have created a “tremendous” opportunity for the trades. Peterson said ERMCO now has 1,200 electricians on site at a data center in Fort Wayne he would not name. He did not disclose specifics of the other projects the company is working on, other than saying that another two are in Indianapolis. Intense competition Data center development not only creates tons of jobs for skilled tradespeople. The pay and incentives are also significant. “We have electricians on some of our work sites, with the amount of time that they’re working in overtime, they’re making, you know, $250- to $300,000 a year in some cases,” Sabey, the data center developer, said. According to Jon Hooker, president and executive director of the Central Indiana Building Trades Council, Meta is paying electricians about $10 above the union pay scale to work on its Lebanon site — which is equivalent to about $5,000 to $6,000 a week. It is “just almost unheard of,” Hooker said. artigo.texto: O Brasil está criando condições para acelerar a instalação de Data Centers, estruturas responsáveis por armazenar e processar os Dados utilizados por serviços digitais, sistemas de Inteligência Artificial e Computação em Nuvem. Sancionada em setembro, a Lei nº 15.504/2026 criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (ReData), que prevê incentivos fiscais para estimular investimentos no setor. Para o advogado especialista em LGPD e professor de Direito Constitucional Newton Moraes, os incentivos previstos na legislação contribuem para fortalecer a soberania tecnológica brasileira. “Sem Data Centers no Brasil, o armazenamento de Dados e a própria operação de sistemas de IA teriam de ser realizados em outros países. Isso significa que uma infraestrutura que será cada vez mais estratégica para a economia e para a sociedade ficaria fora do nosso território”, afirma. Panorama no Brasil Segundo o Ministério de Minas e Energia, o Brasil possui 205 data centers em operação, enquanto os projetos em construção representam mais de R$ 114 bilhões em investimentos. Os pedidos de conexão de novos empreendimentos cresceram 330% entre 2024 e 2025. Apesar desse avanço, o país ainda tem participação reduzida no mercado mundial, ocupando a 10ª posição em participação relativa, atrás de países como Japão e Holanda. O Ministério da Fazenda também aponta uma elevada dependência nacional de serviços digitais prestados no exterior, que atendem cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras. A expectativa é que a nova legislação contribua para ampliar a infraestrutura instalada no País e, consequentemente, reduzir a dependência de estruturas localizadas no exterior. O avanço, no entanto, traz também desafios relacionados à segurança das informações processadas e armazenadas nesses ambientes. Newton chama atenção para a necessidade de que a expansão ocorra acompanhada de mecanismos adequados de proteção. “Quanto maior a quantidade de informações concentradas nesses centros, maior também é a responsabilidade em relação à segurança e à proteção de dados pessoais”, explica. As contrapartidas Os incentivos previstos pelo ReData estão vinculados ao cumprimento de uma série de requisitos. Poderão se habilitar ao regime pessoas jurídicas que implementem projetos de instalação, modernização ou ampliação de serviços de data center no Brasil. Os serviços abrangidos serão estabelecidos em ato do Poder Executivo federal, de acordo com a Nomenclatura Brasileira de Serviços (NBS). A habilitação ao ReData exige compromissos relacionados à sustentabilidade, ao desenvolvimento tecnológico e à oferta de capacidade ao mercado brasileiro. Entre as exigências estão: disponibilizar ao mercado interno, no mínimo, 10% do fornecimento efetivo de capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados a ser instalada com os benefícios do ReData; cumprir critérios de sustentabilidade a serem definidos em regulamento; atender à totalidade da demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de Suprimento ou Autoprodução provenientes de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, conforme disposto em regulamento; apresentar Índice de Eficiência Hídrica (WUE) igual ou inferior a 0,05 L/kWh, com aferição anual; investir no País 2% do valor dos bens adquiridos com os benefícios do ReData em projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento (P&D), em parceria com instituições científicas, tecnológicas e de inovação (ICTs), universidades, empresas públicas ou organizações sociais.

artigo.texto: The construction workers building Meta's largest-ever data center are arriving in a tiny Louisiana town with more than specialized skills and manpower. They've also got cash to spend. It's a fact that local entrepreneurs are leveraging to build new businesses. "It's been a good opportunity for everybody," David Rodgers, the cofounder of Ice Queen, a local business, told Business Insider. "I tell people, you can't stop it unless you have $50 billion. You might as well get on board and go with the flow." Meta said the data center, dubbed Hyperion, will span nearly 10 million square feet in rural Holly Ridge and will support more than 7,500 jobs at peak construction. That's a workforce larger than the population of Aspen, Colorado. While the influx of workers is straining the local housing market and disrupting aspects of daily life, their presence has also boosted the region's economy. Spinning straw into gold Holly Ridge is a very small sliver of the nearly 19,600 residents in Richland Parish, where agriculture has been the main industry for decades. Before Meta arrived, the smattering of towns, villages, and unincorporated areas that make up Richland Parish hadn't seen significant economic growth in years. Tim Allen, a Richland Parish restaurant owner, lived through that stagnation in the nearby town of Rayville. "Rayville has been a small community my whole life, and it's been in decline over the last several years. We have a lot of people whose children are moving out, and they usually don't come back," Allen said. "Growing up, downtown Rayville had multiple businesses, hardware stores, and clothing stores. One by one, they shut down until only a couple of stores were left." When Meta announced its project in 2024, Allen and his family were among those who saw an opportunity to turn things around. "Since Meta's announcement, we've seen old businesses revitalize and new ones open, including ours," Allen said. Holy Tacos opened in April 2025. TJ and Kaycie Weed, also based in Rayville, said the new demographic created by Meta's project has boosted their sales. They first opened their café, HeBrews Coffee & Eats, near the end of 2021. "When we first started, we thought 30 tickets was a good day," TJ said. "Now, we're hitting 30 tickets before the first hour and a half through the drive-thru alone. We're probably hitting 130 tickets now." The café in Rayville is a brick-and-mortar, but the couple has two franchise locations, including a food truck that opened in 2025 directly across the street from the construction site in Holly Ridge. They said the Holly Ridge location opened specifically because of Meta. "Holly Ridge does most of the catering. If it's any of the businesses under the umbrella of Meta, I send it to Holly Ridge," TJ said. The wave of construction workers inspired Rodgers and his former business partner, Linda Edwards, to cofound Ice Queen in 2025. The business sells $3 bags of ice to subcontractors and companies working on the Meta project. The parish has weathered several heat waves this summer, making ice a necessity for outdoor trade workers. Since July, residents have seen temperatures reach 100 degrees Fahrenheit more than two dozen times. The pair keeps the ice bags in a large tractor-trailer parked near the construction site and has a separate ice truck available to make deliveries. Ice was only the beginning, though, and soon Ice Queen transformed into a one-stop shop of sorts for the work crews. Coffee machines. Cups. Sugar packets. Fridges. Microwaves. Straws. You name it, Ice Queen tries to supply it. Robert Cleveland, president and CEO of the local economic development authority, Grow NELA, said the economic growth happening in Richland Parish is undeniable. Data collected by Grow NELA shows that Richland Parish's annual sales tax revenue jumped from $21 million in 2024 to $39 million in 2025. At the end of 2026, Grow NELA expects the parish will see $92 million in annual sales tax revenue. Richland Parish has gained more annual sales tax revenue in 2025 alone than in the last 20 years combined, Grow NELA says. "We have a number of small businesses that have propped up and have grown significantly because of the project," Cleveland said. Supply and demand Part of the business growth in Richland Parish is supplying construction workers with what they need while they are away from home: lodging, food, and basic necessities. Angel and Bryan Crawford, for example, chose to address the housing market gap with their rental company, Parish Line Properties. The couple owns a mobile home park called Antley Pines that opened in 2025. "We added two homes last December, four this May, and our last four in July. All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. A fully-furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom mobile home that's eight miles from the construction site costs an average of $3,000. The couple previously worked in the nursing field, but decided to dive into real estate and property management after becoming empty nesters. "In 2024, we started buying older houses that had been on the market for a long time or needed a lot of work. We had a vision to create a mobile home park and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center," Angel said. The company now owns 18 rental properties, 14 of which the owners have set aside as workforce housing. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," she said. Those long days can be taxing, making places like HeBrews Coffee & Eats popular with workers. Shelbie Stephenson, owner of the Holly Ridge location, said they deliver 450 lunch plates to the Meta work site twice a month. Stephenson said they also do breakfast and coffee catering several times a month. "We have done 900 burritos and 2,500 cups of coffee

artigo.texto: Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) systems are renowned for low electricity generation costs, but their intermittent and non-dispatchable generation poses significant challenges to grid stability and curtailment. Concentrated solar power (CSP), equipped with thermal energy storage (TES), can provide firm, dispatchable power, but its wide deployment is constrained by high capital and operating costs. To address limitations of PV and CSP systems, this study proposes an operation strategy for hybrid PV-CSP plants to utilize the thermal storage capacity of CSP systems. The proposed strategy utilizes stable power supply and grid capacity constraints to guide TES systems operation, providing a methodology for determining supply target power, followed by system simulation, techno-economic evaluation and capacity parameter optimization. Over an annual simulation, the hybrid plant achieved an average monthly target-fulfillment rate of 93.5 %, indicating robust operational performance. The effects of various capacity parameters on system operation are evaluated, with capacity allocation optimized based on metrics of levelized cost of energy (LCOE) and channel utilization rate (CUR). Analysis of capacity parameters demonstrates that the rated output power of CSP systems exerts the most substantial impact on hybrid system operations. Optimization results demonstrate that configuration combining large-scale PV with thermal energy storage-dominated CSP systems (Mode I) could achieve 40–50 % CUR at 0.06–0.07 $/kWh LCOE, while the hybrid system pairing small-scale PV with large-capacity CSP plants (Mode II) attains 70–80 % CUR with 0.08–0.086 $/kWh LCOE. PV-CSP hybrid power systems effectively address operational challenges inherent in sole PV and CSP systems. Bo Wang, Tao Ma, Yanjun Dai, Wentao Xie, Peng Xue, Simulation and techno-economic optimization of a PV-CSP hybrid system with thermal energy storage under stability-oriented operation strategy, Journal of Energy Storage, Volume 150, 2026,120371, ISSN 2352-152X, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.est.2026.120371

artigo.texto: How Chiplets Could Transform Server Design – And Data Centers Chiplets are reshaping CPU design, enabling data centers to do more without increasing space or power consumption. Since the advent of microprocessors more than 50 years ago, CPUs have typically been built as single pieces of silicon. As a result, servers and the data centers that house them have largely been designed around that model. However, that is beginning to change. The growing adoption of chiplets – small modular dies that can be combined in a single processor package – is giving chipmakers a new way to build CPUs. By improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling more specialized processor designs, chiplets could reshape not just server architecture but also how data centers approach compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. What Are Chiplets? A chiplet is a small integrated circuit designed to perform a specific function within a larger processing package. Depending on the design, chiplets may handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as AI acceleration. When combined, chiplets can provide the same overall capabilities as a traditional CPU. The key difference is that, instead of manufacturing a processor as one large monolithic die, chipmakers can build it from multiple smaller dies assembled in a single package. The chiplet concept has existed for decades, and related multi-die approaches are not entirely new. But adoption accelerated in the late 2010s as chipmakers sought more efficient ways to improve processor performance, manage manufacturing complexity, and scale designs across different workloads. The Benefits of Chiplets A chiplet-based approach to CPU design offers several potential advantages. Reduced manufacturing costs. Smaller dies are often easier to manufacture with higher yields than a single large, complex die. If a single die has a defect, the loss is usually less significant than losing an entire monolithic processor. It can also be easier to engineer and optimize a smaller die for a specific function than to design one large chip that must handle multiple functions at once. Design freedom. By separating functions such as compute and I/O into different dies, chipmakers can tailor processor designs more efficiently for different types of workloads and product segments. Potentially higher compute density. In some cases, chiplets allow chipmakers to pack more processing capability into a single processor package, helping to enable more powerful servers without necessarily increasing physical server size. Supply chain flexibility. Because smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than very large monolithic chips, chiplet-based designs may reduce some production constraints. That said, they do not eliminate supply chain risk altogether, because advanced packaging and integration can create bottlenecks on their own. In short, chiplets can make it easier for chipmakers to scale processor designs, improve yields, and optimize hardware for growing demand. What Do Chiplets Mean for Data Centers? Although chiplets directly affect processor design, their impact could extend well beyond the chip itself. One important implication is the potential for increased compute density inside data centers. If chiplets allow server vendors to deliver more processing power within a single server platform, operators may be able to support heavier workloads without expanding physical footprints at the same pace. Historically, higher compute density has often meant higher power draw and greater cooling requirements. Chiplets do not automatically solve that problem. However, if they enable more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt, they could help offset some of the infrastructure strain that typically comes with denser compute environments. A key result of greater chiplet adoption, then, could be data centers that support higher IT loads without requiring proportionally more space or power. In that scenario, existing facilities could become more valuable because operators would be able to do more with the infrastructure they already have. Chiplets may also help reduce the risk of server procurement delays by giving manufacturers more flexibility in how processors are designed and produced. This does not remove supply chain challenges altogether, but it could make sourcing CPUs and servers somewhat easier over time. In the longer term, chiplets could also encourage more specialized server designs. As chipmakers gain flexibility to mix and match dies optimized for different functions, server platforms may become increasingly tailored for workloads such as AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing. That would give data center operators more options, but it could also make infrastructure planning more workload-specific than it is today. A Shift Worth Watching Chiplets are no longer a futuristic concept. They are already becoming an important part of modern processor design, especially as chipmakers look for new ways to improve performance and efficiency. For data centers, the biggest impact may not come from chiplets themselves, but from the servers they enable. If chiplet-based designs continue to improve compute density, efficiency, and workload specialization, they could play a major role in shaping the next generation of data center infrastructure.

James Austin Johnson portrayed Mr. Wonderful during the show’s “Weekend Update” segment. “Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who's to say? But on the flip side, it's going to make me a tremendous amount of money. And I think that's great,” Johnson said while portraying O’Leary in the sketch. MORE | Box Elder County Data Center The real O’Leary said he appreciated the humor in the sketch. “I thought it was a very well-done parody. He even had two watches on!” O’Leary said. “The noise and water pollution — that's only going to affect this area. Colin, you have to understand, I don't live there,” Johnson said while impersonating O’Leary during the sketch. “Look, yes, I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid communist super agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they're not, doesn't mean they aren't,” the impersonator added. ____

artigo.texto: PCBL Chemical Ltd's subsidiary, Nanovace Technologies, has launched Nanovace Advanced Materials Ltd to spearhead innovation in advanced battery materials and next-generation energy storage, targeting critical sectors like electric vehicles and consumer electronics. Key Points - PCBL Chemical Ltd's subsidiary, Nanovace Technologies Ltd, incorporated a new wholly-owned subsidiary on Saturday. - The new entity, Nanovace Advanced Materials Ltd, will focus on advanced battery materials and next-generation energy storage technologies. - Applications for these technologies span electric vehicles, consumer electronics, defence, aviation, and aerospace. - Nanovace Technologies was initially established to develop silicon-based anode materials for lithium-ion batteries. - PCBL Chemical's 2024-25 integrated report highlighted a joint venture with Kinaltek Pty Ltd for nano-silicon-based battery products. PCBL Chemical Ltd's subsidiary Nanovace Technologies Ltd on Saturday said it has incorporated a wholly owned subsidiary to focus on advanced battery materials and next-generation energy storage technologies. Driving Innovation In Energy Storage The new entity -- Nanovace Advanced Materials Ltd -- will focus on applications across electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, consumer electronics, defence, aviation and aerospace, power tools, and energy storage systems, among other industrial and technological sectors, according to a regulatory filing. Nanovace Technologies was established to develop silicon-based anode materials for lithium-ion batteries. PCBL Chemical's 2024-25 fiscal year's integrated report said the company had entered into a joint venture with Australian technology firm Kinaltek Pty Ltd for developing nano-silicon-based products for battery applications. The technology is aimed at improving battery performance, particularly for electric vehicles.

With a reported lifespan of more than 5,000 charge cycles, the batteries could help lower replacement and maintenance costs over the vehicles’ operating lives. Battery Storage Four-hour battery storage now beats gas peaking in 43 markets Storage LCOE falls below open-cycle gas turbines Gas shortages and scale widen the cost gap Stock video by ROMAN ODINTSOV via Pexels Oct 12, 2026 Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas Peaking on Cost in All 43 Wood Mackenzie Markets Four-hour battery storage has reached a cost milestone, with its levelized cost of electricity falling below that of open-cycle gas turbines in every one of the 43 global markets modeled by Wood Mackenzie, according to the firm's latest Levelized Cost of Electricity report. The analysis, reported by pv magazine, also finds that single-axis tracker solar is now the cheapest new-build power source in 43 of the 48 markets studied. Wood Mackenzie principal analyst Ahmed Jameel Abdullah described the economic shift as decisive and widening, noting that gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are lifting peaking costs while expanding battery manufacturing keeps pushing storage costs lower. The report attributes the change to advancing technologies and manufacturing scale that are redrawing global power market dynamics. North America as an exception North America stands apart from the global trend in long-term cost trajectories, shaped by domestic trade policies, supply chain protections, and load pressures. Unlike international markets that benefit from low-cost Chinese equipment exports, developers in the United States and Canada face near-term cost headwinds, with solar costs remaining elevated under tariffs, anti-dumping and countervailing duty actions, and Section 232 import restrictions. Utility-scale solar developers retain a buffer from 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity, but module prices are projected to rise by roughly 5 percent annually through 2030. Distributed generation faces greater pressure, with residential and commercial solar module prices forecast to increase 6 percent in 2027 and a further 14 percent in 2028. Storage incentives and load growth For energy storage, federal tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act continue to offer a competitive advantage, helping offset strict Foreign Entity of Concern sourcing restrictions and domestic supply bottlenecks. A temporary cost increase is anticipated when the Investment Tax Credit phases out in the late 2030s, but hardware commoditization, alternative cell chemistries, and localized manufacturing expansion are expected to bring long-term storage LCOE down 10 percent by 2060. At the same time, substantial load growth from data center development is prompting utilities to reassess capacity planning. Thermal capital costs remain elevated because of a supply deficit cycle in gas generation equipment through the late 2030s, which strengthens the long-term economic case for paired renewables and storage despite near-term headwinds. Faster declines abroad Outside North America, storage and solar costs are declining more quickly owing to unhindered supply chain integration. The convergence of falling storage costs and high gas turbine prices is changing how grid operators plan baseline and peaking capacity, and the underlying economics continue to favor renewable-plus-storage builds over new thermal peaking plants. Abdullah said the structural shift being tracked is no longer only about renewables becoming competitive, but about storage and solar together redefining the economics of a power system. He added that the combination of falling storage costs and strong renewable resources is closing off the economic case for new gas peaking capacity globally. artigo.texto: A Youdera assinala 11 anos de atividade com mais de 2.500 projetos de energia solar realizados em Portugal, Espanha e Suíça e pretende reforçar a aposta em sistemas locais que combinam produção fotovoltaica, armazenamento em baterias e gestão de energia, foi divulgado em comunicado. Segundo a mesma fonte, cinco anos depois de iniciar operações em Portugal, a empresa está a direcionar a sua atividade para soluções de energia descentralizada instaladas nas próprias instalações dos clientes, do lado do consumo, o chamado modelo behind the meter. A estratégia passa por combinar a produção solar com baterias e ferramentas digitais de gestão de energia. Segundo a empresa, a plataforma tecnológica, que recorre a inteligência artificial, permite otimizar a utilização da energia produzida localmente e a eletricidade adquirida à rede. A evolução do modelo de negócio acompanha também um reforço da capacidade de investimento. No início de 2026, a Youdera fechou uma ronda estratégica com a Amundi Energy Transition, associada a um plano de implementação de 150 milhões de euros para infraestruturas de energia distribuída. O financiamento deverá ser aplicado na instalação de novos sistemas, na incorporação de armazenamento em ativos existentes e na aquisição de projetos e portefólios já em operação nos três mercados onde a empresa está presente. “O quinto aniversário de operação da Youdera em Portugal é uma ocasião especial. Temos muito orgulho no trabalho que temos feito no país até aqui”, afirma Pedro Miranda, cofundador e CEO da Youdera. A empresa, acrescenta, começou por financiar projetos solares e evoluiu para um modelo em que constrói e opera sistemas locais de energia nas instalações dos clientes, combinando produção, armazenamento e gestão. A Youdera estabeleceu como objetivo alcançar 500 megawatts (MW) de potência instalada em Portugal, Espanha e Suíça até 2030, através da construção de novos sistemas de geração e armazenamento e da aquisição de projetos e portefólios em funcionamento. Em Portugal, a empresa mantém o foco no desenvolvimento de sistemas locais de energia destinados sobretudo ao setor empresarial, num contexto de procura por soluções que permitam reduzir custos energéticos e aumentar a previsibilidade do consumo. O modelo Energy-as-a-Service adotado pela empresa prevê que os clientes não tenham de realizar o investimento inicial nos equipamentos, ficando a Youdera responsável pelo financiamento, instalação e operação dos sistemas.

artigo.texto: Some Nevada unions love data centers. Now they just have to convince everyone else. Data centers have fast become the political bogeyman of 2026, with nearly every candidate seeking to outfox their opponent in attacks on "Big Tech" and "dirty data centers." In a September poll, nearly 6 in 10 registered voters in Nevada said they oppose the construction of new data centers. Not everybody in the state hates them, though: Electrical and construction unions that benefit from data center projects say the facilities can be a force for good in Nevada — and they're figuring out how they can prove it to everybody else. "There is not a one-size-fits-all situation for how to move forward with this, but there are so many possibilities of how to do that and still check all the boxes of ensuring that ratepayers are protected, that we are good stewards of the earth," said Ronald Young, the political director for the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 357 in Southern Nevada. Some unions see it differently. A few view data centers as threatening their members, doing more to fuel automation via artificial intelligence (AI) than to power Nevada's economy. Advocates for construction counter that while AI acceleration is scary, it's inevitable, making it pointless for Nevada to pass up on economic opportunities that would flow elsewhere. It's led to nuanced discussions as unions representing thousands of workers try to navigate the best approach on young, fast-moving technologies driving demand for new data centers. As 2027's legislative session approaches, unions that work on data center projects say guardrails on their use of water and energy are necessary but that an all-out moratorium could cost Nevada. "Everything's so expensive, and I think if we can turn this into something where locals are getting good-paying jobs, good-paying union jobs, that's a win on top of everything else, right?" Young said. "But it's got to be done smart." Todd Vachon, a professor at Rutgers University who studies labor movements, said he believes concerns about AI will cause a split among organized labor nationwide. "It creates this friction within labor itself," Vachon said, between the primarily blue-collar groups that construct the centers and the white-collar groups who feel threatened by them. "The data centers are actually going to undermine the livelihoods of the white-collar workers if AI advances rapidly and actually does start replacing professional jobs and administrative work, clerical work, writers, creative people, artists." Fears of automation are not theoretical in Nevada, where some service-based workers in casinos and hospitals view AI as an existential threat. In August, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) came to Las Vegas for a roundtable titled Workers over Machines, where he, Rep. Steven Horsford (D-NV) and leaders from trucking, hospitality and other industries discussed how to protect workers without being enemies to growth. Leaders from a range of different unions emphasized in conversations with The Nevada Independent that questions over data centers aren't yet causing major fissures in Nevada's labor community, but there are some disagreements. Brian Lenihan, a steward with the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1107 and an engineer with Clark County, said he is pro-innovation but is skeptical of rampant data center construction, especially in Southern Nevada. He said he distinguishes between data centers that power the internet and "the superpower, water-intensive, noisy, horrific data centers that people don't like." Kenneth Gillingham, an energy professor at Yale, told The Indy there are differences between traditional data centers that have been around for decades and data centers that are now being built to power AI. The latter have greater computational demands, said Gillingham, and therefore require more floor space, more power and more water. Lenihan also said he doesn't find electrical unions' arguments about economic benefits very compelling, arguing those groups could get jobs elsewhere. "Instead of saying we want data centers, what if they said we are going to do a tax cut for everyone to get solar?" he asked. "How much more money do you think IBEW could get from having more electricians wiring up solar facilities?" The electrical unions' view Electrical unions know data centers will be one of the biggest ticket items in the 2027 Legislature, and they say they want more regulations, too. "I don't think the concern is misplaced entirely. … We are in a spot in time where we can either do great things or we could totally screw it up," said Young, adding he disagreed with both those calling for an all-out moratorium and those calling for no regulations. "You need to have some kind of guardrails, because it affects everybody." Jacob Haas, business manager at IBEW Local 401 in Northern Nevada, told The Indy he believes data centers should have regulations similar to those governing "any other building." That means ensuring data centers pay for their own power and don't pass energy price hikes onto consumers, he said. And it means ensuring all facilities use closed-loop cooling systems, a far less water-intensive approach that Southern Nevada has already required of new data centers since 2023. But Haas and Young also emphasized the benefits of data centers when built responsibly. "If data centers weren't here right now, I think Nevada would be in a huge recession," said Haas, adding that roughly 3,000 of his workers are currently staffed on data center projects. He also said the maintenance and upkeep of the centers is so labor-intensive that workers return to the facilities constantly, ensuring jobs aren't just temporary. According to the online tracker Data Center Map, there are 76 data centers built or planned in Nevada. The race among the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturers is becoming more competitive. Sales volumes matter, but battery costs, affordable models, overseas expansion and profitability determine which companies can sustain growth. Its lead continued during the first nine months of 2026, although the companies’ results reveal different strengths and challenges. EV Sales Comparison: Why Vehicle Categories Matter Electric vehicle comparisons require consistent definitions. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) run entirely on electricity, while plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) combine rechargeable batteries with combustion engines. BYD and Geely sell both categories. Tesla sells battery electric vehicles exclusively. Comparing BYD’s combined plug-in sales with Tesla’s deliveries would therefore overstate BYD’s advantage in the fully electric market. The following table compares reported BEV sales for four major manufacturers. It is a selected comparison rather than a complete global ranking. The figures show that Geely Automobile exceeded one million BEV sales and finished ahead of Volkswagen Group in this comparison. Differences in reporting scope still matter when assessing market position. BYD vs Tesla in 2026: Who Is Selling More Electric Cars? BYD sold 1,629,957 passenger BEVs between January and September 2026, according to its September 2026 sales disclosure. Tesla delivered 1,324,681 vehicles over the same period, based on its three quarterly announcements. That puts BYD ahead by approximately 305,000 vehicles, or 23 percent relative to Tesla’s deliveries. These are year-to-date results, so they do not establish the final 2026 outcome. www1.hkexnews.hk BYD’s results also demonstrate why the BEV–PHEV distinction matters.
