Growth in fully electric cars therefore coexisted with weaker overall plug-in sales. www1.hkexnews.hk For manufacturers, a broad product range provides access to different buyers. Compact electric cars target price-sensitive customers, while plug-in hybrids appeal to drivers seeking electric commuting with combustion-engine flexibility. Tesla: High Volumes From a Concentrated Product Range Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, according to its Q3 production and delivery report. Model 3 and Model Y accounted for 478,237 deliveries, approximately 98.3 percent of the quarterly total. Other models contributed 8,295 vehicles. Its reported portfolio includes Geely, Zeekr and Lynk & Co. These figures should not be confused with the entire Zhejiang Geely Holding portfolio, which includes additional automotive businesses. The brand mix creates several routes to growth. Geely addresses mainstream demand, Zeekr competes in premium electric vehicles, and Lynk & Co expands the group’s electrified offering. Financial performance adds another perspective. Geely Automobile reported RMB173.6 billion in first-half 2026 revenue, up 15 percent, and a 17.9 percent gross margin. Within the group, Škoda delivered 174,900 BEVs, increasing 119.8 percent, while Audi delivered 223,000, up 35.6 percent. These examples show how growth across several brands can support group performance even when one major market weakens. Volkswagen’s challenge is to convert growing electric vehicle demand into consistent performance across regions, where prices, competitors and customer preferences differ. artigo.texto: Battery storage is scaling faster than almost any other grid resource in the U.S. As transmission and distribution networks accommodate increasing shares of solar and wind power, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are emerging as one of the most effective technologies to enhance grid flexibility, stability, and resilience. What was once considered a niche solution is now becoming strategic infrastructure. But deployment is outpacing the industry's confidence in how these systems will perform on the grid, under stress, and over decades of service. Closing that gap requires connecting independent testing, grid modeling, and owner oversight across the full project lifecycle. Today's BESS installations play a far broader role than simply storing surplus electricity. Modern battery systems support frequency regulation, voltage control, peak shaving, congestion management, renewable integration, and ancillary services. Their fast response times allow them to react within seconds to grid disturbances, making them valuable assets for balancing increasingly dynamic energy systems. At the distribution level, utilities are evaluating BESS solutions to postpone costly network reinforcements, increase renewable hosting capacity, and improve power quality. Energy storage can support local grids by reducing transformer overloads, mitigating voltage deviations, and managing demand peaks driven by electric vehicle charging and growing electrification. At KEMA Labs, battery research is complemented by the multidisciplinary expertise of the Digital Lab, which combines battery testing with Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) testing and Accelerated Life Testing (ALT). This integrated approach clarifies how batteries, power electronics, control systems, and communication devices interact within BESS architectures. Its expertise also extends to plant controllers and IEC 61850 testing, helping assess communication between grid-connected assets, including BESS, and network operators. Beyond operational benefits, the business case for energy storage is evolving rapidly. BESS operators can stack multiple revenue streams, combining ancillary services, energy arbitrage, capacity or resource adequacy contracts, and congestion management. This evolution is encouraging larger-scale deployment and attracting investment across global markets. However, growth also brings technical and operational challenges. A modern BESS comprises battery cells, racks, Battery Management Systems (BMS), energy management systems, power conversion systems, transformers, cooling systems, and fire protection solutions. Each component influences efficiency, safety, and lifetime. Owners also need confidence in grid interaction, as inverter-based resources respond to disturbances differently from conventional generators. That confidence starts before a project is energized. Grid integration studies, including system impact, harmonic and power quality, temporary overvoltage, insulation coordination, and ride-through assessments, determine whether a BESS will support the grid or introduce new risks. Detailed Electromagnetic Transient (EMT) models capture inverter and plant controller behavior, helping identify control interactions and compliance issues early. Models, however, are only as good as the data behind them. Independent testing laboratories such as KEMA Labs, the testing Division of CESI Group, evaluate batteries under realistic operating conditions. Dedicated facilities can reproduce environmental and electrical stress, including extreme temperatures, humidity, charging and discharging cycles, and accelerated aging scenarios. These tests provide insight into battery performance, reliability, degradation, and expected service life. Recent KEMA Labs’ research on Lithium Iron Phosphate (LPF) batteries demonstrates the value of testing and modeling. Laboratory aging campaigns supported semi-empirical and thermal models for predicting capacity fade, State of Health, and battery lifetime under real-world operating conditions. The study highlighted temperature and State of Charge as key factors affecting degradation, providing insights for battery operation and long-term asset management. The greatest value comes when these disciplines are connected. Laboratory results can validate simulation models so planning studies reflect equipment behavior rather than relying solely on vendor data. Owner's engineering carries that discipline through procurement, factory acceptance testing, commissioning, and performance verification. Within CESI Group, KEMA Labs and EnerNex, the Group’s U.S. grid innovation company, link what is proven in the laboratory with how a system performs on the grid. Once a system is in service, combining laboratory test data with BMS information enables aging models to predict capacity fade, State of Health, and Remaining Useful Life. These capabilities support optimized maintenance, improved operational efficiency, and better-informed investment decisions. As energy storage moves from pilot projects to mainstream infrastructure, utilities and developers should require validated models early, confirm them against test and commissioning data, treat testing and performance verification as core project requirements, and use owner's engineering services to ensure that installed systems match what was studied and contracted. The future power system will require unprecedented flexibility, and battery storage is uniquely positioned to provide it. Realizing that potential will depend on robust testing, accurate modeling, and technical oversight working together across the full lifecycle of every project.

artigo.texto: Lithium-ion batteries use a small amount of glue, called a binder, to hold their internal components together during many charging cycles. Most binders contain fluorine, which means toxic solvents are needed during manufacturing, and hazardous waste is produced when the batteries are recycled. Engineers from the University of California, San Diego, and the Toyota Research Institute of North America have developed a fluorine-free binder that dissolves in water. Their findings appear in Nature Communications. Their studies show that a simple mix of two affordable polymers, polyacrylic acid and carboxymethyl cellulose, can replace toxic ingredients without losing performance. To connect the polymers, the researchers used citric acid, which is also found in citrus fruits. The new binder lasted through thousands of charge cycles and worked with different battery types, including common graphite and silicon anodes. “But that same stability also makes batteries much harder to recycle,” said Zheng Chen, a professor at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering, referring to conventional fluorine binders. Making Battery Recycling Easier Advertisement Traditional battery production uses large drying ovens to remove toxic solvents, which adds extra cost and uses a lot of energy. “Those extra steps significantly increase the cost and energy use — as well as the environmental impact — of battery manufacturing,” said study first author Jiao Lin, a postdoctoral researcher in Chen’s lab. The new design removes those steps completely. To recycle a battery with the new binder, workers soak the parts in water. The binder dissolves, so the electrode material separates easily from the metal foil without leaving behind tough chemical residues. When the team used the recovered materials to make new batteries, they worked just as well as those made with traditional parts. Next, the researchers plan to increase production for commercial use and adjust the formula for different types of batteries in the industry.

artigo.texto: Ataques de drones desativam centros de dados de empresa russa de IA Empresa russa de tecnologia perdeu total ou parcialmente a operação de unidades em 3 regiões do país em 3 dias consecutivos A Yandex, empresa russa de tecnologia e IA (inteligência artificial), informou neste domingo (11.out.2026) que seu centro de dados na região de Vladimir foi totalmente desativado depois de um ataque de drones. Ninguém ficou ferido, mas alguns serviços da companhia estão indisponíveis para os usuários. A unidade de Vladimir é a 3ª instalação da empresa a perder total ou parcialmente a operação em 4 dias, segundo a Reuters. A sequência de ataques afeta a infraestrutura digital da companhia, que tem papel central no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial na Rússia. Ataques em 4 dias Na 6ª feira (9.out.2026), drones ucranianos atingiram um centro de dados da Yandex na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. Segundo a empresa, a unidade ficou parcialmente fora de operação. Na 5ª feira (8.out.2026), um ataque ucraniano desativou o centro de dados da companhia em Sasovo, a sudeste de Moscou. A instalação abriga 2 dos 3 supercomputadores usados no desenvolvimento dos modelos de IA da Yandex. Conhecida informalmente como “o Google da Rússia”, a empresa oferece serviços digitais e desenvolve tecnologias de IA no país. A perda de capacidade em seus centros de dados pode afetar o funcionamento de seus serviços e o desenvolvimento desses sistemas.

artigo.texto: UN carbon market forces cookstove projects to protect against forest loss Cleaner cooking projects in the UN carbon market will have to set aside a share of their credits to insure against the risk that the trees they save are lost to fire, drought or logging, after the market’s regulator rejected calls to exempt the sector. The requirement is part of a new rulebook that the Paris Agreement carbon market regulator – the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body – approved last Friday for programmes that aim to cut emissions by distributing new and cleaner cookstoves in regions that still burn wood or charcoal for cooking. These are the UN mechanism's first rulebooks for cookstoves, one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. Cleaner cooking projects in the UN carbon market will have to set aside a share of their credits to insure against the risk that the trees they save are lost to fire, drought or logging, after the market’s regulator rejected calls to exempt the sector. The requirement is part of a new rulebook that the Paris Agreement carbon market regulator – the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body – approved last Friday for programmes that aim to cut emissions by distributing new and cleaner cookstoves in regions that still burn wood or charcoal for cooking. These are the UN mechanism's first rulebooks for cookstoves, one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. They consist of two methodologies: one for programmes that aim to cut greenhouse gas emissions by distributing more efficient cookstoves that burn less wood or charcoal, and a separate methodology for projects shifting households to lower-emissions cookers running on electricity or liquid petroleum gas (LPG). Mkhuthazi Steleki, the South African chair of the Supervisory Body, said “this decision gives cleaner cooking projects a new pathway under the UN carbon market, with clear rules to ensure that each credit represents a real and credible emission reduction”. - Sep 8, 2026 Industry and NGOs lobby to weaken UN carbon credit rules in “coordinated” push In copycat submissions and a private briefing to government officials, the groups have opposed a proposal to tighten safeguards for emissions offsets - Oct 9, 2026 Launch of Africa Energy Bank delayed again in blow to oil and gas hopes Repeated delays are raising questions about the bank’s momentum and whether it can mobilise investment to finance Africa’s oil and gas ambitions in an era of energy transition Exemption push rejected More efficient cookstove projects earn credits based on the amount of carbon they save by preserving trees that would have otherwise been cut down and burned for fuel. But if those trees later burn in a wildfire or are logged, the carbon stored would be released anyway, erasing the climate benefits of the credits. Several carbon credit developers, conservation NGOs and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) disputed that cookstove projects face this risk, in what critics described as a “coordinated lobbying campaign”. They argued that, unlike forest protection schemes, this type of credit represents a "flow" of avoided emissions rather than a "stock" of stored carbon that can be released. They also warned that requiring a buffer would impose disproportionate costs and undermine the financial viability of these activities. But the UN carbon market regulator was not persuaded by the argument. It decided that projects would have to protect against this reversal risk by handing over a percentage of credits to a so-called “buffer pool” instead of selling them. 'New paradigm' The amount of credits to be given up is calculated by applying different methods for natural risks, like wildfires, droughts or hurricanes, and human-caused ones, such as logging or land clearing. For natural risks, project developers will need to apply local risk values derived from new modelling published by a group of independent scientists. Campaigners have broadly welcomed the decision. Federica Dossi, an expert at Brussels-based advocacy group Carbon Market Watch, said it sets a new paradigm for calculating reversal risk based on empirical data. “This approach is grounded in science and we hope to see this now being adopted by other carbon crediting mechanisms in the voluntary market,” she added. Backers claim this method is more rigorous than current practice in the voluntary carbon market, which largely relies on expert guesswork. artigo.texto: The two candidates running for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District met Wednesday for what could be their only debate before the November election. Republican Michael Alfonso and Democrat Fred Clark met in Duluth, Minnesota, for the debate hosted by WDIO-TV. Among the issues discussed was Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline, which has faced renewed scrutiny following a major natural gas liquids spill in Iron County and environmental concerns surrounding construction of its reroute around the Bad River Reservation. When asked about Line 5, Alfonso expressed support for the pipeline. He also said protecting northern Wisconsin's lakes, forests and farmland doesn't have to come at the expense of building energy infrastructure. “Line 5 is one of these things that brings costs down for every single family in Northern Wisconsin. I really look at this issue and say, if you truly want prices to come down, how can you not support it.” Alfonso had earlier said Clark opposed Line 5. Clark disputed that claim and said his concerns were with Enbridge's environmental record. “I have put out a statement calling on the Wisconsin DNR to hold the Enbridge company accountable for the set of environmental problems they've had. This company has not operated in good faith and until they're willing to do that, we need the state to hold them accountable and stop work until there are reforms.” The candidates were also asked about data centers, which have become a growing concern in Wisconsin over their potential impact on water supplies and electricity costs. Clark called for state and federal regulations to protect communities from the environmental and financial risks of data center development. “We need that badly to protect our water resources, absolutely, to make sure that consumers of energy are held harmless by the huge power demand these things generate, absolutely,” Clark said. Alfonso agreed that water use and electricity costs need to be addressed, but said local communities should decide whether to allow data centers. “If you were to ask me, do I want a data center in Hayward, Wisconsin, where I live? Absolutely not,” Alfonso said. “But I'll tell you what, the federal government does not have a role in stepping in and telling local municipalities what they can and cannot do.” Clark then questioned Alfonso about President Donald Trump's efforts to limit state regulation of artificial intelligence. "So are you willing to tell the president that he's wrong to want to preempt states from having regulations around artificial intelligence and that he's wrong to let Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos basically run the table the way they want to with AI and data centers?” Clark asked. Alfonso responded that Trump supports local control. “President Trump was actually very clear with this. He said, if you're a local municipality and you don't want one, you don't need one. President Trump truly listens to the people,” Alfonso said. “I mean, when we look at issues like the data center issue, it's very clear. People in northern Wisconsin don't want it. But I can't say the same for Kansas. I've never been there. If they want one, it's not the federal government's job to step in and say, no, it's the state or local government.” The full debate is available to watch on WDIO-TV's website.

artigo.texto: Statesboro District 2 candidate Kathleen Keehner focuses on data centers, youth programs Kathleen Keehner is one of three candidates running for Statesboro City Council District 2 STATESBORO, Ga. (WTOC) - Statesboro residents will vote in just over three weeks to fill the city’s District 2 council seat, which has been vacant for nearly five months. The special election is a three-person race. Kathleen Keehner is one of the three candidates seeking the seat. Background Keehner became a homeowner in Statesboro last year when she bought a house to raise her newborn son. She said she is now looking to represent the city’s District 2. “I have a lot of ideas for the future because my son is going to be living here for the foreseeable future,” Keehner said. Data centers Keehner said her motivation for running centers on data centers. In August, Statesboro City Council approved a zoning map amendment that would allow a data center to be built within city limits. Because District 2 was unrepresented, Mayor Jonathan McCollar broke a tie to push the approval despite resident protests. Keehner said she began paying closer attention to local politics when talk of data centers began to increase in the state. She said if elected, she would vote against any data center application. “This race, it’s deeper than just surface level who’s going to win for city council, yeah the city council is made up of five people who vote on decisions, but those decisions can shape the future,” Keehner said. Budget priorities City council members are tasked with approving the city’s annual budget. Keehner said if elected, she plans to devote more taxpayer dollars to creating programs and safe spaces for the city’s youth. “Since we lost the boys and girls club in 2025, we haven’t had any major investments in young people’s programs. So, I would like to reallocate funds, I know that there was a brand new park that they spent over one million dollars on in Whitesville that is farther away from the west side,” Keehner said. Qualifications Keehner does not have experience serving as a public official. She said her qualifications come from being an active member of her community. “Because I do talk to my constituents, I am out here in the streets, I think that qualifies me more than a leader that doesn’t care about the next person, you know,” Keehner said. Keehner said voters should consider who has their best interest at heart. “It’s important to vote for somebody who you know has your best interest at heart, I think that it is important to vote for somebody who doesn’t have deep ties and deep relationships with people who are already proving not to care about you or what you’re concerned with,” Keehner said. artigo.texto: Richardson Electronics, ComEd, trumpet company’s battery storage system plans Richardson Electronics, state lawmakers and ComEd officials gathered Monday to celebrate the Kane County company’s plan to build the largest commercial battery energy storage facility on ComEd’s Illinois grid. “Take it from somebody in the energy industry. This is a very big deal,” said Gil Quinones, ComEd’s chief executive officer and president. The facility, which will have containers with battery energy storage systems, or BESSes, will be built at the rear of Richardson’s headquarters in La Fox. It is intended to serve as a model for potential customers. The facility would be capable of storing up to 5 megawatt-hours of power. “We have learned that standing still is not an option,” said Edward Richardson, chief executive officer and president of Richardson Electronics. His father founded the company in 1947, selling military-surplus electronic supplies such as walkie-talkie batteries. “We’re here because we believe battery energy storage will be claiming an increasingly important role in the future of energy infrastructure,” Richardson said. “The demand for power continues to grow. The ability to store energy, improve reliability and support a more resilient grid becomes increasingly important.” Richardson said the company’s manufacturing experience, engineering expertise and customer relationships help as it grows its global power-management program, which focuses on “green” energy applications. “We believe it has significant long-term potential,” he said. In August 2025, Illinois officials announced the company would receive tax credits for the project through the state’s Re-imagining Energy and Vehicles Program. According to the state, Richardson was investing $8.5 million in the project. The agreement with the state calls for Richardson to add 54 full-time employees at the La Fox site. “The fact is, our energy future depends on having enough power to support growing communities and local economies. Battery storage helps make power available when and where it’s needed most. This is critical for grid stability,” Quinones said. He said batteries will store energy when it is cheap and abundant, to be available when power is scarce and expensive. He said using batteries also “buys valuable time needed to make infrastructure investments needed to bring excess energy onto the grid.” The company is still designing the project. The building size will depend on how many 44-ton battery energy storage systems it will contain, said Scott DuBois, the company’s director of business development. Meanwhile, it is looking to lease space in which to build BESSes, he said. Richardson Electronics sells engineered solutions, green energy products, power grid and microwave tubes and related consumables, power conversion and radio-frequency and microwave components, CT X-ray tubes, and customized display solutions. ssarkauskas@dailyherald.com

artigo.texto: O Ministério de Minas e Energia e a EPE abriram na quinta-feira (8) a consulta pública do PDE 2036. O plano decenal mostra quanto o Brasil deve gastar, onde o consumo de eletricidade cresce e quanto vem do sol e do vento. O PDE 2036, o plano decenal do setor elétrico e de combustíveis, ficou aberto a críticas na quinta-feira (8). O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) e a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) publicaram o Relatório Síntese e marcaram o fim da consulta pública para 6 de novembro, segundo o comunicado do MME. O número que abre o documento é grande: cerca de R$ 3,3 trilhões em investimentos entre 2027 e 2036, de acordo com a nota da EPE. Quanto o consumo de eletricidade deve crescer no PDE 2036? O consumo de eletricidade deve subir 3,4% ao ano e chegar a 979 TWh em 2036. Hoje ele é de cerca de 702 TWh, número que o Eixos trouxe do plano decenal. - Energia renovável perde ritmo no Brasil com cortes de geração e incerteza para investidores - Áustria teve 43.300 tickets em 10 minutos para disputar R$ 215 milhões de subsídio solar que paga R$ 838 por kWp, enquanto no Brasil painel novo já paga 60% do Fio B - Usina solar de Indiana instalou 20 mil painéis por dia com 1.800 operários em 18 meses e está prestes a operar - Agricultor de Illinois tem 10 torres eólicas na fazenda e recebe cerca de R$ 600 mil por ano, mas no Nordeste os relatos vão de R$ 600 a R$ 2 mil por mês por torre A conta é simples: 979 dividido por 702 dá 1,39. É um consumo de eletricidade cerca de 39% maior em uma década. No PDE 2036, a geração acompanha. Vai de 829 TWh em 2026 para 1.133 TWh em 2036, um salto de 304 TWh de geração a mais por ano. Quanto da energia vem do sol e do vento? Solar e eólica juntas respondem por cerca de um terço da geração elétrica em 2036. Em 2026, a fatia é de 28,1%, segundo a EPE. A matriz elétrica continua perto de 90% renovável. Na matriz total, que inclui transporte, indústria e casas, a parcela renovável sobe pouco: de 50,2% para 51,2%. A explicação está no petróleo, que segue forte no PDE 2036. O plano projeta 4,9 milhões de barris por dia em 2036 e 135 milhões de metros cúbicos diários de gás natural, 85% a mais que hoje. Quem puxa a demanda: data centers, carro elétrico e hidrogênio O consumo dos data centers passa de 3 TWh para 30 TWh. É dez vezes mais, e os data centers sozinhos somam 27 TWh por ano a mais na conta do sistema. A eletromobilidade vai de 1 TWh para 15 TWh. Pelo Eixos, os carros leves ficam com 9,4 TWh, os ônibus urbanos com 4,6 TWh e os caminhões com 0,7 TWh. O hidrogênio só entra no consumo de eletricidade a partir de 2031, com 3 TWh em 2036. Quanta bateria e quantos quilômetros de linha o plano prevê? O armazenamento aparece como peça central no PDE 2036. O plano prevê 7,2 GW em baterias, 4,0 GW de resposta da demanda e, pela primeira vez, 2,0 GW em usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis. Somando baterias e reversíveis, são 9,2 GW. Na rede, o PDE 2036 prevê 31,9 mil quilômetros de novas linhas de transmissão e 99,6 mil MVA de capacidade de transformação, de 2026 a 2036. Fora do plano decenal, mas ligado a ele, os primeiros leilões de baterias estão marcados para dezembro, com suprimento a partir de agosto de 2028, informa o Eixos. O motivo, segundo o próprio plano, é ter excesso de energia de dia e falta de potência no começo da noite. E o telhado de casa? A geração distribuída quase dobra A micro e minigeração distribuída, que inclui a solar em telhado, deve passar de cerca de 50 GW para 92 GW. É um aumento de 42 GW, ou 84%, e os data centers e os carros elétricos entram na mesma conta da rede. O Eixos registra que armazenar essa energia em casa pode atrair até R$ 417 bilhões em investimentos até 2036. Como mandar sugestão na consulta pública do PDE 2036 Qualquer pessoa pode contribuir com a consulta pública, do cidadão a empresas. Os caminhos são o portal de consultas públicas do MME e a plataforma Brasil Participativo. O Capítulo 4, “Questões para o Futuro do Setor Energético Brasileiro”, é o espaço aberto para sugerir temas. O MME diz que o conteúdo será consolidado na versão final do plano decenal, depois da avaliação técnica do ministério e da EPE. A consulta pública terá o apoio de dez cadernos temáticos, entre eles Transmissão, Eletromobilidade e Geração de Energia Elétrica, que saem nas próximas semanas, informa o MME. O que o plano ainda não responde é quanto disso vai parar na conta de luz. O PDE 2036 traz projeções de quantidade, não de tarifa, e por isso o consumidor não deve ler os R$ 3,3 trilhões como aumento direto.

artigo.texto: New Peugeot RCZ Vision: solid state battery, 493bhp, and a mad steering wheel A warm welcome back for Peugeot's stylish small coupe. But that wheel? Yeesh... Peugeot is feeling funky. In fact, its new design language is feeling feline, so much so that it’s actually called ‘feline future’. Peugeot wants to be the left-field, extrovert French brand, without being self-consciously wacky. The RCZ Vision showcases the direction of travel. A crisply resolved coupe with echoes of its forebear – which ran from 2009 until ’15 and shifted a healthy 68,000 units – there’s plenty to like on the surface. But actually the bigger stories here are within and beneath, because this car introduces us to two significant developments – both of which are actually coming down the pipe. Core to the RCZ is the STLA architecture, a modular mega-platform that will underpin in excess of 30 new cars across the Stellantis constellation, to the tune of two million vehicles per year by 2035. Coupled to it is a new software and control system called STLA Brain, fast-tracking the company’s ability to deliver autonomous driving capability and innovations such as steer-by-wire. That’s also key to the RCZ Vision. Peugeot was one of the first to genuinely reimagine the car interior, with its odd but also oddly effective i-Cockpit. This new concept car develops the theme in various ways: highlights include ‘mobile’ air vents that can disappear when not in use, an aluminium centre console topped with frosted glass, and a transparent micro LED display screen above the wheel, which can be configured to show as much or as little as the driver wants to see. You might like Well, we say wheel. The dominant innovation inside the RCZ is clearly the so-called Hypersquare, which groups switchgear into four rings. That’ll take some getting used to, but we suspect the ergonomics are sound. Another head-spinner is the arrival of steer-by-wire; yep, there’s no mechanical linkage here, everything is 100 per cent electronic. And fast: the maximum wheel rotation is a little less than one turn compared to the three turns lock-to-lock that we’re used to. A variable steering ratio means that you’re not all at sea at motorway speeds, and vibrations and torque steer are now relics of a different era. The RCZ – and indeed all future Peugeots – will brake-by-wire too. What of the propulsion? The STLA One platform can accommodate ICE, but not here. On the RCZ Vision, we’re talking about a solid-state battery built on a 1,000 volt architecture so that it can charge from 10 to 80 per cent in 10 minutes. Most of the big players are exploring solid state, whose primary benefit is a superior energy density in a more compact configuration. Peugeot is collaborating with a company called Factorial Energy in order to deliver this (Stellantis has a 9.5 per cent equity stake). The company says the RCZ has a power output of 491bhp, is targeting a range of 375 miles, and can deliver 5.4mpkWh overall. Back to the new design language. Peugeot’s design director Matthias Hossann says it’s predicated on five key principles: freedom, courage, elegance, instinct and inner force. Answers on a postcard – if anyone remembers those – as to the meaning of the last one. The RCZ is an undeniably pretty thing, if not as outré as some of its previous concepts (it’s worth looking those up – as far back as you care to go). The horizontal light ‘claws’ are present and correct at the front and rear, and there’s a micro-perforated RCZ graphic across the bumper. The original’s glass bubble roof treatment reappears, and the slinky silhouette is made possible thanks to a battery that’s just 110mm thick. Forged aluminium wheels help reduce weight; they’re 21in upfront, 22in at the rear. Top Gear Newsletter Get all the latest news, reviews and exclusives, direct to your inbox. Note the triangular motifs, another callback to the original. Inside, there’s a dashboard clock from French specialist Serica, enough physical switchgear to satisfy analogue ideologues, and Pelinova recycled leather that uses offcuts that would otherwise be heading to the bin. No word yet on whether the RCZ is destined for production. But a whole heap of the tech and thinking it contains is 100 per cent happening. Good news.

artigo.texto: By Shereen Siewert | Wausau Pilot & Review A Town of Wausau ordinance sharply restricting where and how data centers can be built goes before Marathon County supervisors Thursday, as the county considers its own rules. The board meets at 6 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, in the Assembly Room of the Marathon County Courthouse, 500 Forest St. Thursday’s session is an educational meeting where supervisors review and discuss items; votes are scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20. Public comment is limited to items on the agenda. The Town of Wausau adopted the data center ordinance Aug. 3, following a public hearing that drew 14 residents. According to town minutes, Supervisor Steve Buntin told the audience the town attorney recommended an ordinance because the town had nothing on the books and the state exercises no control over data center siting. The ordinance is modeled on one adopted in the Town of Saratoga in Wood County and is, in Buntin’s words, “very restrictive.” Planning commission minutes note the audience “was not in favor of data centers being located in the township.” Under the ordinance, data centers could be built only in the town’s manufacturing district and only with a conditional use permit. Buildings would have to sit at least 200 feet from every property line, parking lots at least 100 feet, and no structure could exceed 35 feet in height. Noise at the property boundary could not exceed 60 decibels. The definition covers cryptocurrency mining, blockchain processing and server farms. Developers would have to submit an environmental and community impact analysis before any public hearing, including an evaluation of effects on emergency services, water supply, school district budgets and municipal revenue. Any facility relying on private wells would need a water feasibility study mapping every well within 1,000 feet and the geology within a mile. No certificate of occupancy could be issued until the utility verifies that supply lines and substations can carry the load without shortchanging other customers, and until the developer shows the cooling system “will not negatively impact the surrounding region.” Because the Town of Wausau operates under county zoning, state law requires county approval of town ordinance amendments. The county’s review is procedural; the application form signed by town officials states that the county does not assess the legality or enforceability of the language and that the town bears full legal responsibility for the ordinance. The county’s Environmental Resources Committee voted Sept. 29 to forward the ordinance to the full board. The voice vote was not unanimous. At the same meeting, the committee began laying groundwork for a countywide data center ordinance. Committee members directed staff to research state regulations, water usage, cooling systems, electricity demand, noise, lighting, traffic and utility infrastructure, and asked for an educational presentation before deciding which zoning districts might allow data centers. The ordinance itself notes that “the development of data centers is swiftly increasing across the State of Wisconsin.” Rietbrock wind and solar rules Supervisors will also review wind and solar siting ordinances from the Town of Rietbrock, in the Athens and Edgar area west of Wausau. Both cleared the Environmental Resources Committee on non-unanimous voice votes. The wind ordinance incorporates the state Public Service Commission’s wind siting rules, known as PSC 128, including noise limits of 50 decibels during the day and 45 at night and the state’s setback table. The ordinance’s findings run to 25 clauses and cite infrasound, wildlife deaths, property values, drainage, road damage and the town’s desire to “maintain the pastoral, rural nature of this region.” The solar ordinance is unchanged from a version the town board passed in 2025 but never submitted to the county. According to town minutes, the Environmental Resources Committee required a fresh public hearing, which the town held Aug. 25. The town board approved both ordinances that night. Cherokee Park expansion The board will consider buying up to 15 acres of wooded land adjoining Cherokee Park in the Town of Hull at $4,450 per acre, a cost not to exceed $66,750. The 65.5-acre park sits on the Big Eau Pleine River. According to a memo from Parks, Recreation and Forestry Director Jamie Polley, the adjacent landowner approached the county about selling the wooded portion of the property, which includes land along the river that the public cannot currently reach. Adding the acreage would open room for trails and river access, Polley wrote. The owner would be required to survey the land and split off the wooded acres as a separate parcel. Money would come from the county’s Parkland and Products account, which has a balance of about $344,400, or from state Knowles-Nelson Stewardship funds if available. Other business Supervisors will review a resolution authorizing staff to proceed with the fourth phase of construction on the county’s planned new highway facility. The resolution and supporting documents were not included in the agenda packet released Friday. As previously reported, the board will also vote on sweeping roughly $388,750 in unspent American Rescue Plan Act funds from 11 completed projects into the Regional Forensic Science Center. Federal rules require all ARPA money to be spent by Dec. 31. The largest unspent balance, $164,198, comes from medical examiner vehicle purchases. A new Solid Waste Department policy would cut landfill tipping fees for 60 days following any declared emergency. Residents, contractors, haulers and municipalities bringing certified disaster debris to the county landfill in Ringle would pay the contract hauler rate. The board directed staff to write the policy following severe weather events earlier this year. artigo.texto: Why Should Delaware Care? Local governments across Delaware have passed regulations on data centers, citing fears about their massive energy use and effects on the environment. But Dover’s data center moratorium is the first in the state, potentially marking a shift in how far municipalities will go to address these concerns. The Dover City Council on Monday unanimously approved a 18-month moratorium on the construction of data centers in Delaware’s capital city. The moratorium is the first of its kind in Delaware, and follows more than a year of discussions and debate across the state over how much the fast-growing industry could impact power bills and the local environment. Dover’s new ordinance now pauses the city’s official review of proposals for large energy-use facilities, including data centers that use more than 30 megawatts of electricity. That amount of electricity is roughly equivalent to the energy use of 24,000 homes. During the 18-month pause, city officials will research the effects data centers could have on the city; whether they should be allowed to be built; and how to regulate them if they are built. “This is not a ‘no’ to data centers. This is, we need to figure it out before we can say, ‘yes,’” Councilwoman Donyale Hall, who introduced the ordinance, said in an interview. Hall said the council will now decide the most cost-effective way to study the issue. The moratorium passed with little discussion on Monday evening, except from Councilman Brian Lewis, who said called for a ban on construction of the facilities in the city, despite potential economic benefits they could bring. “To me, the environment, people’s health and our infrastructure are more important than jobs in the city,” Lewis said. Dover officials have already been approached about potential plans for more than one data center project in the city, Hall said. She said she did not have information about the developers. And they have not yet submitted a formal application to the city, so the potential projects will not move forward at least until the moratorium is over. While Dover is the first city in Delaware to pass a data center moratorium, it is not alone. Almost every state in the country has at least one municipality that has either banned data centers or imposed a moratorium, according to the artificial intelligence research site, Programs. A boom in the construction of data centers to power the artificial intelligence industry has sparked a nationwide backlash to the facilities. Opponents say they are noisy, use too much water and cause power bills to surge. Proponents say they bring much-needed jobs and tax revenue. New Castle and Kent counties also recently approved rules limiting where a data center could be built in their unincorporated areas. Those regulations include buffer requirements, noise limits and bans on cooling systems that consume large amounts of water. When debating the regulations last summer, Kent County officials also expressed a willingness to consider an outright county-wide ban on the fast-growing industry. Adding to the county regulations are new rules state lawmakers passed in June through a slate of bills. Among those is one that would require developers to supply all of the power a data center facility would use for the first 10 years of its operations.

artigo.texto: GEORGE TOWN: A 31-year-old man was injured while trying to put out a fire at an electric vehicle (EV) battery storage room in Jalan Jelutong yesterday. The Penang Fire and Rescue Department received an emergency call at 3.42pm. Its assistant operations director, John Sagun Francis, said the fire involved a battery storage room measuring about 10sq ft. An estimated 85 per cent of the premises was damaged. "The victim was injured while attempting to put out the fire. "He received initial treatment from the Emergency Medical Rescue Services (EMRS) team before being taken to Penang Hospital for further treatment," he said in a statement. Firefighters from the Jalan Perak station, assisted by teams from the Lebuh Pantai and Paya Terubong stations, were deployed to the scene. John said the team used two water lines fitted with two 60-metre jets and a hose reel to extinguish the blaze. "The fire was brought under control at 4pm and fully extinguished at 4.10pm. "Firefighters then carried out overhaul operations to ensure there were no further hazards," he added. The operation ended at 5.57pm, after which the case was handed over to the Fire Investigation Unit for further action.

artigo.texto: SMM, October 13: Entering September, the sodium-ion battery industry chain's "advancing amid divergence" operating pattern further evolved. The electrolyte segment continued its "capacity without volume release" logic, with top-tier players' shipments highly concentrated and growth mainly flowing to undisclosed major clients. The window for scaled-up breakthroughs is expected to materialize in Q4 with GWh-level order fulfillment. In the battery cell segment, order deliveries were released intensively amid the "September-October peak season" signals, but actual project implementation pace clearly lagged plans, with regional and application-based divergence intensifying. 1. Electrolyte: Ample Capacity in Wait for GWh-Level Batch Implementation According to an SMM survey, sodium-ion battery electrolyte production rose 24% MoM and surged 115% YoY in September, sustaining high growth momentum. Production was highly concentrated, with top-tier players' shipments showing a clear breakaway lead. This round of growth likely flowed to major clients not yet publicly disclosed, and scaled shipment growth is likely delayed to Q4. September data largely reflected early stockpiling and small-batch deliveries on top of existing capacity. From an operational perspective, the number of industry players remains limited. Traditional lithium battery electrolyte leaders still attach relatively low priority to sodium-ion battery business. Apart from a few major clients, they have yet to form bulk supply to publicly disclosed entities, with only sporadic deliveries mentioned in financial reports. Downstream demand exhibited "small-batch, project-based" characteristics—some battery cell manufacturers' sodium-ion battery shipment volumes were relatively small, with cylindrical products shipped only intermittently in small batches, mainly targeting start-stop and small power applications, and no scaled energy storage application has yet formed. On the capacity side, since lithium battery electrolyte capacity is highly interchangeable with sodium-ion battery electrolyte capacity, overall industry capacity is ample with no obvious supply gap. However, it is worth noting that the current high returns in the lithium battery industry may crowd out sodium-ion battery electrolyte capacity. Enterprises' production scheduling priorities will continue to revolve around lithium battery business, leaving uncertainty in the pace of sodium-ion battery capacity release. On prices and raw materials, finished electrolyte prices remained generally stable in September, while core raw materials fluctuated slightly. NaPF6 prices were relatively stable: September production pulled back from August's unusually high level but was clearly better than the same period in previous years' normal levels. The core driver of this round of rise came from marginal improvement on the demand side. Upstream and downstream players across the industry chain generally held no additional inventory, with production strictly following produce-based-on-sales. Downstream electrolyte plants made temporary purchases as needed without advance stockpiling. Despite NaPF6's favorable storage conditions and longer shelf life than similar lithium chemical products, enterprises still scheduled production based on fixed sales, reflecting the industry's prudent judgment on the pace of demand realization. Competitive landscape-wise, the entire industry is waiting for top-tier players to deliver GWh-scale volume signals. Notably, some battery cell manufacturers have adopted low-price selling strategies right after production line commissioning and at the initial mass production stage, a commercial logic that remains to be validated over time. Looking ahead, if demand from key clients ramps up as expected in October, electrolyte and upstream NaPF6 shipments are poised for a step-change increase. SMM expects sodium-ion battery electrolyte production to rise 2% MoM and surge 146% YoY in October. II. Battery cells: Clear peak season signals, but rollout pace falls short of expectations According to SMM survey, sodium-ion battery cell production rose 1% MoM and surged 120% YoY in September, with the sodium-ion battery market showing initial signs of the "September-October peak season." Constrained by the requirement that energy storage projects generally must be connected to the grid before year-end, order deliveries are being released in a concentrated manner; however, from the perspective of project implementation, actual progress is clearly lagging behind plans, with schedule pressure and execution gaps coexisting. Regionally, utility-scale energy storage in China is concentrated in northern regions such as Hebei and Inner Mongolia, while overseas commercial and industrial storage demand is concentrated in Europe and Australia. Domestic commercial and industrial storage has yet to gain traction, presenting a three-way divergence in the demand geography: "northern storage leading, European and Australian commercial and industrial following, and domestic commercial and industrial yet to start." From an operational perspective, mainstream producers' monthly battery cell output remains at the tens of megawatt hours level. On the capacity side, some battery cell manufacturers' new bases in Sichuan will begin production and ramp up in late October, while some existing bases face clear capacity gaps that need to be filled through toll processing. Toll processing business is mostly focused on energy storage projects, with order demand expected to last until year-end. On the technology roadmap, current capacity is concentrated in the polyanion route, demand for cylindrical start-stop battery cells is steadily rising as winter approaches, and orders for prismatic energy storage battery cells remain at high levels, with route and product differentiation trends continuing. artigo.texto: At 5 a.m. in Northern Virginia, chefs are already preparing chicken and chile roja enchiladas, fried shrimp tacos, and big batches of rice and beans to feed thousands of data center construction workers. By late morning, a crew brings the food from the off-site kitchen to a break tent where workers can pick up lunch without leaving the worksite. They don't pay: The Big Tech companies spending billions on AI infrastructure foot the bill. On an average day, National Jobsite Catering serves about 1,500 meals at each of its dozen data center construction sites across Northern Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Nevada, and Georgia, founder Scott Kaplan tells me. The busiest sites serve twice as many. After one to three years, the crews wrap up and move on. Kaplan, whose business used to consist of a fleet of food trucks catering one-off events along the East Coast, designed a venture that can follow them. If you build it, they will cook. National Jobsite Catering is part of the economic ecosystem being generated by America's data center boom. The tech giants leading the AI buildout are expected to spend more than $5 trillion on technology and data centers through 2030, with more than 1,500 data centers already in the works in the US. The room where a worker sleeps, the gym he hits before his shift, his parking spot, his lunch — these are all provided by a growing network of businesses. Local firms in the suburban and rural areas where the bulk of data centers are being built can get a windfall from a single project, but a more lasting proposition is the opportunity to serve site-to-site as construction crews move around. Whether that translates into lasting benefits for host towns is at the heart of growing pushback against the wave of data centers popping up across the country. Kaplan recognized the new opportunity a few years ago when a hyperscaler hired him to bring trucks to a site outside Philadelphia to feed 2,500 workers. "Literally the town that it was in had one restaurant — and it was in a strip club," he says. To avoid a lunch-hour bottleneck, Kaplan proposed preparing meals in a temporary kitchen and bringing them to the site. After replicating this model for other projects, his company now has 20 full-time employees and partners with established local vendors, helping them add equipment and plan production. He estimates a project can employ about 15 local people in kitchen, delivery, and distribution roles. "They know what they're doing," Kaplan says of the local partners. "But they've never cooked for 1,000 to 3,000 people." Since pivoting to data centers exclusively four years ago, revenue has gone up 10X, Kaplan says. Before thousands of construction workers can arrive on-site, they need somewhere to leave their cars — a logistical challenge that's creating a new market. WhereiPark began as a marketplace for city parking spots, but its fastest-growing business now comes from leasing lots near data center construction sites. General contractors have asked WhereiPark to find as many as 2,000 spaces for a project. A church lot used mainly on Sundays might work, as might a struggling shopping center or a nearby fairground or casino. In more remote locations, a contractor may need to grade and stripe land. Local landowners, meanwhile, earn temporary income from unused space without selling the farm. "If there's nowhere for the construction workers to park, the thing doesn't get built," says Joshua Eisen, WhereiPark's chief revenue officer. A team in Toronto does much of the search via property data, calls, and emails; a partner or the general contractor then inspects a prospective lot locally. The company also partners with shuttle operators to ferry workers between the lots and construction sites. For a builder juggling several projects, that means one contact and billing relationship instead of a new search and lease negotiation in every town. A completed facility the size of a Walmart might have just 50 spaces, so most lots return to their previous use. WhereiPark can repeat the search around another project without owning land. With global AI investment expected to exceed a trillion dollars in 2026 alone, companies of all sizes are getting in on the gold rush. Food services and facilities management giant Aramark launched a new division called Nexus earlier this year, which offers hotel-like amenities, fitness centers, and recreation to help attract skilled workers. The company noted that Nexus contracts carry higher-than-average profit margins. Executives projected that three initial data center sites could each generate Aramark about $150 million in annualized revenue once fully running. The data center housing business has a precedent in the oil patch, where companies have long followed temporary crews from project to project. Target Hospitality, a $1.8 billion company that has housed oilfield workers and operated two Texas detention centers for ICE, is building and operating accommodations for data center construction crews, including a $550 million deal for a 4,000-bed facility in North Texas. The company advertises furnished bedrooms equipped with small fridges and microwaves, as well as communal dining, gyms, and WiFi. Its modular assets can be redeployed elsewhere. In August, the company said it has secured contracts representing more than 9,000 beds and $1.4 billion since January. Facing growing opposition, hyperscalers have pitched the AI buildout as an engine of economic development, promising spillover benefits for local areas. Microsoft's "community-first" promise cited its experience in Washington state to estimate that for every direct construction job created, another is generated in sectors including security, maintenance, retail, and food service. While spillovers certainly occur, the exact level varies project to project. artigo.texto: Hoymiles HiOne All-in-One BESS Powers Thai Homes with More Resilient, Flexible Energy Systems By PR Newswire BANGKOK, Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Thailand’s hot and humid climate, growing household electricity demand and the need for greater power reliability are driving more homeowners to look beyond solar generation alone. Hoymiles’ HiOne all-in-one BESS system, paired with HiBox gateway, is helping households in Bangkok make better use of solar power, manage electricity consumption and maintain power availability during grid interruptions. Meeting Thailand’s Growing Residential Energy Needs For Thai households, hot climate drives heavy air-conditioning use, while high electricity costs and power interruptions create demand for systems that offer more than daytime solar generation. The market is also moving toward wider residential solar adoption. According to the Department of Alternative Energy Development and Efficiency (DEDE), Thailand had 3,310 MWp of cumulative rooftop solar capacity by the end of 2024. In 2026, the government also introduced a residential solar feed-in program targeting up to 500 MW of capacity nationwide, allowing eligible households to sell surplus solar electricity to utilities at THB 2.20/kWh under 10-year power purchase agreements. In this context, local installer COMSYS SOLAR has deployed Hoymiles HiOne systems with HiBox gateway across multiple residential properties in Bangkok. Configurations include 10kW or 12kW of solar capacity with 8kWh or 16kWh of storage, allowing each system to be matched to the household’s energy needs. Flexible Solar-plus-Storage for Greater Energy Resilience Hoymiles’ HiOne BESS integrates the inverter, battery and energy management system (EMS) into a minimalist, space-saving design. With maximum efficiency of 98.5% and more than 8,000 battery life cycles, HiOne combines efficient energy conversion with long-term performance. New and existing batteries can be mixed through built-in DC-DC technology, with storage capacity expandable from 8 to 64kWh. Its AI-powered time-of-use (TOU) optimization adjusts charging strategies based on electricity prices and household consumption patterns to maximize self-consumption and reduce electricity costs. The HiBox gateway serves as a central hub for whole-home backup, providing seamless off-grid switching to help keep household appliances running during grid outages. It also supports system expansion through an additional inverter, compatible third-party generators and PV inverters, as well as smart load management through its Smart Port. Hoymiles’ HiOne helps Thai households make better use of locally generated solar power while adapting to changing electricity demand. The multiple installations by COMSYS SOLAR in Bangkok demonstrate how flexible system configurations can meet diverse household energy needs and support more resilient residential energy use. artigo.texto: Developer Returns With A Second Proposal For A Zoning Overlay To Facilitate Apartments In Proximity To Pearl River Transit Station The developer of Jefferson Arms, a proposed 88-unit residential project in Pearl River’s CO (Commercial) zone, returned to the Orangetown Town Board last week asking the town board to advance a proposal that would create a Development Enhancement (DE) Overlay Zone in Pearl River’s downtown. The DE Overlay would allow rental apartments on parcels of land of at least one acre in size and within 1,000 feet of the Pearl River commuter train station. The developer first appeared in May, with a proposal that would allow a 4-story building with 109 apartment units and 132 parking spaces at 10 Jefferson Avenue. In a new iteration, the developer scaled back its project to 88 units (65 units per acre) in a three-story building with below ground parking. Jefferson Arms would have 12 studios, 63 1-bedroom units, 12 2-bedroom units, and one three-bedroom unit for a superintendent. The overlay would apply only to CO (Commercial/Office) zoned land, but would not change the zoning. It would act as an overlay to the existing zoning. Any development would still be subject to review by Orangetown’s land use boards. A proposal to create a zoning overlay in proximity to the Metro North/New Jersey Transit line on Main Street would permit the redevelopment of fallow commercial property in Pearl River. While there are only a few CO parcels large enough (over one acre) to avail itself of the development overlay, the developer’s representative told the board that smaller parcels in the CO zone could be assembled to reach the one-acre threshold. In a presentation to the Town Board last week, the developer, Jefferson Arms LLC, touted the benefits in creating housing opportunities for young professionals, commuters, downsizing seniors, and local workforce residents. Benefits also included additional foot traffic for downtown businesses, as well as enhancing the appearance of the area which is dotted with fallow and underutilized commercial lots. Also discussed was the increase in the taxes the CO lots would pay after conversion to residential use. The owner of the site pays about $69,000 annually in taxes. During the presentation, the owner’s representative alluded to tax revenues from the site many times larger than what is currently levied. The board responded that the 1,000 foot proximity did not make sense, as it could effectively divide individual parcels. A suggestion was made to define the boundaries by streets, not distance from the train station. Changes to the zoning code and the creation of overlays are discretionary with the town board. It has no obligation to act on an application. The Board did not make any decision on the overlay, but referred it to the Town Planner, the Town Planning Board, and the County Planning Department for recommendations and input. BESS Developer Seeks Hardship Exemption From Orangetown Moratorium On Data Centers And Battery Energy Storage Systems A developer of a Batter Energy Storage System (BESS) appeared before the Orangetown Town Board asking for a hardship exemption from the Town’s six-month moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems. A BESS is an engineered installation of rechargeable batteries tied to a utility substation that stores electrical energy and releases it on demand. Batteries are charged in the evening when power demand is low and released during the day or when power demand peaks. The Town of Orangetown passed a six-month town-wide moratorium on new data centers and battery energy storage systems in August. The moratorium allowed for discretionary hardship exemptions. The Orangetown Battery Project, hosted behind a warehouse at 524 Route 303 in Orangeburg, would install about fifteen 30-foot containers of rechargeable batteries adjacent to the railroad tracks in Orangetown’s LO district. The applicant negotiated a contract with the owner of the property in May 2025 and was approved for interconnection with Orange & Rockland in December. It has met with the Orangetown Planning Board several times prior to the imposition of the moratorium. The project does not require any variances, waivers, or zone changes. The batteries would connect to the O&R substation on Mountainview Road. According to NYSERDA, energy storage strengthens and modernizes the electric grid by making it more flexible, efficient, and resilient—benefiting communities, businesses, and households across New York. Battery storage systems pose a unique fire risk, and advances in containment and suppression help local governments manage the risk. The applicant advised the town board that it intended to create a “host community agreement” that would require the operator to finance any equipment the local fire district needed to address a potential fire risk. The town board was inclined to grant the waiver, but a representative of AKRF, a planning firm retained by the town to evaluate the application sought additional information from the developer. The developer agreed to provide the information and the matter was rolled forward to the next town board meeting on October 20th. There was no public comment either in favor or opposed to the application. artigo.texto: EnOcean Pioneer in self-powered wireless standard According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Free Sensors market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Battery Free Sensors market is entering a decisive phase of commercial scale-up, moving from niche, cost-insensitive deployments toward core enablement of low-maintenance monitoring across energy storage and renewable integration systems. The central demand driver is predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems (BESS), where conventional battery-powered sensors impose recurring replacement labor, downtime, and hazardous-waste liabilities over 20-30 year asset lives. Battery-free sensors that harvest ambient RF, thermal, kinetic, or solar energy eliminate those costs and unlock continuous condition monitoring at scale. Demand is bifurcating between high-reliability nodes for mission-critical grid and industrial assets and ultra-low-cost, high-volume nodes for distributed environmental and condition monitoring across vast renewable fleets. Adoption is not a simple sensor swap: it requires re-architecting data acquisition networks, affecting gateway placement, communication protocols, and backend analytics, which locks in system integrators and controls providers as key channel gatekeepers. Supply chain maturity is uneven, with energy harvesting components and ultra-low-power ASICs facing scale and performance constraints, while mechanical vibration harvesters remain application-specific. Project economics are dominated by total cost of ownership, where eliminated battery replacement labor, downtime, and disposal justify a significant upfront premium. Competitive advantage is shifting from component performance to system integration expertise and software analytics, as value migrates from data collection to predictive maintenance and operational optimization. Regulatory and standards bodies are beginning to formalize maintenance-free monitoring requirements in safety-critical applications, creating compliance-driven demand pull in regulated utility and industrial segments. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market through 2035, covering deployment use cases, buyer environments, upstream dependencies, qualification requirements, pricing architecture, and country capability differences. The baseline scenario for the Battery Free Sensors market through 2035 assumes continued acceleration of renewable capacity additions and grid modernization, with BESS deployments growing at a double-digit pace in most regions. Under this scenario, battery-free sensor demand is forecast to expand at a 14.2% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, lifting the market index to 380 by 2035 (2025=100). The strongest demand pull comes from predictive maintenance for BESS, where operators face mounting pressure to reduce OPEX and safety liabilities associated with battery-powered sensor replacement in hard-to-access or hazardous installations. As BESS asset fleets age, the labor and downtime costs of conventional sensor maintenance compound, making the total cost of ownership case for battery-free sensors increasingly compelling. Adoption will be fastest in utility-scale energy storage and commercial and industrial backup power, where asset criticality and maintenance access constraints are most acute. The commercial and industrial segment will also benefit from tightening functional safety standards and insurance requirements that favor maintenance-free monitoring. Supply-side constraints, particularly specialized low-power PMIC design and fabrication capacity, will moderate growth in price-sensitive, high-volume applications, but will not derail the overall trajectory. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will lead in volume terms, supported by China's dominance in BESS manufacturing and deployment, while North America and Europe will drive value growth through higher qualification and safety requirements. Latin America and the Middle East and Africa will remain smaller but fast-growing markets, underpinned by utility-scale solar and storage tenders. Key risks to the baseline include slower-than-expected BESS deployment, delays in standards formalization, and persistent cost premiums that slow adoption in cost-sensitive segments. However, the structural drivers of maintenance-free monitoring, digitalization of asset management, and the imperative to reduce hazardous waste from battery disposal are expected to keep the market on a strong upward path through 2035. Utility-scale energy storage is the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for battery-free sensors, primarily driven by predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems (BESS). As grid operators and utilities deploy massive BESS fleets to integrate renewable energy and provide grid services, the challenge of monitoring thousands of battery modules, thermal management systems, and power conversion equipment becomes acute. Conventional battery-powered sensors require periodic replacement, which is costly and disruptive in high-voltage, hard-to-access installations. Battery-free sensors that harvest ambient RF, thermal, or kinetic energy enable continuous monitoring of cell voltage, temperature, vibration, and state of health without maintenance. Through 2035, demand will be propelled by the need to reduce OPEX, enhance safety, and extend asset life. Key demand-side indicators include BESS capacity additions, average asset age, maintenance cost per sensor, and regulatory requirements for safety monitoring. The sector will increasingly favor sensors integrated with analytics platforms that predict failures before they occur, shifting value from hardware to software and services. artigo.texto: Um ataque com drones ucranianos atingiu o centro de dados principal da Yandex em Vladimir, na Rússia, na manhã de 11 de outubro, forçando a suspensão temporária das operações e interrompendo mais de 80 serviços digitais. Segundo os dados avançados pelo Vietnam.vn, a investida afetou desde aplicações de consumo e ferramentas de inteligência artificial até à infraestrutura corporativa em nuvem da empresa. Terceiro ataque à infraestrutura do gigante tecnológico Este incidente representa o terceiro ataque direcionado aos servidores da multinacional russa num intervalo de apenas quatro dias. A vaga de investidas começou a 8 de outubro com uma ação contra um centro de dados em Sasovo, na região de Ryazan, que provocou um incêndio e obrigou ao encerramento total da infraestrutura responsável por suportar serviços da rede ferroviária russa (RZhD), da operadora MegaFon e de vários órgãos de comunicação social. No dia seguinte, a 9 de outubro, outra instalação em Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscovo, foi visada, tendo a Yandex confirmado a desativação de múltiplos módulos de hardware. O complexo de Vladimir, visado na ação mais recente, foi projetado para albergar até 2.880 racks de servidores, constituindo um dos polos centrais de processamento do grupo. Serviços afetados e impacto na rede elétrica A interrupção no centro de Vladimir provocou falhas imediatas em várias aplicações de consumo, incluindo a assistente de voz Alice, o Yandex Music, a plataforma de videoconferência Telemost e os sistemas de domótica Yandex Smart Home. No setor empresarial, a plataforma Yandex Cloud registou quebras nos serviços de computação, armazenamento e bases de dados, afetando soluções como Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL e ClickHouse. As ferramentas de IA da empresa, como a API YandexGPT, o SpeechKit e o Vision OCR, também ficaram inoperacionais. O impacto estendeu-se a plataformas de comércio eletrónico, instituições bancárias, serviços de transporte por aplicação e cadeias de retalho na Rússia e em países vizinhos. Em paralelo, a autarquia de Vladimir confirmou que os ataques danificaram subestações locais e provocaram um corte geral de eletricidade, embora cerca de 80% do fornecimento tenha sido restabelecido durante a manhã. O Ministério da Defesa russo declarou ter intercetado 479 drones em 16 regiões, ao passo que analistas militares apontam que a degradação continuada destas infraestruturas visa comprometer a logística, a governação e as capacidades de comando digital do país.

artigo.texto: Yandex Go taxi and delivery services in Kazakhstan have been disrupted for 36 hours following a drone attack on Russian technology giant Yandex’s data center in Vladimir, leaving users, drivers and couriers unable to access the app. "Yandex Go services are currently operating with errors or may be temporarily unavailable," the company’s Kazakhstan press service said. "We cannot yet name exact timelines, but we are doing everything possible to bring them back as soon as possible." The outage shows how Ukraine’s apparent campaign against Yandex data centers in Russia is spilling into neighboring countries that rely on the company’s services, including Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Belarus and Armenia. Yandex Go Kazakhstan said personal data of Kazakh users is stored on servers in Kazakhstan, but that its services rely on distributed infrastructure. "Individual technological components may be located on servers in different countries. Therefore, technical problems in one component can affect service availability in several countries," it said. The company did not directly confirm that the outage was caused by the attack in Russia. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development announced Sunday that the servers holding users' personal data were in the country and working normally, but some key components for taxi and delivery services are abroad. It said it was working with Yandex and local providers to restore services. In Uzbekistan, Yandex said some Yandex Go services were unavailable or working intermittently, without saying whether the problem was linked to the attack. Services in Kyrgyzstan were working normally, Russian media outlet TASS reported. Yandex said search, its Alisa voice assistant, maps, mail and taxi services were gradually being restored in Russia, though some functions remain unavailable. The company limited some features of its Disk cloud storage. "We deliberately limited some functions of Yandex 360, including Disk, to preserve the main thing, the operability of services," Yandex told RBC. Yandex said it agreed with cloud providers VK Cloud, Selectel and K2Cloud to quickly host clients’ data and services. Its shares fell more than 5% in early trading on the Moscow Exchange on Monday, TASS reported. Replacing damaged equipment could take about six months, market sources told Kommersant. "These were very large data centers, and since their construction, a global shortage and rising prices for computing capacity began, especially for AI accelerators. Equipping them promises to be expensive and long," said Sergey Kudryashov of Strategy Partners. Russia’s Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadaev said his ministry and the Defense Ministry are working on protecting data centers, TASS reported. Drones struck Yandex data centers in Sasovo in the Ryazan region on Oct. 8, Kaluga on Oct. 9 and Vladimir on Oct. 11, shutting the Vladimir facility completely. Yandex has five data centers, four in Russia and one in Finland that was disconnected because of sanctions. "Two can play at this game," Andriy Kovalenko, former head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, wrote after the first strike, as the Yandex outage spreads beyond Russia.

artigo.texto: Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners committed more than €270 million to Kilmarnock South, a 350 MW / 1,400 MWh battery energy storage project in southern Scotland. The investment is being made through Copenhagen Infrastructure IV, the firm’s fourth flagship fund. CIP has taken a final investment decision on the project, and construction is underway. Commercial operations are expected to begin in the first quarter of 2028. Kilmarnock South is designed as a four-hour-duration lithium-ion battery energy storage system. Once operational, it is expected to become the longest-duration battery storage asset in CIP’s U.K. portfolio. The project will store excess Scottish wind power that might otherwise be curtailed and return that electricity to the grid when network capacity is available. Kilmarnock South represents CIP’s fourth investment in transmission-connected battery energy storage in Scotland. The project joins Coalburn 1, Coalburn 2, and Devilla. Coalburn 1 reached commercial operations in August 2026. When all four projects are fully commissioned, CIP’s Scottish battery storage portfolio is expected to provide 1.85 GW of power capacity and 4.4 GWh of energy storage. CIP said that level of storage represents nearly one-third of Great Britain’s current operational battery energy storage capacity. The portfolio would have enough energy storage capacity to meet the electricity demand of more than 5.5 million households for two hours. Kilmarnock South was developed by Noriker Power, which will continue managing the project’s construction phase. The project also has an optimization agreement with Shell Energy Europe designed to provide long-term contracted revenue. KEY QUOTES: “CIP is pleased to add Kilmarnock South to our growing portfolio of UK battery projects, which, once commissioned, will be the longest-duration BESS asset in our UK fleet. Well-sited battery energy storage projects provide valuable power system flexibility which enables the full benefits of low-cost renewables to be captured, strengthening security of supply and helping to both cut and stabilise energy bills for consumers.” Nischal Agarwal, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners “A former coal mine at Coalburn is now home to one of Europe’s largest batteries storing clean power, while at Kilmarnock South, a new GBP 232 million battery will store even more Scottish wind power for when it’s needed most. Together, these projects mean less homegrown power going to waste, greater energy security, and lower bills over the long term.” Michael Shanks, U.K. Energy Minister

artigo.texto: Home › Policies & Regulations ›Finance Ministry Clarifies 10 Percent Customs Duty on Stationary and Grid-Scale BESS Finance Ministry Clarifies 10 Percent Customs Duty on Stationary and Grid-Scale BESS The Ministry of Finance has clarified that stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion BESS qualify for a concessional 10 percent Basic Customs Duty (BCD), while consumer power banks remain subject to the applicable 20 percent tariff rate. October 13, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey The Ministry of Finance has clarified that stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are eligible for a concessional Basic Customs Duty (BCD) rate of 10 percent, distinguishing them from consumer power banks, which are excluded from the concession and remain subject to the applicable 20 percent tariff rate. The clarification follows reports of divergent assessment practices among customs field formations for BESS classified under tariff item 8507 60 00. Some formations had been treating stationary, grid-scale and industrial BESS as power banks and denying them the concessional duty rate. The Ministry has clarified that the term ‘Power Bank’ applies only to lithium-ion battery devices equipped with charging and discharging ports and designed to function as external charging devices for cellular mobile phones or portable electronic devices. Consequently, stationary, grid-scale and industrial lithium-ion BESS falling under the specified tariff item are not covered by the power-bank exclusion and should not be denied the 10 percent concessional BCD rate merely on that basis. The clarification aims to address inconsistent customs assessments by establishing a clear distinction between portable consumer charging devices and stationary energy storage systems. The concessional duty provision continues to exclude battery packs used in the manufacture of electrically operated or hybrid vehicles, lithium-ion batteries or battery packs for cellular mobile phones, and power banks.
